bullets: A new audit found that all 761 traceable tumor test images in a widely used brain magnetic resonance imaging benchmark came from patients also represented in training. Patient-disjoint cross-validation—keeping each patient wholly within one split—reduced reported overall accuracy from roughly 99% to 95%, while simply removing pixel duplicates did not produce the same correction. Why it matters: If you evaluate medical imaging models, image-level deduplication is insufficient when multiple images can come from one patient. Model-selection claims from this benchmark need patient-disjoint splits to measure generalization to unseen patients rather than recognition of patient-linked features. Evidence: E045. High confidence.

EvoProbe is a new framework that continually regenerates large language model agent tasks using diagnostic feedback. It scores verifiable subtasks, evaluates complete action sequences with evidence-supported judges, and extracts phase-level bottlenecks rather than relying only on final success rates. GraceBench and HICO-Bench independently reflect the same captured-feed pressure toward diagnosing trajectories and verifying resulting plans. Why it matters: If you maintain an agent evaluation suite, EvoProbe offers a design for updating tasks around observed failure modes instead of adding undirected examples. Its phase-level evidence can distinguish whether a product change fixed planning, tool execution, or another stage even when the aggregate success score barely moves. Evidence: E001, E159, E125. High confidence.

Doc2Harness is a new two-stage benchmark that evaluates the software harness around a coding agent—the tools, interfaces, and control logic that let the model work—rather than holding that harness fixed. Its first stage asks a model to construct a complete candidate harness from an interface contract and a development document covering twelve frontier harnesses. Why it matters: If you are choosing a coding-agent stack, this separates model capability from harness engineering. It enables comparisons of whether a model can build the surrounding execution system, rather than attributing all downstream task success to the model used inside a preselected harness. Evidence: E012. High confidence.

MMA-SafetyBench is a new safety benchmark for multimodal agents that inserts deceptive visual elements, such as forged system alerts, into an agent’s observation stream. It contains 1,083 adversarial trajectories across web, desktop, mobile, document, and video tasks, targeting visual semantic hijacking: interface content that diverts an agent from its authorized task. Why it matters: If your agent acts through visual interfaces, text-only prompt-injection tests do not cover this attack path. This benchmark lets a safety review test whether the agent follows authorization boundaries when malicious instructions appear as meaningful on-screen content during a multi-step task. Evidence: E008. High confidence.

RCA-Bench is a new benchmark for whether an agent chooses an appropriate autonomy level. It separates substantive decisions reserved for humans from authorization to execute, then grades responses as ACT, CONFIRM, or ESCALATE across 60 expert-validated organizational scenarios and six domains. Its release includes 1,440 responses from four models under baseline and policy-guided prompting. Why it matters: If you are setting deployment permissions for workplace agents, this evaluates the delegation decision itself rather than only task correctness. The three-way outcome can reveal whether a policy prompt reduces unauthorized action, causes excessive escalation, or appropriately requests confirmation. Evidence: E006. High confidence.

BenchChecker is a new contamination-audit framework for bug-fixing benchmarks. It uses textual model outputs and public repository history to look for evidence that benchmark patches may have appeared in training, and its source description says the method works with both open- and closed-source models. Why it matters: If you compare coding models whose training data are unavailable, this provides a possible audit path without inspecting model weights or private corpora. Contamination findings can determine whether a high repair score supports deployment selection or mainly reflects exposure to persistent repository patches. Evidence: E024. Medium confidence.

J-tau is a new Japanese benchmark for tool-using customer-support agents, localized from the English-centric tau-bench through translation, adaptation of locale-specific entities such as addresses and currencies, and human review. Its construction also identified and fixed two flaws in the original benchmark. Why it matters: If you are selecting an agent for Japanese customer support, a translated English test may preserve unrealistic entities and interaction assumptions. J-tau provides a locale-adapted alternative, while the reported fixes mean scores should not be treated as directly interchangeable with results from the uncorrected source benchmark. Evidence: E013. High confidence.
bullets_zh: 一项新审计发现，在一个广泛使用的脑部磁共振成像基准中，所有可追溯的 761 张肿瘤检测图像均来自训练集中也出现过的患者。采用患者不重叠的交叉验证——确保每名患者的数据全部归入同一个划分——后，报告的总体准确率从约 99% 降至 95%，而仅移除像素级重复图像并未带来同样的修正效果。Why it matters: 如果你评估医学影像模型，当多张图像可能来自同一名患者时，仅进行图像级去重并不足够。基于该基准的模型选择结论需要采用患者不重叠的数据划分，才能衡量模型对未见患者的泛化能力，而非对患者相关特征的识别能力。Evidence: E045. High confidence.

EvoProbe 是一个新框架，可利用诊断反馈持续重新生成大语言模型智能体任务。它对可验证的子任务进行评分，借助有证据支持的评判器评估完整动作序列，并提取阶段级瓶颈，而非仅依赖最终成功率。GraceBench 和 HICO-Bench 也分别反映出同样的趋势：所采集的信息流正日益侧重于诊断执行轨迹并验证由此产生的计划。Why it matters: 如果你负责维护智能体评估套件，EvoProbe 提供了一种围绕已观察到的失败模式更新任务的设计，而不是无明确方向地添加样例。即使总体成功分数几乎没有变化，其阶段级证据也能区分产品变更究竟修复了规划、工具执行还是其他阶段。Evidence: E001, E159, E125. High confidence.

Doc2Harness 是一个新的两阶段基准，它评估的是编码智能体周边的软件框架——即让模型得以工作的工具、接口和控制逻辑——而不是将该框架固定不变。其第一阶段要求模型根据接口契约和一份涵盖十二个前沿框架的开发文档，构建一个完整的候选框架。Why it matters: 如果你正在选择编码智能体技术栈，这一基准可以将模型能力与框架工程区分开来。它支持比较模型能否构建周边执行系统，而不是把所有下游任务成功都归因于预选框架中使用的模型。Evidence: E012. High confidence.

MMA-SafetyBench 是一个面向多模态智能体的新安全基准，会在智能体的观察流中插入欺骗性视觉元素，例如伪造的系统警报。它包含横跨网页、桌面、移动端、文档和视频任务的 1,083 条对抗性轨迹，针对的是视觉语义劫持，即通过界面内容让智能体偏离其获授权任务。Why it matters: 如果你的智能体通过视觉界面执行操作，仅包含文本的提示注入测试无法覆盖这条攻击路径。该基准可让安全审查测试智能体在多步骤任务期间，当恶意指令以有实际含义的屏幕内容形式出现时，是否仍会遵守授权边界。Evidence: E008. High confidence.

RCA-Bench 是一个用于评估智能体能否选择适当自主程度的新基准。它将保留给人类的实质性决策与执行授权区分开来，然后在 60 个经专家验证、涵盖六个领域的组织场景中，将响应评定为 ACT、CONFIRM 或 ESCALATE。其发布内容包括四个模型在基线提示和政策引导提示下生成的 1,440 条响应。Why it matters: 如果你正在为工作场所智能体设置部署权限，该基准评估的是委派决策本身，而不只是任务正确性。这种三分类结果可以揭示政策提示是减少了未经授权的操作、导致过度升级，还是恰当地请求了确认。Evidence: E006. High confidence.

BenchChecker 是一个面向缺陷修复基准的新污染审计框架。它利用模型的文本输出和公开代码仓库历史，寻找基准补丁可能曾出现在训练数据中的证据；其来源说明称，该方法同时适用于开源和闭源模型。Why it matters: 如果你要比较训练数据不可用的编码模型，这提供了一条无需检查模型权重或私有语料库的潜在审计路径。污染调查结果可以帮助判断较高的修复分数是否足以支持部署选型，还是主要反映了模型曾接触长期存在于代码仓库中的补丁。Evidence: E024. Medium confidence.

J-tau 是一个面向工具调用型日语客服智能体的新基准。它以英语为中心的 tau-bench 为基础，通过翻译、调整地址和货币等特定地区实体以及人工审核完成本地化。其构建过程还发现并修复了原基准中的两个缺陷。Why it matters: 如果你正在为日语客户支持选择智能体，经过翻译的英语测试可能仍保留不符合实际的实体和交互假设。J-tau 提供了一个经过地区适配的替代方案；与此同时，鉴于所报告的修复，其分数不应被视为可与未经修正的源基准结果直接互换。Evidence: E013. High confidence.
briefing.caveat: This briefing covers a keyword-filtered, nonrepresentative feed. Only 189 of 899 corpus evidence records were injected for analysis, so these findings do not represent a full reading of the captured corpus. Brave and OpenReview were unavailable, and several attention collectors had failed or unread requests; no field-wide prevalence claim follows from this evidence.

evidence_items.summary: Static benchmarks for large language model (LLM) agents face saturation and data contamination risks, motivating continual updates to evaluation tasks. However, aggregate scores and success rates offer limited insight into specific problem-solving bottlenecks and provide limited guidance for subsequent task design. We propose EvoProbe, an evaluation-driven benchmark evolution framework that integrates task generation, diagnostic evaluation, and feedback-driven regeneration into a closed loop. It combines verifiable subtask outcome scoring with evidence-supported multi-judge trajectory evaluation and distills phase-level bottlenecks, success patterns, and failure patterns into diagnostic feedback for generating new executable tasks. Across two rounds of cybersecurity experiments, evaluations of eight models on 66 tasks reveal phase-level performance differences and common failure patterns beyond aggregate scores. In a cross-round comparison with the Examiner model set and solver configuration held fixed, all eight models achieve lower Outcome scores on the updated tasks, with relative decreases of 11.8\% in mean Outcome and 40.0\% in mean Pass\textasciicircum{}3. These results support using fine-grained diagnostics to guide iterative task updates and probe agents' current capabilities and limitations.
evidence_items.title: EvoProbe: Evaluation-Driven Benchmark Evolution for LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: TORRENT (the Traceable, Observation-constrained, Rapid-Response, Episode–gauge–watershed Network of Testbeds) converts reported flash floods in the contiguous United States into traceable episode–gauge–watershed testbeds for reproducible hydrological-response analysis and model intercomparison. The dataset is organised in three levels. Level 1 preserves the national inventory of 42,466 NOAA/NCEI flash-flood episodes for 1996–2025 (110,251 event records; 342,238 location records), retained without hydrological screening. Level 2 documents observation availability for 5,424 recent CONUS episodes (2021–2025), annotating USGS stream-gauge and USGS/FEMA Short-Term Network high-water-mark (HWM) availability for the full population rather than pre-selecting cases; 4,599 of those episodes have discharge availability at a queried nearby gauge. Level 3 provides 806 episode–gauge–watershed evaluation packages (160 episodes, 208 gauges), each requiring a retrievable NLDI contributing watershed, at least one temporally confirmed in-basin high-water mark, and a detected discharge response. Successive screening on Level 3 yields 175 strict flash-flood testbeds, 115 after deduplication, 54 with in-basin NCEI corroboration, and 31 with a Log-Pearson III return period of at least 2 years. Two documented post-selection reviews — direct flood-control influence and recent-wildfire applicability — remove ten further testbeds and define a conservative primary benchmark of 21 testbeds representing 14 episodes and 21 gauges. Every removed testbed remains in Level 3 with the reason recorded as a flag, so users can widen or narrow the sample themselves. The full 13,315-pair screening audit trail ships as data/L3/l3 candidate pairs.csv, so the entire funnel can be re-derived from the archive alone.
evidence_items.title: TORRENT: a benchmark-ready flash-flood dataset for the contiguous United States

evidence_items.summary: Data, models and code accompanying the IEEE SSRR 2026 paper One Operator, Many Robots: Natural-Language Command of UAV–UGV Teams for Search, Victim Detection, and Rescue. The paper extends Swarm-Steward, a natural-language multi-robot coordination system, with live aerial victim detection, geolocation, operator confirmation and UGV deployment, and evaluates it in twelve outdoor search experiments. What’s new in version 2.0 (October 2026) Single-source specialists for every YOLO26 size: 20 detectors fine-tuned on HERIDAL, LADD, NOMAD or SARD alone (sizes n, s, m, l, x), each evaluated on all four sources and on the pooled validation set (125 results). Dataset rebuild script: downloads the AerialPerson-Mix images from the original providers and verifies every image against the released labels and SHA-256 checksums. Camera-ready figures and reports, including precision–recall operating points for all five sizes. Version 1.0 (June 2026) remains available. The concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20643213 always resolves to the latest version. Contents A detector.zip — the deployed AerialPerson-YOLO26l detector (PyTorch), the YOLO26 n/s/m/l/x size sweep, the 20 single-source specialists with their cross-source evaluation, confidence-threshold analysis, reports, figures and plotting scripts. B aerialperson mix.zip — the AerialPerson-Mix definition: single-class YOLO labels for 3,985 images (3,188 train / 797 validation) from SARD, HERIDAL, LADD and NOMAD, per-source manifests, dataset YAML, image checksums and the rebuild script. Source images are not redistributed. C search experiments.zip — curated data from the twelve outdoor experiments: run manifests, per-drone telemetry summaries, gimbal/altitude precision tables and candidate records, covering four victim placements, one-, two- and four-UAV teams, and DJI Mini 4 Pro UAVs over an area of about 200 m × 240 m.
evidence_items.title: Swarm-Steward SAR Perception-to-Response Artifacts: AerialPerson-YOLO26l, Dataset Splits, and Field Evaluation Data

evidence_items.summary: AI agents for autonomous scientific discovery must decide which experiments to run under a limited budget. Most benchmarks for science agents provide fixed datasets, while others that support active experimentation largely rely on simulation. We introduce Autonomous Science Bench, an initial release comprising six budgeted design-build-test-learn campaigns grounded in published experiments across biology, chemistry, and materials science. Agents select batches of designs, receive measurements from a lab service, and use the results to guide subsequent experiments before delivering a predictive model. Success requires passing two calibrated gates: a discovery gate, which evaluates the designs the agent measured, and a learning gate, which evaluates its model's ranking of held-out designs. In a pilot evaluation of eight agent-model configurations and 144 trials, the best configuration succeeds in 67% of trials, while the hardest campaign is solved in only three of 24 attempts. The two gates reveal different weaknesses: some agents build accurate rankings but find too few promising designs, while others find promising designs but fail to predict which unseen designs will perform well. These differences are obscured by overall success rates alone. We release version 0.1 of the campaigns, lab runtime, and public leaderboard at https://yibow.me/autonomous-science-bench.
evidence_items.title: Autonomous Science Bench: Evaluating AI Agents for Autonomous Scientific Discovery

evidence_items.summary: Contextual forecasting seeks to improve time series forecasting by incorporating forward-looking information, such as planned events, external conditions, and expert expectations. However, reliable evaluation remains difficult: existing benchmarks often have limited domain coverage, lack standardized history-future splits, or provide text that is not guaranteed to inform the future. We introduce GIFT-Eval-CTX, a benchmark that isolates whether forecasting methods can translate verified future information into accurate numerical trajectories. Built upon GIFT-Eval, GIFT-Eval-CTX contains 10,000 instances across 20 datasets. Each instance provides structured effects derived from the realized future: Macro effects describe horizon-wide behavior, while Micro effects specify localized changes. We construct these annotations with an agentic pipeline combining LLM-based discovery and deterministic code validation. We benchmark TSFMs, frontier LLMs, and tool-using agentic systems. The results show that structured effects reduce aggregate relative MASE by 40.7% for GPT-5.6 Sol and 29.6% for Claude Opus 4.8 relative to history-only prompting. The evaluated MoiraiAgent system achieves the best overall result. We further analyze the contributions of structured effects and agentic systems to performance, and identify opportunities for future research.
evidence_items.title: GIFT-Eval-CTX: A Benchmark For Contextual Forecasting Model Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models accelerate software development but introduce severe security vulnerabilities. This systematic review investigates security risks in automated coding, benchmark limitations, and the role of human developers. Findings indicate that models frequently generate insecure code and faulty patches due to training data biases. Additionally, the models themselves are susceptible to direct attacks. Current evaluation methods suffer from data contamination and lack robust security metrics. Consequently, human oversight remains essential. Safer integration of automation will require more security-aware model architectures, stronger security-specific benchmarks, and more effective human-AI collaboration frameworks to mitigate these systemic risks.
evidence_items.title: Security in LLM-Assisted Coding: A Systematic Literature Review

evidence_items.summary: Independently authored skills can impose incompatible requirements, competing preferences, and redundant instructions when jointly loaded by an LLM agent. We propose SkillFusion, an offline compiler that reconciles these interactions into a reusable merged skill. Its central idea is to make composition decisions explicit through typed, scoped constraints linked to their source directives. A type-scope gate selects candidate interactions, while selective fallback revisits pairs potentially missed by structural pruning. A classifier identifies interaction types, and an adversarial verifier re-examines uncertain judgments. The resolver applies conditional routing or explicit priorities to hard conflicts, verified abstraction to soft conflicts, and deduplication to redundant instructions. Source-linked checks guide synthesis and compression, and metadata synthesis supports discovery of the merged skill. The resulting artifact retains associated scripts and resources and can be reused across tasks and executor models. SkillFusion achieves the highest mean Success among evaluated non-oracle methods on all three agent benchmarks and on both transfer benchmarks across three executor models. At the largest tested instruction configurations, it achieves over 2.5 times the Success of unresolved multi-skill loading, highlighting the growing value of reconciliation as composition becomes more demanding. The code will be open-sourced after the review process concludes.
evidence_items.title: SkillFusion: Towards Reliable Multi-Skill Composition for LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: The evaluation of coding agents generally strives to be as realistic as possible. In our study, we collect 4,782 agent sessions of real software engineers in JetBrains IDEs, which we call Production Sessions. Since our subject is interactive agents, we study the sessions with at least three user messages (33% of the sample). These long sessions differ from issue-derived benchmark tasks in two ways: (i) user requests span a far wider mix of task types - questions about the project's code, planning, review, refactoring, execution - and (ii) users switch between types throughout a session. Long-session samples from three public interaction corpora exhibit markedly different Task Flows (the distributions of session lengths, task types, and type-to-type transitions), so no single interaction distribution is universally realistic: benchmarks should name a target use case and calibrate to measurements from it. We present SWE-TaskFlow, an approach for transforming any issue-derived benchmark: it preserves the verified tasks and tests while steering the interaction toward a target Task Flow through prompt splitting and verifiable repository QA, with a TaskFlow Alignment Score (TFAS) for selecting among generated trajectories. In a pilot on 700 SWE-Bench Pro tasks, solving the task sequentially in several steps approximately doubles agent cost without a stable change in resolve rate: the interaction protocol itself is an important dimension of evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Coding-Agent Benchmarks Should Match Their Users' Task Flows

evidence_items.summary: Playing the user with a large language model is standard in scalable evaluation, and has a repeatedly diagnosed failure: the simulated user is excessively cooperative, so a system under test can score by the number of questions it asks rather than by making the user willing to speak. We answer with a disclosure gate conditioning information release on the companion agent's behaviour: its state is a ladder of five ordered gates, merged onto three observable depth layers. We specify, ablate, and audit it. The gate is a load-bearing component of the environment: on a published companion-agent benchmark's English corpus, withdrawing per-example gate statements from training displaces the ranking of the 12 systems beyond the noise band of a seed re-run, while per-system scores show no detectable change. We state two acceptance criteria: a ranking must be order-preserving, and absolute scores must be scale-stable. Only one candidate passes both -- the simulator we release -- correlating at 0.993 with the published leaderboard. Prompting a frontier model instead barely moves the ranking while shifting every score up, invisible to ranking-only checks; we supply the specification, ablations, and downstream sensitivity analysis the benchmark's environment lacked.
evidence_items.title: Disclosure-Gated User Simulation for Companion-Agent Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Operational facilities accumulate extensive local telemetry, but agent-ready interactive evaluations with source-verifiable answers are costly to construct from such archives. Site-specific measurement histories also motivate a local conversion workflow that can operate where raw operational data must remain under organizational control. We introduce BTS-AgentBench, a deterministic compiler that transforms read-only telemetry and equipment metadata into tool-backed, multi-turn agent tasks, phase-level targets, evidence and executable evaluation contracts. The BTS release includes 532 episodes across nine families; a second-corpus port produces 204 XAI4HEAT episodes. Frozen-input replay reproduces released artifacts byte-for-byte, and independent raw-source checks cover all 89 BTS and 41 XAI4HEAT test episodes. Replayable provenance links 1,170 trial identities to recorded execution and scorer conditions, while 1,125 completed traces retain model responses and tool results. An obligation-level comparison of 216 scored failures found that linked records exposed additional recorded failed obligations in 202 cases (93.5\%), including tool arguments, stream identity, state carryover and missing interaction steps. The pipeline thereby supports source-grounded task generation, exact reconstruction and auditable diagnosis of agent executions. Code, released benchmarks, and reproduction instructions are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/telemetry-benchmark-reproduction-3D68
evidence_items.title: BTS-AgentBench: A Deterministic, Replayable Pipeline from Read-Only Telemetry Logs to Agent Benchmarks

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as data-science agents, combining abstract reasoning with advanced tool use. Yet the relevant benchmark landscape largely divides into symbolic causal reasoning benchmarks without realistic data analysis or data analysis benchmarks without causal data-generating structure or a range of causal data science tasks. Existing causal evaluation datasets are often restricted to curated examples from existing sources, with diversity coming from limited templatized variations rather than from systematic generation of novel synthetic causal structures. We introduce CausalDS, a benchmark for evaluating causal reasoning in agentic data-science workflows. Each benchmark instance is a scene consisting of a sampled structural causal model (SCM) with generated observational data and an accompanying synthetic natural-language story grounded in a real domain. We ground the composition of the benchmark components in empirical distributions obtained from real-world datasets, thus retaining empirical structure while reducing the memorization risk through completely synthetic generation. From each scene, we then derive tasks spanning all three of Pearl's rungs. Most tasks include a data science coding component, where the model typically needs to use several tools to arrive at the final answer due to imperfect observations. Abstention is tested directly: for targets the graph does not identify, the graded answer is to abstain. The benchmark thus jointly evaluates symbolic causal reasoning, data science, uncertainty quantification, abstention, and tool use/coding. Because the generator is fully synthetic, the exam is not a fixed dataset: composition, difficulty, and size are parameters, and fresh exams can be drawn at will.
evidence_items.title: CausalDS: Benchmarking Causal Reasoning in Data-Science Agents

evidence_items.summary: RCA-Bench is a benchmark for evaluating whether large language models (LLMs) select appropriate levels of autonomy when responding to organizational requests. It uses a two-gate decision framework distinguishing human-reserved substantive decisions from execution authorization, with three possible autonomy outcomes: ACT, CONFIRM, and ESCALATE. The benchmark contains 60 expert-validated organizational scenarios across six domains. The accompanying experimental dataset comprises 1,440 valid responses from four LLMs evaluated under Baseline and Agent Delegation Policy (ADP)-guided prompting conditions, with three repetitions per scenario. The repository includes benchmark scenarios, expert-established reference labels, experimental responses, prompting procedures, execution configurations, reproducibility scripts, statistical analysis, and supporting audit documentation. The overall classification accuracy was 87.92%. Although ADP-guided prompting produced a descriptive improvement, the scenario-cluster bootstrap confidence intervals did not establish a statistically conclusive improvement. The package is intended to support transparent evaluation, independent verification, and future research on risk-calibrated autonomy, human oversight, and authorization-aware AI agents. The included documentation specifies the scope of the licenses, known reproducibility limitations, and considerations concerning third-party model outputs.
evidence_items.title: RCA-Bench v1.0: Benchmark Scenarios, Experimental Responses, and Reproducibility Materials for Risk-Calibrated LLM Agent Autonomy

Version v0.2 adds the repeated-run evaluation reported in the revised paper (runs/round2), golden validation cases for fault-section localization and two optimization families, repeated-run tooling, and runner fixes for packet isolation and timeouts.

evidence_items.summary: We present MARL-BattleGrounds (MARL-BGs), an easy-to-use JAX-native benchmark for heterogeneous and competitive multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), designed to be sample-efficient, computationally efficient, and researcher-centric. MARL benchmarks are typically simple and efficient, like SMAX, where winning reduces to unit micromanagement, or rich and costly, like Dota 2. MARL-BGs fills this missing middle. Its first mode, Team Deathmatch, is a simultaneous turn-based game between two teams of five heterogeneous agents. The five classes have distinct basic, passive, and ultimate abilities designed to synergize with allies and counter enemies. Our 52 hand-designed maps with diverse obstacles include a 12-map curriculum and ten held-out validation and test maps. MARL-BGs provides two canonical evaluation modes. First, eight endgame scenarios form a hard generalization challenge: each asks a team to win an unseen, nearly lost position against a strong reactive controller within 5-10 ticks. Second, a monthly round-robin tournament retrains each submission on equal compute, plays it against every member of the current "Big Nine" field, and publishes the Elo results on the official leaderboard. All entrants are publicly released as downloadable opponents. MARL-BGs records 11,192 metrics per game in 28 topics. We also include three strong scripted opponents, an analytical replay viewer, and off-the-shelf tools for self-play, cross-play, curriculum learning, and zero-shot coordination evaluation. We even provide an API for LLM-based agents and use it to evaluate Qwen3.5-9B against our strongest policy. In our BattleClient, humans can play alongside or against any mix of policies, enabling human-AI evaluation. We benchmark MARL-BGs with six additional deep MARL baselines, which we release. On one RTX 5090 with 1,024 parallel games, the simulator runs 50,000 5v5 game steps per second.
evidence_items.title: MARL-BattleGrounds: A Novel JAX-native Benchmark for Heterogeneous and Competitive Multi-agent RL

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal agents increasingly rely on visual interfaces to perceive state and select actions, creating an attack surface not captured by text-only safety evaluations. We study Visual Semantic Hijacking, in which deceptive but semantically meaningful interface elements, such as forged system alerts, cause an agent to depart from its authorized task. We propose a trajectory-guided procedure that identifies candidate injection points and inserts reproducible visual payloads into the observation stream. Using this procedure, we construct MMA-SafetyBench, which contains 1,083 adversarial trajectories across web automation, desktop GUI control, mobile navigation, document understanding, and video processing. Across nine evaluated models, Attack Success Rate (ASR) reaches 87.96%, while Semantic Compromise Rate (SCR) reaches 98.09%. A 1--3--5 scoring scheme distinguishes target-matching outputs, semantic disruption without a target match, and successful preservation of the benign task. Controls covering all nine models and five domains show that attacks persist under neutral prompts. A safety-priority prompt lowers ASR without eliminating the failure mode.
evidence_items.title: MMA-SafetyBench: A Benchmark for Multimodal Agent Safety Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Ultrathin multimode fiber (MMF) probes promise minimally invasive endoscopic access to sub-millimeter anatomy, but far-field imaging through a single small-core collection fiber yields severely speckle-dominated recordings dominated by multiplicative, signal-dependent interference that obscures fine structural details. While fully supervised physics-guided models achieve state-of-the-art despeckling fidelity with large-scale paired datasets, generating extensive clean ground truth (GT) references demands substantial experimental effort, limiting scalability in resource-constrained biomedical settings. Self-supervised approaches, conversely, struggle with the structured non-stationary patterns of coherent speckle due to their reliance on additive or pixel-independent noise models. We introduce a physics-informed, semi-supervised CycleGAN framework that overcomes these constraints by training primarily on abundant unpaired speckled patches augmented by only 1% clean references for identity regularization. Multiplicative speckle is converted to additive noise in the logarithmic domain; an attention-augmented UNet generator selectively preserves salient features; and optimal weighted convolution (OWC) modules embedded in outermost layers and discriminator input incorporate spatial density weighted prior that exploit the spatial correlation structure of coherent speckle patterns. Quantitative evaluations on paper and metal datasets demonstrate superior PSNR/SSIM over self-supervised baselines and standard CycleGAN, with reconstructions closely approaching fully supervised benchmarks without requiring paired speckled-clean data for training. This design offers a practical complement to paired training paradigms, enabling high-fidelity despeckling in scenarios where clean references are scarce-such as dynamic in vivo imaging, photon-limited deep-tissue probes, or clinical biopsies-thus advancing speckle-free ultrathin MMF endoscopy toward routine microanatomical interrogation.
evidence_items.title: Toward Practical Speckle-Free Imaging in Multimode Fiber Endoscopy via Semi-Supervised Cycle-Consistent Generative Networks With Optimal Weighted Convolution

evidence_items.summary: This dataset comprises 59 high-resolution agar plate images, including 57 images collected from heterogeneous bacterial samples across multiple plating dilutions and four culture media: MacConkey (MAC), de Man, Rogosa and Sharpe (MRS), Plate Count Agar (PCA), and Violet Red Bile Agar (VRBA), alongside two negative controls. The 57 experimental images and corresponding human-derived reference annotations were used to benchmark AgentCount, an automated colony enumeration pipeline integrating SAM 3-based image segmentation with LLM-assisted reporting. The dataset is publicly available to support reproducibility and independent evaluation of automated microbial colony counting methods.
evidence_items.title: High-Resolution agar plate image benchmark dataset for automated colony enumeration

evidence_items.summary: Agents driven by large language models are increasingly deployed on long-horizon tasks, where they use tools and modify real workspaces. How well they perform depends as much on the harness around the model as on the model itself. Existing benchmarks measure downstream task success under a fixed harness, leaving harness engineering itself unexplored. We propose Doc2Harness, a two-stage benchmark that evaluates long-horizon harness engineering directly. In Stage 1, a build model operating inside a fixed builder harness receives an interface-only contract skeleton and a development document that consolidates behavior across twelve frontier harnesses, and then constructs a complete candidate harness in an isolated container. In Stage 2, the frozen candidate harness runs in containers separate from the construction environment, one per test case, and is driven end to end by a scripted mock model. We score each test case using four observable channels, namely the requests sent to the model, the files on disk, the process exit code, and the command output; positive controls rule out vacuous passes. Across nineteen frontier models, each evaluated with three independent builds on 328 test cases, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest pass rate at 53.05%, while the weakest model reaches 27.44%, a gap of roughly twenty-six percentage points. Even the strongest model fails nearly half of the test cases, and failures cluster around how cross-cutting functionality is split across modules. To our knowledge, Doc2Harness provides the first deterministic benchmark for measuring long-horizon harness engineering.
evidence_items.title: Doc2Harness: Benchmarking LLMs on Long-Horizon Harness Engineering of Coding Agents

evidence_items.summary: We present J-tau, the first publicly available Japanese benchmark for evaluating tool-using LLM agents in interactive customer-support scenarios. While tau-bench is widely used to evaluate LLM agents, it is English-centric and cannot evaluate agents in other languages. Existing multilingual extensions offer no public Japanese version and rely primarily on machine translation, leaving locale-specific entities such as addresses and currencies inconsistent with the target region. To enable reliable evaluation in Japanese, we carefully localize tau-bench through machine translation, entity adaptation, and human review. During this process, we also uncover and fix two flaws in the original tau-bench: invalid tasks and a score aggregation error that inflates certain models' results. Experiments show that J-tau yields fewer evaluation errors than a naively machine-translated counterpart and that our fixes resolve both flaws.
evidence_items.title: J-tau: A Fully Localized Japanese Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction

rationale: Also found via Hugging Face Papers
evidence_items.summary: In long-horizon tool-calling tasks, LLM agents can fail not only because of tool-use errors, but also because of ineffective interaction with users. Yet existing benchmarks largely assume cooperative and behaviorally stable users, leaving the effect of emotional variation on agent reliability underexplored. We introduce $\tau$-Emotion-Bench, a ten-domain benchmark for evaluating tool-calling agents under controlled emotion-conditioned user interactions while preserving the underlying task objective. To scale both benchmark construction and agent training, we introduce Tracer, a scalable agentic data-generation pipeline that constructs grounded, policy-valid tasks and collects trajectories through an interactive agent--user--environment harness. By allowing dissatisfied users to terminate inefficient interactions, the harness provides an interaction-aware signal that filters trajectories with excessive user dependence and favors effective tool use. Experiments with two user simulators show that frontier agents remain unreliable, with substantial gaps between average task success and consistent task completion. Tracer-generated supervision consistently improves Qwen3 models across scales, generalizes to unseen domains, and transfers to $\tau$-Bench and $\tau$-Trait. Behavioral analyses further show that higher task success is associated with a better balance between tool execution and necessary user follow-up. Overall, $\tau$-Emotion-Bench and Tracer provide a scalable framework for evaluating agent reliability under diverse user behaviors and improving tool-calling agents through interaction-aware supervision.
evidence_items.title: $\tau$-Emotion-Bench: Exposing the Interaction Fragility of LLM Agents through Real-World User Emotions

evidence_items.summary: Language-model (LM) agents are increasingly evaluated on repository-level software engineering (SWE) benchmarks derived from GitHub issues and pull requests. Although these benchmarks cover a broad range of development tasks, they provide limited insight into a common yet technically distinct challenge: migrating an existing implementation from one operating system (OS) to another while preserving behavior on both. We introduce OS-Bench, an executable benchmark for cross-OS code migration between Linux and Windows. Motivated by case studies showing that cross-platform features are frequently implemented on one OS before support is added for another, OS-Bench identifies migration opportunities by comparing execution coverage collected from the same repository on both systems. Platform-specific regions are then verified, organized into five migration scenarios, and transformed into repository-level tasks with target-platform tests and source-platform regression tests. The resulting benchmark contains 140 validated tasks from 111 repositories across C, C++, C#, Go, and Rust, comprising 91 Windows-to-Linux and 49 Linux-to-Windows migrations. We evaluate six models with SWE-agent, Claude Code, OpenHands, and Win-agent. The best configurations achieve only 26.4% success on Linux-target tasks and 20.4% on Windows-target tasks while preserving correctness across both systems. These results indicate that cross-OS migration is a challenging and underexplored capability, and OS-Bench is a testbed for improving platform-aware SWE agents.
evidence_items.title: OS-Bench: Evaluating SWE Agents on Cross-OS Code Migration

evidence_items.summary: Searching text-rich knowledge graphs requires following relations while examining textual evidence. Predefined graph interfaces constrain what evidence agents can access, even when they write code to combine tool calls or process retrieved subgraphs. We propose direct knowledge graph interaction (DKGI), a harness in which language model agents create graph access tools directly over complete node and edge files. The agent writes Python code to follow relations, combine node sets, and select textual evidence, interleaving execution with shell search and file inspection. This lets agents process large node sets in bulk while returning selected text for the model to assess. Execution feedback guides tool creation and revision, while the evolving tools determine what evidence the agent gathers next. On benchmark datasets spanning three domains, training-free DKGI exceeds the strongest published baseline by at least 6.7 Hit@1 points on every graph, even with a minimal harness. Controlled ablations show the benefits of multi-turn programming over shell-only access and predefined graph tools, while trajectories show agents revising code to extend searches or address errors. These findings highlight the value of allowing tool creation and tool use to co-evolve during graph search. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/leopoldwhite/DKGI.
evidence_items.title: Knowledge Graphs as Files: An Agent Harness Where Tool Creation and Tool Use Co-Evolve

rationale: Also found via Hugging Face Papers
evidence_items.summary: A robot following a multi-step instruction needs to act on the right objects in the right order, even as the scene changes. It must also maintain awareness of task progress and determine when to advance. To address these challenges, we introduce Orchestra, an agent harness that separates task planning and execution management from action generation. Orchestra decomposes a complete multimodal instruction into ordered subtasks, tracks completed steps, and updates the locations of relevant objects and destinations during execution. It maintains a shared context containing the active subtask, spatial grounding, and recent observations. An action policy uses this context to generate actions, while a separately trained progress evaluator estimates when to advance to the next subtask. To evaluate whether robots trained on atomic instructions and short trajectories can execute longer subtask sequences, we introduce a benchmark named RMBench-Compose. Orchestra achieves a mean success rate of $68.22\%$ across nine RMBench tasks, outperforming Mem-0 by $26.22$ percentage points. On RMBench-Compose, it achieves an Average Success Length (ASL) of $7.35$ subtasks, $2.46$ times that of HarnessVLA. Across four real-world multi-step tasks, it improves mean ASL by $25.0\%$ over Orchestra using the base $\pi_{0.5}$ policy. These results show that Orchestra helps robots carry out longer sequences of subtasks while preserving the requested subtask order and acting on the specified objects. Our code and project page are available at https://youpengwen.github.io/Orchestra.
evidence_items.title: Let the Mind Conceive, Let the Hand Achieve: Following Multimodal Instructions for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation

evidence_items.summary: Long-term memory has become a core component of large language model (LLM) agents. As agents accumulate personal information over long-term use, users increasingly ask them to delete sensitive or outdated facts. A memory system should honor such requests. It should remove exactly what was requested and keep the rest of its memory intact. However, existing memory benchmarks evaluate only memory writing, retrieval, and organization, so whether agents can forget at the user's explicit request remains under-evaluated. To address this gap, we propose Bemula, the first benchmark dedicated to memory unlearning. It comprises 50 multi-session dialogue instances, 135 forget requests of six types, and 1,742 test questions. Each dialogue has a control version without the requests, so that only systems that have stored the target can earn credit for forgetting. Across the paired versions, five test suites measure storage, removal of the requested information, preservation of unrelated memories, relearning of similar facts, and resistance to extraction attacks. On Bemula, we evaluate six mainstream memory systems under three backbone LLMs, together with the Full Context LLM on two of them. The results are negative. Across all evaluated systems and backbones, no system passes more than 1.5% of forget requests end to end, and most pass none at all. These systems either leave the requested information extractable under simple attacks or delete far more than requested. Memory unlearning therefore remains an open challenge for agent memory design. We release our data and code at https://github.com/Nboxff/bemula-benchmark.
evidence_items.title: Can Agents Forget When Asked? A Benchmark for Memory Unlearning in LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: Agent evaluation harnesses are software systems that run test suites, generate inputs, and decide outcomes with test oracles. This paper audits such software for reliability defects that score tables cannot reveal. We introduce an oracle-integrity auditing approach with five state-integrity invariants and three known-answer controls. We evaluate it by injecting seven oracle defect classes across two task domains and a synthetic domain. All injected defect classes are detected, and the repaired oracle has no false positives. Applied to an agent benchmark, the audit reveals a reward-function defect that changes the environment state before post-run scoring. Across 4,320 episodes, replay-based correction changes database-pass labels from 4,194 to 2,883 and reduces measured success from 94.3% to 65.5%. We also study configuration-dependent measurement effects. A component ablation over 3,240 episodes shows that the agent's policy documents, tool descriptions, and tool error strings influence observed trajectory reliability, with tool descriptions showing the largest exploratory effect (-9.2 pp) and error strings the smallest (-5.3 pp). A second task domain reverses the sign of the language effect, so the result is bounded to the tested configuration. Finally, we report a portability boundary: the auditing approach cannot validate a second independently implemented benchmark because the required reference terminal state cannot be reconstructed from its recorded API-call log. The paper releases a replication package containing the auditing suite, fault-injection catalogue, frozen records, deviation logs, and offline analysis entry points without network access, API keys, or model calls.
evidence_items.title: When Agent Evaluation Becomes Unreliable: An Empirical Study of Oracle Failures and Configuration-Dependent Measurement in an LLM Agent Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Healthcare agents must transform longitudinal clinical evidence into reliable actions through heterogeneous tools and stateful workflows, conditions under which model-centric systems may lose context, misuse tools, fail to verify consequential transitions, or cross authorization boundaries. Existing medical-agent benchmarks primarily emphasize terminal task outcomes, making it difficult to determine whether execution failures arise from the agent model, the runtime harness, or their interaction. We present the Medical Harness Protocol, an outcome-preserving framework that independently evaluates seven healthcare-specific process dimensions: Care Action Fulfillment, Clinical Resource Competence, Patient-Evidence Alignment, Clinical Workflow Continuity, Clinical Auditability, Closed-Loop Verification, and Clinical Conduct Boundaries. A normalized intervention trace further tracks whether runtime support is available, activated, delivered, adopted by the agent, and propagated into subsequent behavior. We instantiate the protocol as MedHarnessBench, comprising 342 executable tasks across FHIR/EHR operations, healthcare-administration interfaces, and multimodal clinical tools. Across more than 16,000 controlled task executions, MedHarness yields broad improvements in terminal task success, intermediate subtask completion, and healthcare-specific process quality. We further evaluate MedHarness against multiple general-purpose harnesses and use controlled single-fault perturbations to verify the sensitivity and discrimination of the seven-dimensional evaluation. These results demonstrate that healthcare-specific runtime support can substantially improve both task completion and execution quality, while revealing failures that terminal outcomes alone cannot capture. Code and resources are available at https://github.com/Tomry1114/Awesome-Agent-Harness-for-Healthcare.
evidence_items.title: MedHarnessBench: A Unified Benchmark for Healthcare Agent Evaluation

rationale: Also found via Hugging Face Papers
evidence_items.summary: Words are increasingly becoming an interface for action: large language models (LLMs) can now invoke tools, operate devices, and make decisions that affect the physical world. However, current benchmarks largely evaluate LLMs through static text responses, offline tool calls, or simulated tasks, leaving open the question of how well they can act in real physical environments. We present a benchmark for measuring LLMs in closed-loop physical interaction, where models control a harness system connected to real-world components including robotic arms, cameras, and sensors. In each task, the model must issue instructions, receive physical feedback from the environment, interpret the resulting state, and adapt its next action accordingly. This setting evaluates capabilities beyond language understanding, including grounded perception, action planning, tool selection, spatial reasoning, feedback-driven correction, and robustness to execution uncertainty. Through experiments with representative LLMs, we characterize their ability to translate linguistic reasoning into physical actions and identify common failure modes such as hallucinated state changes, poor recovery from unexpected outcomes, and unstable long-horizon plans. Our benchmark aims to provide a systematic foundation for evaluating LLMs as interactive agents that connect words, tools, and the physical world.
evidence_items.title: Words to World: Benchmarking LLMs in Interactive Physical Environments

evidence_items.summary: We present OpenTWBench, an open evaluation suite for Taiwan-domain knowledge in large language models, built around two benchmarks. tw-exam-bench contains 255,854 four-option questions across 148 academic subjects, from fifteen years of Taiwan's national examinations published as open data by the Ministry of Examination; answer keys agree across 31,312 duplicated question groups at 99.91%, with all 27 disagreements accounted for. A reviewed second pass withdrew 2,180 items whose stems depend on a figure the text does not carry; all scores use the remaining 253,674. tw-formosa-bench contains 1,696 difficulty-curated questions about everyday and contemporary Taiwan - the Taiwan that licensing examinations never ask about - generated from a community-curated corpus under a discipline in which no model writes a ground truth, and curated against a frozen seven-model pool so that the pool scored at the passing margin (46.9-74.6%, median ~54%); a leave-one-out experiment shows the selection preserves model ranking (near-zero bias). Within six weeks the frontier had cleared that band: of 108 models now on the public board, 22 score above its ceiling, the best 91.6%. We also document how much of a score comes from the apparatus rather than the model. On identical questions, switching answer extraction from pattern matching to an explicit \boxed{} answer moves accuracy from 20.8% to 93.9%; a single placeholder character in a system prompt moved one model from last (58.2%) to first (83.9%) on the same benchmark; doubling the thinking budget from 8k to 16k tokens bought 0.2% while shuffling which questions failed; and a three-judge validation panel proved to be one judge in disguise, two members approving 92-99% of everything shown. We release all datasets, per-item difficulty data, curation manifests and a leaderboard at https://opentwbench.ai
evidence_items.title: OpenTWBench (Open Taiwan Benchmark): Taiwan-Domain Knowledge Evaluation for Large Language Models, and How the Measurement Apparatus Shapes the Score

evidence_items.summary: With the increasing complexity of smart home environments, trigger-action-program (TAP) conflicts have emerged as critical issues, occurring when multiple automation apps compete for control over shared devices or interact in unintended ways. While existing approaches detect and resolve such conflicts using predefined rules or expert knowledge, they fail to account for the significant variability in individual pReferences for conflict resolution and significantly degrade the automation-system utility. To address this gap, we propose a preference-aligned conflict resolution (PaCR), a novel agentic framework that resolves conflicts while aligning with users’ personalized preferences for automation behavior. PaCR employs a two-step conflict resolution process: first, it interactively gathers contextual information from smart home configurations to generate conflict resolution agents (CRAs) with user profiles that accurately depict user preferences and characteristics; then, the agents, acting as users, utilize the semantic reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to assist in generating personalized conflict detection and resolution strategies. Due to the agentic conflict-resolving feature, we evaluate the effectiveness of PaCR with existing datasets at scale. PaCR demonstrates strong capabilities in addressing conflicts based on users’ needs and significantly improves conflict resolution efficacy and interpretability, offering a user-centric approach to managing smart-home automation conflicts.
evidence_items.title: PaCR: An Agentic Preference-Aligned TAP Conflict Handling

evidence_items.summary: Legal reasoning is a fundamental capability for large language models (LLMs) to complete legal AI tasks such as legal judgment prediction. In legal practice, this reasoning is shaped by legal philosophy: a judge's view of the nature and sources of law guides how legal materials are interpreted and applied, so judges working from the same statutes and precedents can reach different judgments. Existing research has largely overlooked whether LLMs can understand legal philosophy and apply it in legal reasoning, an ability we call \textit{legal-philosophical reasoning}. To fill this gap, we introduce LePhilBench, a benchmark for evaluating the legal-philosophical reasoning of LLMs that comprises two benchmarking tasks and a dataset. The two tasks evaluate how well LLMs understand legal philosophy and how well they apply it in legal reasoning, respectively. The dataset is manually and meticulously constructed. Its test set contains 220 U.S. Supreme Court opinions. A law professor designed fourteen annotation questions on legal philosophy, and three law-trained annotators with formal training in jurisprudence answered all fourteen questions for every opinion, yielding 9,240 legal-philosophical labels. LePhilBench takes the first step toward exploring legal-philosophical reasoning in LLMs.
evidence_items.title: How Do LLMs Understand Legal Philosophy? Diagnosing Legal-Philosophical Reasoning in LLMs

rationale: Matched: benchmark, dataset, evaluat, test set
evidence_items.summary: Identifying protein-ligand binding sites (pockets) is important for understanding protein function and developing drugs. However, no public method has leveraged co-folding models for novel pocket prediction; furthermore, this task lacks a suitable benchmark as existing benchmarks are within the training distribution of co-folding models. We therefore developed PocketWatch,a curated dataset of biologically relevant ligand pockets. The PocketWatch test set consists of unseen pockets stratified by sequence similarity, structural similarity, and crypticity to enable evaluation of generalization to novel and challenging pockets. Using this dataset, we develop zPocket, a method that trains pocket-prediction heads on top of frozen features from co-folding models. We show that zPocket heads outperform baseline methods across all stratifications. Our best zPocket model achieves overall per-target AUPRC of 0.745 compared to 0.598 and 0.595 for the strongest baselines, VN-EGNN and UniSite-1D retrained on the PocketWatch split (0.559 and 0.531 when using the published weights); the widely used P2Rank reaches 0.477. We further show that zPocket can be used to outperform baseline methods on top-N+2 recall of predicted pocket centroids through clustering per-residue predictions or using zPocket to rescore centroids proposed by other models. Finally, we explore two applications of zPocket: crystallographic fragment screens and a proteome-scale scan for uncharacterized pockets on human proteins. Together these results suggest that zPocket heads built on co-folding trunk features can greatly advance ligand binding site prediction.
evidence_items.title: zPocket: Better Pocket Finding with Frozen Co-Folding Features

evidence_items.summary: Vision-based document retrieval has improved rapidly, but current evaluation settings still emphasize short documents and single relevant pages. This leaves an important gap between leaderboard performance and realistic long-document retrieval, where the evidence needed to answer a query may span multiple pages or even multiple documents. We present VL-DocIR, a page-level benchmark for evidence-complete visual long-document retrieval. VL-DocIR is built from 29,641 HTML-born documents rendered into 388,548 page images from Wikipedia, arXiv, PubMed, and SEC proxy statements. It contains 271,760 queries across 23 domains and six evidence structures, covering single-page, within-document multi-page, and cross-document evidence configurations. Evidence annotations are grounded to rendered pages and HTML element identifiers, and queries are filtered with a cleaning pipeline targeting clarity, correctness, closedness, and the absence of explicit layout references. We evaluate leading single-vector and multi-vector visual retrievers together with diagnostic retrieval settings such as document-context scoring, query splitting, reranking, and round-robin ensembles. The strongest evaluated configuration reaches 69.3 nDCGAll@10 and 80.6 RecallAll@10 under structure-balanced Macro evaluation, but source- and evidence-structure breakdowns show that cross-document retrieval remains substantially harder than single-page retrieval, and that document-context scoring is especially helpful for within-document multi-page queries. VL-DocIR exposes these failure modes and provides a more demanding target for visual long-document retrieval. The new dataset and code will be made publicly available at https://yufanchen96.github.io/VL-DocIR.
evidence_items.title: VL-DocIR: A Benchmark for Vision-Based Long Document Information Retrieval

authors: Serin Atiani (Princess Sumaya University for Technology
rationale: Matched: benchmark, dataset, evaluat, judge model
evidence_items.summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed in contexts requiring adherence to ethical and legal norms, yet their alignment with internationally recognized human rights standards remains underexplored. We introduce UDHRBench, a large-scale benchmark for operationalising the evaluation of large language model compliance with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The dataset comprises 1,124 human rights confronting questions covering all 30 articles and 4,496 responses from four large language models (ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini, and Fanar), manually annotated by experts for alignment, with high inter-annotator agreement ($\kappa = 0.801$). Our analysis reveals systematic and non-trivial misalignments, showing that violations typically arise through seemingly rational reasoning: appeals to efficiency, risk management, or scientific neutrality, rather than explicit rejection of rights. We further propose an LLM-as-a-Judge framework for automated evaluation using zero-shot and few-shot prompting, achieving 89.8\% weighted F1-score in detecting human-rights misalignment, alongside a novel Alignment Leniency Score that quantifies how judge models resolve ambiguous cases. The dataset, annotations, and code will be released as open-source resources (https://sina.birzeit.edu/UDHRBench).
evidence_items.title: UDHRBench: Benchmarking Human Rights in Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Large language models are increasingly used as scientific assistants, yet we still lack reliable ways to evaluate whether they can investigate a system rather than merely answer a prompt. A useful evaluation must let agents choose experiments, interpret finite evidence, and make causal decisions, while keeping the environment coherent across repeated observations and interventions and preserving objective ground truth. We introduce ACED-BENCH (Active Causal Evidence and Decision Benchmark), a neuro-symbolic benchmark built around this requirement. The key idea is to separate the readable scientific surface from the formal causal world: LLMs generate natural-language scenarios and task text, while hidden probabilistic graphical models define the causal graph, data-generating process, intervention semantics, validation checks, and oracle answers. This yields scientific worlds that are natural for agents to investigate but exact enough for scalable, programmatic evaluation. The main leaderboard ACED-CORE contains 180 tasks: 60 set-valued causal ancestry/descendancy questions and 120 constrained causal-decision tasks. We also report ACED-QUAL, a 150-question yes/no qualification check using the same hidden-PGM interface. We evaluate seven contemporary LLMs and two earlier-generation models across three active agent designs. ACED-QUAL checks whether agents can use the interface to draw conclusions from evidence, while ACED-CORE tests whether they can decide what evidence to collect and when to commit to an answer. Evidence-ledger analysis localizes failures within the investigation: agents test the wrong intervention, lose relevant evidence, or continue after sufficient evidence has appeared. These results suggest that reliable AI co-scientists need explicit support for experiment design, evidence retention, answer commitment, and stopping.
evidence_items.title: ACED-Bench: Evaluating How LLM Agents Acquire and Act on Causal Evidence

evidence_items.summary: Modern video games provide a measurable testbed for AI models, combining abilities of visual understanding, instruction decomposition, goal planning, and precise action control over multiple temporal horizons. Existing datasets and benchmarks, however, either cover a narrow range of games, lack language instructions, or rely on high-variance online rollouts. To address these challenges, we introduce GameHorizon, a unified data and evaluation suite that measures gameplay capabilities at different horizons for diverse model families. GameHorizon Suite consists of three components. First, GameHorizon-Annotator is a scalable and automated annotation pipeline for multi-horizon instructions. Second, utilizing the pipeline, we construct GameHorizon-Data, the first large-scale AAA gameplay dataset with temporally aligned videos, player actions, and multi-horizon instructions. It comprises 5,000 hours of recordings from 21 games, collected by 100 human expert players. Third, we build GameHorizon-Bench with reproducible offline and stepwise online testing. The offline track enables reproducible evaluation using thousands of standardized questions organized into three primary tasks and a series of diagnostic variants, while the online track tests whether offline scores reflect actual gameplay capabilities and localizes failures to specific steps within long-horizon gameplay. Based on our GameHorizon Suite, we evaluate 47 models through more than one million model invocations, revealing a meaningful hierarchy of task difficulty and pronounced differences in model capabilities. Our work can provide a standardized yardstick for evaluating gameplay capabilities across horizons and model families. We will release our dataset, annotator, and benchmark to facilitate future research.
evidence_items.title: GameHorizon Suite: Multi-Horizon Data and Evaluation in Gameplay

rationale: Matched: benchmark, dataset, evaluat, synthetic data
evidence_items.summary: Synthetic tabular data support use cases like data sharing, model development under access restrictions, and rapid prototyping of analytical workflows. Modern generative models are evaluated by their statistical similarity, correlation structure, privacy, and downstream machine-learning utility. However, such evaluations leave a gap: they rarely test the structure that matters for analytical queries. We present TabQueryBench, a query-centric benchmark for evaluating synthetic tabular data with SQL-shaped analytical queries. TabQueryBench distills 12 public query sources into 44 reusable query templates and grounds them to each dataset through a policy-guided template-to-SQL pipeline. Across 49 datasets and 11 generative models, it produces more than 100 executable queries per dataset while preserving cross-model comparability. Our evaluation reveals a substantial gap between conventional and query-centric fidelity. Even the strongest model, RealTabFormer, reaches only 0.76 +/- 0.23 query-centric fidelity compared with 1.00 for real data. Failures are most pronounced for high-cardinality attributes and local or tail queries, while model quality also trades off against generation cost. These results show that synthetic data can appear statistically realistic yet still fail to preserve the analytical behavior of real data, motivating query-centric fidelity as a necessary complement to existing evaluation metrics. We open source TabQueryBench to facilitate research in this direction.
evidence_items.title: TabQueryBench: A Query-Centric Benchmark for Synthetic Tabular Data

evidence_items.summary: Parametric knowledge in large language models (LLMs) is a cornerstone of their success, yet remains poorly understood. Existing knowledge benchmarks typically rely on predefined questions (e.g., "What is the birth date of M.L. King?"), evaluating only knowledge that benchmark designers explicitly choose to query, a problematic availability bias. In this paper, we introduce open knowledge evaluation, a new paradigm for benchmarking the stated knowledge of LLMs. Instead of asking narrow questions, it evaluates models on the knowledge they choose to surface in response to open-ended elicitation prompts (e.g., "Tell me everything you know about M.L. King"). This shifts the focus from predefined answer retrieval toward characterizing the knowledge models naturally express. We instantiate this paradigm with BeQu (Beyond Questions), a benchmark of 10,000 entities paired with reference corpora for statement verification. Using BeQu, we evaluate a broad range of language models and analyze the effects of reasoning effort, model scale, prompt format, and knowledge domain. Data and leaderboard are available on this work's GitHub repository and at ANONYMIZED.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Questions: Evaluating the Stated Knowledge of LLMs
