evidence_items.summary: Procedures whose attempts share state, such as search trees, shared-prefix sampling and self-debugging loops, can be scored by a pass@k computed from the total number of successes over all their attempts. We ask what that pooled total supports. In the model where each of R runs draws a latent success rate and makes n conditionally independent attempts, no function of the pooled total is unbiased for pass@k when R, n and k are all at least 2, whether pass@k is read as the procedure's chance of success within k attempts or as the success chance of k independent attempts. The distribution of the total still determines the independent-attempt target for every k and the procedure target for k ≤ n; we give the complete classification of when an unbiased function of the total exists. Per-run counts, by contrast, are known to admit unbiased estimators of the procedure target for k ≤ n and of the independent-attempt target for k ≤ R. Below that run threshold, at R = k − 1 runs, the delete-one jackknife over the runs' first attempts has exact worst-case bias 3.86 percentage points at k = 4 and 2.91 at k = 16, far above the minimax bias 2 · 4^−k, and the same values are lower bounds on the worst case of the jackknife over the runs' success fractions; yet in ten of eleven recorded benchmark cells from eight designs the jackknife's mean error against held-out runs is within 0.44 points, and −2.02 in the eleventh. An evaluation that logs only the pooled total, once R, n, k ≥ 2, gives up unbiased estimation that per-run counts would allow.
evidence_items.title: What a Pooled Success Total Supports for pass@k: Identification, Unbiased Estimation, and a Jackknife Below the Run Threshold

evidence_items.summary: Visible-light anti-uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) detection is important for low-altitude UAV early warning by providing direct appearance and semantic cues. However, in fixed-viewpoint scenarios, UAV targets near the field-of-view (FOV) periphery often suffer from off-axis imaging degradation, which weakens local cues and hinders reliable detection. Existing approaches primarily focus on general small-target representation, whereas explicit modeling of FOV-peripheral degradation and weak-cue attenuation remains insufficient. To address this limitation, we propose WCMA-UAV, a wavelet-guided context modeling and aggregation network for fixed-viewpoint visible-light anti-UAV detection. WCMA-UAV is built around three coordinated components: the wavelet-coupled context module (WCCM), the hierarchical parallel aggregation unit (HPAU), and the progressive attention refinement head (PARH), forming a functional progression from degradation-aware feature extraction through structure-preserving aggregation to progressive refinement. Experiments on the DUT anti-UAV benchmark show that WCMA-UAV achieves the highest average precision (AP) among the compared detectors on both the official test set and the validation set, with the validation set containing a larger proportion of tiny UAV targets. These results indicate that WCMA-UAV improves weak-cue UAV detection near the FOV periphery.
evidence_items.title: Wavelet-Guided Context Modeling and Aggregation Network for Anti-UAV Detection

evidence_items.summary: What binds large language models on auditable, hypothesis-driven decision tasks, where every candidate can be checked against the evidence? On the public TCMEval-SDT benchmark for Traditional Chinese Medicine syndrome differentiation (200 cases), the binding constraint is output discipline and reasoning structure, not model capability alone: two years of model scaling move zero-shot scores by only -0.03 to +0.08, while output-discipline failures (non-terminating reasoning, format non-compliance, large run-to-run spread) persist even in frontier models. We test this with a model-agnostic agent framework formalizing decision making as a five-stage closed loop, enforced by a candidate x evidence matrix falsification protocol: every candidate is judged against every evidence item, at least half of the candidates must be falsified before a conclusion is licensed, and survivors are emitted in a machine-verifiable single-line format. Across five base models, the effect is sign-conditional on zero-shot output discipline: it rescues models whose discipline fails (DeepSeek-V4-Flash: +0.267/+0.271, entirely termination rescue), reduces a high-variance model's run-to-run standard deviation from 0.218 to 0.007 (Kimi K3), and significantly costs already-disciplined models (-0.087 to -0.120 on budget-matched Qwen3-4B/32B). Ablations attribute the cost to the candidate-bounded format layer and show the effect is independent of injected knowledge content (protocol-knowledge decoupling). The protocol also transfers to misinformation-robust mathematical reasoning, detecting injected false premises at 89.8% recall with a 6.8% false-positive rate (MCC 0.54; a flag-everything baseline scores 0) and restoring accuracy to the no-misinformation ceiling. Where zero-shot output discipline is weak, the reasoning protocol sets the floor; base-model capability always sets the ceiling.
evidence_items.title: Output Discipline Sets the Floor: A Falsification-Guided, Model-Agnostic Agent Protocol for Auditable Hypothesis-Driven Decision Making

evidence_items.summary: Repeated event forecasting requires extracting predictive signals from noisy evidence and evaluating their value across successive decisions. We introduce JockeyBench, a benchmark and evaluation protocol that studies this problem through historical Japanese horse racing. The protocol combines time-gated evidence, priced tools, paired frozen-program controls, and two workflows: executing an LLM-written predictor or acquiring evidence for a fresh per-race LLM forecast. Evaluation separates forecast quality, benchmark-specific net utility, and retrospective betting returns and risk under fixed decision rules. Across 28 model--scaffold configurations on 324 races, paired tests identify seven revision gains and two declines after multiple-testing correction. Yet every configuration has negative mean profit under capped-Kelly settlement. In a four-model comparison, the reusable-program workflow has higher mean betting profit and lower research fees, although both workflows lose on average. Further diagnostics reveal that mean probability bias reverses on selected bets and that profitable individual runs can depend on concentrated returns. These findings motivate evaluating predictive competence, adaptation, resource use, and decision value separately when assessing agents for repeated event forecasting.
evidence_items.title: JockeyBench: Evaluating LLM Agents on Horse-Racing Decision-Making

evidence_items.summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance in visual perception and spatial reasoning, leading to growing interest in using them as high-level planners for embodied AI. However, physical tasks require models to integrate spatial information, reason over temporal states, and generate multi-step plans under various constraints, raising the question of whether current VLMs can reliably support such reasoning and planning independently of execution. We introduce Plan-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating the high-level reasoning and multi-step planning capabilities of VLMs relevant to embodied worlds, while isolating the influence of action execution. It covers three complementary dimensions, spanning 16 subclasses and 699 curated samples. Extensive evaluation of 28 VLMs reveals room for improvement, with even the strongest model achieving only 75.0% accuracy. We further find that model scaling generally improves these capabilities. Ablation studies also indicate larger models show increasing potential as high-level planners. Overall, Plan-Bench provides a lightweight probe for evaluating VLMs' reasoning and planning capabilities relevant to embodied environments and assessing their potential as decision makers for physical tasks. Our benchmark and code are available at https://github.com/MinneFeng/Plan-Bench.
evidence_items.title: Plan-Bench: Can Existing VLMs Go Well Beyond Perception to Reason and Plan in Embodied Worlds?

evidence_items.summary: Cross-modal Geo-localization (CMGL) matches ground-level text descriptions with geo-tagged aerial imagery, which is crucial for pedestrian navigation and emergency response. However, existing studies are constrained by narrow geographic coverage and simplistic scene diversity, failing to reflect the immense spatial heterogeneity of global architectural styles and topographic features. To bridge this gap and facilitate universal positioning, we introduce CORE, the first million-scale dataset dedicated to global CMGL. CORE comprises 1,034,786 cross-view images sampled from 225 distinct geographic regions across six continents, offering an unprecedented variety of perspectives in varying environmental conditions and urban layouts. We leverage the zero-shot reasoning of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) to synthesize high-quality scene descriptions rich in discriminative cues. Furthermore, we propose a physical-law-aware network (PLANET) for cross-modal geo-localization. PLANET introduces a novel contrastive learning paradigm to guide textual representations in capturing the intrinsic physical signatures of satellite imagery. Extensive experiments across varied geographic regions demonstrate that PLANET significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, establishing a new benchmark for robust, global-scale geo-localization. The dataset and source code will be released at https://github.com/YtH0823/CORE.
evidence_items.title: Global Cross-Modal Geo-Localization: A Million-Scale Dataset and a Physical Consistency Learning Framework

evidence_items.summary: The African mining industry continues to face a serious communication gap between technical safety documentation and the language used by the workforce. Safety manuals, operating procedures, and regulatory guidance are often produced in English or French, while many workers communicate in isiZulu, chiShona, and other local languages. This mismatch is not just inconvenient; it can be dangerous in safety-critical settings where misunderstandings may contribute to preventable incidents. This paper reports on Talk MINING, a domain-adapted multilingual large language model built on InkubaLM and trained on mining-specific text, question–answer pairs, and multimodal hazard data. The model was developed using Hugging Face tools and evaluated with both quantitative and qualitative methods. Results show a marked improvement over the baseline model, with overall accuracy rising from below 50% to 82%, and strong gains across isiZulu, chiShona, and English. The project also includes a web-based prototype that allows users to take photos of mining conditions and receive guidance in a local language. This paper presents the full pipeline for Talk MINING, including document preparation, translation and localization, model training, evaluation, deployment, monitoring, and validation. Beyond benchmark performance, the system is designed for practical deployment in environments where connectivity is limited and literacy levels vary—supporting both text queries and image-based hazard input through a mobile-ready prototype. The work contributes a reproducible pipeline, a curated multilingual mining corpus, and an open evaluation framework that can serve as a foundation for extending domain-adapted AI to other African languages and safety-critical industries. Ultimately, Talk MINING demonstrates that closing the language gap in mining safety is not only technically feasible but achievable with relatively modest model size when domain adaptation is done rigorously.
evidence_items.title: A Domain-Adapted Multilingual Large Language Model for Mining Safety in African Languages

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has fundamentally transformed information interaction, yet their application in environmental science and engineering (ESE) is hindered by multimodal data formats, dynamic context requirements, and hallucination risks. To transition from general-purpose models to domain expert agentic systems, this Perspective introduces a three-pillar framework for ESE-LLMs: domain perception, knowledge grounding, and action capability. Implementing these capabilities introduces potential pitfalls such as geographic representation bias, catastrophic forgetting, and source authenticity vulnerabilities, which require strategic model blending and careful data curation to overcome. Furthermore, rigorous evaluation must extend beyond standard knowledge benchmarks to systematically assess factuality, fairness, consistency, and safety using both human and automated metrics. Finally, we present a decision-guided deployment workflow that helps researchers in ESE fields integrate LLMs into their workflow. Ultimately, achieving trustworthy environmental intelligence relies on continuous evaluation, robust governance, and sustained interdisciplinary collaboration to safely deploy agentic ESE-LLMs for high-stakes environmental challenges.
evidence_items.title:
Putting Large Language
Models into Environmental Context

evidence_items.summary: Literature snowballing is a widely used technique for identifying relevant studies in secondary research, but its manual screening effort is substantial. Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise for supporting systematic reviews, yet their effectiveness for snowballing-specific reference screening remains largely unexplored. We evaluate three contemporary LLMs—OpenAI GPT-5, Google Gemini 3.5 Flash, and Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5—on a purpose-built benchmark of four datasets spanning two research domains (photoplethysmography and bin packing). For each of 20 seed articles, balanced candidate sets are constructed from references of the seed (positives) and references of other seeds (negatives) using automatically derived labels, with strict screening at a confidence threshold of 0.70. In cross-domain conditions, all models achieve near-perfect precision (\(\ge 99.8\%\)), indicating that broad topical discrimination is trivial. In within-domain conditions, precision drops to 55–\(73\%\), exposing the core challenge of fine-grained relevance assessment. GPT-5 attains the highest F1 scores (\(77.7\%\) BPP, \(73.9\%\) PPG) by balancing precision and recall, while Claude maximizes recall (up to \(98.7\%\)) at the cost of many false positives.
evidence_items.title: Experimenting with Snowball Sampling of Research Papers using Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Modified nucleic acids play important roles in biology and biotechnology. However, their chemical and structural diversity as well as effects on nucleic acid structure and intermolecular interactions remain incompletely characterized. The performance of structure prediction and co-folding algorithms for modeling modified nucleic acids and nucleic acid–protein complexes has also not been evaluated. Here, we systematically analyze ribose-based modified nucleotides present in structures deposited in the Protein Data Bank. Modified nucleotides are primarily localized to the nucleobase, where they exhibit chemical and structural diversity shaped by molecular size, topological shape descriptors, and polarity-related properties. We develop MODNAP, the first curated dataset of experimentally determined structures containing modified nucleotides. Using MODNAP, we benchmark AlphaFold 3 on 1039 nucleic acid and nucleic acid–protein complex structures spanning a range of nucleotide modifications, tertiary folds, and biological functions. AlphaFold 3 achieves success rates exceeding 80% at an RMSD threshold of 2.5 Å. However, its accuracy in positioning modified nucleotides is variable and decreases for structures not explicitly represented in training. PoseBusters analysis reveals frequent intramolecular validity failures, primarily due to non-ideal ribose ring geometries. Together, these results establish MODNAP as a resource for evaluating and improving structure prediction methods for modified nucleic acids.
evidence_items.title: The MODNAP benchmark set for modeling ribose-based modified nucleic acid and nucleic acid–protein complexes: a case study with AlphaFold 3

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) promises structured, traceable development of complex systems, but high modeling effort remains a key adoption barrier. The textual notation of SysML v2 turns model construction into a text-to-text generation problem, opening new avenues for large language model (LLM) automation. This paper presents AMADEUS (Agentic Model-Aided Development Engineering Utilizing SysML), a conceptual framework for integrating agentic AI into systems engineering workflows in automated driving. The AMADEUS framework comprises three contributions: (1) a work package concept that operationalizes a domain-specific Systems Engineering methodology into discrete units executable by agents and maps each section to orchestration patterns such as actor-critic validation and role-based routing, (2) two complementary architecture patterns, typed operations exposed by a dedicated model server and direct SysML v2 text editing in a Git-based workflow, with a comparative analysis, and (3) an empirical benchmark evaluating three late-2025 frontier AI agents (OpenAI Codex, Google Gemini 3 Pro, Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.5) against a human expert reference on seven SysML v2 modeling tasks of varying complexity. The evaluation provides initial evidence that AI agents achieve comparable quality (average score 3.69 vs. 3.86 on a 0–4 scale) while reducing modeling time by a factor of approximately 12 and per-task execution cost by a factor of 3,500. Transformation tasks achieve average $$S {total} \ge 3.6$$ S total ≥ 3.6 out of 4, while deduction-heavy tasks reveal remaining gaps, suggesting that the engineer’s role shifts from model creator to model reviewer.
evidence_items.title: AMADEUS: A Conceptual Framework for Integrating Agentic AI into Model-Based Systems Engineering

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents have shown strong capabilities in interactive problem solving, tool use, and long-horizon task execution. However, they may also acquire sensitive or private knowledge during training and expose it during deployment. Retraining a model from scratch to remove such knowledge is prohibitively costly, making machine unlearning a more practical approach. Machine unlearning aims to remove targeted undesirable knowledge from trained models without retraining from scratch while preserving general utility. When language models are deployed as agents, parameter-level unlearning becomes insufficient: forgotten information may still persist in memory artifacts or be reacquired via tool calls. In this paper, we formulate the problem of agent unlearning as removing private information from an LLM-based agent across three information channels: parametric knowledge, persistent memory, and tool-call acquisition. To study this problem, we introduce we introduce Agent Unlearning Benchmark (AUBench), a controlled benchmark that extends the fictitious-author setting of TOFU into an agent environment with persistent memory, an offline web snapshot, tool-accessible documents, and provenance-tracked interaction trajectories. By evaluating existing parameter-level and memory-level unlearning methods in this setting, AUBench reveals the gap between model-level forgetting and system-level agent unlearning, and provides a foundation for developing unlearning methods that operate across the full lifecycle of LLM agents.
evidence_items.title: Can Agents Truly Forget? Explore Machine Unlearning for LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used for vulnerability analysis, yet existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of exploitation that depends on interactions among network protocol components. Such vulnerabilities arise from inconsistencies in message interpretation, timing, state, or trust assumptions across participants. We introduce ProtoArena, a black-box, multi-component, dynamic benchmark with 80 cross-component vulnerability-exploitation environments spanning 11 protocol and application domains and 7 attack categories. Tasks are primarily informed by published protocol-attack mechanisms. Agents interact with running systems through scoped interfaces to achieve security-effect objectives without target source code. Three information levels assess guided reproduction, exploitation with mechanism and topology context, and effect-directed black-box exploration. A hybrid verifier combines rule-based checks with LLM review of independently collected traffic and logs. We evaluate five LLMs. Claude Opus 4.8 achieves the highest observed success rates: 48.8% under L1 guidance and 12.5% under effect-directed black-box L3. In a separate DNSBomb optimization experiment, it achieves a peak downstream-response to average query-input byte-rate ratio exceeding 171,000 times. The results show that agents can achieve verifiable exploitation effects in some cross-component environments, but success with limited black-box information remains low and varies across domains and attack categories. All experiments use controlled, explicitly authorized targets; they do not test production systems or disclose previously unknown vulnerabilities.
evidence_items.title: ProtoArena: Can AI Agents Discover and Exploit Real-World Cross-Component Protocol Vulnerabilities?

evidence_items.summary: Historical digital libraries hold millions of scanned pages spanning centuries of human knowledge. However, high-fidelity content accessibility through automated question answering remains largely unsolved. Large language models offer a promising path but historical documents pose particular challenges such as OCR noise, archaic spelling, mixed layouts and domain shift from modern training corpora. Moreover, large language models exhibit sharply divergent competence across these challenges. Selecting the wrong model silently degrades retrieval quality at scale, with no easy way for digital library practitioners to know which model to trust for a given document. To address this challenge, we investigate adaptive LLM selection as a core problem for historical digital libraries. We construct a large-scale benchmark of 84,441 multiple-choice questions derived from 5,941 scanned pages of bilingual English and Chinese historical periodicals. We systematically evaluate 50 open-source LLMs ranging from 0.5B to 9B parameters, producing a page-level binary correctness matrix of 50 × 5, 941 entries. Our analysis reveals that model performance is highly page-dependent: the per-page oracle accuracy reaches 86.1% while the static best model achieves only 42.8%. We further show that our routing models include the oracle-best model in the top-3 candidate models for more than 61% of pages, offering a practical path toward efficient deployment. Gains are largest on the most challenging pages, including tabular content, Chinese-language text and hard pages where the dominant model consistently fails. Expert validation further confirms that adaptive selection decisions derived from automatic MCQs are consistent with historian judgement. Our benchmark and methodology establish a reproducible framework for studying and deploying adaptive LLM selection in historical digital library pipelines.
evidence_items.title: Adaptive LLM Selection for Question Answering over Historical Digital Libraries

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are aligned to human preferences, after pre-training and supervised fine-tuning steps. However, standard RL alignment steps such as RLHF do not focus on factuality of LLMs, hence they may generate non-factual information, which could result in unintended consequences. In response, a number of factuality alignment approaches have been proposed in the literature which claim to improve factuality of LLMs on their own benchmarks. However, these methods have not been reproduced independently and are also not comparable since each uses a different base model, training data, evaluation set, judge, and metric. In this paper, we present the first independent reproduction of five factuality alignment methods, which span on-policy RL (PPO, GRPO, and Dr.~GRPO) and offline preference optimization (DPO and KTO), and compare them on a common benchmark with common evaluation metrics. We found that none of these methods reproduces in full, and on the common benchmark none of the methods significantly outperforms the base model. On closer inspection, the rewards optimize for format, length, or brevity rather than factuality and relevance, whereas the choice between on-policy and offline training matters little. Furthermore, the evaluation metrics and benchmarks are also part of the problem since they do not measure relevance of text to the prompt. Since there is no ground truth associated with the prompts, the reliance on LLM judges and retrieval for verification also makes the evaluation fragile. We release our code, data, and checkpoints.
evidence_items.title: Do Factuality Methods Make LLMs More Factual? Reproducibility and Fair Comparison

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong zero-shot reasoning across diverse domains, but their potential for Human-Object Interaction (HOI) remains unexplored. Unlike traditional HOI approaches that rely on extensive labeled datasets and fixed interaction taxonomies, MLLMs offer flexible reasoning, making them well-suited for dynamic, real-world scenarios. In this work, we present the first systematic study of MLLMs for HOI recognition and detection within a pipeline that combines an external object detector for entity localization with zero-shot multimodal reasoning for interaction understanding. We introduce a benchmark framework for principled zero-shot evaluation, consisting of (i) a unified taxonomy of zero-shot prompting strategies, and (ii) a methodology that transforms token-level logits into interaction scores, enabling fair comparison with specialized HOI models under standard metrics. To support prompt-based evaluation, we additionally construct new question-answer annotations for standard HOI datasets, transforming them into a format suitable for MLLMs. Building on this, we propose two visual prompting strategies, namely Objects as Context and Black Other Objects, that guide MLLMs to target objects while preserving scene context. Experiments on HICO, HICO-DET, and V-COCO demonstrate state-of-the-art zero-shot performance, achieving 53.50 mAP on HICO and 23.69 mAP on HICO-DET. Overall, our work provides a principled benchmarking framework for MLLMs in HOI, opening the door to new models and datasets and enabling flexible open-world interaction understanding.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking Multimodal Large Language Models for Zero-Shot Human-Object Interaction

evidence_items.summary: Wheel-legged robots operating in outdoor spaces shared with humans require accurate perception, socially compliant navigation, future-scene reasoning, and scene reconstruction. However, existing datasets typically support these capabilities in isolation and rarely provide dense spatial and behavior-level supervision on real wheel-legged platforms. We introduce LynxScenes, a large-scale real-world dataset and benchmark collected with a LYNX M20 wheel-legged robot. It contains approximately 100K 30-s navigation clips spanning 833.6 h and 3,294.7 km, with 3.0M annotated frames. The synchronized recordings include four fisheye cameras, dual LiDARs, IMU, odometry, and robot states. Annotations comprise 20.82M oriented 3D boxes across 27 categories, 13.89M road-structure annotations, and 20 navigation instructions organized into three layers and aligned with continuous future trajectories. LynxScenes supports four complementary tasks: instruction-conditioned trajectory prediction, BEV-based perception of 3D objects and road structures, future scene prediction, and multi-view scene reconstruction. For trajectory prediction, we further introduce a log-replay-based pseudo-closed-loop evaluator that measures safety, progress, and instruction compliance beyond trajectory imitation. Extensive evaluations across representative navigation, perception, world-model, and reconstruction methods reveal substantial remaining challenges in close-range outdoor robot navigation. The dataset and evaluation toolkit are planned for public release.
evidence_items.title: LynxScenes: A Large-Scale Real-World Benchmark for Outdoor Wheel-Legged Robot Perception, Navigation, Imagination and Reconstruction

evidence_items.summary: The rapid advancement of cybersecurity agents in vulnerability discovery has increased the need for benchmarks that evaluate their capabilities accurately. However, synthetic benchmarks lack realism, real-life benchmarks are prone to contamination, and many existing benchmarks have already been saturated by current models. We therefore set out to develop a benchmark that is realistic, reproducible, resistant to contamination, and challenging. Our key insight is that real-life business-logic vulnerabilities are subtle and exercise complex application interactions, making them naturally demanding. The difficulty lies in specifying evaluation criteria precise enough to faithfully measure model capabilities while keeping the tasks free of data-leakage. We introduce AnonVul, a cross-language benchmark of 132 application-level business-logic vulnerabilities, built by a semi-automated pipeline that anonymizes each task, injects oracles from expert-written specifications, and differentially verifies proof-of-concept exploits. The benchmark spans nine languages, with two evaluation tracks on black-box and grey-box settings, where each task runs in a sandbox with specialized oracles embedded in key exploitation steps. We evaluate six state-of-the-art vulnerability-discovery agents on the AnonVul benchmark, measuring discovery success, cost-effectiveness, anonymization sensitivity, oracle validity, and failure modes. Our results show that AnonVul remains challenging, with the best agent succeeding in only 23.11% of attempts. On a matched cohort of 20 vulnerabilities, restoring software identity increases discovery from 21.25% to 40.83%, highlighting the importance of controlling recognizable software knowledge when evaluating vulnerability discovery.
evidence_items.title: Discovery or Memorization? A Faithful Benchmark for Real-World Business-Logic Vulnerability Discovery

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language models are increasingly used to identify and describe places, yet their recognition and knowledge of specific cultures remain poorly understood, particularly in underrepresented regions such as the Philippines. This study introduces the Tanawpamana Dataset, a repository of Philippine heritage site images with metadata based on the Talapamana registry of the National Commission for Culture and the Arts of the Philippines. We also introduce the Tanawpamana Benchmark, comprising 4,046 tasks designed to evaluate models'recognition and knowledge of heritage sites. Evaluating seven vision-language models, we find that they struggle more with fine-grained visual discrimination among similar heritage sites than with coarse recognition, and that their geographic knowledge is weaker when inferred from image inputs than from text.
evidence_items.title: Tanawpamana: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models on Philippine Cultural Heritage Sites

evidence_items.summary: Benchmarks report what an Artificial Intelligence (AI) agent can do on a task suite, but not whether one released version has been engineered with the controls that make it reliable, safe and observable, or how strongly that is shown. This paper proposes AgentStripes, an evidence-graded maturity model for AI agents. It defines levels (0 to 7 stripes), process areas (12 areas holding 40 capabilities), three gates (basic, safety, proof) that hold an agent at a level however high its score, and evidence grades E0 to E5. Each applicable capability receives a rating from 0 to 3 and a separate evidence level; these are combined into a credit, aggregated into a severity-weighted score and converted into stripes that the gates limit. Instruments gather evidence, language-model judges interpret it under explicit criteria, and the arithmetic is deterministic. The model is compared with standards at topic level without a claim of conformance, and an unexecuted validation protocol is specified. An empirical evaluation (exploratory, non-confirmatory) of 30 public Python agent repositories, with static evidence only, is a demonstration and not a validation: static evidence caps every final stripe at 2, 26 repositories end at one stripe and 4 at two, and this distinction is unreliable, since re-judging changed the final stripe of 4 of 22 repositories (engine, dossier and panel changed), whereas none of 8 panel-only repeats, all at stripe 1, changed. The parameters are expert conventions without outcome based calibration, and the stripes have not been shown to predict reliability or safety.
evidence_items.title: AgentStripes: An Evidence-Graded Maturity Model for AI Agents

evidence_items.summary: Generative AI has achieved remarkable success in de novo protein design, yet protein engineering typically begins with existing, characterized proteins. The primary demand is targeted local editing, e.g., engineering a specific region to optimize affinity, alter immunogenicity, or improve stability, while strictly preserving core catalytic motifs and overall scaffold integrity. However, no standardized framework currently exists for carrying out and evaluating such edits. In current generative-design workflows, researchers often need to manually specify complex low-level parameters and rely on repetitive, trial-and-error sampling and evaluation across generative backends to search for viable conformations. While large language models (LLMs) offer an intuitive interface to express these goals using natural language, prevailing structure-generation models cannot directly interpret high-level human instructions. To bridge this gap, we introduce PROTEAN, a standardized benchmark for text-guided protein structural editing. PROTEAN comprises 380 sub-tasks spanning six intervention families and evaluates a two-stage pipeline in which an LLM translates natural-language goals into backend-specific geometric constraints and a generative model remodels the protein backbone. A two-tier evaluation separates geometric compliance, including target attainment and off-target scope fidelity, from biophysical realizability assessed by inverse folding and refolding consistency. Across five frontier LLMs paired with three backends, strict end-to-end biophysical success starts at just 7.0%. Ablation studies show that LLM constraint compilation is already highly accurate, whereas the main bottlenecks are backend-specific scope leakage and refolding failure. PROTEAN provides an open testbed for developing autonomous, multi-backend macromolecular design agents.
evidence_items.title: PROTEAN: Beyond De Novo Generation - Can LLM Agents Perform Text-Guided Protein Structure Editing?

evidence_items.summary: Game-theoretic benchmarks claim that large language model (LLM) strategic decision-making varies across game types, interaction structures, and capability dimensions. However, they only evaluate strategic performance across individual fixed models. In parallel, contemporary LLM routers pick models under quality-cost trade-offs, but with no notion of a strategic structure. They do not account for an opponent that might be unknown, and that can adapt over time and shift the feedback signal. To address this, we extend the game-theoretic evaluations and define strategic selection as the meta game layered on top of the base game. In each round, a strategic selector fields an LLM from a portfolio of models to navigate a game payoff matrix that is latent and learned online. We find that the evaluation signal is game-specific, and that extracting a reliable signal requires a much higher number of seed runs $N$ compared to traditional benchmarking setups. Evaluating across 5 games and 10 LLMs, we show a model's strategic competence varies significantly depending on the game setup and the opponent faced. Building on this, we implement a suite of selector methods and find that approaches that rely on query embeddings or LLM self-reflection do not consistently capture the underlying strategic signal. A lightweight multi-armed bandit algorithm performs more reliably across games, though it still falls short of the best fixed model. Finally, we show that simple non-stationary and adversarial bandit variants fail to outperform a stationary bandit baseline, pointing to a gap in how current methods handle a shifting opponent in strategic settings.
evidence_items.title: Choosing LLMs for Strategic Agent Interactions

evidence_items.summary: Recent coding large language models (LLMs) can synthesize dynamic 4D worlds from natural language, but the resulting content remains a visual artifact. It lacks physical semantics such as the collision geometry, mass, friction, inertia, and joint structure, required to enable it to simulate the physical world, and its dynamics are scripted to look plausible rather than designed to execute. What is needed is an executable world: one that a physics engine can load and step, resolving contact physically. We present Code2Worlds-2, an extension of Code2Worlds that turns 4D world generation into an embodied world simulation. We keep the original dual-stream generation pipeline intact and append two modules. First, a SimReady Scene Compiler that turns a generated visual scene into a simulator-compatible representation: it assigns collision meshes via convex decomposition, estimates physical attributes with a vision-language model, infers a lightweight support graph, instantiates the engine's contact, friction, and dynamics constraints, and applies a gravity settling pass, before exporting the scene as MuJoCo MJCF. Second, a Simulator-in-the-Loop 4D Refiner that implements an automated agent harness-a compile, simulate, critique and refine loop-that converts visual dynamics into executable rigid and articulated dynamics and evolves the physical settings rather than only the code, replacing the purely visual motion critic with a simulator critic that inspects penetration depth, collision pairs, stability, contact forces, joint limits, and robot reachability. We further propose SimCode4D, a state-based benchmark with five task templates for evaluating embodied simulation. Experiments on SimCode4D and across natural, indoor, industrial, urban, and service scenes show that Code2Worlds-2 produces physically plausible, simulator-compatible, and robot-interactable scenes.
evidence_items.title: Code2Worlds-2: Physically Plausible Agent Harness for Embodied World Simulation

evidence_items.summary: Authors routinely point to the datasets and software their studies use through URLs in their papers, which we call OADS-URLs. Many no longer lead to the resource they point to. How much of the cited open access datasets and software (OADS) is still reachable is not well understood, leaving web archives no basis for deciding which endangered resources to preserve first. My dissertation measures the availability and discoverability of OADS-URLs at scale and how fast they decline. We built two benchmarks, sURL-3K and OADS-1K. On sURL-3K we evaluated our proposed extraction method, VisURLX, against heuristic baselines. VisURLX reads rendered page images with a multimodal large language model and is the most accurate, at an F1 score of 86.86%. On OADS-1K we developed EnSU, which classifies each URL by resource type and provider at a macro F1 of 90%. With the pipeline that best trades accuracy against cost and EnSU, we will build OADS Repo from about 16 million scholarly documents and measure how availability and discoverability differ across discipline, provider, host, venue, and institution, and how fast OADS-URLs disappear. The results will show how much of the endangered record can be preserved and which OADS to capture first.
evidence_items.title: Toward Preserving Open Access Datasets and Software in Scholarly Documents

evidence_items.summary: Ambiguous or incomplete task specifications complicate both execution and clarification for language-model agents. Yet agents'responses to these information gaps remain poorly characterized across models and execution harnesses. We present AM-Bench, a benchmark built from 48 tasks adapted from Terminal-Bench 2.0 and Harness-Bench. Each task includes a fully specified reference and six variants spanning ambiguous or missing goals, context, and constraints. We evaluate every pairing of five models and four harnesses over 20,160 runs. Our results reveal distinct execution deficits: goal gaps hinder completion, context gaps increase token use, and constraint gaps weaken compliance without necessarily preventing completion. Missingness lowers success more than ambiguity in all three domains. These effects also reshape system comparisons: advantages under complete information need not persist, and rankings depend on model $\times$ harness pairings and the evaluation criterion -- completion, success, or repeat consistency. Estimates based on observed clarification requests and matched fully specified runs further suggest that clarification could recover unfinished work while leaving most constraint violations unresolved. Together, these findings motivate joint model-harness evaluation across information conditions and targeted clarification of unresolved requirements before dependent actions. To support future research on agents under task underspecification, we provide the AM-Bench project repository at https://github.com/s4-lab-cuhksz/AM-Bench.git.
evidence_items.title: AM-Bench: Understanding Agents under Task Underspecification across Models and Harnesses

evidence_items.summary: Discovering what drives an outcome from data is central to science and often requires deciding what is worth investigating before a specific hypothesis is known. Yet most existing hypothesis generation settings substantially narrow this search by providing a research question, target relationship, or curated context. We introduce open-ended multiple hypothesis discovery, where a system receives only a large tabular dataset and an outcome and must discover multiple data-supported hypotheses without knowing in advance the relevant variables, functional forms, conditions, or number of underlying mechanisms. To study this problem, we introduce a benchmark built from structural causal models grounded in real-world data schemas, containing 351 planted hypotheses across 15 tasks and five domains, with 53--65 variables and 1M--10M rows per task. The causal model is hidden from the discovery method and retained only by the evaluator, allowing proposed hypotheses to be tested through interventions and separating observational discovery from causal validation. We further propose HypAgent, which treats the dataset as an interactive environment and performs iterative search by proposing candidate directions, triaging and refining promising hypotheses, and removing explained signal so that each accepted discovery redirects subsequent search. HypAgent achieves 0.47 precision, 0.51 recall, and 0.49 F1, compared with 0.35 F1 for the strongest baseline. Our analysis shows that many failures occur after a relevant variable has already been surfaced, suggesting that correctly characterizing a mechanism's functional form and conditions, rather than merely identifying relevant variables, remains a key challenge in open-ended discovery.
evidence_items.title: Searching for What Matters: Open-Ended Discovery of Multiple Hypotheses with Agentic Data Exploration

evidence_items.summary: Language models are increasingly expected to support users in stressful or uncertain situations, where warmth and empathy are desirable. While recent work associates warmer models with reduced reliability, we show that this conclusion is incomplete. Prior studies often train primarily on empathetic dialogue, making it difficult to separate tone effects from SFT-induced distribution shift. We revisit this issue at both the model and evaluation levels. We study prompting, SFT, and RL for inducing warm behavior, and comprehensively evaluate capability preservation using an 11-dataset benchmark suite and EMOFACT under emotional contexts. Across multiple model families, we find that warmth effects are task- and model-dependent, while task-aligned adaptive tone can improve empathy and targeted reliability, although some capability trade-offs remain. We further introduce human-validated empathy evaluators specifically developed to assess empathetic model responses. Our results suggest that models can be more supportive in social interactions while remaining reliable.
evidence_items.title: Empathy Is Not the Scapegoat for Declines in Factuality and Reliability

evidence_items.summary: Using results reported in scientific papers requires more than extracting the values. A system must also determine whether each value is correct and whether results from different papers are comparable. Two papers may report accuracy on the same dataset but use different data splits, metric variants, or conditions, which papers often omit. Large language models can turn papers into structured result records, but extractors can read the wrong value, and their confidence may not reflect correctness. This study asks how numerical scientific results can be extracted, audited, compared, and queried when their evidence, uncertainty, and experimental protocols are incomplete or heterogeneous. We propose protocol-qualified records that preserve source evidence, reliability estimates, and reported conditions, flagging those that could not be recovered. We hypothesize that such records support more accurate conclusions than extraction-only, leaderboard, and retrieval approaches. Three core aims build and evaluate the records, a fourth combines them in question answering, and an optional fifth studies how conclusions change over time. Preliminary work includes a multi-agent extraction framework, error prioritization over 47,613 facts, and a pilot census in which an estimated 45% of candidate pairs showed real numerical differences, mostly from protocol rather than scientific conflict.
evidence_items.title: From Extracted Numbers to Comparable Evidence: Protocol-Qualified Scientific Result Records

evidence_items.summary: Graph fraud explanation generation emerges as an important task, which requires jointly leveraging graph structure and content information to produce human-readable explanations for a given risk label. An intuitive approach is to adapt existing graph-enhanced large language models (LLMs), which inject graph structure into LLMs via graph-conditioned instruction tuning or structure-aware embeddings. However, existing methods face two key challenges in graph fraud explanation generation: a lack of evaluation protocols tailored to explanation quality, and a mismatch between the granularity of graph information they provide and what explanation generation requires. In this paper, we propose FRaud Explanation Generation via Agentic Graph Context NavigaTION (FRACTION), a framework for graph fraud explanation generation. To evaluate explanation quality, we introduce a task-specific rubric that assesses faithfulness, graph grounding, helpfulness, consistency, and conciseness, and validate it against human judgments. To focus on fine-grained details of relevant neighbors without reading the entire neighborhood, we equip a language model with graph tools that progressively disclose neighbor records. To train our graph agent, we propose a rubric-guided trajectory distillation strategy through which the agent learns both tool-use behavior and structured explanation generation. Experimental results on three fraud datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines under a human-aligned rubric.
evidence_items.title: FRACTION: Fraud Explanation Generation via Agentic Graph Context Navigation

evidence_items.summary: Generative AI is becoming part of how scientific content is being produced, evaluated and communicated. Large language models (LLMs) can write science news, simulate readers, retrieve evidence, generate scientific hypotheses, write code, and execute research workflows. These capabilities create opportunities for accelerating scientific discovery and broadening access to scientific information, but they also introduce risks related to hallucination and trustworthiness. This doctoral dissertation studies how generative AI can support scientific content production and dissemination, while preserving trust, comprehension, and replicability. The completed work includes three components: (1) detecting LLM-generated science news through SANews and GFS, (2) evaluating science communication through reader learning using KnowledgeGain and LLMSim, and (3) benchmarking LLM agents for research replication with ReplicatorBench and ReplicatorAgent. The proposed work extends these directions toward learning-optimized science news generation, MESH for multimodal evidence-grounded hypothesis generation, and MERIT, a simulation-grounded framework for evaluating autonomous AI co-scientists and hypothesis testing in computational materials discovery. The overarching goal is to develop evaluation methods and AI systems that make scientific outputs not only fluent and scalable, but also grounded, useful, and interpretable.
evidence_items.title: Applications of Generative AI for Advancing Scientific Content Production, Evaluation and Dissemination

evidence_items.summary: Automated post-training transforms pre-trained large language models (LLMs) into models capable of handling diverse domains by automatically constructing and optimizing a recipe of coupled decisions over data sources, data processing, cross-domain composition, and training configuration under a limited experimental budget. Existing automation either searches predefined recipe spaces that enable systematic optimization but remain fixed rather than adapting their available choices to the target tasks, or uses open-ended agents that discover task-specific choices but leave them implicit in trial-level edits, limiting their systematic reuse and recombination across trials. To fill this gap, we introduce optimization over a task-adapted recipe space, a novel paradigm that can adapt the recipe space itself to the target tasks while representing its choices explicitly for systematic reuse, recombination, and joint optimization. We instantiate this paradigm with Structured Recipe Optimization (SRO), comprising an LLM-based Recipe-Space Designer that constructs the task-adapted recipe space and a Multi-Domain Recipe Optimizer that uses structured trial evidence to guide LLM candidate construction and multi-objective Bayesian trial selection. Extensive experiments show that SRO achieves the highest average score in all evaluated target-model and agent-LLM combinations. In joint post-training across three capability domains and six benchmarks, SRO reaches 41.1 versus 15.4 for the strongest baseline on Qwen3-1.7B with GPT-5.4, and 53.8 versus 40.8 on Qwen3-4B with DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Our code is available at https://github.com/RuohLiuq/SRO.
evidence_items.title: LLM Agents for Automated Post-Training via Structured Recipe Optimization

evidence_items.summary: While it is known that quantization of large language models (LLMs) reduces memory usage via lower-bit weights, studies quantifying the resulting impact on energy usage and carbon intensity are scarce. We present the first unified evaluation of weight-only quantization strategies for LLM inference across varying input/output lengths and GPUs, highlighting differences in energy efficiency in addition to accuracy degradation and runtime. We study quantized inference on Llama 2 7B, Phi 3.5 Mini Instruct, OLMo 1B, Qwen 2.5 7B, and Qwen 2.5 14B across GLUE MNLI, MMLU, HumanEval, and GSM8K datasets, evaluating 10 post-training quantization (PTQ) strategies on NVIDIA H100, A6000, A100, and L4 GPUs. We identify a novel trend showing that quantization techniques tend to exhibit peak energy efficiency relative to full-precision baselines when inputs are sufficiently long and outputs are short. Furthermore, we show that quantization strategies become marginally more energy-efficient relative to full-precision models as batch sizes increase, though gains are modest. Notably, fused-kernel implementations such as EETQ int8 and Bitsandbytes int8 offer the highest energy savings, up to 4x compared to FP32 on short text generation, with negligible accuracy loss. Finally, we observe that energy usage closely tracks runtime on our evaluated benchmarks, indicating that, in practice, latency optimization can serve as a reliable proxy for reducing the environmental footprint of LLM services. We conclude with suggested directions for strategically selecting low-carbon quantization strategies based on specific inference requirements.
evidence_items.title: Towards Green AI: Evaluating Energy Efficiency for Quantized LLM Inference

evidence_items.summary: Automated radar waveform recognition classifies the waveform and modulation type of a received signal. As new waveform variants appear over time, a deployed classifier must learn them without retraining from scratch. Catastrophic Forgetting occurs when learning new waveforms overwrites prior knowledge. Continual Learning (CL) methods tackle this challenge, but prior radar studies only evaluate a few methods on narrow benchmarks. Practitioners lack evidence on which method to deploy or which mechanisms are effective. This work presents the first large-scale benchmark of continual learning for radar waveform recognition. Eighteen CL methods are evaluated on a sequential ten-task problem, drawn from four public datasets spanning 54 waveforms, under task- and class-incremental (TIL, CIL) settings and single- and multi-epoch regimes. Methods that retain data from old tasks lead both TIL and CIL settings. Plain replay alone closes 77-88% of the gap between the lower and upper practical limits under TIL, but only 46-55% under CIL. The internal mechanisms of the leading methods are ablated and statistically tested to identify effective mechanisms. Each ablation is paired against its full method over n=6 training seeds, topped up to n=12 when inconclusive, and p-values are Holm-Bonferroni corrected within each method's family. Ablation results show that several mechanisms confer smaller but statistically significant gains. Combining these mechanisms improves the leading F1 score by 3.4-5.5% and 2.7-4.9% under TIL and CIL, respectively, and the combined models exceed every benchmarked method in both settings for all SNRs. These results give researchers of radar waveform classification systems a mechanism-level basis for design.
evidence_items.title: Overcoming Catastrophic Forgetting: Continual Learning for Radar Waveform Classification

evidence_items.summary: Visual reasoning is an important capability for vision-language models (VLMs) to understand visual evidence, spatial structure, constraints, and state changes. Existing evaluations mainly rely on real-world data or procedurally generated tasks. Real-world data preserve natural complexity, while procedural games provide controllable generation and verifiable solutions. However, it remains unclear whether abilities measured in toy games correspond to real-world visual reasoning and whether game examples can support transfer. We introduce Game2Real-Bench, a benchmark that studies these connections across four capability groups, including fine-grained perception, spatial reasoning, constraint reasoning, and sequential planning. We construct 1,000 procedurally generated game samples with executable verification and curate 400 real-world samples aligned by shared reasoning requirements rather than visual similarity. We evaluate 25 representative VLMs and observe strong game-to-real consistency, with Pearson and Spearman correlations of 0.935. We further study one-shot game-to-real transfer on four models. Constraint reasoning improves for several models, while fine-grained perception declines with game demonstrations. We also construct Game2Real-Dataset with nearly 24K verified game samples across 18 tasks and 65 QA families. Our benchmark, dataset, and code are available at https://github.com/QingAnLiu/Game2Real-Bench.
evidence_items.title: Game2Real-Bench: Do Toy Games Reveal and Transfer to Real-World Visual Reasoning?

evidence_items.summary: Scientific data repositories can be FAIR yet unsearchable: column names such as NEE_CUT_REF, SSA637, or lel carry meaning only for specialists, so a non-expert cannot find, filter, or plot the data at the variable level. We generate natural-language descriptions for opaque columns with a language model at ingestion, from their names, statistics, and sample values, and store them as curator-reviewable catalog metadata for search and a natural-language visual-discovery interface. Our clearest result is on findability: across three collections from a live repository, the descriptions make opaque columns retrievable by natural-language query, raising pooled mean reciprocal rank from 0.46 to 0.79, and a control shows the gain comes from the descriptions’ content—generic or shuffled text does not reproduce it. Downstream, in a within-model NL2Vis ablation, the benefit is conditional: enrichment raises translation accuracy in two of six model–collection cells and leaves the rest flat or slightly negative, in a pattern that tracks a column’s opacity to the model and the model’s accuracy headroom, so the single-collection lesson that “enrichment helps weaker models” does not generalize. A quality evaluation against curator references finds description accuracy governed by how familiar the model is with a naming convention; how opaque the name looks to a person does not predict it, so a human-unreadable but standard schema is described well while errors concentrate on unfamiliar specialized vocabulary, where curator review should focus. We release the questions, descriptions, and evaluation harness as a benchmark.
evidence_items.title: LLM-Based Semantic Metadata Enrichment for Findable Scientific Data Collections

evidence_items.summary: We present scalable-htr, a user-friendly open-source Python library for end-to-end segmentation and transcription of historical manuscripts. Built upon Kraken but extensible to other engines, the tool provides a framework for reproducible experimentation and efficient, large-scale inference on high-performance computing (HPC) environments. The tool facilitates systematic benchmarking across datasets and models by computing quantitative end-to-end metrics, and it generates interactive visualizations that allow users to qualitatively assess model adaptation to their target domains by inspecting segmentation and transcription results directly on the images. By combining systematic evaluation with scalable transcription, scalable-htr has been designed to assist researchers and cultural heritage professionals convert digitized manuscript collections into machine-readable data. The tool is demonstrated via a case study on medieval notarial manuscripts.
evidence_items.title: scalable-htr: A Framework for Scalable and Reproducible Handwritten Text Recognition on Historical Documents

evidence_items.summary: Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) have become a major source of online education, generating large volumes of learner reviews that provide valuable insights into course quality and learning experiences. However, manually analyzing this feedback is time-consuming, while existing transformer-based summarization models often struggle to balance summary conciseness with information preservation. In addition, most evaluation frameworks rely solely on automatic metrics and rarely consider user preferences. To address these limitations, this study proposes ClusSumm, a user-centered hierarchical clustering and adaptive transformer framework for summarizing MOOC learner reviews. A domain-stratified dataset containing approximately 8,000 Coursera course records across eight educational domains was constructed through automated web scraping. Eight state-of-the-art transformer models, including BART, PEGASUS, T5, FLAN-T5, DistilBART, LED, LongT5, and BigBird PEGASUS, were benchmarked to establish comparative baselines. ClusSumm first applies K-Means clustering with silhouette-based optimization to group semantically similar reviews, followed by TF-IDF sentence ranking to remove redundant content. An adaptive summarization strategy then assigns clusters to different transformer models according to their complexity, and a hierarchical BART-based fusion module generates the final summary. Experimental results show that ClusSumm achieves a summarization ratio of 12.65% while maintaining ROUGE-1 and ROUGE-2 precision scores of 98.31% and 90.12%, respectively. A user-calibrated composite evaluation further demonstrates that the proposed framework produces concise summaries that better align with user preferences than existing benchmark models. These findings highlight the effectiveness of combining semantic clustering, adaptive summarization, and user-centered evaluation for scalable educational feedback analysis and intelligent learning analytics.
evidence_items.title: ClusSumm a user centered hierarchical clustering and adaptive transformer framework for efficient summarization of MOOC learner reviews

evidence_items.summary: The translation of deep learning architectures from controlled experimental settings into real-world cancer diagnostics is heavily bottlenecked by domain shift and demographic bias. While models routinely achieve near-perfect retrospective performance on internal datasets, validation across external multicenter cohorts incurs a systemic and severe performance degradation, with an average metric drop of 0.16 AUC. This review provides a comprehensive metasynthesis of contemporary algorithmic mitigation paradigms designed to alleviate distribution discrepancies, evaluating techniques ranging from classical stain normalization and adversarial feature alignment to test-time adaptation and large-scale self-supervised pathology foundation models. Our analysis reveals a critical dichotomy between raw diagnostic performance and algorithmic equity: current optimization frameworks that successfully elevate aggregate macro metrics frequently do so by obscuring or actively exacerbating underlying demographic and subpopulation disparities. To achieve safe, equitable, and universally reliable clinical artificial intelligence, the field must transcend static validation habits. We outline a future roadmap anchored on three critical axes: establishing intersectional disparity indices as primary regulatory endpoints, standardizing multivendor metadata-rich benchmarks, and prioritizing.
evidence_items.title: Mitigating Domain Shift and Dataset Bias in Deep Learning Models for Cancer Diagnostics.

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) can support drug discovery, but benchmark performance alone does not establish experimental, operational or clinical benefit. This keynote review distinguishes predictive generalization, experimental confirmation, workflow utility and clinical outcomes, separating demonstrated failures from missing validation. We critically examine quantitative case studies of benchmark bias, prospective hit finding and clinical development, alongside data quality, reproducibility, uncertainty and governance. Practical recommendations link each intended use to appropriate comparators, evaluation designs and acceptance criteria. The aim is not to presume that AI fails to translate but to specify what evidence is needed to demonstrate reliable prospective use in drug discovery.
evidence_items.title: From artificial intelligence promise to translational practice in drug discovery: Reproducibility, validation and evidence-based implementation.

evidence_items.summary: Most artificial intelligence models for electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation rely on task-specific supervised learning, requiring dedicated labeled datasets for each diagnostic task and limiting scalability across diverse cardiac conditions. This study investigated whether vision-language learning from paired ECG recordings and summary reports could enable transferable ECG representations without task-specific supervised training. We developed ECG-VLM, a contrastive vision-language model consisting of a Transformer-based image encoder and a text encoder, trained on 800,034 paired 10-s ECG recordings and summary reports from the MIMIC-IV-ECG database. Cardiac condition detection was performed using natural-language prompts without condition-specific retraining or fine-tuning. Performance was evaluated on an internal test set and externally validated using the LSAS-ECG dataset (45,151 recordings) across 14 cardiac conditions, together with retrieval and subgroup analysis. ECG-VLM achieved diagnostic performance across 14 cardiac conditions, with AUROC ranging from 0.679 to 0.981 on the internal test set and from 0.691 to 0.991 on external validation. Performance was strongest for rhythm abnormalities (mean AUROC 0.948 internally and 0.921 externally) and lower for morphological conditions. Compared with the previously reported signal-based ECG-CLIP framework, ECG-VLM achieved comparable performance for rhythm abnormalities while improving AUPRC for several morphological conditions. Performance remained broadly consistent across external validation and demographic and clinical subgroups. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of vision-language supervision from paired ECG recordings and summary reports for learning transferable ECG representations without task-specific supervised training. This framework provides a basis for future extension of vision-language learning to ECG images encountered in routine clinical practice.
evidence_items.title: Language-supervised electrocardiogram interpretation with vision transformer

evidence_items.summary: Educational inequalities are largely rooted in parental resources; yet, it has been proposed to distinguish between parental and child cultural capital. This raises the question of whether children’s cultural activities can promote educational attainment independently of parental resources and thus foster social mobility. Drawing on cultural reproduction theory, the cultural mobility model, and rational choice theory, we analyze the effect of children’s cultural activities on educational attainment as well as potential underlying mechanisms. Using a large-scale German panel dataset and entropy balancing, we report two main findings. First, children’s participation in highbrow cultural activities and arts education courses outside school increases the likelihood of attaining an upper secondary degree. Second, decision-making processes (secondary effects) mediate a larger share of these effects than academic achievement (primary effects). We conclude that children’s cultural capital contributes to educational attainment independently of parental resources, highlighting its potential for promoting social mobility.
evidence_items.title: Do Students' Cultural Activities Affect Educational Attainment Beyond Parental Influence? Examining the Underlying Mechanisms

evidence_items.summary: Free, open-source web security scanners are widely adopted in small projects, yet there is little quantitative evidence on what they miss, what they wrongly report, and what they cost to run on a developer’s own machine. This paper presents a reproducible benchmark: a small Flask application with 13 documented weaknesses, each verified by an executable test (12 observable by black-box testing), built in a vulnerable and a hardened version. We evaluate ZAP (formerly OWASP ZAP), Nuclei and Nikto against this ground truth over 10 repeated runs and report precision, recall and F1, false positives on the hardened build, scan time, peak memory and CPU use, and the marginal value of combining tools. ZAP detected 7 of the 12 observable weaknesses, Nuclei 3 and Nikto 2 to 3; no tool detected four weaknesses (access control on an admin page, direct object reference, SQL error disclosure and unrestricted file upload) under the configurations used. Adding Nuclei or Nikto to ZAP raised recall from 0.58 to 0.67 at a cost of 117 s or 33 s, and a third tool added nothing on this benchmark. A test-first track shows that an executable security check written for each weakness fails on the vulnerable build and passes on the hardened build (13 of 13).
evidence_items.title: A Reproducible Empirical Evaluation of Automated Web Security Testing Tools for Small Applications

evidence_items.summary: Deep learning (DL) models are now routinely deployed in safety and mission-critical domains such as medical diagnosis, autonomous driving, financial fraud detection, and cybersecurity. While these systems achieve strong performance on standard benchmarks, their robustness under adversarial manipulation, distribution shift, and operational perturbations remains insufficiently characterized from a Software Quality Assurance (SQA) perspective. This paper introduces a structured SQA framework for robustness evaluation of neural networks that incorporates adversarial testing, fault injection, coverage analysis, and runtime monitoring as integrated activities in the quality lifecycle. The framework accounts for architectural properties and the stochastic nature of learned models and is grounded in both software engineering theory and practical machine learning practice. We instantiate the framework on representative architectures ResNet-50 and VGG-16 for vision, an LSTM classifier, and BERT-base for natural language processing- and report empirical results across adversarial robustness, distribution shift robustness, coverage, and runtime indicators.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating the Robustness of Deep Learning Architectures: An SQA Framework for Neural Networks

evidence_items.summary: Summary When drilling risks such as kick events occur, rapidly identifying the root causes and recommending effective mitigation measures is critical for well control and operational safety. Traditional incident analysis mainly relies on expert experience and rule-based diagnostics, which are time-consuming and often lack systematic interpretability. This paper proposes a Large Language Model (LLM)-based framework to automatically interpret risk causes and generate mitigation recommendations following drilling risk events. Historical drilling incident reports, operational logs, engineering guidelines, and mitigation case records are first collected to construct a drilling risk knowledge base. A word embedding model is then domain-fine-tuned using drilling-related corpora to enhance semantic representation of domain-specific terminology and operational context. Based on the enhanced embeddings, a knowledge retrieval mechanism identifies relevant historical cases and engineering knowledge. The retrieved knowledge and event descriptions—including drilling parameters and operational records—are provided to a Large Language Model, which performs structured reasoning to interpret possible causes and generate recommended mitigation measures. The proposed framework is evaluated using drilling incident datasets covering 45 wells and 56 recorded risk cases from wells drilled in western China oilfields, together with associated drilling reports and operational documentation. Experimental results show that domain-fine-tuned word embeddings significantly improve semantic retrieval performance, increasing relevant case retrieval accuracy from 0.713 to 0.863. With the enhanced knowledge retrieval, the LLM can effectively identify key contributing factors and produce structured explanations of incident causation.
evidence_items.title: A Large Language Model Framework for Risk Cause Interpretation and Mitigation Recommendation in Drilling Operations

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) show promise for clinical decision support but are limited by opaque knowledge and inconsistent decision-making. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mitigates these issues by injecting verifiable passages from a curated corpus at inference time. Using 2,400 real patient pathways from the MIMIC-CDM dataset, we evaluated RAG configurations over information gathering, diagnostic accuracy, treatment recommendations and guideline retrieval, identifying key factors for integrating RAG into clinical AI-agents. Across eight general and medical LLMs spanning 1B to 70B parameters, RAG consistently increased mean diagnostic accuracy from 55.64% to 64.29%, an 8.65-points gain (P=0.0039). In a matched three-backbone analysis, RAG improved physical-examination, imaging and laboratory clinician test-ordering alignment by 5.17 points and treatment alignment by 3.97 points, while surfacing verifiable guideline citations for clinicians. Benefits depended on retrieval design, with autonomous query rewriting producing the clearest effect on retrieval fidelity and downstream performance. These findings demonstrate that guideline-grounded RAG can improve both the outcomes and clinical-decision pathways of LLM-agents while increasing their traceability and transparency.
evidence_items.title: Towards guideline-grounded clinical decision-making: a multi-scale study of retrieval augmented generation based large language model agents
