evidence_items.summary: This research investigates the deepest and most decisive layer of digital sovereignty: Artificial Intelligence, focusing on foundational models, computational power, and hardware infrastructure. By analyzing the State of Qatar’s strategic transition from a technological consumer to a producer—manifested in the national AI model “Fanar” and the establishment of the “QAI” company—the study explores the boundaries of strategic independence for small states. While Qatar has successfully secured a genuine sovereign asset through developing massive, culturally contextualized Arabic datasets that address structural linguistic gaps, critical analysis reveals a profound dependency on foreign foundational models and cloud architectures. The research further delves into the geopolitics of semiconductors, illustrating how hardware monopolies and export controls act as a rigid ceiling to absolute sovereignty, increasingly weaponized within the US-China technological rivalry. Consequently, the study reconceptualizes digital sovereignty for small states not as absolute autarky, but as a dynamic spectrum of “managed dependency.” To navigate this unequal global technological order, the state of Qatar must employ strategic multilateral partnerships, leverage open-source architectures, and capitalize on their sovereign wealth to mitigate vulnerabilities. Ultimately, a small state’s digital sovereignty is measured by its capacity to manage these dependencies, protect its socio-cultural specificity, and maximize its geopolitical margin of maneuver within entrenched structural constraints.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence Sovereignty and Technological Dependency

organizations: Department of Master of Computer Applications  ASM’s Institute of Business Management & Research, Pune, Maharashtra, India
evidence_items.summary: With the growing use of digital images in online communication and social media, verifying whether an image is authentic has become increasingly important. Image manipulation techniques such as copy-move, splicing, inpainting, and object removal can change the meaning of visual information. At the same time, JPEG compression and repeated recompression can weaken the forensic traces that are useful for detection. This review looks at two AI-based approaches for detecting digital image forgery. The first study combines Error Level Analysis (ELA) with the VGG-16 convolutional neural network to classify images as original or tampered. The second study focuses on compressed images shared through social networks and uses a modified ShuffleNet V2 architecture for lightweight forgery classification. The two studies are reviewed based on their objectives, datasets, preprocessing or feature representation, deep learning architecture, compression conditions, findings, and limitations. The comparison shows that ELA with VGG-16 can help expose compression-related manipulation artifacts, while the modified ShuffleNet V2 approach focuses on the practical challenge of detecting forgery after JPEG and social-network recompression. The review highlights dataset diversity, compression robustness, computational efficiency, and generalization across different manipulation and sharing conditions as important research gaps. Keywords— Artificial Intelligence, Digital Image Forgery, Deep Learning, Error Level Analysis, VGG-16,ShuffleNet V2, Image Compression.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence Approaches for Digital Image Forgery Detection

evidence_items.summary: Virtual reality enables studying active visual search and gaze behavior under naturalistic, free-viewing conditions while preserving experimental control. However, free head-eye coordination, extended 3D space, dynamic target trajectories, and headset-specific field of view and eye-tracking constraints mean that findings from traditional 2D paradigms cannot be assumed to generalize to immersive environments. Interpreting gaze-based outcomes in VR requires bench-marks that establish how basic target properties influence detection. We used target eccentricity, size, and speed as benchmark predictors of visual detection in an immersive VR coin-foraging task. Using in-headset eye-tracking, participants guided a gaze-controlled avatar to collect coins that varied in gaze-relative eccentricity, size, and speed. We modeled gaze-based observation probability, observation latency, dwell time, gaze-coin angular distance, and saccade dynamics. Observation probability was analyzed using mixed-effects logistic regression, whereas latency was analyzed with a censoring-aware Cox framework that retained never-detected coins. Eccen-tricity and size showed the clearest benchmark effects. Peripheral and small coins were less like-ly to be detected. Speed’s role was more nuanced. Although slow coins were detected more of-ten in a binary model, this advantage did not persist in a censoring-aware survival analysis, suggesting that speed influenced the opportunity for observation more than momentary salience. Consistent with this interpretation, slow coins produced longer dwell times, and gaze-coin an-gular distance and saccade measures indicated that target properties shaped both the geometry and effort for acquisition. These findings establish a feature-based benchmark for gaze-based de-tection in immersive visual search and demonstrate the importance of modeling missed targets as censored detection opportunities.
evidence_items.title: A Benchmark for Gaze-Based Target Detection in Immersive Virtual Reality: Effects of Eccentricity, Size, and Speed on Observation and Detection Dynamics

evidence_items.summary: This study examines the use of machine learning for predicting default risk within the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) 7(a) loan program using publicly available loan-level data obtained through the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA). Using 488,772 resolved loans originated over fifteen fiscal years from FY2010 through FY2024, the study compares a traditional logistic regression benchmark with Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and an ensemble model. Gradient Boosting produces the strongest out-of-time predictive performance, achieving an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) of 0.9178 compared with 0.7641 for the logistic regression benchmark, representing a 20.1% relative improvement. The model also reduces the Brier Score by 44.5%, indicating substantially more accurate probability forecasts. Loan term, initial interest rate, and the SBA guarantee ratio emerge as important predictors of default. Default outcomes also vary considerably across industries, with Transportation (9.84%), Arts and Entertainment (9.70%), and Wholesale Trade (8.52%) exhibiting the highest default rates, while Agriculture (4.09%), Finance and Insurance (4.60%), and Healthcare (4.81%) exhibit the lowest. Across the study period, among the resolved-loan sample has an overall default rate of 7.47%, with annual rates ranging from 5.48% in FY2013 to 16.27% in FY2023. The findings demonstrate the potential value of machine learning for credit risk prediction in government-guaranteed small business lending while highlighting the importance of out-of-time model validation. More broadly, the study provides evidence relevant to SBA policymakers, participating lenders, and the responsible development of AI-assisted credit risk assessment tools for small business lending.
evidence_items.title: Can Artificial Intelligence Improve Credit Decisions? Evidence from Large-Scale Lending Data

evidence_items.summary: This paper presents an empirical study of a multi-persona large language model (LLM) consensus architecture deployed in a live retail FinTech platform for equity and options trade signal generation. Grounded in a prior quantitative trading framework (Anton, 2025) and building upon academic antecedents in multi-agent LLM systems (Xiao et al., 2024), the Edge Stack Trading platform deploys a six-persona AI analyst panel producing structured, constrained verdicts across a real-time multi-signal scoring architecture. Analysis of nine live trade reports generated between April and May 2026 reports a preliminary 87.5% directional accuracy rate across eight assessable signals in an exploratory proof-of-concept evaluation, with unanimous panel consensus strongly correlated with system confidence extremes. Inter-model disagreement functions as an auditable risk signal, and model API failures produce identifiable, recoverable degradation patterns consistent with graceful degradation requirements for financial AI systems. The architecture addresses the 2026 conference theme of Reliable and Deterministic AI for Financial Systems through structured verdict formats, role-constrained persona prompting, and explicit multi-signal deterministic scoring as mechanisms for AI governance in retail financial decision support. One incorrect signal (Palantir) reveals a boundary condition in which extreme valuation risk overrides technical alignment, informing a specific architectural recommendation. Implications for HBCU financial technology education, democratized institutional-grade AI analysis, and regulatory auditability are discussed.
evidence_items.title: Ensemble LLM Consensus Architectures for Deterministic Trade Signal Generation: An Empirical Study of Multi-Persona AI Panels in Retail FinTech Applications

evidence_items.summary:
This systematic review evaluates the effectiveness, diagnostic accuracy, and implementation outcomes of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted screening tools for depression and anxiety in primary care settings, with a focus on literature published since the advent of advanced large language models. A systematic search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, and Cochrane Central from January 2020 to September 2025. Ten studies met the inclusion criteria, comprising randomized controlled trials, pragmatic trials, and validation studies. Included studies demonstrated that AI-assisted tools (including conversational chatbots, machine learning models using voice and behavioral data, and digital decision-support systems) can achieve high diagnostic accuracy, with balanced accuracy up to 88.2% and Area Under the Curve (AUC) up to 0.82. Clinically, AI-assisted interventions were associated with higher depression remission (e.g., 27.3% vs. 12.0%) and better anxiety outcomes than treatment-as-usual in individual trials. Feasibility and acceptability were generally favorable, with completion rates often exceeding 60-70% and user satisfaction reaching 79%, even among older adults. Key challenges included limited external validation, demographic homogeneity, and insufficient reporting on ethical safeguards.
AI-assisted screening tools show potential to improve the detection and management of depression and anxiety in primary care, with encouraging accuracy, clinical effectiveness, and user engagement in the available studies. However, the evidence base is small and heterogeneous, and future research needs to address gaps in generalizability, long-term efficacy, ethical oversight, and seamless workflow integration to ensure equitable and responsible implementation.
evidence_items.title: Effectiveness of AI-Assisted Screening Tools for Depression and Anxiety in Primary Care: A Systematic Review

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents built for teaching tend to leak evaluation: they praise right answers, hint after wrong ones, and drift toward explaining. This note records the design of Talk It Through: Newton's Laws, a prompt-engineered agent for introductory mechanics that probes understanding instead of tutoring. In a short conversation, a student commits to a prediction about each of Newton's three laws, explains it in everyday words, and defends it against a changed case built from the student's own words that alters exactly one variable of the original scene. The agent never confirms, corrects, or hints during the conversation and scores only at the end. Each law receives one of four outcome codes: held, caved, self-corrected, or misconception survived. We define cave detection, the identification of a correct initial idea that is abandoned under a single changed case, as a measure of robustness that right/wrong item scoring cannot see. We summarize design rules found through more than 40 scripted simulation runs. All results reported here come from simulated prototype testing; no real-student data have yet been collected. A full design paper and an IRB-approved classroom study are in preparation.   Preprint, not peer reviewed.

evidence_items.summary: Self-distillation in agentic reinforcement learning has produced a growing number of methods. However, existing evaluations often reuse published baseline scores under differing experimental conditions, provide few direct comparisons among contemporaneous methods, and give limited attention to training stability and computational cost. These limitations obscure the source of reported gains and the practical strengths and weaknesses of competing methods. Costly agent training further motivates a common basis for comparison. To address these gaps, we compare ten representative methods against GRPO on ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, Search-QA, and WebShop across three model sizes. Our study comprises 132 training runs totaling 12,124.4 recorded H800 GPU-hours, with repeated evaluations over eight rollout seeds for the pretrained backbones and all eleven trained methods. Beyond final task performance, we examine training progress, stability, and measured computational cost. Our evaluation yields three key findings. First, gains over GRPO remain limited in scope, with no method consistently outperforming it across settings. Second, strong final performance can mask unstable training. Third, additional training cost does not consistently translate into better performance. We establish this benchmark to support fair, comprehensive comparison and guide future research toward reliable and cost-effective improvements in agent training. Project page: https://aim-uofa.github.io/Self-Distillation-AgentRL/
evidence_items.title: More Methods, Better Agents? A Reality Check on Self-Distillation in Agentic Reinforcement Learning

evidence_items.summary: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become more capable and widely deployed, concerns about privacy and safety have become increasingly pressing. Machine unlearning offers one approach to addressing these concerns by removing designated information from trained models while preserving unrelated capabilities. However, fragmented implementations and evaluation protocols, incomplete robustness testing, and limited understanding of metric reliability make progress in MLLM unlearning difficult to assess systematically. We introduce Open-MMUnlearning, an open-source, extensible framework that integrates target-model preparation, multimodal data processing, unlearning, and evaluation through shared interfaces and structured configurations. The framework supports five benchmarks spanning privacy, safety, and copyright, eight MLLMs from four model families, and twelve unlearning methods. Its evaluation suite jointly assesses forgetting effectiveness, retained utility, and robustness to model interventions, adversarial inputs, and membership inference attacks. Using a common evaluation protocol, we compare ten representative unlearning methods. In this comparison, GD and MIP-Editor tie for the highest overall score: GD achieves the highest Forget Quality, while MIP-Editor preserves more Model Utility. We further introduce a metric meta-evaluation protocol that tests faithfulness using models with controlled exposure to target knowledge and robustness under quantization and relearning. Among the thirteen evaluated metrics, BLEU achieves the highest aggregate reliability score. KS-Test attains the highest faithfulness AUC but performs less well on robustness. Together, the framework and these findings support reproducible comparison of MLLM unlearning methods and systematic assessment of evaluation reliability.
evidence_items.title: Open-MMUnlearning: Unifying Methods and Evaluation for MLLM Unlearning

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Sanskrit morphology provides a setting for comparing explicit suffix rules and language-model predictions under changes in word order. This exploratory study evaluates a Python suffix classifier and supplied Gemini prediction files for 100 Bhagavad Gita entries representing 98 distinct verse identifiers. The corpus contains 614 split-token occurrences and 280 selective reference annotations. Natural and scrambled inputs preserve the same token multisets. A scoring audit identified repeated matching and unconditional credit for ambiguous outputs in the original symbolic evaluator. Using one-to-one annotation matching and candidate-set membership, the unchanged symbolic classifier achieved compatibility on 228/280 annotations (81.43%) in each order. The supplied natural and scrambled Gemini CSVs each achieved 242/280 compatible predictions (86.43%), after resolving one scrambled-token transcription mismatch by its input position. Only two of 614 paired Gemini classifications changed; neither affected the annotated score. The comparison shows no decrease in compatibility under scrambling and documents stable compatibility in this recorded comparison, alongside limitations from selective annotations, candidate ambiguity, and incomplete model metadata. The results describe robustness of these outputs under the supplied permutations rather than general word-order invariance or full morphological parsing accuracy.
evidence_items.title: Comparative Analysis of Rule Based Symbolic Logic and a Large Language Model in Sanskrit Morphological Analysis

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate plausible responses without using the relevant evidence or meeting task constraints. We separate the Modality Gap in cross-modal correspondence and evidence use from the Intent Gap in behavior relative to specified constraints, goals, and human expectations. Six dimensions organize the review: architecture, objective functions, data construction, training, evaluation, and applications. The first four control evidence access, optimization targets, supervision, and updates. Comparing mechanisms and supervision assumptions shows what interface compatibility, target imitation, preference learning, and verifiable rewards can each demonstrate about alignment. Evaluation at the representation, task, and behavior levels tests these choices through controlled input changes and reward-model validation, and we interpret each gain together with its model, task, and evaluation setup instead of comparing scores across conditions. Studies in robotics, safety, healthcare, recommendation, and climate decision support share three requirements: traceable evidence, valid supervision, and constraint-sensitive decisions. Stronger representations or higher benchmark scores can leave the claimed alignment mechanism unresolved, which motivates four research directions: evidence-consistent alignment across modalities, verified self-correction and test-time alignment, targeted repair from failure diagnosis, and reliable transfer to underrepresented settings.
evidence_items.title: Alignment in Multimodal Large Language Models: A Survey

evidence_items.summary: Background/Objectives: Hip osteoarthritis (OA) is a highly prevalent musculoskeletal disorder associated with substantial functional impairment and healthcare burden. Although evidence-based clinical practice guidelines exist, including the 2021 guideline of the German Society for Orthopaedics and Trauma Surgery (DGOU), their implementation in routine practice remains incomplete. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly consulted for guideline-related information, but the concordance of their answers with guideline recommendations is uncertain. This benchmark study evaluated the guideline concordance, comprehensiveness and length of answers generated by five widely used LLMs to questions derived from the 2021 German S3 guideline on evidence- and consensus-based indication criteria for total hip arthroplasty in hip OA (EKIT-Hip; AWMF register no. 187-001; lead society DGOU). It did not evaluate the effectiveness or safety of clinical decision support. Methods: In a cross-sectional, single-run benchmark study, 26 structured, context-free questions covering five of the six thematic complexes of the guideline (diagnosis and imaging; assessment of the level of suffering; evaluation of alternative therapeutic options; contraindications; optimisation of modifiable risk factors) were derived from the guideline recommendations and submitted between 9 November 2024 and 25 February 2025 through the consumer web interfaces of five LLM-based systems (GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-4o mini, Gemini Advanced and Consensus Premium), yielding 130 responses (one per system–question pair, each in a newly initiated chat session). Responses were evaluated by three board-certified orthopaedic surgeons blinded to model identity, using a four-point accuracy scale and a five-point comprehensiveness scale. Only a single consensus score per response was recorded, so inter-rater reliability could not be assessed.
evidence_items.title: Guideline-Concordant Answer Quality of Five Large Language Models on Indication Criteria for Total Hip Arthroplasty in Hip Osteoarthritis: A Single-Run Benchmark Against the 2021 German S3 Guideline (EKIT-Hip)

evidence_items.summary: The integration of natural language understanding into conversational commerce requires robustly extracting structured intents from idiomatic text. While cloud-based models are highly capable, their latency, privacy risks, and operational costs necessitate efficient local alternatives. To address this, we empirically evaluate locally deployed, open-weights Large Language Models (LLMs) on parsing multi-intent shopping cart commands into deterministic JSON schemas. We benchmark multiple models across minimal, extended, and few-shot prompting paradigms, utilizing a dual-axis framework to simultaneously measure extraction quality (operation F1-score, exact match, schema validity) and hardware performance (latency, GPU power consumption). Our evaluation highlights a fundamental trade-off between schema compliance and computational overhead, demonstrating how advanced prompting techniques improve parsing accuracy while measurably impacting inference latency and power draw. Ultimately, this comprehensive profiling identifies optimal model configurations for resource-constrained environments: a well-chosen 3-8B parameter model (specifically Granite4 3B) paired with few-shot prompting recovers over 95% of the quality of the largest evaluated model at a coarse indicative estimate of 40× lower operational energy per command, establishing a practical baseline for deploying cost-effective LLMs as efficiency candidates in resource-constrained environments.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking Local Large Language Models for Structured Knowledge Extraction in Conversational Commerce

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) have recently emerged as a promising backbone for time-series forecasting, yet most existing LLM-based forecasters are still optimized with purely supervised objectives such as MSE or MAE. Such point-wise training is often misaligned with the sequence-level properties that matter in real deployments, including waveform fidelity, trend consistency, and robustness under distribution shift. Reinforcement learning (RL) is a natural candidate for sequence-level optimization, but directly transplanting RL recipes from natural language processing to time series is difficult because forecasting involves continuous outputs, long-horizon credit assignment, multi-objective rewards, and unstable policy updates. To address these issues, we propose TSLLM-BO , a two-stage framework that first learns a strong supervised forecaster and then performs structure-aware behavioral alignment through reinforcement learning. The framework combines three key ideas: 1) a time--text alignment architecture that links temporal patches with semantic prompts in a frozen LLM backbone; 2) a differentiable composite reward that jointly optimizes point accuracy, waveform consistency, and trend alignment; and 3) Dynamic Policy Clipping (DPC) , which adapts the PPO trust region over training to stabilize long-horizon optimization. Extensive experiments on standard long-horizon forecasting benchmarks show that TSLLM-BO consistently outperforms strong LLM-based and deep forecasting baselines, especially under long prediction horizons, cross-dataset transfer, and noise/missingness perturbations. These results suggest that behavioral alignment, rather than supervised fitting alone, is a practical route for endowing LLM-based forecasters with stronger temporal structure awareness and deployment robustness.
evidence_items.title: Structure-Aware Behavioral Alignment of Large Language Models for Robust Time Series Forecasting

evidence_items.summary: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in educational settings creates pedagogical opportunities while raising environmental concerns regarding data center energy consumption and physical infrastructure footprint. This systematic review synthesizes scientific evidence on the algorithmic carbon footprint of AI tools implemented in environmental education programs. Adhering to the PRISMA 2020 statement and an adapted PICoS framework (Population: educational stakeholders; Phenomenon of interest: AI carbon/energy auditing; Context: environmental/sustainability education; Study design: empirical and theoretical studies), systematic searches were conducted across Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and ERIC up to 6 August 2026. Seven studies met the eligibility criteria: 5 empirical, 1 scoping review, and 1 theoretical-conceptual synthesis. Quality appraisal utilized MMAT (2018 version) for primary empirical studies and an adapted SANRA (2019 version) for non-empirical documents, followed by qualitative narrative synthesis. Results indicate that, within the reviewed corpus (n = 7), studies predominantly examine conversational agents and large language models (LLMs) applied to sustainability education, while highlighting a critical measurement gap regarding the empirical auditing of energy consumption and physical infrastructure during model training and inference. Conceptual frameworks synthesized across non-empirical literature hypothesize a potential misalignment between educational content promoting planetary conservation and the environmental opacity of underlying technological deployments. Key limitations include inferential fragility due to a small, methodologically heterogeneous evidence base restricted to higher education settings.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of Algorithmic Carbon Footprint and Artificial Intelligence (AI) Tools in Environmental Education Programs: Systematic Review

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning, is reshaping cardiovascular imaging and electrocardiography (ECG) by enabling automated acquisition support, quantification, disease detection, and risk prediction. Yet, high retrospective accuracy does not by itself establish transportability or clinical benefit. This narrative review first outlines the AI development lifecycle, with emphasis on data and label quality, architecture selection, patient-level data partitioning, calibration, external validation, and prospective evaluation. It then critically examines representative advances in ECG, echocardiography, cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), cardiac computed tomography (CT), and nuclear cardiology. Particular attention is given to three rapidly evolving areas: AI-enhanced ECG, video- and vision-language echocardiography, and volumetric CT and CMR analysis. We compare convolutional, transformer-based, hybrid, and generative approaches; summarize explainable-AI methods, including gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM), SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), integrated gradients, and occlusion testing; and analyze failure modes arising from label, sampling, demographic, device, and temporal bias. Quantitative examples show that performance can deteriorate across institutions, demographic groups, and acquisition settings despite apparently strong internal validation. Future progress will depend on prospective workflow-based trials, multimodal foundation models with transparent benchmarks, lifecycle governance and regulation, and continuous post-deployment surveillance.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence in cardiovascular imaging and electrocardiography

evidence_items.summary: As digital self-triage becomes more widely used, quality assurance requires evaluation of both emergency recognition and overall agreement with clinical judgement, including how these outcomes differ across generations of large language models. The Benchmark Self-Triage (BeST) project intends to provide a framework to compare systems for digital self-triage against a medical 'gold standard' in Germany. In a first step developing the method and demonstrating its potential we developed a representative set of patient vignettes and compared two regulated medical-device triage systems, SmED and Infermedica, with five structured OpenAI configurations spanning multiple model generations: gpt-4.1, gpt-5.4, gpt-5.6-luna, gpt-5.6-sol, and gpt-6-astra. An LLM-based patient actor covered 480 physician-curated vignettes derived from German routine triage data. A pool of seven physicians provided preliminary reference classifications and consensus for 480 vignettes. Recommendations were mapped to three urgency categories 'emergency', 'acute', and 'not urgent' and evaluated using winsorised weights derived from routine triage frequencies. Weighted emergency sensitivity ranged from 51.3% (95% CI 35.5-66.3%) for gpt-4.1 to 99.9% (99.7-100.0%) for gpt-6-astra. Weighted exact three-category agreement (accuracy) ranged from 54.4% to 68.8%; gpt-4.1 achieved the highest agreement despite the lowest emergency sensitivity. No system performed best across all urgency categories. The later-generation OpenAI configurations showed a more precautionary triage profile resembling SmED, with higher sensitivity for emergency cases; gpt-6-astra showed the strongest shift. This cross-sectional comparison across model generations suggests a shift towards more precautionary triage behaviour, without establishing a longitudinal improvement in accuracy. These findings highlight the limitations of overall agreement for evaluating self-triage and support category-specific assessment.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark Self-Triage (BeST): Comparing Self-Triage Systems and Multiple Generations of OpenAI Models Against Preliminary Expert Consensus

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The integration of AI into fact-checking has significantly enhanced the speed and scale of misinformation detection across digital platforms. AI-driven fact-checking systems can now access information in real-time, leveraging machine learning, natural language processing, and large language models. However, the same AI systems that enhance speed and scalability in verification also introduce new ethical and technical concerns. Biases embedded in training data, opaque algorithmic decision-making, and inconsistencies in human oversight can undermine fairness, accuracy, and accountability. Without robust safeguards, AI fact-checking may unintentionally propagate misinformation, exacerbate societal biases, and erode public trust in automated verification. This chapter examines the epistemic challenges AI fact-checking faces, namely bias, fairness, and accountability, against the backdrop of accelerating misinformation. It traces the evolution of verification technologies, evaluates the risks of static governance models, and proposes adaptive, participatory epistemic infrastructures as essential to sustaining public trust. It calls for a shift from technical optimization toward democratic and ethically anchored verification ecosystems.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Fact-Checking

evidence_items.summary: LLMs are increasingly being embedded into a variety of distributed agentic systems, in the form of agents with APIs, microservices, workflows, and external tools for task completion. Systems need to be able to handle requests that are worded differently but mean the same thing, to make sure routing is consistent, caching can be reused, latency is reduced, reliability is ensured, and governance is supported. Conventional intent representations, beyond simply conveying what users want with their intent and respective slots, do not encode information about user authorization, policies with implications for execution, side effects of actions, locality of execution, and operational implications of intents. Prior work has provided frameworks for normalization, capability discovery and routing in distributed agentic systems, but all this work is done independently and thus does not provide a unified pipeline for handling requests in distributed systems. The main contribution of this paper is to propose a unified framework describing the normalization, discovery, routing, execution control and runtime feedback in distributed agentic systems. The core of this work is the introduction of a canonical representation of intent, called an intent record, which can convey all kinds of semantic information, as well as context, policy, and operational information about the system as a whole, including its uncertainty, to be used by the system’s routing layer. We also introduce a new constraint-first multi-criteria routing process. A reference architecture is also given for such sorts of systems. The architecture’s main functional components are semantic control and its decoupled, cross-governance-deterministic execution. An evaluation framework for the proposed approach in the future is also presented. This framework is not validated through implementation or benchmarking experiments. Such an empirical evaluation is left for future work.
evidence_items.title: AI-Based Intent Normalization and Service Routing in Distributed Agentic Microservices

organizations: University of East London
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models and agentic artificial intelligence provide the reasoning layer of autonomous aerial and ground robots, but the architectures remain fragmented across the two communities. This systematic review, reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 statement, searched ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, ProQuest, EBSCO, and Google Scholar from January 2020 through April 2026. Of 5298 records, 2228 remained after duplicates were removed and 124 studies were included: 67 aerial, 41 ground, and 16 on both platforms or a generic architecture. Six patterns appear, from a language model used only as a task-specific tool to an end-to-end foundation model, such as vision-language-action models. Open-loop pipelines, closed-loop pipelines, hierarchical executives, and multi-agent systems lie between those extremes. The model carries semantic reasoning, task decomposition, and tool orchestration, while classical planners and controllers retain trajectories, safety, and real-time control. Memory appears in 62 of 124 studies (50%) and function calling in 37 (30%), yet only 13 (10%) run the model onboard and 44 (35%) validate a physical robot. Aerial systems emphasize long-range vision and mission planning; ground systems emphasize local perception and interaction; both follow the same hybrid pattern. A suitability matrix shows that specialized vision models remain preferable for geometric perception. Designers should match the pattern to the task dynamics and choose the model for latency, safety, and where inference runs, rather than for benchmark score alone. Hallucination, spatial reasoning, inference latency, and the lack of standardized evaluation still limit deployment.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Models and Agentic AI Architectures for Aerial and Ground Robots: A Systematic Review, Taxonomy, and Design Guidelines

evidence_items.summary: Introduction Undetected calibration drift in autonomous ocean sensors corrupts temperature and salinity records underpinning climate reanalysis, seasonal forecasting, and marine ecosystem assessments. With 15–20% of active Argo floats showing meaningful drift at any time and correction workflows taking three to six months, scalable autonomous quality control is urgently needed. Methods We present DriftGuard, a five-component autonomous framework integrating a physically-informed heterogeneous sensor graph over 135 nodes, a Hybrid Temporal Transformer and Graph Attention Network (HybridTGAT), a cross-sensor consistency loss, a conformal prediction wrapper, and a LangGraph-orchestrated three-stage agentic loop supported by a 2,183-chunk RAG store. Results Evaluated on Argo float profiles (116 floats, North Atlantic, 2021–2024), NDBC buoy time series (15 stations, 2019–2024), and the expert-labelled AdapAD benchmark, DriftGuard achieves a GAT-level ROC-AUC of 0.8376, an AdapAD zero-shot AUC of 0.8423, and detects gradual drift types an average of 84.7 readings earlier than the operational Argo QC Test 16 baseline. Operational fleet evaluation across 131 sensors identifies 13 floats in a CRITICAL state requiring correction within 24 hours. Discussion DriftGuard is the first system in the marine sensor domain to unify graph-based spatial reasoning, temporal modelling, autonomous LLM-driven correction, conformal uncertainty certificates, and closed-loop retraining within a single operational pipeline, demonstrating readiness for real-world deployment.
evidence_items.title: DriftGuard: an agentic hybrid temporal transformer and graph attention network framework for autonomous calibration drift detection and correction in distributed marine sensor networks

evidence_items.summary: Data and code behind "openPASO: an agentic open-source multi-physics and multi-code framework for verifiable computer simulations" (Hermann, Shojaei, Scheider, Cyron). The archive holds what the paper's numbers rest on: the source of the evaluated openPASO, the 22 evaluation instances, their manufactured solutions (released after grading), the fingerprints recorded before the runs, every run with its grade, and the analysis. The evaluation in brief Three openly downloadable AI models (Qwen3.5-27B, Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B) solved 16 single-code and 6 coupled finite-element problems, each with and without openPASO, with three seeds per problem. Every instance's manufactured solution was drawn fresh and kept sealed (stored encrypted) until grading; the agent received only the data derived from it and reported its computed values at a fixed grid of points. The single-code runs used openPASO at commit ec8db887, the coupled runs at commit f1787b80; every run's ledger records its commit. A small out-of-family test, made after the evaluation under the same protocol, ran two instances of families never used in development; its runs used commit df984f6f, identical to f1787b80 in every archived file ( out of family.tar.gz ). A component test of openPASO's parts and a test of the six coupled development families that did not meet the development requirement ran the 27B AI model under the same protocol, with an analysis fixed before the first run, at commit ac7ce420 ( component test.tar.gz ).
evidence_items.title: openPASO evaluation archive: blind evaluation of AI models solving single-code and coupled finite-element problems with and without openPASO

evidence_items.summary: Out-of-fold probability calibration and multi-family stacking metrics | computer science | beginner | classification | deep learning | tabular | english
evidence_items.title: Tabular Calibration & Stacking Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Can AI agents carry out research on open scientific problems? We introduce Into the Unknown, a benchmark that provides an agent with a science paper along with a research direction to pursue and tasks it to write a follow-up paper. We work with scientists at US Department of Energy (DOE) national laboratories, who each contribute an unpublished follow-up direction from their own work together with the necessary conditions a submission must meet. While assessing the quality of a follow-up paper is challenging in general, using these conditions to form a rubric makes evaluation more tractable for research problems that have no reference answer. We have nine frontier agents write 15 follow-ups each, spanning quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning domains. None of the 135 submissions satisfies all the conditions, and 114 fail our integrity check, most often because the paper claims work that was never done or reports numbers that contradict the recorded evidence. Overall, agents readily produce papers that look like follow-ups, but none meets the standard of the domain scientist, leaving substantial headroom. Our code and data are publicly available.
evidence_items.title: Into the Unknown: Benchmarking AI agents on open scientific research problems

evidence_items.summary: LLM agents are becoming increasingly capable of handling daily workspace tasks by interacting with application environments through tool calls. However, as agents read and write sensitive user data across email, documents, and other applications, a central privacy question is whether they preserve contextual integrity (CI), that is, whether the information flows they produce comply with context-specific disclosure constraints. Existing work either focuses on model-level privacy leakage or evaluates agents in limited application environments with manually constructed disclosure constraints. In this work, we introduce AgentCIScope, a unified platform and benchmark for evaluating agent-level contextual integrity through executable, multi-step tasks across diverse, realistic application environments. AgentCIScope transforms public and synthetic privacy cases into executable agent tasks, with disclosure constraints grounded in three criteria: governing privacy policies, persona-based agreement, and a predefined sensitive-attribute taxonomy. Based on AgentCIScope, we evaluate 12 agents on 936 tasks and find that strong task-completion capability does not guarantee contextual-integrity preservation: single-run leakage rates range from 32.5% to 94.4%, while repeating each task five times further increases leakage by 4-19 percentage points. Leakage varies substantially across attributes: personal preferences and booking details have average leakage rates of 84.7% and 76.5%, compared with 17.1% for credit-card information and 29.4% for SSNs; environments: calendar has the highest average leakage rate as an information source, while WhatsApp ranks highest as an information destination; and governing privacy policies. AgentCIScope provides deep insights into agent privacy leakage and serves as a unified testbed for developing privacy-preserving agents.
evidence_items.title: AgentCIScope: Grounded Contextual Integrity Evaluation for LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: Absorption and scattering coefficients for the Jerlov optical water types, taken from the primary literature with the provenance of every value recorded. Values that a published table got wrong are flagged rather than silently repaired, and quantities the data do not determine are refused rather than guessed. Twenty-two entries are documented, nine of them confirmed defects in the source literature: duplicated rows in Solonenko & Mobley (2015) Table 7, a transcription error in the small-particle scattering coefficient that propagated into their published coefficients, a Data Availability Statement that gives the DOI of an unrelated dataset, and a reprint whose stated unit is out by a factor of ten. Three further entries were open questions that obtaining the 1968 first edition settled. The same Jerlov water type is in circulation with beam attenuations differing by a factor of five, which is why every coefficient here carries the source it came from. Every shipped table can be regenerated from its primary source by the scripts in tools/ , and each generation step checks the result against the equations of the paper it came from.
evidence_items.title: jerlov: inherent optical properties of the Jerlov optical water types, with provenance

evidence_items.summary: Live, open-source benchmark for comparing AI coding agents on real GitHub issues
evidence_items.title: linny006/agent-eval-harness

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent systems to automate complex computer-use workflows, yet existing benchmarks mostly assume consistent, cooperative environments. In contrast, real-world collaboration rarely runs on consistent information: peer or sub-agents frequently report outdated states, issue contradictory instructions, or compete over shared permissions and files, forcing agents to check others' outputs and verify ground truth in the environment. Evaluating such conflict resolution remains challenging: manual authoring cannot scale across complex systems, while unconstrained LLM generation produces narrative drift, answer leakage, and unsatisfiable rubrics. We introduce CLASHarness (Conflict-Loaded Agent Scenario Harness), a controllable framework for generating verifiable multi-agent conflicts in computer use, with a benchmark of 600 multi-round tasks. By combining hierarchical scenario planning with an eight-step verified micro-pipeline, CLASHarness pre-commits decisive visual facts before rendering and compiles hybrid code and semantic graders directly from executed reference trajectories, guaranteeing every task is solvable by construction. Evaluating 15 frontier models on CLASHarness reveals three core bottlenecks. First, when sub-agent outputs conflict with the environment, weaker models blindly follow misleading information, whereas stronger models inspect visual evidence to verify ground truth. Second, resolving conflicts is much harder than finding them: while agents can spot inconsistencies, actively fixing system state drops task success significantly. Third, coordination protocols remain a universal bottleneck: even frontier models fail over 58% of closing actions, often forgetting to release shared locks or hand off tasks. CLASHarness provides a scalable, verifiable foundation for building reliable multi-agent systems.
evidence_items.title: CLASHarness: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Conflict in Computer Use via a Controllable and Verifiable Generation Pipeline

evidence_items.summary: For repository-grounded coding agents, a functionally correct patch is not necessarily an acceptable one: developers also constrain how the task must be carried out-modification scope, workflow order, validation, tool use, and reporting. This capability, which we call engineering constraint following, remains largely invisible to current evaluations. We introduce ANCHOR (Assessing Naturalistic Constraint Hierarchies and Ordering in Repository-Grounded Agentic Coding), a benchmark built on naturalistic, multilingual repository tasks spanning eight language groups. ANCHOR combines (i) a hierarchical taxonomy of 10 categories and 78 leaf types distilled from real developer interactions, (ii) an automated pipeline that instantiates task-grounded atomic constraints and composes them into typed AND/THEN/PRIORITY relations, and (iii) a trajectory-grounded evaluation framework that checks both the code diff and the execution trajectory with rule-based and LLM judges. Across 19 agent configurations spanning 2 scaffolds and 10 foundation models on 358 tasks, the strongest measured system, Claude Opus 4.8 under Cline, reaches 70.1% atomic compliance and 63.7% relation compliance, while 19.0% of tasks pass every scored checklist item under the strict all-item FCCR criterion. A five-engineer audit of constraints from 50 instances reports 94% feasibility, 94% repository consistency, and 96% realism. In the primary paired set (14 configurations), the mean signed change in task completion after adding constraints is +0.7 percentage points; individual changes vary in both directions. These results distinguish functional success from constraint compliance, with failures concentrated in workflow ordering, tool-use discipline, and reporting, and substantial interactions between models and scaffolds.
evidence_items.title: ANCHOR: Assessing Naturalistic Constraint Hierarchies and Ordering in Repository-Grounded Agentic Coding

evidence_items.summary: A spatial answer depends on the reference frame specified in language and its supporting visual evidence. Item accuracy alone obscures whether correctness persists when either changes. We introduce Frame Evidence, a benchmark of 320 matched triplets and 960 Chinese multiple-choice questions from captured and rendered scenes. One family compares three grounded reference frames over fixed images. The other pairs image deletion annotated as insufficient with answer-preserving addition. Joint metrics require correct answers across all three frames and paired evidence variants. Across 20 configurations on 288 held-out questions, GPT three-shot reaches 50.00\% item accuracy, but the best three-frame group accuracy is 5/48 (10.42\%), reached by GPT two-shot. Few-shot prompting and task-specific adaptation improve item accuracy without consistently improving joint correctness. Input controls show where images support matched success, while repeated executions reveal answer instability beneath similar scores.
evidence_items.title: Frame Evidence:A Benchmark for Reference Frames and Visual Evidence in Multi-Image Spatial Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Chatbot Arena ranks language models with the Bradley-Terry model, which gives each model one score and so assumes Luce's choice axiom. Choice theory predicts where this fails: near-copies are told apart more decisively than their scores imply. On 1.8 million Arena votes, votes between versions of one model are 1.37 times as decisive as Bradley-Terry predicts, between sizes of one generation 1.26 times and between models of one lab 1.12 times; a release a year later gives consistent multipliers, and the effect survives alternative tie treatments, prompt subsets and topics, and timing checks. How alike two models' answers are worded and formatted tracks the effect. A correction with four to six parameters predicts held-out votes better than Bradley-Terry and than models with hundreds of parameters, mostly by modelling ties; frozen and carried to new releases in a test fixed in advance, its gains are concentrated in ties, and better head-to-head odds are not established. The leaderboard order barely moves. With language-model judges and three-answer menus, a near-copy takes votes mostly from its twin when choices are pooled over prompts (log-odds shift +0.10, 95% interval 0.05 to 0.16); within a prompt the shift is smaller and clear for two of four judges.
evidence_items.title: Similar Models, Broken Odds: Where Luce's Axiom Fails in Chatbot Arena

evidence_items.summary: Formal verification proves that a program satisfies its specification, but says nothing about whether the specification captures what the author meant. As LLMs increasingly write both code and specifications, a gap between the author's natural-language requirement and the specification becomes a live risk. A machine-checked proof of a property narrower than the one requested is worthless but passes every check. Closing this gap is solving the spec formalization problem: given a natural-language requirement, produce a formal artifact whose meaning matches it. To measure the gap, we curate an end-to-end benchmark for spec formalization spanning four formal languages: Dafny contracts and Lean 4, Isabelle and Rocq theorem statements. Each of its 3,234 rows pairs a natural-language requirement with a formal artifact and a label established by execution, by proof, or by the benchmark it is drawn from. A third of the rows are meaning-preserving rewrites of the artifact that keep the faithful label, so a judge cannot score by detecting that a row was edited. We introduce claimcheck, a tool that detects incorrect formalizations: the formal artifact is translated back into plain English by a model that never sees the requirement, and a separate model, the judge, decides whether the informalization and the requirement express the same guarantee. On all four languages it gains 8.2 to 9.8 points of macro recall over a single call shown the requirement and the artifact, and 4.2 to 6.0 over that call handed the same list of meaning-preserving rewrites. Showing the judge the artifact as well costs 1.4 to 4.5 points. Across four judges that also see the artifact, the gain shrinks as the judge gets stronger, to within a point of the informed single call for the strongest.
evidence_items.title: claimcheck: Measuring and Improving Specification Faithfulness

evidence_items.summary: Current ASR models perform well on general benchmarks but still struggle with acoustically ambiguous words. Visual context can aid recognition in screen-based scenarios, yet existing benchmarks provide limited insight into the benefits of different types of visual evidence. To address this gap, we introduce ScreenASR-Bench , a tiered benchmark with three progressively challenging levels: Explicit Textual Evidence (ETE), based on direct on-screen text; Explicit Visual Evidence (EVE), using visible content rather than on-screen text; and Implicit Semantic Evidence (ISE), requiring scene-level inference. Extensive experiments on ASR models, Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) and Omni models show that incorporating visual context substantially improves recall over the audio-only setting across all three model families. The gains are largest for ETE and smallest for ISE, indicating that models leverage direct visual evidence more effectively than indirect semantic cues. To facilitate future research on visually grounded speech recognition, we publicly release ScreenASR-Bench.
evidence_items.title: ScreenASR-Bench: A Tiered Benchmark for Speech Recognition with Visual Context

evidence_items.summary: Self-evolving agents are usually scored by endpoint Gain: held-out success after an update minus success before. That difference can credit a frozen rescore as evolution. We introduce Trace Evolution Bench (TEB), a protocol that separates that rescore from a context or weight update, together with three frozen 80/20/40 packs. An update is accepted only when validation does not fall, held-out identifiers never enter the update, and a text update is not ranked with a weight update. The primary scoreboard is coding, graded by hidden unit tests in a closed workspace. On that pack (40 held-out tasks, one family), DeepSeek v4 Pro under no_evolve never changes its policy yet moves 7.5, 5.0, and 12.5 percentage points across three seeds. Of nine text-update cells inspired by GEPA, ACE, and ExpeL, seven have positive excess above that seed's own band, and one gepa_llm seed moves down by the width of its band (-12.5, regression 0.48). GLM and MiniMax do not reproduce that seven-of-nine pattern. No method stays above its own band on every seed of all three models: GLM has two paired cells above their own bands, and MiniMax expel_llm seed 44 is a third (regression 0.30). The methods were fixed on a validation screen before held-out was read. Office, graded by rule-bounded delivery, and manufacturing table QA are separate packs: office DeepSeek does not exceed its own bands (widest 17.5 points), and manufacturing has no paired positive excess beyond its seed band.
evidence_items.title: Trace Evolution Bench: Measuring Whether Agents Improve from Their Own Environment Traces

evidence_items.summary: Object-goal navigation has made substantial progress in semantic perception and exploration, yet persistent memory for multi-object navigation and cross-floor navigation are still commonly addressed separately. We present LifelongCrossNav, a framework for sequential multi-object ObjectNav in unknown multi-floor indoor environments. Within each episode, the agent receives an ordered sequence of object-goal queries while continuously maintaining a shared sparse 3D semantic voxel memory. This memory incrementally accumulates geometric structure, traversability states, and vision-language features, allowing subsequent object-goal queries to retrieve previously acquired scene information without rebuilding the map. To support persistent search across floors, LifelongCrossNav combines support-aware 3D traversability mapping, stair-specific perception, and direction-aware stair traversal. A unified navigation policy coordinates same-floor frontier exploration, live and historical point-of-interest retrieval, stair navigation, and target-object search and approach. We further introduce HM3D-MFMON, a benchmark for sequential Multi-Floor Multi-Object Navigation built on HM3D scenes, including a dedicated subset in which completing the full sequence of object-goal subtasks requires at least one floor transition. Experimental results show that LifelongCrossNav consistently outperforms a representative planar persistent semantic-map baseline on HM3D-MFMON, demonstrating that persistent 3D semantic memory and cross-floor traversability modeling effectively support sequential multi-object navigation in multi-floor environments.
evidence_items.title: LifelongCrossNav: Persistent 3D Semantic Memory for Cross-Floor Multi-Object Navigation

evidence_items.summary: Many recent document embedding models are trained on document-as-image representations, embedding rendered pages as images rather than the underlying source. Meanwhile, existing benchmarks for scientific document retrieval, such as ArXivQA and ViDoRe, treat documents as images of pages, implicitly favoring such representations. In this work, we argue that this paradigm is not well-suited for text-rich multimodal scientific documents, where critical evidence is distributed across structured sources, including text, tables, and figures. To study this setting, we introduce ArXivDoc, a new benchmark constructed from the underlying LaTeX sources of scientific papers. Unlike PDF or image-based representations, LaTeX provides direct access to structured elements (e.g., sections, tables, figures, equations), enabling controlled query construction grounded in specific evidence types. We systematically compare text-only, image-based, and multimodal representations across both single-vector and multi-vector retrieval models. Our results show that: (1) document-as-image representations are consistently suboptimal, especially as document length increases; (2) text-based representations are most effective, even for figure-based queries, by leveraging captions and surrounding context; and (3) interleaved text+image representations outperform document-as-image approaches without requiring specialized training.
evidence_items.title: Document-as-Image Representations Fall Short for Scientific Retrieval

evidence_items.summary: This record contains trained object-detection models developed within the Digital Innovation In the Forest value chain (DIIF) project. The models detect the end face of a log. The single object-detection class is: 0 = logend The models were trained using the dataset and reproducibility code published separately as: DIIF — Log-End Image Dataset and Reproducibility Code [10.5281/zenodo.22894169] The dataset combines locally acquired log-end images with selected images from published external datasets. The external source images are documented in the training dataset record and can be restored using the accompanying reproducibility tools. Models included This record contains two trained model runs: Faster R-CNN / Detectron2 YOLOv8s The model packages retain the project naming and associated configuration and metadata files. ONNX models and inference Both model families are provided as ONNX exports, but they use different architectures and input/output formats. Their inference scripts are therefore different and are not interchangeable. Detectron2 ONNX The Detectron2 export expects an input tensor named: image The input is a float32 BGR image converted from HWC to CHW. The Detectron2 workflow does not apply YOLO-style /255 normalization. The exported model returns bounding boxes, class IDs, scores, and image-size information. Use the Detectron2 folder inference script: python code/detectron2 onnx inference folder.py \ model outputs/detectron2/logend faster rcnn r50 fpn/model final.onnx \ input-dir annotated dataset/images/test \ output-dir outputs/detectron2/logend faster rcnn r50 fpn/predict onnx The script processes all supported images in the input directory and saves annotated output images. YOLOv8 ONNX The YOLOv8 export uses dynamic input dimensions and the training/export size of 960 × 960 for inference. Input images are processed using aspect-ratio-preserving letterboxing rather than being stretched directly to a square.
evidence_items.title: DIIF - Trained Log-End Detection Models

evidence_items.summary: Safety-aligned language models often refuse a harmful request stated directly but answer the same request inside a role-play or narrative wrapper. We measure this vulnerability across languages and registers: attack success on Qwen3-1.7B is already 89.4% in English and 93.0% in modern Chinese, and reaches 95.7% in Classical Chinese. We build GUISE, a benchmark for systematically studying this vulnerability. It includes parallel requests in English, modern Chinese, and Classical Chinese, matched harmful and benign pairs, wrapper types held out for evaluation, and a stricter criterion that counts warn-then-answer responses as attack successes. Representation analysis shows that language and register move harmful-request representations only slightly away from the model's refusal direction, whereas narrative wrappers move them much farther away. We propose AXIS, which combines preference optimisation with a rotation objective that aligns harmful-request representations with the refusal direction and a commitment objective that trains the model to refuse completely rather than produce a warn-then-answer response. Across Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B and GLM-4-9B, AXIS achieves the highest combined safety and usability score among the compared methods.
evidence_items.title: How Narrative Wrapping Affects LLM Refusal: A Cross-Language Benchmark and Defense

evidence_items.summary: Open-ended scientific discovery often requires repeatedly proposing and evaluating candidate solutions. LLM-based systems can support this process by generating and refining executable solutions from verifier feedback. Methods such as TTT-Discover use test-time training (TTT) to update the solution-generating LLM from verifier feedback, adapting its generation policy to improve subsequent proposals on the target problem. However, this becomes expensive when reliable execution requires a large model, since training must maintain gradients, optimizer states, and policy statistics while repeatedly generating long, structured outputs. It also complicates credit assignment: outcome-level verifier feedback must jointly evaluate the high-level strategy and its low-level implementation. In this work, we introduce Guidance-TTT, which separates these roles. A compact guidance model is trained at test time to propose high-level strategic changes, while a frozen execution model implements them as complete executable solutions. At each step, the system selects a promising previously discovered solution, proposes a change, executes and verifies it, and updates only the guidance model using an adaptive group-relative RL objective. This concentrates test-time learning on short strategic decisions while retaining the implementation capability of a substantially stronger model without adapting it. Without web access, Guidance-TTT produces strong solutions across four distinct domains: combinatorial optimization (Polyomino Packing), heuristic programming (AHC058), machine learning (Lasso), and GPU kernel optimization (TriMul). Across these tasks, it outperforms the best solutions reported in prior work while remaining competitive with state-of-the-art results on public online leaderboards. Code is available at https://github.com/Human-Agent-Society/reef/tree/guidance-ttt-support.
evidence_items.title: Evolving in Thought Space: Training a Small Model at Test Time Unlocks Better Discoveries

evidence_items.summary: Soft state representations assign states nonnegative class weights that sum to one, but agreement with reference labels does not guarantee accurate prediction of the next weight vector. We derive lower confidence bounds on the minimum population root-mean-square prediction error over linear predictors with a prescribed spectral-norm limit. The bounds compare within-class successor variation with retained within-class input variation, with an alternative based on reference-label deviation. They are estimated from independent transition pairs without fitting a prediction matrix to the evaluation data. A bound above a chosen error tolerance excludes that accuracy for every admissible predictor at the stated confidence level; a bound of zero does not establish whether an accurate predictor exists. For coordinates constructed from Kernel Affine Hull Machine reconstruction scores, we relate the reference class's affinity advantage over competitors to label agreement. The class-centered population bound equals the optimum in a four-state example. Using 117,000 previously generated evaluation datasets from fixed four-state designs, we compare the finite-sample certificates with an empirical-risk-minimization baseline. For one Van der Pol representation selected before evaluation, the label-based bound is positive in all 64 independent evaluation datasets at the fitted matrix's spectral norm. Separately, exact matrix propagation under deterministic dynamics yields a Koopman interpretation of the coordinate-function span. The certificates help identify forecasting targets that cannot be reached by refitting a fixed representation within a specified predictor class and evaluation distribution.
evidence_items.title: Prediction Limits and Koopman Closure of Geometry-Induced Soft State Abstractions

evidence_items.summary: Automatic safety judges -- for example Llama Guard, or GPT-4o given a grading prompt -- produce the numbers behind reported jailbreak success rates, defense evaluations, and safety leaderboards. We ask whether these judges grade what a reply contains or how it sounds. We place a fixed piece of text before or after a model reply (a style wrapper) and leave the reply itself unchanged byte-for-byte, so any change in verdict is an error of the judge. Over 600 JailbreakBench replies (300 harmful, 300 refusals), 9 wrappers, and 8 judges, using paired tests and a measured per-judge repeat-disagreement rate (the noise floor), we find that most judges barely move but specific judges have specific, cheap blind spots. A token refusal ("I can't help with that") placed before the unchanged harmful text flips 19.9% of GPT-4o-mini's correct "unsafe" verdicts to "safe" (noise floor 0.5%; 18.2% under majority-of-three re-scoring), yet moves Claude only 0.4%. The deployed Llama Guard 4 guard model is evaded by an "educational course" preface on 12.3% of harmful replies, and the flips persist across repeats, while a second deployed guard (gpt-oss-safeguard-20b) is immune. Changing only the grading prompt to ignore tone cuts the GPT-4o-mini attack roughly tenfold on the same model, so the weakness lives in the judge, not in the content. Pure tone-only decoration that adds no new claim still flips up to 2.1% of verdicts on the vulnerable judges, several times their noise floors. On this artifact set the judges also disagree about which target model is safest, and a bootstrap shows the ranking is unstable before any wrapper is added. We release the data, wrappers, code, and per-verdict labels.
evidence_items.title: Style Over Substance: Content-Invariant Wrappers Flip LLM Safety-Judge Verdicts

evidence_items.summary: LLM-generated peer reviews are increasingly common at major venues, yet their deficiencies are hard to detect because they are uniformly fluent and well-structured. Existing work either classifies authorship without judging quality, or scores quality with features designed for human-written reviews; no prior system detects deficiencies in LLM-generated reviews at the level of individual defect types. To bridge the gap, we introduce TADDLE, a Tool-Augmented Agent for Detecting Deficient LLM-Generated Peer Reviews, together with the first expert-annotated benchmark for this task. Our benchmark comprises 1,800 reviews on 50 ICLR 2025 papers, multi-label-annotated by 18 domain experts against a taxonomy of six defect categories (plus a non-deficient label). TADDLE decomposes detection into four specialized analysis tools -- Verify, Correct, Complete, and Transform -- orchestrated by an agent; an integrator synthesizes their outputs into binary and multi-label classifications via two-stage semi-supervised learning. Experiments show that TADDLE performs strongly on binary detection and the multi-label classification task. We release the benchmark and code at https://github.com/AquariusAQ/TADDLE.
evidence_items.title: TADDLE: A Tool-Augmented Agent for Detecting Deficient LLM-Generated Peer Reviews

evidence_items.summary: In recent years, multilingual Large Language Models (LLMs) have become an inseparable part of daily life, making it crucial for them to master the rules of conversational language in order to communicate effectively with users. While previous work has evaluated LLMs' understanding of figurative language in high-resource languages, their performance in low-resource languages remains underexplored. In this paper, we introduce MasalBench, a comprehensive benchmark for assessing LLMs' contextual and cross-cultural understanding of Persian proverbs, which are a key component of conversation in this low-resource language. We evaluate eight state-of-the-art LLMs on MasalBench and find that they perform well in identifying Persian proverbs in context, achieving accuracies above 0.90. However, their performance drops considerably when tasked with identifying equivalent English proverbs, with the best model achieving 0.79 accuracy. Our findings highlight the limitations of current LLMs in cultural knowledge and analogical reasoning, and they provide a framework for assessing cross-cultural understanding in other low-resource languages. MasalBench is available at https://github.com/kalhorghazal/MasalBench.
evidence_items.title: MasalBench: A Benchmark for Contextual and Cross-Cultural Understanding of Persian Proverbs in LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Socio-economic causal effects depend heavily on their institutional and environmental contexts. The same intervention can produce different, even opposite, effects across regulatory regimes, market conditions, time periods, or populations. This poses a challenge for large language models (LLMs) in decision-support roles: can they infer the direction of a causal effect under a specified context, and revise that judgment when the context changes? To address this, we introduce EconCausal, a large-scale benchmark of 10,490 context-annotated causal triplets extracted from 2,595 high-quality empirical studies in top-tier economics and finance journals, constructed through a rigorous four-stage pipeline with multi-run consensus, context refinement, and multi-critic filtering. Across 19 models, we observe source-sign over-transfer in cross-context prediction. While top models reach ~84% accuracy in single-context prediction, mean accuracy is 74.75% overall but drops to 44.27% when source and target signs disagree. On these cases, accuracy is 11.54 percentage points (pp) lower with the signed source example than with the target input alone. Mean accuracy is below 60% under corrupted source signs. Models also struggle to predict study-reported nonsignificant effects (19.16% accuracy). The dataset and benchmark are publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/econcausal-benchmark-6F12.
evidence_items.title: EconCausal: A Context-Aware Economic Reasoning Benchmark for Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: We introduce Physics, a benchmark for evaluating foundation models on advanced physics problem solving. It contains 1034 annotated, open-ended problems from PhD-qualifying exams across six core physics domains. Solving these problems requires applying domain-specific knowledge to physical setups and carrying out multi-step mathematical reasoning. Each problem includes a worked solution and independently checked reference answers. An LLM-based grading protocol evaluates individual answers and complete multi-part problems, supporting numeric, symbolic, and text responses. We evaluate 53 proprietary and open-weight models. On test problems without figures, high accuracy is concentrated in a small group of thinking models, with the strongest open-weight models approaching proprietary performance. Most open-weight models still solve fewer than half of these problems. Our analysis of Qwen3.5-9B reveals failures in applying physics knowledge and interpreting figures, with misread figures affecting several subquestions.
evidence_items.title: Physics: Benchmarking Foundation Models on University-Level Physics Problem Solving

evidence_items.summary: AI agents are demonstrating increasingly strong offensive and defensive cybersecurity capabilities in the real world. Current benchmarks mostly evaluate agents in isolation against static targets. Real cyber operations, however, are dynamic and coupled: security postures constantly change as attackers and defenders adapt to each other in real time. Static benchmarks quickly saturate and miss an agent's ability to attack and defend simultaneously under live pressure. To address this gap, we present CyberArena, a dynamic, symmetric adversarial benchmark built around multi-round attack-and-defense combat. In isolated sandboxes, two agents compete under identical rules, acting concurrently as both attackers and defenders over continuously changing services. This converts static targets into evolving, semi-open challenges, directly testing an agent's speed and precision in discovering, exploiting, and patching vulnerabilities. To sustain the benchmark's longevity, an automated agentic pipeline continuously generates, reviews, and validates new environments. Furthermore, because pairwise contests are notoriously hard to quantify, we introduce a dynamical model that maps match dynamics into unified, multidimensional scores across offensive, defensive, and domain-specific capabilities. Evaluating 12 frontier LLM agents across 40 challenges in 466 matches, CyberArena separates model capabilities where single-agent baselines hit a ceiling. The trajectories read like a fight rather than an exam: defenders patch one hole and miss the next and certify repairs on stale evidence, while capable agents think a move ahead, planting backdoors for later rounds and, in one case, writing their own packet sniffer to watch the opponent. Beyond a benchmark, CyberArena serves as an adaptable, scalable experimental platform for future research on cybersecurity agents.
evidence_items.title: CyberArena: Benchmarking AI Agents in Live Symmetric Attack-and-Defense Combat

evidence_items.summary: "RFJ-Bench is a multimodal benchmark dataset for automated radiology report generation in rheumatology. It contains 2,239 finger joint posteroanterior (PA) X-ray examinations from 2,124 unique patients, retrospectively collected at Dazhou Central Hospital between October 2020 and March 2024 under an IRB-approved protocol with waived informed consent. Each case pairs a de-identified hand radiograph (8-bit grayscale PNG, longest side up to 1024 pixels, with Protected Health Information stripped from DICOM headers) with six structured clinical fields \u2014 chief complaint, history of present illness, past medical history, auxiliary examinations, primary diagnosis, and current diagnosis \u2014 plus patient sex and age at examination, and an expert-written reference diagnostic report produced by attending radiologists.Every clinical field and every reference report is provided in both the original Chinese and an English translation, and ready-to-train instruction files are supplied for two prompt scopes (six clinical fields, or chief complaint only) in both ms-swift and LLaVA-Rad formats.The cohort spans eight disease categories, with rheumatoid arthritis (n = 1,542) the largest, followed by undetermined arthralgia\/arthritis (n = 360), hand osteoarthritis (n = 253), and smaller groups of gouty arthritis, connective tissue disease-related arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis. The cohort comprises 1,709 female and 415 male patients (mean age 55.3 \u00b1 11.4 years, range 9\u201388).The dataset is partitioned at the patient level into training (70%), validation (10%), and test (20%) subsets by stratified random sampling over disease category (seed 42), yielding 1,572 \/ 221 \/ 446 images.

evidence_items.summary: Determining whether an image is AI-generated does not establish whether the situation it depicts is factually supported. We formulate Image Factuality Assessment: given an image and a generic verification instruction, a system returns a supported or refuted verdict with an evidence-grounded explanation. Without a supplied textual claim, the system must progressively refine factual questions during investigation and align external evidence with the specific situation depicted. We introduce EviLens, an expert-reviewed benchmark of 10,174 supported and refuted images from controlled construction and web collection, covering twelve factual error types and evaluating both verdict accuracy and evidence sufficiency. We develop EviScene, a multimodal ReAct agent that interleaves visual inspection, external retrieval, and evidence analysis, using new findings to refine its questions and revisit relevant image details. We train a compact policy with supervised fine-tuning on reviewed teacher trajectories, followed by privileged on-policy self-distillation applied to verified decisions from the policy's own investigations. On the 1,527-image test set, the trained Qwen3.5-9B agent achieves 79.05% balanced accuracy and a Strict Evidence Sufficiency Rate (SESR) of 52.26%, improving over the same-backbone base agent by 6.71 and 9.37 percentage points, respectively. Its SESR is the highest among the evaluated agents.Code, models, and data will be released at https://github.com/wangzian828/EVISCENE and https://huggingface.co/ZiAnwang/EviScene.
evidence_items.title: EviScene: Beyond "Is It AI?" for Agentic Image Factuality Assessment
