evidence_items.summary: As GUI agents are increasingly deployed for mobile task automation, their reliability depends not only on final task outcomes, but also on whether they reach these outcomes through stable interaction trajectories. In automation workflows, unnecessary actions, detours, and execution errors can add noise to collected data, introduce irreversible side effects, or undermine trust, even when the agent eventually completes the task. It is therefore important to systematically diagnose the execution stability, including whether an agent deviates from a feasible path, enters a loop, becomes stagnant, or recovers from unstable actions. Existing benchmarks, however, primarily assess final task success or a small set of intermediate milestones, leaving step-level execution behavior unclear. To bridge this gap, we introduce GraceBench, an online evaluation framework that represents the reachable interaction space of mobile applications as UI Transition Graphs (UTGs), providing a structural reference for step-level execution diagnosis. To support reliable alignment between dynamic UI observations and graph states, GraceBench uses video-grounded trajectory evaluation over this graph-aligned representation, assessing process stability beyond final success with metrics such as deviation rate, loop burden rate, and recovery ability. GraceBench contains 169 tasks spanning 10 applications and constructs 10 UTGs with 2,909 canonical GUI states and 3,116 observed transitions. Across 3,718 trajectories, GraceBench shows that outcome scores hide execution instability: GPT-5.6 Sol achieves the highest success rate (SR) but the lowest recovery ability, 51.24% of successful runs still contain a deviation or loop, and trajectories with the same success rate (SR) and completion rate (CR) can differ substantially in recovery behavior. Code and data will be released on https://iaie-physicalai.github.io/GraceBench.
evidence_items.title: How GUI Agents Fail: GraceBench for Execution Stability Diagnosis

evidence_items.summary: Pediatric speech and language assessment supports the early identification of communication difficulties and access to timely intervention. Large language models (LLMs) and related generative artificial intelligence technologies are increasingly being incorporated into systems that analyze children’s speech and language data. However, evidence regarding their application in pediatric assessment remains limited and fragmented. This scoping review aimed to map and critically examine research on LLM-enabled systems used to assess children’s speech, language, and communication abilities. Four databases were searched, and seven studies met the inclusion criteria. Data were charted according to study design, purpose, participant and target-population characteristics, assessment domain, type of LLM, model input, role of the LLM, additional artificial-intelligence components, evaluation methods, and reported outcomes. The findings provide preliminary evidence of technical feasibility and agreement with human or reference-based assessments. However, the evidence remains limited because of small or restricted datasets, the use of synthetic data in some cases, limited real-world validation, and concerns regarding fairness and generalizability across languages and clinical populations. Further research is necessary to establish clinical validity, reliability, and appropriate use of LLM-enabled systems before their broader implementation in pediatric speech and language assessment.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model-Enabled Systems for Pediatric Speech and Language Assessment: A Scoping Review

evidence_items.summary: Chemical language models (CLMs) are pretrained on large corpora of molecules with the aim of learning representations that transfer to diverse downstream tasks. Here, we systematically study the effects of pretraining using a series of such CLMs across 64 molecular property prediction datasets. We find that the downstream gains of pretraining in CLMs do not scale and performance saturates below gradient-boosting baselines. Across the regimes evaluated, only supervised pretraining on traditional physico-chemical descriptors consistently improves downstream performance for the CLMs tested whereas some forms of pretraining result in models worse than a randomly initialized encoder. While models can resolve molecular structure well, they do so no better than a randomly initialized model, suggesting that, at best, CLMs learn descriptor-like properties in addition to low-level token statistics during pretraining, but surprisingly little chemistry beyond what classical molecular features already capture.
evidence_items.title: Does Pretraining Teach Chemical Language Models Chemistry?

evidence_items.summary: Safety programs at research institutions, industrial facilities, and public agencies routinely accumulate tens of thousands of free-text observation records per year, documenting unsafe behaviors, near-misses, safety conversations, and best practices, yet these records are seldom analyzed beyond simple counts. We present SafeLens, an interactive system for AI-augmented exploratory analysis of large-scale organizational safety observation corpora. SafeLens addresses this gap through a four-stage pipeline: (1) multi-dimensional structured filtering over a Parquet-encoded corpus of 468,397 real safety records; (2) stratified adaptive sampling (SAQS) that guarantees representation of all interaction-type strata; (3) large language model (LLM) inference that returns ranked insight objects in three categories: riskiest behaviors, common patterns, and best practices; and (4) an interactive Streamlit dashboard with statistical charts, scrollable insight panels, a data viewer, and a conversational chat interface with persistent session memory. The demonstration allows users to issue live queries against the full corpus, inspect individual records, rate insight quality, and observe how the system’s sampling strategy affects result coverage. A built-in evaluation dashboard captures all human-AI interaction metrics in real time. A full demonstration of the system is presented in the supplementary video here1.
evidence_items.title: SafeLens: AI-Augmented Exploratory Analysis over Organizational Safety Records for Actionable Insights Generation

evidence_items.summary: Recent scientific language models achieve strong performance by scaling model size and training on large domain-specific corpora; however, they primarily rely on raw textual data and lack explicit mechanisms for knowledge abstraction and reuse. In this paper, we present StemForce-LM, a framework for transforming unstructured scientific literature into structured, reusable supervision for language model training. The proposed approach generates concept-conditioned question–answer pairs that decouple underlying principles from document-specific context, enabling cross-document knowledge integration. The framework consists of four stages: domain corpus curation via citation graph expansion and prompt filtering, concept-conditioned knowledge extraction through constrained prompting, information integration via Q/A-based fine-tuning, and evaluation using debiased pairwise comparisons. We evaluate the framework on a stem cell mechanobiology testbed (StemForce-LM) and demonstrate improved domain-specific reasoning accuracy, strong performance against substantially larger models. These results indicate that structured knowledge extraction provides an effective and scalable alternative to raw data scaling for advancing scientific language models.
evidence_items.title: From Fragmented Literature to Reusable Knowledge: Concept-Conditioned Information Integration through LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Academic genealogies are fragmented across proprietary dissertation records and crowdsourced resources with uneven coverage. Mainstream bibliographic databases do not encode advisor–advisee relationships. This study develops computational methods to infer advisor–advisee relationships from disambiguated PubMed coauthorship networks and bibliographic metadata, using dissertation records to establish ground truth. The work proceeds in three stages. First, an interpretable probabilistic logistic regression model, Model M, is trained on 3.2 million advisee–coauthor pairs, incorporating 53 contextual bibliometric features spanning academic age, authorship position, institutional affiliation, grant funding, demographics, citation behavior, and retraction history. Model M achieves Precision@1 and Recall@1 of 0.749 and recovers the true advisor among the top five candidates with over 95% Recall@5. Second, large language models, specifically gpt-5.4-nano and gpt-5.4-mini, are evaluated for advisor inference directly from publication metadata and for reranking Model M’s top candidates. LLMs demonstrate the ability to reason over bibliometric metadata at the paper level, although profile-level LLM reranking does not outperform Model M alone. Third, the best-performing approach will be applied to the full disambiguated PubMed corpus to produce a large-scale, discipline-diverse academic genealogy dataset.
evidence_items.title: Toward Contextual Mentorship Inference: Bibliometric Modeling and LLM-Informed Reasoning over Scholarly Publication Metadata

evidence_items.summary: Egocentric multimodal assistants see through the user's eyes and guide what the user does next, so their outputs directly shape physical actions, including those that affect bystanders. Yet existing safety evaluations do not distinguish whom a response would harm, and score only whether a model refuses. Pooling all harms into one refusal rate hides two failures: a model may protect one target but not another, and it may refuse without understanding the risk, or understand it and comply anyway. We present STOU, a benchmark of 2,902 egocentric video-audio and video-text queries whose potential harm targets the user (Self), co-present individuals (The Others), or society at large (Others). Our evaluation decouples safety understanding from refusal behavior: beyond refusal, we score whether the model recognizes the user's intent, the presence and target of harm, and its downstream consequences. Across 10 open and closed source omnimodal and multimodal LLMs, we find that refusal varies systematically with the harm target, and that models often recognize a harm yet still assist with it. These results show that refusal rates alone cannot certify an assistant as safe, and that safety alignment must account for who would be harmed. Project page: https://onedayoneyeah.github.io/safety-for-whom
evidence_items.title: Safety for Whom? Benchmarking Understanding Beyond Refusal in Egocentric Multimodal Assistants

evidence_items.summary: Pretraining generalist Earth observation foundation models requires data that combine several sensors, varied temporal sampling and, increasingly, text, yet open datasets rarely provide all three in one consistent, easily accessible form. We introduce MajorTOM:Elliot Pretrain, a collection of 279,166 tiles of 10 km drawn from the Major-TOM grid by clustering AlphaEarth embeddings. Each tile stacks Sentinel-2 L1C, Landsat-8/9, Sentinel-1 RTC, Copernicus DEM and ESA WorldCover on a shared 1056x1056-pixel, 10 m grid, complemented by cloud masks, OpenStreetMap entities and ERA5 weather. The tiles are partitioned into three temporal regimes, Monotemporal (250,000 tiles, one acquisition), Monthly (12,500 tiles, twelve acquisitions spread over the annual cycle) and Burst (16,666 tiles, six acquisitions within 30 days), and are released as 6.3 TB of Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs indexed by TACO v3 Parquet metadata, a standard that allows cloud streaming, efficient data access, and filtering before any pixel is read. A companion library derives sensor-tagged fact sheets, captions and 16 families of vision-language tasks from these layers at load time. We test our design choices in short pretraining runs of OlmoEarth-Base. First, a 25% subset of Major-TOM Core-S2L2A curated with AlphaEarth embeddings matches or exceeds the full corpus on 8 of 9 benchmarks. Second, on Elliot-Pretrain, adding Landsat-8/9 improves or matches Sentinel-2 only pretraining on every benchmark. Third, using DEM and WorldCover as prediction targets during pretraining further improves 8 of 9 benchmarks, while giving the same maps to the encoder as inputs degrades 5 of 9. Fourth, Sentinel-1 helps on 7 of 9 benchmarks, particularly on benchmarks with radar inputs. Fifth, rule-based captions match a small language model at no cost. The dataset is openly available at https://source.coop/major-tom/elliot-pretrain.
evidence_items.title: MajorTOM:Elliot Pretrain, A Multi-Sensor, Multi-Temporal Pretraining Dataset for Earth Observation

evidence_items.summary: We introduce LensErase, a general-purpose mask-based Erase Anything foundation model designed to cover a broad spectrum of real-world erase scenarios. LensErase supports diverse objects, visual text, watermarks, associated visual effects, multiple-object removal, and a wide range of object scales, aspect ratios, and image resolutions. First, to enable such broad coverage, we construct LensErase-100M, a large-scale dataset containing 101.07 million paired source-mask-target examples spanning diverse erase scenarios. Second, we pretrain LensErase from the text-to-image model Lens, adapting its strong generative prior to mask-based erasing. To efficiently incorporate the source image and erase mask, we propose Mask-Aware RoPE, a 3D rotary positional encoding that directly injects mask information into the source-image tokens without introducing a separate mask token sequence. Finally, we refine the model through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning with contract-guided, region-aware rewards, and apply TraceFusion at inference to preserve high-fidelity content outside the effective edit region. Across six public benchmarks and the proposed LensErase-Bench, LensErase achieves substantial improvements under both reference-based objective metrics and reference-free VLM evaluation. We hope LensErase can serve as a foundational model for erase-related applications and systems.
evidence_items.title: LensErase: A Foundation Model for Erase Anything

evidence_items.summary: How can we build an agent that thinks beyond human language, yet still acts through it in the external environment? Modern LLM agents still reason and interact through text, while latent reasoning offers an efficient internal medium but lacks native tool access and reasoning transparency. We bridge these two directions with Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents), which dynamically navigate between latent reasoning and text-based interaction throughout a unified generation process. Architecturally, a lightweight HybridLink enables seamless transitions between text and latent modes, while the agent's continuous working memory preserves lossless hybrid context across multiple turns. These designs preserve tool-integrated agentic capabilities while making latent thoughts directly inspectable. Building on this architecture, we further develop dedicated post-training algorithms for hybrid reasoning: HybridSFT stabilizes tool-integrated hybrid generation by teaching the backbone to coordinate with HybridLink, then HybridRL scales reasoning by learning when to think in latent space and when to act through text. We evaluate HybridAgent at 3 model scales across 11 benchmarks covering mathematics, science, medicine, search, and agentic reasoning. Compared with frontier LLM Agents and agentic frameworks spanning both text-based and latent methods, HybridAgent consistently improves performance by 10.4%, while delivering 35.5%-54.7% token reduction, 1.8x-2.6x faster inference, and 2.7x-3.7x cost savings. Code and data are available at https://github.com/togethercomputer/HybridAgent.
evidence_items.title: Hybrid Reasoning Agents

evidence_items.summary: Tool-call judges evaluate argument values proposed by LLM agents. We find that they accept a correct value less often when their input holds no reference for it, that is, no text that says what the value should be. This happens when the value is a default value from the function schema that the user did not mention, when it has to be inferred, or when the text it comes from was cut from the judge input. We call this drop in acceptance the derivation gap. It appears across all seven judges we evaluate, including System One models CLM and Jev. The gap is not only a truncation artifact: correct default values have the largest gap on a benchmark with no truncation. A controlled source-relocation test shows that judges follow the reference in their input: they favor a visible incorrect value over a correct value whose source is hidden. We introduce DeRef (Derived Reference): a separate model reads the full history without seeing the candidate and writes a reference for the judge. Across three benchmarks, DeRef improves overall argument AUROC for all judges tested. On the controlled test, it raises AUROC from chance or below to between 98.40 and 99.59.
evidence_items.title: Judges Follow the Reference: The Derivation Gap in Verifying Tool-Call Arguments

evidence_items.summary: Deep research (DR) agents address open-ended information needs through multi-step reasoning, long-horizon web search, and evidence synthesis. However, existing benchmarks primarily focus on academic research or synthetic tasks, leaving DR agents' capabilities in real-world life and professional productivity settings insufficiently evaluated. To bridge this gap, we introduce LifeSearch, a challenging benchmark comprising 203 Chinese and English tasks derived from real-user query seeds across 7 concrete life and productivity domains. With more than 4,500 hours of human annotation, we construct over 4,000 expert-written, fine-grained rubrics, covering both report-content criteria for coverage and accuracy and concrete criteria specifying values, units, dates, and URLs. We conduct extensive experiments on 12 advanced DR agents under a unified evaluation harness, systematically analyzing their performance patterns and failure modes. We find that even the best-performing frontier agent, GPT-5.6 Sol, achieves a score of only 63.4%, leaving substantial room for improvement on realistic life and professional DR tasks. We select the grading configuration by comparing candidate LLM judges against human rubric labels, and a human ranking study shows strong alignment between aggregate benchmark scores and human judgments (Spearman's ρ= 0.89, Kendall's τ= 0.81). LifeSearch provides a rigorous evaluation framework and foundation for advancing DR agents toward real-world life and productivity.
evidence_items.title: LifeSearch: Benchmarking Deep Research Agents for Real-World Life and Productivity

evidence_items.summary: LLM-based multi-agent collaboration is increasingly used to solve complex tasks by dividing work among specialized agents and integrating complementary expertise. Yet existing systems and evaluations largely rest on an implicit perfect-colleague assumption: collaborators provide correct and complete information and respond promptly to requests. In realistic teamwork, however, collaborators may return information that does not answer the intended question, provide insufficient detail to support a decision, or fail to respond to a request. To separate task-solving competence from the ability to recover an unreliable evidence-gathering process, we introduce the Unreliable Colleagues Benchmark (UnCoBench), which organizes behavioral failures through Misaligned, Incomplete, and Missed settings. The main agent need to verify contextual correctness, diagnose information gap and track unresolved dependencies in order to obtain the correct evidence for solving the task. We also introduce a verifiable and scalable automated generation pipeline that pairs LLM-based scenario generation with executable checks of answer uniqueness and role necessity. Results across ten models show that similar reliable-setting performance can result in different robustness to unreliable evidence. Trace analysis reveals frequent omissions of corrective follow-up, and the recovery behavior involves inefficient waiting and redundant queries. These findings show that robust collaboration requires not only sound reasoning, but also targeted action to diagnose evidence failures, recover relevant information, and integrate it into decisions. Our data and source code are available at https://github.com/iNLP-Lab/UnCoBench.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Perfect Teammates: Multi-Agent Collaboration with Unreliable Colleagues

evidence_items.summary: Recent years have witnessed rapid progress in joint audio--visual generation. However, audio--visual synchronization remains a challenge, as generated speech and sound often temporally misalign with visual events. A key bottleneck is the lack of human-annotated data, reliable evaluation benchmarks, and synchronization-aware evaluation models for generated audio--visual outputs. To address these limitations, we conduct a comprehensive study spanning data, benchmarking, and reward modeling. We first introduce SyncReward-Data-80K, a dataset containing 80K professional synchronization ratings for clips from eight audio--visual generators. A taxonomy-guided construction pipeline covers four sound-event families: Speech, Onset, Instrument, and Ambient. We further construct SyncReward-Bench, a held-out benchmark of 1K clips, each independently rated by multiple professionals. Using this benchmark, we systematically evaluate specialized synchronization metrics and omni-modal models, revealing their substantial misalignment with human judgments. Finally, we develop SyncReward, a reward model that combines semantic--temporal contrastive pretraining on real clips with human supervision on generated clips. As an evaluation metric, SyncReward achieves the strongest agreement with human ratings among the evaluated methods. As a reward, it improves synchronization through inference-time best-of-N selection and reinforcement learning based post-training. We will release the data, benchmark, model, and code at https://github.com/WeChatCV/SyncReward.
evidence_items.title: SyncReward: Human-Aligned Synchronization Reward for Audio-Visual Generation

evidence_items.summary: AI coding agents now write much of the code that ships, yet whether that code is secure remains unclear. We introduce the Last Secure Code Benchmark, a comprehensive evaluation of secure code generation by coding agents. Built from 150 real vulnerabilities, its 450 tasks span seven widely used languages (Java, C, C++, JavaScript, Python, PHP, and Go), 24 CWEs including 21 of the 2025 CWE Top 25 and 8 of the Top 10 KEV weaknesses, more than any benchmark we compare with, and three vibe-coding scenarios: filling in a function, writing a file, and building a repository's source tree from scratch. Every task asks only for functionality, through a specification that never mentions security, and hidden functional and security tests grade the result. Across six frontier agents, 73.6% to 91.3% of tasks pass functionally, yet even the strongest, Claude Fable 5, produces code that is both functional and secure for only 25.1% of tasks, and the others for 16.4% to 24.7%. The best model only passes 12% of the vulnerability scenarios across all vibe coding setting, posing strong concern on the security of the code written by vibe coding.
evidence_items.title: Last Secure Code Benchmark: Is the Code You Vibe Secure?

evidence_items.summary: Understanding and tracking a dynamic world are fundamental to visual intelligence. Existing video benchmarks provide limited insight into whether models can maintain a coherent understanding of evolving world state. Building such a benchmark from real-world videos is challenging because the underlying world state is partially observable, making annotations hard to obtain. To close this gap, we introduce Video-Arena, a benchmark that turns competitive games into scalable, verifiable tests of how well models understand evolving world states from videos. Specifically, inspired by how humans understand dynamic events, we evaluate spatiotemporal world state understanding and tracking through three task categories: perceiving critical events, interpreting state updates, and tracking the resulting states. Our pipeline can generate videos and aligned reference labels from game records at scale. To keep evaluation affordable and reproducible, we curate a golden set of 180 tasks across 9 games and run evaluations under two protocols: native visual understanding and tool-assisted agentic analysis. The best-performing systems achieve F1 scores of and under the two protocols, respectively. The result highlights that native models struggle to perceive events reliably, while tool-assisted systems improve event recovery but still struggle to interpret state updates and track the resulting states consistently over time. Our project page is in https://videoarena-bench.github.io
evidence_items.title: Video-Arena: A Scalable Agentic Video Benchmark for Spatiotemporal Capability

evidence_items.summary: As robotic hardware and learning methods advance, humanoids need tools to perform tasks beyond their inherent physical limits. Successful tool use requires selecting a suitable tool and coordinating manipulation and, when needed, locomotion to complete the task. Existing benchmarks do not jointly evaluate these capabilities on a humanoid. We introduce HumanoidToolBench, an 18-task benchmark spanning three scenarios, three execution levels, and two tool-set modes, together with ToolBook, a dataset of 3.1k demonstrations collected in simulation and on a real Unitree G1. Evaluation of seven policies in simulation and three on the real robot reveals substantial gaps between selecting a suitable tool and completing the task. Focused GR00T N1.7 probes show reduced selection accuracy on unseen tools and continued task execution under unrelated instructions. Code and data are available at https://snu-pi.github.io/HumanoidToolBench/.
evidence_items.title: HumanoidToolBench: Benchmarking Humanoid Tool Use from Selection to Mobile Execution

evidence_items.summary: This dataset presents the raw data from the project "Monitoring Success in Natural Forest Reserves, Canton Aargau", which documents the early ecological state of 18 selected Natural Forest Reserves in the Canton of Aargau, Switzerland. It establishes a baseline for future success control, capturing the status approximately 20 to 40 years after management cessation. The project uses a paired comparison design across the 18 reserves and adjacent managed forests serving as reference areas. Data collected between 2015 and 2023 cover three ecologically relevant organism groups: wood-inhabiting fungi, saproxylic beetles and bats. Species were surveyed by identification of fungal fruiting bodies, Polytrap flight-intersection traps and bioacoustic recording. The biodiversity data are linked with metrics of forest habitat quality: quantity and quality of standing and lying deadwood (decay stage, size, orientation), canopy closure, shrub cover and the diameter of the largest living trees. The data are organised in five interlinked tables following the Darwin Core standard and provided as UTF-8 encoded CSV. NWR-Aargau dataset-metadata.xlsx documents every variable and follows the metadata template of Annals of Forest Science. README dataset.md describes the file structure and the conventions used.
evidence_items.title: Data on Early Biodiversity Responses (Saproxylic Fungi and Beetles, Bats) to Management Cessation in Temperate Forest, Canton Aargau, Switzerland (2015–2023)

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Objective To characterise the reporting completeness of clinical trials involving large language model (LLM) interventions using established reporting guidelines. Design Systematic review and meta-research analysis. Data sources Bibliographic databases (Embase, Medline, and CENTRAL) were searched for trial reports and protocols, and trial registries (ClinicalTrials.gov and World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform) were searched for trial registrations published from 1 January 2017 to 6 December 2025. Eligibility criteria Trial reports, trial protocols, and trial registrations describing clinical trials of LLM interventions in medicine. LLM interventions used for a healthcare function in a clinical trial setting included patient education, clinical documentation, communication support, triage, care navigation, management recommendations, or clinical decision support. Eligible studies prospectively assigned human participants to the intervention and evaluated a health related biomedical or behavioural outcome. Main outcome measures Overall study level and item level reporting completeness assessed using reporting guidelines matched to study design and purpose, including TRIPOD-LLM (Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis Or Diagnosis—LLM), CONSORT (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials) 2025 and CONSORT-AI, SPIRIT (Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials) 2025 and SPIRIT-AI, CHART (Chatbot Assessment Reporting Tool), and the WHO Trial Registration Dataset (version 1.3.1). Two reviewers independently screened and extracted trial and intervention characteristics, and three calibrated raters assessed item level reporting completeness. Results The systematic search yielded 461 records, including 68 trial reports, 15 protocols, and 378 registrations.
evidence_items.title: Reporting completeness of clinical trials evaluating large language model interventions in medicine: systematic review

evidence_items.summary: Processing technical terms in documents is essential for digital libraries and knowledge organisation, supporting applications such as scholarly search, information retrieval, and domain terminology construction. While document-level term identification, a sub-task of automatic term extraction (ATE), has been tackled as a sequence labelling task, the emergence of large language models (LLMs) opens new avenues for prompt-based extraction. However, evaluation practices have persistently relied on simple success or failure against a single gold standard, without analysing how model behaviours align with human annotations, especially on borderline cases where annotators disagree. To address this issue, this study investigates to what extent LLMs can perform term identification using prompt instructions mirroring human annotator conditions. By evaluating multiple commercial and open-weight LLMs against double human annotations in ACL RD-TEC 2.0, an ATE benchmark, we show that LLMs achieve performance close to human annotators (up to 76.6% F1, within 5 percentage points of the inter-human agreement of 81.6%), with open-weight 30B-scale models outperforming larger commercial counterparts. Crucially, our analysis reveals a distinctly conservative nature: LLMs reliably extract terms on which humans consistently agree, but omit terms on which humans disagree. Our findings reveal the limitations of relying on a single gold standard, highlighting the need for annotator-aligned prompting and controllable precision–recall tuning.
evidence_items.title: Can Large Language Models Identify Technical Terms in Documents Like Human Annotators?

evidence_items.summary: Background Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate medical assessment items, but their reliability for disease-specific question writing remains uncertain. We benchmarked seven LLMs for epilepsy single-best-answer multiple-choice question generation under a standardized blueprint, focusing on structural compliance, clinical accuracy, expert-rated quality and educational usability. Methods Each model completed the same 60 prespecified tasks spanning foundational knowledge, clinical cases, treatment decision-making, and diagnostic evaluation and longitudinal management, yielding 420 questions. Tasks were delivered through an identical single-turn prompt without model-specific optimization, web search or external tools. Objective evaluation assessed structural compliance, keyed-answer accuracy, textual characteristics and response time. Two blinded clinical reviewers independently rated content rigor, clarity, distractor quality, educational usefulness, cognitive alignment and overall usability on five-point scales. Results After one standardized corrective prompt, all 420 questions met structural requirements, although first-pass compliance ranged from 83.33% to 100%. Keyed-answer accuracy varied substantially, from 61.67% to 98.33%, with Claude-5 achieving the highest accuracy. GPT-5.6 obtained the highest composite expert score (median, 3.75), followed by Claude-5 (3.67) and Kimi-K3 (3.50). Distractor quality was a common limitation, with median scores of only 2–3 across models. Only 2 of 420 questions (0.48%) were judged directly usable without revision, both generated by GPT-5.6; 119 (28.33%) were usable after minor revision and 299 (71.19%) required substantial revision. Longer outputs were associated with better cognitive alignment but not with content rigor or clarity, while response time was unrelated to overall usability.
evidence_items.title: Leveraging large language models to generate multiple-choice questions for epilepsy education

evidence_items.summary: Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) plays a central role in global food and nutritional security, but its productivity is challenged by biotic and abiotic stresses. Its large, polyploid genome and extensive repetitive sequences complicate the identification of genetic variation and the dissection of complex agronomic traits. This review examines emerging genomic resources and the complementary contributions of transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics and epigenomics to wheat improvement. High-throughput genotyping platforms, including SNP arrays, genotyping-by-sequencing and DArTseq, facilitate genetic diversity analysis and the identification of genomic regions associated with agronomic traits. Pan-genome approaches extend analyses beyond a single reference assembly by capturing structural, copy-number and presence–absence variation. Functional omics studies provide information on transcriptional regulation, protein responses, metabolite accumulation and chromatin-associated mechanisms involved in development and stress adaptation. The review also considers the use of artificial intelligence and machine learning for integrating complex datasets, predicting yield-related traits, automating phenotypic assessment and supporting genomic selection. Examples from wheat demonstrate the potential value of combining molecular information with computational approaches, although the reliability of predictions depends on data quality, representation and appropriate validation. Together, these advances provide complementary tools for identifying candidate genes and interpreting genotype–phenotype relationships. Their integration with reliable phenotypic information and established breeding practices may support more efficient wheat improvement while acknowledging the technical and biological challenges of translating molecular findings into breeding outcomes.
evidence_items.title: Advancing Wheat Improvement through Multi-Omics and Artificial Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Modern computer-aided synthesis planning (CASP) tools, particularly retrosynthesis planning, are becoming practical aids for the ideation stage of chemical synthesis design. However, the same target molecule can be synthesized via substantially different routes depending on the purpose: a discovery or medicinal chemistry route used to obtain small quantities during early development, or a manufacturing route optimized for industrial-scale production. While CASP tools have been extensively studied and benchmarked for the former, their ability to support manufacturing route design remains largely unexplored. Performance of CASP tools is usually measured by benchmark experiments, which typically report the fraction of target molecules for which a tool can generate a synthesis route, connecting the target molecule through a sequence of intermediates to starting materials. Sometimes, to assess the quality of the generated routes, they are also manually compared with expert-designed routes reported in the literature. Currently, public benchmark datasets focused on process and manufacturing chemistry are lacking. In this study, we take a first step in this direction by analyzing one of the main sources of process chemistry research, the Organic Process Research & Development (OPRD) journal. We reviewed OPRD papers published between 1997 and 2022 and selected 2507 papers reporting multi-step synthesis routes. We then separately collected and digitized the target molecules of corresponding synthesis routes as SMILES strings. This resulted in a collection of 2219 unique target molecules, each paired with the DOI of the original publication reporting their corresponding synthesis route. This benchmark can therefore be used to assess how many process-chemistry targets modern CASP tools can solve and, for solved targets, to compare predicted routes with the expert-designed routes reported in the literature.
evidence_items.title: Digitalizing Manufacturing Chemistry Targets: A Benchmark for Retrosynthesis Tools

organizations: Automatics Research Group, Department of Engineering, Universidad Tecnológica de Pereira (UTP), Pereira 660003, Colombia
evidence_items.summary: Background/Objectives: Predicting time-to-conversion from mild cognitive impairment (MCI) to Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a critical clinical challenge. Most survival analyses rely on static baseline variables, ignoring the temporal dynamics of serial neuroimaging. We benchmark seven survival model families using a novel temporal MRI descriptor pipeline on ADNI. Methods: A cohort of 661 MCI patients (250 conversion events, 37.8%, median follow-up 42.0 months) was constructed from ADNI. FreeSurfer volumetrics of six brain regions were summarised into three time-based descriptors each (atrophy rate, trajectory variability σ, and time-weighted cumulative mean μ) under strict anti-leakage constraints, yielding 18 neuroimaging features which, combined with six clinical variables (age, sex, education, MMSE, ADAS-13, and APOE-ε4), form a 24-dimensional covariate vector. Cox PH, Weibull AFT, Exponential, RSF, GBST, DeepSurv, and DeepHit were evaluated under stratified 5-fold cross-validation and assessed on an independent OASIS-3 cohort (n=78) as an exploratory analysis. Results: All seven models achieved C-index 0.853–0.863 (Δ=0.010), with Cox PH reaching 0.863±0.027 using only routine structural MRI. Time-dependent AUC ranged from 0.856 (12 months) to 0.938 (48 months). Risk stratification by quartile yielded highly separated Kaplan-Meier curves (log-rank p<0.001). On OASIS-3 (n=78, exploratory), classical models showed preliminary cross-cohort consistency (Weibull AFT 0.760±0.063, RSF 0.759±0.049), while deep learning degraded substantially (DeepSurv 0.551±0.116); these results are hypothesis-generating and should not be interpreted as confirmatory given the small per-fold sample size (EPV ≈ 1). Conclusions: The temporal MRI descriptor pipeline achieves a C-index of 0.863 using only routine structural MRI, without PET or CSF biomarkers, demonstrating strong discriminative performance on ADNI MCI-to-AD conversion.
evidence_items.title: Predicting MCI-to-Alzheimer’s Conversion: A Systematic Benchmark of Classical, Machine Learning, and Deep Survival Models

evidence_items.summary: Accurate and computationally efficient inverse kinematics is a fundamental requirement for industrial manipulators in intelligent manufacturing, where positioning, assembly, and handling demand reliable pose computation under nonlinear constraints. However, the inverse mapping of six-degree-of-freedom manipulators may admit multiple solutions, become ill-conditioned near singularities, or violate joint limits, while metaheuristic comparisons rely on heterogeneous protocols emphasizing best-run results. Herein, a statistical benchmark of five metaheuristics is presented for solving the inverse kinematics of a UR3 manipulator: Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES), Multi-Verse Optimizer (MVO), Non-Dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II), Salp Swarm Algorithm (SSA), and Whale Optimization Algorithm (WOA). A master–slave architecture separates the stochastic search from a deterministic evaluator that computes an unweighted full-pose residual subject to joint bounds and a Jacobian-determinant screening penalty. Three poses represent reoriented, nominal-height, and near-singular upper-workspace conditions, each assessed over 1000 independent runs with fixed algorithm settings. Nonparametric tests are interpreted with Cliff’s Δ effect sizes. The results reveal distinct accuracy–time trade-offs: CMA-ES obtains the smallest best-run objective at modest runtimes, MVO yields the smallest mean objective but the longest runtimes, and WOA is the fastest with higher residuals. The findings support algorithm selection for offline inverse-kinematics computation and supervisory robotic planning.
evidence_items.title: Soft Computing Optimization of Industrial Robot Inverse Kinematics for Intelligent Manufacturing: A Statistical Benchmark of Metaheuristic Algorithms

evidence_items.summary: In this study, a high-fidelity multi-physics framework was established through the direct link between the continuous energy Monte Carlo (MC) neutronics code McCARD and the subchannel thermal-hydraulic (T/H) analysis code MATRA. A relaxation scheme suppressed numerical oscillations due to the stochastic nature of the MC method and ensured stable convergence of the Picard iteration. The SMART benchmark problems served to evaluate the accuracy and numerical stability of the developed system through a stepwise verification procedure. First, closed-channel calculations assessed the physical consistency of the fundamental T/H models in the two codes. The subsequent open-channel calculations quantified the effects of cross-flow and turbulent inter-channel exchange. The numerical results show that explicit consideration of lateral heat and mass transfer between adjacent subchannels substantially reduces local coolant-temperature peaks and produces temperature distributions that more closely represent the relevant physical phenomena. The coupled framework also captures distinct pin-wise power variations, particularly near the periphery, due to subchannel-scale T/H feedback that the single-physics model does not account for. Consequently, this study demonstrates that the McCARD/MATRA external multi-physics code system can represent the multi-physics phenomena required for high-fidelity safety analyses and provides a reliable technical basis for SMR design optimization.
evidence_items.title: Multi-Physics Analysis of SMART Small Modular Reactor Benchmark Problems Using the Coupled McCARD/MATRA Code System

evidence_items.summary: Machine-learning and deep-learning models are increasingly applied to financial-market forecasting, yet their reported accuracy is often measured in price levels and rarely tested against a stringent benchmark under changing market conditions. It therefore remains unclear whether added model complexity delivers genuine, resilient predictive value or merely reflects the persistence of the underlying price series. This study addresses that gap by evaluating one-day-ahead gold-price forecasts within a transparent, leakage-resistant, benchmark-centred framework during a major structural regime shift. Using daily COMEX gold futures (2014–2026), we compare Ridge Regression, SVR-RBF, Random Forest, GARCH(1,1), and a bidirectional LSTM against a naïve random walk, with ARIMA and exponential-smoothing benchmarks, using strictly chronological splitting, training-only preprocessing, a return-space target, and two-sided and one-sided Diebold–Mariano tests. Structural-break analysis confirms a pronounced regime shift, with the gold price rising from roughly USD 1051 to USD 5318/oz and volatility breaks falling inside the out-of-sample period. All models attain near-unity price-level R2 but non-positive return-space R2, and none of the flexible models significantly outperforms the naïve benchmark; only a heavily regularised linear model shows a marginal one-sided edge attributable to gold’s upward drift rather than to learned structure, while GARCH’s contribution lies in calibrated uncertainty rather than point accuracy. Increasing model complexity did not yield resilient incremental predictive value, and the study offers a reproducible template for benchmark-based evaluation of forecasting systems.
evidence_items.title: Financial Resilience Under a Major Gold-Price Regime Shift: A Benchmark-Based Assessment of Machine Learning, Deep Learning, and Econometric Models

evidence_items.summary: Human-robot collaboration has relied on task models that are specified in advance for each product. Embodied foundation models and agentic artificial intelligence change this premise, because a robot can now interpret an open goal, plan, act, monitor the outcome and recover from failure. This review examines what that change means for collaboration. A critical narrative review was conducted over 231 sources. Embodied intelligence, agentic intelligence, autonomy and collaboration are distinguished, and four collaboration modes are defined by the roles of the human and the robot. Four system architectures are compared: modular agentic, end-to-end embodied, hierarchical agentic embodied, and human-centred shared autonomy. Six groups of enabling technologies and five collaboration mechanisms, from autonomy allocation to failure recovery, are analysed. Applications in six domains, from manufacturing to domestic service, are assessed by the maturity of their evidence. Reported systems are validated mainly on single cells and short tasks, human factors are measured in few studies, and verified safety layers remain separate from learned reasoning. An evaluation framework and research directions for seven open challenges are proposed. The review gives researchers and system builders a basis for bringing embodied and agentic AI into human-robot collaboration and for evaluating the systems that result.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Embodied AI for Human–Robot Collaboration: Architectures, Technologies, and Future Directions

evidence_items.summary: Selecting which large language model to trust for querying a digitised historical collection is a concrete, unresolved problem for digital libraries. This is not only a collection-level question: model performance is highly heterogeneous even within a single collection, varying from page to page as layout, language, and content type shift, so that no single model can be trusted uniformly across a collection’s pages. We demonstrate, in this paper, an interactive tool for exploring the benchmark and the multi-model evaluation underlying our companion paper on adaptive LLM selection for historical document question answering. The demonstration exposes, page by page, 5,941 scanned pages of the Chinese Economic Journal (1923-1937), 84,441 multiple-choice questions automatically generated from them and the resulting 50 × 5, 941 binary correctness matrix obtained by evaluating 50 open-source LLMs. Rather than presenting model heterogeneity only through aggregate statistics, the demonstrator lets practitioners and researchers inspect, for any page and any question, which of the 50 models answered correctly and which did not, directly grounding the case for adaptive model routing in observable evidence. We describe the resource the demo is built on, walk through the views of the tool, and outline usage scenarios for digital humanists, historians, NLP researchers as well as digital library practitioners.
evidence_items.title: An Interactive Tool for Exploring Multi-LLM Correctness on Bilingual Historical Digitised Documents

evidence_items.summary: Educational digital libraries may grant large language model (LLM) tutors access to worked solutions, but access to repository content should not automatically authorize a model to reveal final answers. This study evaluates whether LLM tutors can leverage private solution context to generate pedagogical hints without disclosing final answers to students. Four models, two general instruction-following models and two math-specialized models, are evaluated across 5,000 aligned problem–message cases per condition, constructed from 500 MATH benchmark problems paired with ten fixed student prompts that ask for, or attempt to confirm, the final answer. Three prompting strategies are compared: a plain assistant prompt, a basic tutoring prompt, and a two-step method that generates a private solution before producing numbered hints. The basic tutoring prompt reduces detected answer leakage from 47.4% to 0.3% for GPT-4o-mini and from 30.2% to 1.0% for LLaMA-3.1, but produces no comparable improvement for Qwen2.5-Math or DeepSeek-Math. Under identical strict hint rules, adding private solution context has minimal effect on GPT but significantly improves tutoring compliance for LLaMA; Qwen produces the most accurate private solutions yet shows the highest leakage and solution-to-hint overlap. These results indicate that private solution access can support hint generation in some architectures but is not a reliable answer-withholding mechanism on its own. For educational digital libraries, access to solution content and authorization to disclose it should be treated as distinct access-control decisions.
evidence_items.title: Strong Solvers, Leaky Tutors: Evaluating Answer Leakage in LLM Math Tutors

evidence_items.summary: Large language model agents can follow complex human instructions to solve real-world tasks. In practice, however, initial instructions are often incomplete. In our analysis of 100 user-agent trajectories from SWE-chat, 56\% of initial instructions omit requirements that later emerge as necessary, and 52\% of the useful follow-up requirements could have been inferred from the project. A user states requirements from their own understanding of the task, and these \textbf{stated requirements} often differ from the \textbf{true requirements} that completing the task imposes. An agent should therefore treat the instruction as evidence rather than as the objective, inferring the true requirements from the instruction and the environment and satisfying them even when the user is not yet aware of all of them. We call this ability \textbf{outcome alignment}. In this work, we construct \textbf{TiGanEval}, a benchmark of software engineering and research tasks. In every task the user genuinely lacks part of the requirements, each requirement stays discoverable from the code and runtime behaviour of the environment, and requirements the agent infers are separated from those the user adds after observing delivered work. These properties together make outcome alignment measurable. Evaluating eight frontier models including GPT-5.6-Sol, we find outcome alignment broadly missing: the models lose 53 to 67 points of success rate when moving from the full specification to the partial instruction, and consequence feedback across four submissions does not close the gap. Furthermore, a plan-mode harness cannot compensate for the missing ability of the model itself, which places outcome alignment among the abilities the next generation of models should be developed for.
evidence_items.title: Instructions Are Evidence, Not Objectives: Measuring Outcome Alignment of Agents

evidence_items.summary: Post-training quantisation reduces the memory cost of large language models, but it remains unclear whether compression preserves language skills of regional varieties as reliably as their standard-language counterparts. We study this question for Bavarian, Standard German, and English using BAVGROUND, a multiple-choice benchmark, where 206 source questions are aligned across all three languages. Across 14 open-weight 7B--10B instruction models, we compare BF16 with 8-bit GPTQ and two 4-bit settings, GPTQ and AWQ. Eight-bit GPTQ remains close to BF16 and largely preserves the relative behaviour of the three languages, while 4-bit quantisation was found to be much less stable. The two 4-bit methods reduce average accuracy by about 1.4--1.5 percentage points and change 11.9--16.0% of BF16 decisions, with changes concentrated on examples where the BF16 model is already uncertain. This instability does not translate into a consistent Bavarian disadvantage. Although Bavarian, a low-resource dialect, has lower baseline accuracy than German and English, the language most affected at 4 bits varies across models and quantisation methods. Calibration further shapes these cross-language effects: the relative Bavarian--German effect changes with calibration language, while changing the calibration source has little average effect on GPTQ-4 but can affect AWQ-4 much more strongly. Free-form evaluation on five models further shows that 4-bit compression can degrade generated responses even in settings where multiple-choice accuracy changes only modestly, while 8-bit GPTQ remains comparatively stable. Overall, our results show that quantisation robustness for regional language varieties depends on the model, quantisation method, calibration data, and evaluation setting, and cannot be measured by aggregate multilingual accuracy alone.
evidence_items.title: Lightweight but Linguistically Fair? Quantisation Robustness across Bavarian, German, and English

evidence_items.summary: Soil organic carbon (SOC) is an indicator of agricultural soil condition and carbon storage, but numerical outputs from large language models (LLMs) require validation before use in monitoring or management. We evaluated seven general-purpose LLM configurations on three direct-response tasks: estimating 0--10 cm SOC concentrations for 308 Australian paddocks under two information conditions, calculating SOC stock in 120 matched scenarios, and comparing 300 paddock pairs. References were measured SOC records or deterministic calculations; response validity, repeated-call dispersion and estimated API cost were assessed separately. Additional measured soil attributes reduced concentration mean absolute error by 13--62\% across configurations, although high-SOC underprediction and paddock-specific errors persisted. Six configurations were highly accurate in stock calculations using equation-native units without coarse fragments, but accuracy declined with physically equivalent alternative units. Pairwise accuracy was 90.5--94.6\% overall and 59.1--70.9\% for 52 closely separated pairs; some configurations were sensitive to presentation order. Nearly all outputs were parseable, without necessarily being correct. The benchmark identifies three distinct requirements for AI-mediated SOC assessment: agreement with measured concentrations, unit-consistent stock calculations and reliable discrimination between sites. These findings support task-specific validation and auditable calculations, rather than unverified use of LLM outputs as ecological evidence.
evidence_items.title: How Reliable Are Large Language Models for Soil Organic Carbon Assessment? An Australian Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Background: Recent work has brought large language models (LLMs) into clinical variant interpretation. In most existing approaches, the model is confined to text-level operations, retrieving, extracting, compacting, and summarizing heterogeneous evidence, while the genuine genetic evaluation is delegated to a separate deterministic engine. Other tools employ LLMs to mine functional evidence for a single ACMG criterion, to rerank a classifier's output, or to answer isolated variant questions. Integrative genetic reasoning, by contrast, demands multi-source evidence weighing for each variant, reconciliation of inheritance with observed zygosity and parental genotypes, joint interpretation of variants in the same gene, and the derivation of a case-level conclusion. Moreover, to protect patient privacy, this must be done on hospital premises. Methods: o build an end-to-end variant interpreter that runs on local infrastructure, we benchmarked 13 small language models (SLMs) on 150 multiple-choice genetics questions and selected Qwen3.5-9B. In IVA (Intelligent Variant Analyser), a four-stage pipeline, the model assigns ACMG/AMP criteria, applies de novo, dominant, recessive, and X-linked inheritance logic to trios, and writes a structured report, while deterministic code handles retrieval, phasing, point summation, citation checking, and formatting. We evaluated IVA on synthetic scenarios, 16 solved trios, and 327 solved singleton cases of visual impairment, on a single GPU. Results: On the benchmark, Qwen3.5-9B reached a mean accuracy of 0.81, compared with 0.89 for a 1.6-trillion-parameter cloud model. In the 16 trios, IVA reported every previously identified pathogenic, likely pathogenic, or uncertain-significance variant of interest (sensitivity 100%; precision 39.5%). In the 327 singleton cases, it recovered 93% of the expert-reported causative variants and classified 82% of them as pathogenic or likely pathogenic (precision 43%). Failures fell into four recurrent classes: omission, unverified mechanism, mismatch between reasoning and label, and arithmetic errors. Conclusions: A small language model running on local hardware can serve as the reasoning layer for case-level and trio-based variant interpretation when it is surrounded by deterministic safeguards. Because its outputs are not deterministic, analyst review and prospective multicenter validation remain necessary.
evidence_items.title: IVA, a locally deployable Intelligent Variant Analyser based on a small language model for complete case-level and trio-based genomic interpretation.

evidence_items.summary: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have attracted increasing research attention due to their bidirectional attention and arbitrary order decoding. However, there are two issues in dLLMs inference: the decoding difficulty is dominated by the tokens on the right side of the block, and the block-wise decoding inherently suffers from boundary contextual discontinuity. To tackle these limitations, we propose HaloBlock, a difficulty-aware adaptive halo mechanism for dLLM inference. We first leverage bidirectional cumulative entropy to characterize block decoding difficulty. Then, based on the bidirectional decoding difficulty, we adaptively allocate bidirectional halo regions on both sides of each block to mitigate boundary contextual discontinuity. The difficulty-aware design of HaloBlock smooths cross-block context propagation and lowers decoding difficulty for hard tokens, yielding better generation quality and faster convergence. Evaluated on LLaDA-8B-Instruct, Dream-7B-Instruct and LLaDA-1.5 across mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks, HaloBlock demonstrates consistent accuracy improvements and higher inference efficiency. Source codes are publicly available at https://github.com/PolyU-VCLab/HaloBlock.
evidence_items.title: HaloBlock: Faster and Better Decoding for Diffusion Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary:
OBJECTIVES
Large language models (LLMs) have the potential to be integrated into diagnostics workflows, yet their reliability in pre-analytical diagnostic stewardship remains uncertain. We aimed to evaluate the performance of six LLMs answering common pre-analytical questions in the domain of medical microbiology. Next, we propose a blueprint to evaluate LLMs in medical microbiology.


METHODS
We compared general-purpose models from OpenAI (GPT-3.5, GPT-4) and Meta AI (Llama2-7B, Llama2-13B), alongside two domain-enhanced versions (customised GPT-4 agent and Llama2-7B Medical) in a hybrid evaluation framework. First, we quantified the response length (word count), then assessed the similarity between LLM-generated responses and expert-reviewed reference answers (BLEU/ROUGE scores, BERTScore). Finally, thirty-three medical professionals rated the accuracy and completeness of the LLM-generated responses on a 1-7-point scale.


RESULTS
Responses of OpenAI models showed greater similarity to the reference set and significantly outperformed Meta AI-based models in accuracy and completeness. The customized generative pre-trained transformer (GPT) matched performance of OpenAI's general-purpose models, while generating significantly shorter responses (p<0.001). Quality ratings varied markedly between professionals, as medical microbiologists and experienced infectious disease specialists assigned significantly lower scores compared to infectious disease trainees and medical students (p<0.001).


CONCLUSIONS
We observed considerable variation in LLM performance and highlight differences in perceived response quality across professional groups, emphasizing the need for critical appraisal when consulting LLMs for pre-analytical guidance.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of six generative large language models answering pre-analytical questions in medical microbiology.

evidence_items.summary: Machine unlearning for large language models seeks to remove specified knowledge while preserving general capability, yet current methods often treat an entire response as the unit of forgetting. This coarse granularity causes unnecessary utility loss when the forget target is only a small set of sensitive facts embedded within otherwise benign explanations. In this paper, we introduce Decouple to Forget (D2F), a targeted unlearning method inspired by semantic mediation that separates sensitive factual content from non-sensitive meaning and surface expression. For each example to be forgotten, D2F extracts a fact-level"mediator"representation from the answer, identifies which parts are sensitive, and removes only those parts while leaving the rest of the structure intact. We then generate counterfactual answers grounded in this mediator that preserve non-sensitive content but exclude sensitive facts, employing preference-based contrastive optimization to reduce the likelihood of information leakage while maintaining helpfulness and fluency. Experiments across various benchmark datasets show that D2F achieves a better balance between forgetting and retention than strong baseline methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/JingyueCong/D2F.
evidence_items.title: Decouple to Forget: Semantic Mediation for Sensitive Unlearning in Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Frontier large language models (LLMs) and diffusion models can generate realistic chest radiographs, raising concerns for dataset integrity when provenance metadata are absent. We compared authenticity judgments by two radiologists, two nonradiologist physicians, and three frontier LLMs (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Claude Opus 4.8) on 160 posteroanterior radiographs: 40 real NIH ChestX-ray14 images and 120 synthetic images generated from text by three pipelines. Each evaluator judged every image once; the LLM evaluation was repeated twice 3 months later. Balanced accuracy was the primary metric, given 75% synthetic prevalence. The two best evaluators reached nearly identical balanced accuracy from opposite operating points: Gemini 3.5 Flash had the highest point estimate (77.9%; specificity 100%, sensitivity 55.8%) and RAD1 was a close second (75.8%; specificity 55.0%, sensitivity 96.7%), a paired difference of - 2.1 percentage points (95% CI, - 5.8 to 1.2). On repetition, LLM judgments were not fully reproducible and this ordering did not hold. Nonradiologists performed near chance. All four human readers detected diffusion-generated images at 82-100%, whereas the radiologists misclassified 38-45% of real images and the conservative LLMs reached perfect specificity yet detected only 32-72% of LLM-generated images. With laterality markers and borders masked, specificity was 62.5% (Gemini) and 85.0% (GPT-5.5) against 90-100% in same-day unmasked runs. Interevaluator agreement was low throughout (Fleiss' kappa among LLMs 0.213). A frequency-domain baseline reached 98.3% balanced accuracy within this dataset but 12% sensitivity on a held-out generator. Human readers and LLMs failed on different images; visual authenticity assessment alone may be insufficient for provenance verification.
evidence_items.title: Complementary Error Profiles of Human Readers and Large Language Models in Detecting AI-Generated Chest Radiographs: A Comparative Reader Study.

evidence_items.summary:
BACKGROUND
Trauma registries are crucial for evaluating the prognosis of injuries and the quality of trauma care. However, the calculation of Injury Severity Score (ISS) remains a predominantly manual process, which is labor-intensive, potentially error-prone, and difficult to scale. Automating this process is a critical step toward enhancing the efficiency and quality of trauma registry data.


OBJECTIVE
This study conducts a feasibility test on the use of large language models (LLMs) to automatically calculate ISS from free-text discharge diagnoses. We specifically investigate the efficacy of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to enhance LLM accuracy by incorporating knowledge from the Abbreviated Injury Scale. We compare the performance of baseline LLMs against models augmented with both a standard RAG and a novel, domain-specific RAG framework.


METHODS
In this retrospective validation study, we used deidentified, free-text discharge diagnoses from trauma patients at Chang Gung Memorial Hospital (Linkou, Taiwan) in 2022. Against a physician-verified gold standard, we compared the performance of three systems: (1) baseline LLMs, (2) LLMs with standard RAG, and (3) LLMs with domain-specific RAG, for which the retriever was fine-tuned on trauma-related ICD-10 (International Statistical Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision) codes. Performance was evaluated on a physician-verified test set across exact ISS prediction, tolerance-based accuracy, and ISS severity categories.


RESULTS
Baseline state-of-the-art LLMs achieve modest exact-match (EM) accuracy, ranging from 47.3% to 64.7%. Standard RAG did not produce consistent gains (54.3% to 60.3%), whereas the domain-specific RAG substantially improved accuracy (62.7% to 75.3%). Performance gains were most pronounced in patients with moderate to severe injuries. GPT-4.1 with domain-specific RAG reached the highest EM accuracy (75.3%, 95% CI 66.1%-82.7%), compared with 70.0% for the deterministic International Classification of Diseases and R statistical software (ICDPIC-R) baseline. Tolerance-based and categorical analyses confirm substantial gains with the domain-specific RAG framework in clinically relevant ranges.


CONCLUSIONS
This single-center feasibility study suggests that LLMs augmented with a domain-specific retriever can calculate the ISS from free-text discharge diagnoses with overall accuracy comparable to that of a deterministic coding tool, with the advantage concentrated in the most severe injuries. This approach may help alleviate the administrative burden of manual coding, enhance standardization, and improve the quality of trauma registry data. Future multi-institutional validation is needed to confirm these findings.
evidence_items.title: Automating Injury Severity Score Calculation From Free-Text Discharge Diagnoses Using Domain-Specific Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models: Retrospective Validation Study.

evidence_items.summary: Theory of mind (ToM), the ability to reason about others'mental states, underlies effective communication and coordination. Its higher-order form enables reasoning over nested perspectives in strategic interactions. However, existing evaluations often equate belief-nesting depth with reasoning order, allowing nominally higher-order questions to admit lower-order shortcuts. We formalize effective order through the distinct events supporting successive belief prefixes, revealing widespread order inflation across existing benchmarks. We introduce HopToM, with certified full-order questions and controls for lower-order alternatives. Under direct prompting, mean accuracy across four frontier LLMs falls from 73.5% at first order to 20.0% at fourth order, and human participants also struggle. Causal interventions link a recurring class of errors to evidence for shallower belief prefixes. We introduce HopTrace, a plug-and-play inference-time method that encodes each interaction once into perspective records and resolves nested queries deterministically. On certified narrative questions, it improves fourth- and fifth-order accuracy by 22.0 and 38.5 percentage points over strong prompting baselines, while using 20-39 times fewer tokens than multi-call methods. These results sharpen how higher-order ToM is evaluated and offer a practical way to improve perspective reasoning in interactive agents.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Belief Nesting: Rethinking Higher-Order Theory of Mind in Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Repetition counting requires identifying and enumerating action cycles over time. While state-of-the-art video language models describe actions fluently, they fail to reliably count how many times an action repeats. To investigate this limitation, we introduce RepProbe, a benchmark of 42K real and synthetic video clips containing exactly k in [1, 20] complete repetitions, with controls for clip position, temporal coverage, and duration. These controls allow us to study the counting failure directly and locate where in the model it arises. Counting accuracy collapses at high counts across the video language models we evaluate, and controlled experiments show this collapse is not explained by frame sampling alone. We compare model outputs with linear probes trained on the final-layer representations used to generate those outputs. We find a consistent representation-to-output dissociation: substantial count information remains linearly decodable even when models fail to report the correct count. Further analysis shows this failure arises primarily at the output stage, where answers concentrate on a small set of preferred numbers rather than the available count information. The dissociation holds on both real and synthetic videos and is not explained by clip duration, position, or scene content. These results indicate that models encode repetition structure but do not reliably report it in their outputs. Project page: https://arenaa.github.io/RepProbe-webpage/
evidence_items.title: RepProbe: Can Video Language Models Count Repeated Actions? A Diagnostic Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: With the rapid development of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), evaluating their video understanding capabilities has become increasingly important. Existing video understanding benchmarks cover only part of the evaluation dimensions, limiting systematic diagnosis of omni-modal video understanding. We introduce OmniCompass, a holistic benchmark for omni-modal video grounding and understanding. OmniCompass defines two evaluation tracks: OmniCompass-VL assesses vision-language models on tasks requiring visual evidence, while OmniCompass-AV assesses omni-modal models on tasks requiring joint audio-visual evidence. Each track includes three complementary tasks: temporal grounding (TG), spatial grounding (SG), and question answering (QA), assessing when a referenced target appears, where it is, and what happens. QA covers five perception and three reasoning categories in OmniCompass-VL, and three perception and two reasoning categories in OmniCompass-AV. OmniCompass-VL contains 820 videos and 2,460 instances across domains and three duration types: short, medium, and long. A narrative- and audio-rich subset forms OmniCompass-AV with 240 videos and 720 instances. Each instance is evaluated under two paired settings: text-only and text+image, specifying the same target through text and visual-language guidance. All instances are manually annotated with multi-round quality verification. Evaluations of 50 MLLMs show that open-source models still lag behind proprietary counterparts, particularly in audio-visual understanding. Precise temporal and spatial grounding remains challenging even for leading models, and their predictions still exhibit inconsistencies across the paired target specifications.
evidence_items.title: OmniCompass: A Holistic Benchmark for Omni-Modal Video Grounding and Understanding

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance on diverse vision-language tasks, but their computational demands limit deployment under constrained budgets, particularly on edge devices. Many works focus on Knowledge Distillation (KD) and try to transfer knowledge from powerful teacher models to students. In addition to reducing model size, visual token compression provides a complementary route to efficiency, but introduces mismatched visual token counts that complicate direct token-wise knowledge transfer. To mitigate this, we propose DVTR-KD, a knowledge distillation framework based on \textbf{D}ense \textbf{V}isual \textbf{T}oken \textbf{R}econstruction, which reconstructs the teacher's dense visual tokens from the student's compressed tokens. We reconstruct visual states after the final LLM layer and at the input to an intermediate layer identified as important for visual-information readout. At the intermediate layer, reconstruction is supervised through the teacher's response predictions rather than by direct token-wise KL or MSE matching. An auxiliary attention-readout loss complements this response-level supervision by aligning how the student and the original teacher integrate contextual information when predicting responses. Evaluations on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that DVTR-KD improves the performance of token-compressed students while retaining the inference efficiency afforded by visual token compression.
evidence_items.title: DVTR-KD: Distilling Vision-Language Models via Intermediate Visual Token Reconstruction

evidence_items.summary: Task-oriented dialogue understanding remains underexplored for Bangla, particularly in multilingual settings involving English and romanized Bangla (Banglish). We introduce BanglaTOD, a parallel tri-lingual benchmark comprising 209 multi-turn dialogues across nine Bangladesh-specific service domains and 64 intents. Each conversational turn is aligned across Bangla, English, and Banglish, yielding 4,689 language-specific turn records annotated with intents, token-level slots, state updates, and accumulated dialogue states. We establish context-aware baselines for joint intent classification and slot filling using mBERT, BERT-base-uncased, and BanglaBERT. Cross-language analysis reveals substantial performance differences across models and linguistic representations, while removing dialogue history reduces intent accuracy by 19.0--25.7 percentage points. BanglaTOD provides a foundation for multilingual dialogue understanding and future dialogue state tracking research in Bangladesh-specific conversational applications. The dataset is publicly available at \href{https://huggingface.co/datasets/afri7here/BanglaTOD}{Hugging Face}.
evidence_items.title: A Benchmark for Bangla Task-Oriented Dialogue Understanding

evidence_items.summary: Large language models have evolved from single-turn chatbots into interactive agents capable of long-horizon reasoning. In real deployments, MCP tool services can return noisy feedback and users may intervene to correct the agent, but existing methods provide limited supervision for reflection learning and failure recovery. To bridge this gap, we propose Agent-Reflex, a general training framework for incentivizing proactive reflection in agents. Specifically, Agent-Reflex comprises three stages. First, Environment Reflection Skill Discovery (RSD) injects grounded tool-feedback perturbations into environment scaling, samples a capability-diverse LLM pool, mines matched success-failure pairs, and summarizes reusable reflection meta-skills. Building on this skill library, we then apply Reflective Supervised Fine-Tuning (ReSFT) that converts each skill into supervision for self-reflection, skill recovery, and user-centric correction, strengthening complementary reflective behaviors. Finally, we propose On-Policy Reflective Policy Optimization (ORPO) to combine agentic reinforcement learning under noisy interactions with reflection-guided on-policy distillation to further elicit proactive reflection. Built on Qwen3-8B, Agent-Reflex reaches 58.6 overall on five long-horizon tool-use benchmarks and 29.1 on AgentNoiseBench, surpassing strong environment-scaling and reflection baselines. Experiments on six challenging agent benchmark suites demonstrate the effectiveness of Agent-Reflex. Further analyses show that Agent-Reflex improves agents'robustness to noise while maintaining stable training dynamics, supporting scalable agent training. Our code is available at https://github.com/RUC-NLPIR/Agent-Reflex.
evidence_items.title: Agent-Reflex: Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively

evidence_items.summary: Cu-C materials and interfaces are central to diamond thermal management, metallization, graphene growth and carbon-coating technologies, but atomistic simulations across these applications require a potential that describes metallic Cu, diverse carbon bonding, heterogeneous Cu-C interactions and close atomic encounters. Here we develop NEP-CuC, a transferable neuroevolution potential trained on a dataset of 2,727 uniformly relabelled configurations selected from a heterogeneous Cu-C candidate pool. Disagreement within an ensemble of five independently trained models provides an internal indicator of model sensitivity. A Ziegler-Biersack-Littmark (ZBL) correction describes short-range nuclear repulsion, while a runtime D3(BJ) correction supplements dispersion-sensitive calculations. Tests on source-derived held-out and independent external datasets, together with structural, elastic, defect, interfacial, vibrational and finite-temperature transport benchmarks, establish broad but property-dependent physical fidelity across elemental Cu, diverse carbon environments and heterogeneous Cu-C configurations. Large-scale simulations of amorphous-carbon formation and orientation-dependent shock compression of Cu further test transferability under strongly non-equilibrium conditions. For Cu/diamond interfaces, the same potential describes deposition, annealing and tensile response: preparation history leaves persistent differences in interphase structure, while the mean peak nominal tensile stress at 500 K decreases from $12.35\pm0.71$ to $6.65\pm0.98$ GPa as the incident Cu energy during the initial deposition stage increases from 1 to 50 eV. NEP-CuC provides an atomistic framework for linking processing, interfacial structure and physical response across Cu-C systems, with direct relevance to Cu/diamond thermal-management interfaces, diamond metallization and non-equilibrium Cu-C processing.
evidence_items.title: A Transferable Machine-Learned Potential Enabling Large-Scale Copper-Carbon Simulations from Equilibrium to Extreme Conditions
