evidence_items.summary: We propose a unified spatial-density signal to score token importance for both inference phases: bipartite merge for prefill and KV eviction for decode, yielding measurable gains in each stage. To isolate the two phases, we split benchmarks by scoring logic. Prefill probes (MMBench, POPE, ScienceQA) evaluate only the first decoded token; their accuracy reflects prefill logits argmax before any decode KV eviction. Full-pipeline probes (TextVQA, DocVQA, MM-Vet) assess the complete generated sequence and capture both phases. We identify a critical evaluation pitfall: decode pruning claims validated solely on prefill probes measure prefill quality, not decode performance. Experiments show discarding all visual KV during decode barely affects prefill-probe accuracy but degrades TextVQA and MM-Vet drastically; this insensitivity stems from the scoring rule, not compression intensity.Evaluated on seven model variants (InternVL-3.5, Qwen3-VL, LLaVA-1.5) and three full-pipeline benchmarks, our method achieves a three-way Pareto frontier across compute, memory and accuracy. Density-based prefill compression maintains strong accuracy, scales linearly with visual token count, and delivers 100x faster token selection at high resolution. For decode, density top-k KV eviction consistently outperforms strong baselines H2O, SnapKV and StreamingLLM on TextVQA and MM-Vet across three retention ratios. At 0.125 keep ratio on TextVQA, it surpasses H2O by 9.6 points; InternVL-3.5 models (2B to 38B) maintain a 7 to 10 point advantage. Compression scales favorably with model size: every measured 8B to 38B model transition reduces accuracy loss instead of worsening it. We suggest MM-Vet or DocVQA as mandatory full-pipeline validation for any decode-phase claims. Our code is available at https://github.com/Kai-Liu001/TwinPrune
evidence_items.title: TwinPrune: Density-Aware Two-Phase Token Pruning for Vision-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Dialogue and collaborative assistants repeatedly judge what a partner knows, believes, or intends. Typed decision models offer a potential alternative to generative large language models for bounded Theory of Mind (ToM) selection. We present Jev-ToM, comparing five typed decision models and seven generative baselines on 11,117 English text questions from nine ToM benchmarks across six capability groups. TypeSafe Jev reaches 73.2% source-balanced accuracy including native controls and ranks first or second across all six capabilities, leading beliefs, goals/desires/intentions, and emotions. Other typed models show distinct strengths across tasks. Separate resource comparisons suggest that Jev could reduce the cost and waiting time of repeated ToM selection. Confidence-based selection remains benchmark-dependent, and supplied reasons can repair errors or overturn correct answers depending on their attachment. Candidate expansion reveals distinct selection and output-validity problems. Related-question cues account for most of Jev's downstream gains, with task-dependent effects from predicted states. The findings motivate testing Jev as a ToM selection component in assistants, with task-specific confidence calibration, candidate design, and output validation as integration priorities.
evidence_items.title: Jev-ToM: Evaluating Theory of Mind in Typed Decision Models

evidence_items.summary: Time-series analysis is increasingly studied in multimodal settings, yet most benchmarks pair temporal signals with text or with visualizations derived from the same signal. This leaves open whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can integrate time series with real-world visual evidence. We introduce MMTA (multimodal temporal analysis), a benchmark of tri-modal tasks with diverse cross-modal complementarity patterns among time series, text, and vision. MMTA spans nine domains -- robotics, autonomous driving, human action, manufacturing, AR assistance, healthcare, recommendation, finance, and climate -- under video+TS and image+TS layouts, with a 3,524-sample test split covering classification and forecasting. The benchmark standardizes heterogeneous real-world sources into a shared schema with domain-specific prompts, provenance documentation, and success-weighted metrics that penalize both wrong answers and failed generations. Evaluating eight open-source and proprietary MLLMs reveals a shared bottleneck: representing time series as text creates very long token sequences and weakens fine-grained alignment with visual evidence, especially in long-video settings. We then introduce TimeOmni-v, a multimodal LLM extension with a dedicated time-series encoder, temporal positional alignment, modality-aware token layout, and a forecasting head. TimeOmni-v improves long-video classification and time-series inference efficiency, showing that MMTA not only exposes representation and grounding failures but also motivates targeted model design.
evidence_items.title: MMTA: Benchmarking Multimodal Temporal Analysis with Time Series, Text, and Vision

evidence_items.summary: Rapid advances in artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) have significantly promoted using text-to-image (T2I) models to generate images with specific affective intentions. However, the emotional effects conveyed by generated images frequently deviate from target expectations, and it remains unclear whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can reliably interpret the emotion of AI-generated visual content. Existing affective benchmarks are predominantly built on natural images, while affective studies of generated images have largely focused on emotions expressed in portraits, lacking a unified benchmark for studying the emotions expressed and evoked by generated images. We therefore introduce EmoGenie, a benchmark of emotion for AI-generated images that evaluates capabilities in T2I generation and MLLM understanding across expressed and evoked emotions. It comprises 6,400 images generated by eight T2I models using 800 emotion-targeted prompts, annotated with question-answer (QA) pairs, termed EmoGenie-QA, and continuous human ratings, termed EmoGenie-Assess. EmoGenie-QA contains 90,000 closed-set questions in single-image and image-pair settings, as well as 1,057 open-ended questions for emotion description. EmoGenie-Assess benchmarks continuous affective and aesthetic prediction using 13,175 mean opinion scores (MOSs) aggregated from human ratings in terms of valence, arousal, dominance, and aesthetic quality. We further develop EmoProbe, which combines emotion question answering with response-aligned, dimension-specific regression heads for continuous score prediction. Experimental results show that EmoProbe achieves superior results on emotion-related QA tasks, while its affective and aesthetic predictions correlate better with human ratings, demonstrating its state-of-the-art capabilities of unified coarse-to-fine affective understanding for AI-generated images.
evidence_items.title: EmoGenie: Benchmarking and Evaluating Expressed and Evoked Emotion in T2I Generation with MLLMs

evidence_items.summary: Textual reasoning before acting has improved vision-language-action (VLA) models, but at the cost of latency: every action conditioned on the reasoning text must wait for autoregressive decoding. We show that actions do not need to wait for or condition on the generated reasoning to benefit from it, because the reasoning supervision already improves the backbone representation. We introduce TacitVLA, a reasoning VLA whose action expert never attends to the reasoning it generates for the current call. On long-horizon tasks where the reasoning text also serves as episodic memory, it can generate each entry during action execution rather than before acting. We evaluate it in a controlled study on four benchmarks spanning manipulation and autonomous driving, memory and non-memory tasks: RoboMME, RMBench, LIBERO, and PhysicalAI-AV. On all four, TacitVLA matches the performance of its explicit-reasoning counterpart at up to 3.4x lower latency, and matches the latency of the same architecture trained without reasoning at up to +17.1% success. In absolute terms, it surpasses the best previously published results on the RoboMME Counting suite (82.7% vs. 66.8%) and RMBench (77.5% vs. 56.5%), and reaches 72.9% on LIBERO-Plus and a 52.5% scene score on the public split of the PhysicalAI-AV closed-loop driving challenge. Project page: https://tacitvla.github.io.
evidence_items.title: TacitVLA: Reasoning Vision-Language-Action Models Without Reasoning Latency

evidence_items.summary: Web resources rarely carry the educational metadata that teachers use to judge whether a resource fits their lesson, and dedicated educational repositories that do carry it cover only a fraction of what teachers find through web search. Closing this gap in real time, at the point of search, requires classifiers that are fast enough to run per query and that target a vocabulary specific to the teacher’s curriculum and grade structure, for which labelled training data is scarce. We investigate whether Large Language Model (LLM)-generated labels and paraphrases can train small, fast classifiers for this task. Across nine LRMI-aligned educational metadata properties for STEM education in Lower Saxony, Germany, matching model complexity to property difficulty reaches micro F1 > 0.8 for every property at inference latencies under 15ms, with models compact enough for client-side, browser-based deployment. We report this as preliminary, ongoing work: evaluation for six properties currently relies on LLM-generated labels validated against a 50-page human-annotated sample, and train/test splits do not yet separate resources by website, which we flag as open validity questions for the digital libraries community to weigh in on.
evidence_items.title: Real-Time, Context-Specific Educational Metadata Enrichment of Learning Resources on the Web

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are becoming an integral part of the software development lifecycle, and the capabilities granted to them allow an agent to act with the user's authority on any resource it can access. The reach that gives an agent its utility is equally available to an attacker who can steer it. Anything an agent ingests can carry an injected instruction, and since the model does not reliably distinguish instructions from data, indirect prompt injection should be mitigated by mediating the effects the agent produces. Such mediation faces a structural difficulty. Legitimate work and the first step of an attack often look alike when an individual action is observed, and what separates them lies later in the trace, so a monitor limited to allow and deny is forced to decide before the evidence accumulates. We present Kairos, a reference monitor at the isolation boundary of an unmodified, opaque agent, where a tool call, a shell command, and a script the agent writes all cross the boundary as the same file and network operations, so that confinement holds regardless of the agent's behavior. A declarative policy that states which sources are trusted decides most effects deterministically and defers the rest, which are held while the agent continues speculatively. A decision oracle with bounded authority, such as a language model or a human, releases or refuses each deferred effect on the trace. Across three benchmarks and three agent models, Kairos outperforms existing defenses in the trade-off between attack success and utility. In particular, on AgentDojo, it reduces attack success from 47.0\% to 2.7\% while its benign utility stays at the level of the undefended agent.
evidence_items.title: Kairos: Transactional Security Enforcement at the System Boundary for LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: Frontier language-model agents can now improve robots on their own: they write control code, test it, and keep what works as skills and memories for the next task. We introduce SEAR (Self-Evolving Agentic Robotics), a framework and benchmark built around two questions. Is the agent really learning, or just trying more often? And does what it learns still help on new tasks, in a new simulator, and on a real robot? The framework runs an agent in three modes: it writes code that becomes the policy (code-as-policy), acts live in the control loop (agent-as-policy), or works as a researcher that fine-tunes a vision-language-action model (auto-research). The benchmark adds controls that separate retained experience from repeated attempts, familiar tasks, privileged simulator state, larger budgets, and luck. Across seven frontier language models, 330 simulated and five physical tasks, and over four years of agent runtime, we highlight three findings. First, the learning curve of a robotic agent depends both on the overall time budget and the task difficulty relative to model capability. Harder tasks make longer sessions worthwhile; on easier tasks, re-rolling short attempts does just as well. Second, control code and shared routines transfer across tasks and simulators, while task-specific solutions do not. On a real robot, we observe a performance gap between agent-designed practice and novel human-designed scenes. Third, different models evolve more effectively in different ways. Some do best acting live, others writing code first. And a text-only model keeps pace with a comparable multimodal one: perception helps with error assessment, but agentic reasoning and tool use can matter more. We release the benchmark and codebase to support future research.
evidence_items.title: SEAR: Self-Evolving Agentic Robotics

evidence_items.summary: Long-context inference makes the key-value (KV) cache a major memory bottleneck for large language models. We propose BELT, a low-rank KV cache compression framework. Its key-side objective targets attention distributions rather than raw keys or pre-softmax logits, yielding a quadratic surrogate with a closed-form low-rank solution. A learned global rank allocator uses differentiable soft selection during training and hard selection at deployment to meet a user-specified component budget. Experiments demonstrate improved model quality under aggressive compression and increased decoding throughput at comparable accuracy. Evaluated across three LLMs and multiple benchmarks, BELT achieves up to 70% low-rank KV cache compression while outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 23.3 points on LongBench, and up to 17.8x overall KV cache reduction when combined with quantization. With Triton-based GPU kernels and a quantized cache, BELT delivers up to 2.7x speedup for the attention module and 3.3x end-to-end decoding throughput.
evidence_items.title: BELT : BEhavior-Aligned Low-Rank KV Cache Compression with Learned Top-k Rank Allocation

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges to predict which of two candidate answers a human evaluator would prefer, providing a scalable alternative when human evaluation is too costly. Unfortunately, LLM judgments can exhibit systematic biases. Prior work has documented position, verbosity or model family of the candidate answers influencing the judge decision rather than their quality, while additional biases may remain undocumented. $\textit{Multicalibration}$ provides a natural framework to address this problem: each bias corresponds to miscalibration on an identifiable group, $\textit{e.g.}$, family bias manifests as overconfidence in answers generated by models belonging to the same family of the judge. The challenge is to fix miscalibration simultaneously across many, potentially unknown groups. To this end, we introduce $\mathrm{CaLLM}$, a post hoc framework that multicalibrates an LLM judge, thereby bounding all such biases simultaneously. We prove that $\mathrm{CaLLM}$ bounds the bias of every group whose error structure is captured by an available representation, and that augmenting it with explicit bias groups further reduces the residual bias. We then derive theoretical conditions under which $\mathrm{CaLLM}$ improves the judge's accuracy, rather than trading it for calibration. Finally, we evaluate $\mathrm{CaLLM}$ across pairwise preference benchmarks, showing that it reduces the multicalibration error on both specified and unspecified bias groups, while improving predictive performance of the judge.
evidence_items.title: A CaLLM Judge is a Better Judge: Mitigating Bias in LLM-as-a-judge

evidence_items.summary: Scientific progress relies on acknowledging epistemic boundaries and charting forward directions. However, limitations and future work are systematically omitted or hedged to improve publication prospects. With escalating submission volumes, reviewers increasingly rely on Large Language Models (LLMs), yet zero-shot models generate superficial, hallucinated, or author-echoing feedback. This thesis presents a unified framework to discover, evaluate, recommend, and generate scholarly limitations and future work. First, we introduce LimTopic and FutureScope, using hybrid BERTopic, LLM pipelines to uncover thematic limitation patterns and model thirteen years of NLP future work trajectories. Second, to resolve metric inflation from surface metrics, we establish BAGELS and FutureGen, introducing atomic Limitation Units (LUs) for fine-grained PointWise evaluation and RAG-based future work generation with iterative critique loops. Third, we construct citation knowledge graphs with GraphSAGE to recommend paper-specific limitations. Finally, SciLimAgents couples intrinsic (LimitAgents) and novelty (NovAgents) specialist agents over a 120K-paper shared memory, aligned via on-policy preference optimization and composite process rewards. Across extensive benchmarks, our frameworks demonstrate substantial gains over frontier baselines, establishing a principled foundation for AI-assisted scientific quality assurance.
evidence_items.title: Towards Automated Analysis of Scientific Limitations and FutureWork

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal LLMs are typically trained by first aligning a vision encoder with a language model via projector training on large image-caption datasets, followed by joint training of the full multimodal model. Despite its widespread use, the role of the projector training stage remains poorly understood. We find that (i) using only $10$ to $20\%$ of the data for training the projector already recovers most downstream performance gains, and (ii) projectors trained on different datasets can be linearly interpolated while largely preserving performance. These results suggest that projector training mainly performs a coarse alignment, which many different projectors achieve equally well. Motivated by these findings, we propose PORTAL, a training-free projector initialization that requires neither paired image-caption data nor gradient-based optimization, but only per-modality summary statistics. PORTAL computes an optimal-transport-based map between Gaussian approximations of the vision and language feature distributions on a shared principal subspace, so that the projector training stage can be skipped entirely. Without any paired data, PORTAL matches the standard pipeline trained on 558k image-caption pairs across six LLM backbones, two vision encoders, and 16 benchmarks. It outperforms that pipeline in $3$ of $7$ (vision encoder, LLM) settings and reaches an average $98\%$ of its score across the other four.
evidence_items.title: Rethinking Projector Training in Multimodal LLMs

evidence_items.summary: The rapid advancement of image-to-text extraction systems and large language models (LLMs) poses new challenges for educational assessment by making assignment materials easy to transcribe and solve with minimal human effort. To address this problem, we present AIRRI (Artificial Intelligence Resilient Reading Interface), a framework for generating machine-resistant educational content, a dataset of higher-education assignments for evaluation, and an initial evaluation of the human readability of AIRRI machine-resistant text designs. AIRRI employs two categories of machine-resistance techniques. First, AIRRI applies image transformations including character spacing, word spacing, line spacing, character opacity variation, stripe overlays, and image noise. Second, AIRRI applies decision-based adversarial attacks: RayS, SurFree, and ADBA. We evaluate AIRRI against three image-to-text systems: Tesseract, EasyOCR, and the transformer-based GOT-OCR2 model. Our results show that AIRRI substantially degrades automated text extraction performance. AIRRI increased character error rates for EasyOCR (6.9% to 55.9%), Tesseract (2.3% to 100.0%), and GOT-OCR2 (30.7% to 48.1%). Word error rates increased for EasyOCR (24.9% to 96.7%) and Tesseract (10.7% to 100.0%). Among the evaluated decision-based attacks, ADBA consistently produced the largest degradation in image-to-text performance, while RayS and SurFree produced more moderate reductions. EasyOCR and Tesseract were generally more susceptible to both image-based and adversarial perturbations than the transformer-based GOT-OCR2 model. Our findings suggest that AIRRI can significantly reduce the reliability of image-to-text-to-LLM workflows, increasing the effort required for AI-assisted assignment completion.
evidence_items.title: AIRRI: Towards a Human-Readable, Machine-Resistant Reading Interface

evidence_items.summary: Understanding facial behaviour in video requires answering three fundamental questions: when a key facial expression occurs, where the model attends on the face at that moment, and why that evidence is necessary rather than merely correlated. Today's multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can label and describe video, but they rarely provide faithful explanations, especially for small facial movements that change over time. We present VideoFace-X-LLM, a framework for explainable facial video understanding comprising two key components. First, we introduce ExplainFace, a weakly supervised video-text corpus for facial behaviour understanding, automatically constructed from CelebV-HQ videos and validated through human evaluation and a two-model audit (at most 2.3% contradictions), demonstrating consistent gains across two backbone architectures. Second, H-TCC (Hierarchical Temporal Spatial Causal Concepts), which finds the key temporal moments (When), the facial regions (Where), and verifies its causal necessity (Why) through targeted occlusion. Fine-tuning on ExplainFace raises appearance Macro F1 from 19.48% to 32.87% (+13.39), with gains of +4.38 on actions, +6.77 on temporal emotion, and +11.84 F1 on deepfake detection. We also measure the explanations pointing lift, face/edge lift, stability, an Adebayo sanity check, and a necessity test rather than only showing examples. Our models, code, and corpus are available on request for research use.
evidence_items.title: When, Where, and Why: Hierarchical Causal Explainability for Video Face Understanding with MLLMs

evidence_items.summary: Identifying scientific limitations is essential for transparent reporting and rigorous critical appraisal. However, zero-shot large language models (LLMs) often produce generic critiques, repeat author-stated limitations, and overlook paper-specific methodological and contextual weaknesses. We propose LimAgents, a training-free multi-agent framework in which role-specialized workers extract explicit limitations, analyze methodological weaknesses, adopt a peer-review perspective, and examine cited literature. Workers can refine their outputs through feedback from a Leader Agent, after which a Master Agent consolidates and de-duplicates the resulting limitations; ablations show that refinement benefits GPT-4o mini but not Llama 3 8B. For evaluation, we construct a validated, non-exhaustive reference set by combining author-stated limitations with OpenReview critiques and decomposing them into atomic Limitation Units through multi-model consensus. We evaluate generated limitations using human-calibrated, LU-level semantic matching with two independent LLM judges. Across multiple backbones, LimAgents achieves the highest F1 across both baseline-comparison backbones. In terms of reference-aligned coverage, it achieves improvements of 4.41 and 15.51 points over the Llama 3 8B and GPT-4o mini zero-shot configurations, respectively. Furthermore, LimAgents yields substantial gains in overall F1 scores, exceeding competing baselines by 12.30–20.91 points when utilizing Mistral 7B, and 5.31–34.18 points with Qwen 2.5 3B. Code: https://github.com/IbrahimAlAzhar/LimAgents_limitation_generation_with_LLM_Agents | Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/IbrahimAlAzhar/LimAgents
evidence_items.title: LimAgents: Multi-Agent LLMs for Generating Research Limitations

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) can produce fluent and confident responses even when those responses lack sufficient support or contain factual errors. Reliable question answering therefore requires models not only to generate answers, but also to recognize when they cannot provide a well-supported response and abstain accordingly. This capability is particularly important in scientific domains, where inaccurate responses can cause real-world harm. This paper systematically investigates the abstention behavior of LLMs in challenging scientific multiple-choice answering tasks. We evaluate several LLMs on multiple modified versions of a scientific multiple-choice question answering dataset, varying both the availability of the correct answer and the wording of the abstention option. Our findings demonstrate that LLMs often struggle to abstain consistently when the correct answer is absent, and that their abstention behavior is sensitive to model family, abstention wording, and reasoning settings.
evidence_items.title: Exploring the Abstention Ability of LLMs using Scientific Reasoning in Critical Fields

evidence_items.summary: Digital libraries increasingly provide access to large collections of mathematical content, including textbooks, research articles, educational resources, and community question-answering forums. Effectively searching these collections remains challenging because mathematical queries combine natural language with symbolic notation, where symbols often have context-dependent meanings and essential assumptions are frequently left implicit. These characteristics make query ambiguity difficult to identify, reducing retrieval effectiveness and increasing user effort. Despite its importance for mathematical digital libraries, mathematical query ambiguity detection has not previously been studied as a benchmark task. This paper introduces MathDisAm, the first benchmark for mathematical query ambiguity detection. The benchmark contains 1,000 queries, evenly divided between ambiguous and unambiguous instances, derived from Math Stack Exchange. Ambiguous variants are created through targeted omission operations, while corresponding unambiguous versions provide explicit clarification. All instances are manually validated by human annotators to ensure annotation quality. Baseline experiments with three transformer-based classifiers show that the domain-adapted MathBERT achieves 90.0% accuracy, outperforming the general-purpose RoBERTa-base (86.5%) and BERT-base-uncased (86.0%). Error analysis indicates that domain-specific pre-training substantially reduces false positives, although all models continue to struggle with missing mathematical context and inconsistencies that are difficult to recognize from symbolic notation alone.
evidence_items.title: MathDisAm: Towards Math Query Disambiguation

evidence_items.summary: Video understanding benchmarks are the primary yardstick for measuring progress in video-language modeling, and a growing body of work relies on them to claim improvements. The reported benchmark scores in these works, however, are almost always produced by frameworks (e.g., lmms eval) used as black boxes: certain evaluation choices like frame sampling, preprocessing, and input formatting are inherited from preset defaults and seldom inspected carefully. We show these unexamined choices are a major source of variance. Even for the same model checkpoint, evaluation configuration alone can shift accuracy by up to 19.5pp. Hence, it is unclear whether reported gains reflect genuine improvements in capability or differences in evaluation setup. Moreover, many benchmark samples offer little evidence of visual capability, since they can be answered without the video, and the full suites are expensive to evaluate. We address these issues in two parts. First, we curate existing suites for discriminability and efficiency, producing Meta-Video, a balanced 1,000-question benchmark over 791 videos spanning diverse tasks and durations, which largely preserves model rankings, at 5 times inference speedup for a full-frame count sweep experiment (4-128 frames). Second, we establish a standardized evaluation protocol by sweeping the configuration space to isolate choices that measurably affect results, distill them into best practices and reporting standards, and release reproducible reference scores across five models and seven benchmarks. We hope that the proposed evaluation framework and the Meta-Video benchmark will support video understanding research by providing a reproducible and efficient foundation to measure progress in a reliable way.
evidence_items.title: Meta-Video: Efficient Standardized Evaluation for Video Understanding

evidence_items.summary: Recovering high-quality images from degraded underwater observations is crucial for underwater exploration. Polarization observations show promise as an effective source of complementary physical cues for recovering target radiance under clear-water conditions. However, existing methods have yet to jointly model raw intensity information and polarization cues to enable image restoration driven by an understanding of mixed degradations (color casts, haze, and low light). To overcome these limitations, we propose PolUR, a unified multimodal language-driven framework that jointly uses polarization and RGB information to identify degradation types and severity levels through structured semantic instructions and enhances joint restoration representations under the guidance of degradation-aware semantic features to improve restoration robustness under mixed degradations. We further construct a new benchmark named MixPolar, which contains underwater images exhibiting real-world degradations and their corresponding degradation descriptions. MixPolar supports systematic evaluation of degradation perception, image restoration, and performance on downstream tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PolUR effectively integrates polarization and RGB information, achieving competitive performance in degradation perception and image restoration, while also demonstrating generalization capability and utility for downstream tasks.
evidence_items.title: PolUR: Polarization Aware Multimodal Degradation Perception for Underwater Image Restoration

evidence_items.summary: Rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) evaluates responses against explicit criteria to construct rewards, offering a viable way to train large language models on open-ended tasks. However, standard methods compress criterion-level feedback into scalar rewards and assign uniform token advantages, leaving structured rubric supervision underutilized. Recent work seeks finer-grained guidance by treating rubrics as privileged information to derive self-distillation targets, but the resulting learning signal is not grounded in criterion outcomes and can lead to reward degradation. This motivates us to reframe the problem as criterion-aware credit assignment, where privileged rubric information serves as a relevance cue for credit allocation rather than a source of imitation targets. Accordingly, we propose CoCA, which derives criterion-level credits from group-relative outcomes and allocates them across tokens based on criterion-induced distribution shifts, yielding both outcome-grounded and fine-grained learning signals. Empirically, CoCA achieves an average gain of +4.2% over standard rubric-based RL across medicine and science benchmarks, demonstrating more effective learning on open-ended tasks.
evidence_items.title: CoCA: Criterion-Aware Credit Assignment for Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning

evidence_items.summary: Chemical safety knowledge is scattered across heterogeneous institutional collections—safety data sheets, reactivity handbooks, regulatory databases, and tens of thousands of incident reports—yet no deployed system provides unified, query-driven access to these resources for laboratory researchers. We demonstrate ChemSafe, an AI-powered decision-support system that addresses this information access problem by integrating large language models with a corpus of 74,000 DOE incident reports and multiple authoritative safety data sources. Given a natural-language experiment description, ChemSafe produces a structured safety report containing chemical hazards with GHS pictograms, incompatibility warnings, exposure limits, relevant historical incidents, activity-based work controls with risk levels, and emergency response procedures. The system employs a hybrid retrieval architecture combining keyword search (BM25), semantic embeddings, cross-encoder reranking, and LLM-based relevance evaluation. An ablation across four retrieval strategies reveals that pure vector search is insufficient for this specialized corpus (P@5 = 0.032), while keyword-based and hybrid methods achieve near-perfect incident retrieval (P@5 = 0.936, NDCG@5 = 1.000), underscoring the importance of lexical matching in technical safety domains. ChemSafe is deployed at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, reducing safety review time from hours to minutes.
evidence_items.title: ChemSafe: Hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Decision Support for Laboratory Chemical Hazard Assessment

evidence_items.summary: Large language models are attractive text compressors because next-token probabilities can be converted into code lengths. In practice, however, the main bottleneck is often not modeling quality but systems cost: a compressor must obtain logits quickly enough to compete with strong classical baselines. This paper examines systems optimizations for LLM-based compression, including multistream pipelined arithmetic coding and target-interval capture, and evaluates their trade-offs across inference engines, configurations and datasets. We evaluate LLM-based text compression on three different inference engines: Transformers, vLLM, and TensorRT-LLM. Notably, we obtain a speedup of 18.84x compared to prior work's Transformers implementation and a maximum recorded inference speed of 181 kilobytes per second at a compression ratio of 7.17, when running on an NVIDIA A100.
evidence_items.title: High-Throughput LLM-Based Compression and What It Takes: A Systems Study of Inference Engines and Entropy Coding Optimizations

evidence_items.summary: Evidence synthesis methods, such as systematic reviews (SR), require research teams to find, select, evaluate, and synthesize all available evidence to answer a specific research question in a reproducible and transparent, bias-reduced manner. Early in the process, teams must screen all unique titles and abstracts gathered from a comprehensive search, which can result in thousands of records. Therefore, the process often takes months to years to complete. In this research, we conduct a set of experiments using open-source Large Language Models (LLMs) with small parameters hosted on local servers to screen titles and abstracts against pre-defined eligibility criteria respective to each topic. We use two cases from real SRs for which titles and abstracts screening has already been completed by dual, independent human screeners, which we use as our “ground truth”. The goal of this work is to contribute to developing an AI-enabled workflow to reduce the time and labor required for the relevance screening phase of SRs. Therefore, we start by focusing on metrics such as recall to ensure we don’t miss any relevant results during automatic screening. As the value of these methods depends on a comprehensive corpus and missing relevant records can impair the quality of results, recall is the topmost priority. Our results suggest that AI may indeed aid with initial relevance screening, but more research is needed before full adoption. Repeated runs also demonstrated that models have deterministic results across different prompt variations.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating and explaining LLM classification for automatic screening in Systematic Reviews

evidence_items.summary: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) enables large language models (LLMs) to learn from multi-turn interactions with verifiable outcomes. Textual skills can improve exploration by distilling prior interactions into reusable guidance. However, existing skill-based RL approaches often either assume skill injection is beneficial or rely on indirect feedback or rollout-intensive evaluation to assess its utility. Our pilot studies show that rollout-based utility estimation for skill credit assignment is costly and unstable under limited sampling, while skill benefits vary across candidates and depend on the current policy's competence on each query. To address these challenges, we introduce SkillScaffold, a policy-adaptive training scaffold that combines low-cost skill-utility estimation with selective skill injection. By reusing outcome-verified training trajectories, SkillScaffold generates candidate skills and estimates their utility through outcome-aware likelihood comparisons, without candidate-specific environment rollouts. The resulting utility guides whether and which skill to inject, retaining skill-free execution when no candidate is estimated to help. Joint training enables the Generator to produce skills tailored to the evolving Executor. Scaffolded RL encourages skill internalization for skill-free inference. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, ScienceWorld, and $\tau^2$-Bench demonstrate gains over strong agentic-RL and skill-based RL baselines across both short- and long-horizon tasks. Ablations and further analyses support the importance of utility-based selection and abstention. Our code is available at https://github.com/Vaidurya00/SkillScaffold.
evidence_items.title: SkillScaffold: Scaffolding Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Policy-Adaptive Skill Credit Assignment and Selective Injection

evidence_items.summary: Visual token pruning for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) appears highly effective, with existing methods retaining over 95% of unpruned performance on common VQA benchmarks using a quarter of the visual tokens or fewer. However, our extensive evaluation of ten methods across three MLLM families and five ability groups reveals a critical gap: strong general performance often comes at the cost of severe degradation on fine-grained tasks such as OCR and visual grounding. We trace these failures to two limitations of the prevailing paradigm of retaining the highest-ranked native patches. A single importance ranking overlooks the complementary evidence required by different tasks, while sparse patch selection disrupts both image content and spatial integrity. To address these limitations, we propose Bifocal, a training-free, two-stage pruning method built on a mixed-granularity framework. It allocates separate budgets to query-focused and image-intrinsic evidence, complemented by a pooled coarse representation of the entire image. Before the LLM, Bifocal matches question words to visual regions through a soft conjunction balanced against norm-debiased image saliency, while selecting image-intrinsic evidence to maximize representational coverage. Inside the LLM, it further prunes tokens using density-adjusted text-to-image attention. With roughly a quarter of the original visual tokens, Bifocal is the only evaluated method to retain over 90% of unpruned performance in every ability group across all three models, and ranks first on average in all nine model-budget settings. The code is available at: https://github.com/EIT-NLP/Bifocal
evidence_items.title: Bifocal: Training-Free Mixed Granularity Visual Token Pruning for Multimodal LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Large language models increasingly tackle tasks that require multi-step reasoning, where errors in intermediate claims can affect the final answer. Self-consistency (SC) improves reasoning by voting over sampled final answers, but its vote leaves intermediate disagreements unresolved. To address this problem, we introduce DDRG (Disagreement-Driven Verification Guided by Reasoning Graphs), a framework for selective correction from a frozen bank of reasoning traces. Our insight is that graph alignment can expose claim-level disagreements and provide correction evidence without expanding the sampled trace bank. DDRG builds source-grounded claim graphs and sends localized conflicts to an answer-blind verifier. A verifier-supported refutation that reaches the majority answer's supporting path triggers one focused repair; otherwise, DDRG returns the exact SC vote. Experimental results across five benchmarks show that native zero-shot DDRG improves macro-average accuracy over direct answering by 8.65 and 15.83 percentage points for Qwen2.5-7B and Llama3.1-8B. It also exceeds CoT, the evaluated GoT and GoV question-answering adaptations, and SC on this macro metric. DDRG links local verification to selective correction without enlarging the initial candidate bank.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Answer Voting: Fine-Grained Correction of LLM Reasoning through Graph Alignment across Sampled Traces

evidence_items.summary: Vision language models (VLMs) are used in creative tasks such as visual storytelling, design ideation, art interpretation, and advertising. Yet we lack principled ways to measure the lateral reasoning of these models compared to human potential. We introduce CREATE, a semi-automatically constructed benchmark containing 155 visual Remote Associates Test problems. These problems require a solver to find an underlying connection among three seemingly dissimilar images. We conduct a human study (N=25) to validate and ground the quality of our benchmark, and evaluate 11 VLMs. Our findings show that most VLMs underperform humans on this task. Our experiments indicate that the associative ability of VLMs depends on the cue concepts provided in the text and does not universally extend to visual puzzles.
evidence_items.title: CREATE: Creativity Evaluation of VLMs using the Visual Remote Associates Test

evidence_items.summary: Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST) parsing has historically been dominated by discriminative models based on pretrained encoder-only language models. The recent availability of high-quality generative language models has made it unclear whether RST parsing is better approached as a generative task. In this work, we investigate whether generative language models are better at parsing RST than traditional discriminative ones. We find that at matched parameter counts, discriminative parsers perform much better than generative ones, though much larger generative models sometimes outperform them. Generative models hold a particular advantage in elementary discourse unit (EDU) segmentation, and we report new state-of-the-art results on the RST-DT benchmark in end-to-end parsing as well as segmentation.
evidence_items.title: Worth Their Weights? Evaluating Generative Models for Discourse Parsing

evidence_items.summary: Visual question answering models often produce plausible responses even when the available visual evidence is insufficient to support a valid answer. Although prior work has introduced benchmarks and abstention mechanisms for unanswerable visual questions, it remains unclear which signals derived from a frozen vision-language model reliably indicate answerability on unseen image-question pairs. We systematically evaluate answerability signals on a stratified 10K subset of UNK-VQA using frozen InstructBLIP, covering predictive uncertainty, cross-modal alignment, visual grounding, visual dependence, internal representations, and learned probes. Answerability discrimination remains weak, with test AUROC largely confined to 0.50-0.54. CLIP alignment yields the highest point estimate but does not significantly outperform generation confidence under paired bootstrap analysis. Targeted removal of question-relevant visual evidence causes substantially larger changes in answer confidence than same-size random masking, yet intervention sensitivity provides essentially no answerability discrimination. Increasing probe capacity, combining multiple signals, and adding reason-aware supervision do not provide robust improvements, while post-freeze cross-validation yields similarly weak discrimination. Selective-answering analysis shows limited usable coverage under low-risk operating criteria. Failure-mode analysis shows that the relative utility of individual signals varies across perturbation mechanisms. Taken together, these results show that, on our UNK-VQA subset with frozen InstructBLIP, visual dependence, uncertainty, semantic alignment, and static representations are not robust standalone proxies for answerability. Our findings emphasize the need to distinguish a model's reliance on visual evidence from whether that evidence is sufficient to support an answer.
evidence_items.title: Visual Dependence Does Not Imply Answerability: A Systematic Analysis of Answerability Signals in Frozen InstructBLIP

evidence_items.summary: A common practice in instance retrieval is to grow the gallery size to improve a benchmark's discrimination capability. One prominent example is ILIAS, which adds up to 100 million distractor images. The prevailing assumption is that faithful evaluation demands web scale, and that indexing all 100M images through the backbone is the unavoidable price of a comparable number. That price is steep: hundreds of GPU-hours and ~200 GB of descriptors per model, paid again for every method or ablation. We show the web-scale indexing price is largely avoidable: evaluation itself obeys a scaling law. The number of distractors that outrank a positive is Binomial in the gallery size. We define the per-query retrieval hardness, a gallery-scale agnostic quantity that yields a retrieval metric at any scale, and demonstrate it can be derived from a small random sample. The underlying sampled-rank machinery is long established in recommender-system and biometric evaluation, but to our knowledge has never been adapted to visual retrieval. We make the law per-query and estimable, and validate it at true 100M scale on ILIAS and INSTRE, and on the full 759k-distractor Google Landmarks v2 pool. Concretely, within a 5% sample (a flat 20x less indexing), every backbone's tail-aware (EVT) estimate has converged onto the large-scale mAP, to within ~0.01 (mean absolute error 0.005), across five backbones, three benchmarks, and two distractor pools (mAP@1000 at 100M on ILIAS/INSTRE; the official mAP@100 at the full 759k pool on GLDv2); the recommender-systems count baseline over-predicts everywhere (+0.037 to +0.068). This is an order of magnitude better than naively reporting the metric on the same subset (+0.08 to +0.13). We release code and the per-query hardness to facilitate faster, cheaper, and greener retrieval evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Web Scale on a Budget: Tail-Aware Retrieval Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Egocentric video understanding spans diverse capabilities, modalities, and evaluation formats, yet these are often studied in isolation despite their tight coupling in real-world interaction. We propose the Ego-Action-World interaction loop as a unifying principle: the wearer perceives the world, forms goals, acts, changes the world, and uses feedback to guide subsequent behavior. Based on this view, we introduce EgoOmniWorld, a benchmark organized around four complementary interaction structures: Node captures ego, action, and world states; Edge captures directed relations among them; Chain captures linked dependencies; and Loop captures feedback-closed interactions. We develop an interaction-first, evidence-grounded data pipeline that extracts structured interactions from egocentric videos, grounds them in visual and auditory evidence, and generates questions according to their interaction structure. Required modalities and single- or multi-turn formats follow naturally from the supporting evidence and dependencies. EgoOmniWorld contains 24,166 QA groups, including 20,284 training and 3,882 test samples. Experiments on representative open- and closed-source multimodal large language models reveal substantial and uneven limitations across interaction structures. Models trained on EgoOmniWorld improve in-domain interaction understanding and generalize to existing egocentric benchmarks. EgoOmniWorld provides a unified foundation for evaluating and advancing egocentric video understanding. Data, code, and models will be released.
evidence_items.title: EgoOmniWorld: Unifying Egocentric Understanding via Ego-Action-World Interactions

evidence_items.summary:
SUMMARY
Analysis of Compositions of Microbiomes with Bias Correction (ANCOM-BC) and its successor ANCOM-BC2 are critical algorithms for differential abundance analysis. Designed for handling compositional data, they feature the ability to estimate the unknown sampling fractions and correct the bias induced by their differences. While the original R package implementing the two methods is robust for standard dataset sizes, the increasing magnitude of modern multi-omics studies presents computational challenges, often resulting in a runtime bottleneck for high-dimensional data. Here, we present native Python implementations of both ANCOM-BC and ANCOM-BC2 in the scikit-bio package, significantly accelerating the workflow and enabling their application to large-scale datasets. By leveraging vectorization with NumPy and numerical optimization in SciPy, we enhanced the efficiency of both methods without compromising their statistical accuracy. The benchmarking results revealed a dramatic increase in performance in both simulated and real datasets. We demonstrated that our Python implementations generated test results matching the original R code, while achieving 380- and 147-fold faster runtimes and 97.4% and 96.2% lower memory consumption on the largest tested dataset, respectively. The Python implementations allow for the analysis of datasets that are significantly larger than previously possible, and enable applications to alternative omics data types and complex statistical models that vary greatly by the number of samples, features, and covariates.


AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION
https://github.com/scikit-bio/scikit-bio.


SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
N/A.
evidence_items.title: Efficient and scalable Python implementation of ANCOM-BC and ANCOM-BC2 for omics differential abundance testing.

evidence_items.summary: Deep learning has enabled substantial advances in oncology, including cancer detection and diagnosis, medical image analysis, tumor characterization, treatment planning, response assessment, and outcome prediction. However, conventional data-driven models often require large annotated datasets, exhibit limited generalization across heterogeneous clinical settings, and lack explicit mechanisms for incorporating the physical, physiological, and biological principles underlying cancer development and treatment. Physics-informed deep learning (PIDL) integrates governing physical laws, mechanistic models, physiological constraints, and domain knowledge into deep learning frameworks, providing a principled approach for learning from sparse, noisy, and heterogeneous oncological data. This review presents a task-oriented synthesis of PIDL methods across oncology, encompassing neural networks, Kolmogorov-Arnold networks, convolutional and vision architectures, neural operators, generative models, and hybrid physics-data-driven frameworks. Their applications are examined across cancer detection and diagnosis, image reconstruction and analysis, tumor characterization, quantitative imaging, tumor progression, treatment response, radiation therapy, treatment planning, and multimodal clinical modeling. Based on the synthesized methodological and application-level evidence, we develop task-optimized PIDL workflows that align the clinical task with appropriate data representations, physical constraints, model architectures, and validation strategies. We further analyze key challenges, including physical-model fidelity, computational scalability, uncertainty quantification, domain generalization, standardized benchmarking, and clinical validation.
evidence_items.title: Physics-Informed Deep Learning in Oncology

evidence_items.summary: Question answering (QA) over digital library collections allows users to obtain facts directly from digitized historical sources such as newspaper archives. Systems for this task typically follow the retrieve-then-read paradigm, in which a retriever first locates candidate passages in the collection and a reader then extracts or generates the answer from them. An answer that is never retrieved can never be read, so retrieval bounds end-to-end performance. How retrieval behaves depends on the retriever family. Lexical retrievers match the query’s surface forms, while dense retrievers match semantic representations. In the historical setting, both must bridge what we term the diachronic vocabulary gap, the mismatch that arises because users formulate queries in contemporary language whereas the target documents preserve the vocabulary of their period. This gap remains understudied. Existing historical QA benchmarks generate their questions from the source passages, so the questions inherit period wording and grant lexical matching an overlap that authentic user queries would not provide, and benchmark results may consequently overestimate real-world effectiveness. We examine this issue on ChroniclingAmericaQA, a large-scale QA benchmark over historical American newspapers. We construct a modern-query counterpart of the benchmark by re-expressing each question in present-day language under automatic validation, with answers and passages held fixed. A human preference study supports the construction. On both question sets we evaluate lexical, dense, and domain-adapted retrievers together with extractive and generative readers. We find that lexical retrieval is accurate but degrades sharply under modern phrasing, that dense retrieval is robust but less accurate, and that the degradation propagates to answer quality. Since the two retriever families fail on complementary queries, we combine them and empirically characterize the lexical–semantic trade-off, selecting the interpolation weight on held-out data. The resulting hybrid achieves the highest retrieval accuracy on both question sets. As digital libraries move from page delivery to question answering, the language their users bring belongs in the evaluation itself, and our benchmark and empirical analysis are a step in that direction.
evidence_items.title: Old Stories, New Readers: Evaluating Retrieval and QA over Historical Newspapers under Diachronic Vocabulary Change

evidence_items.summary: Research databases accumulate rich metadata, including subject keywords, themes, geographic and cultural references, but much of this data remains largely isolated, making it difficult to retrieve and reuse across different databases. The key problem is semantic grounding: without stable identifiers, databases that describe the same cultural practice or geographic region cannot recognise that they do so. We present Context-Aware Routing for Entity Linking (CAREL), a training-free, cost-efficient pipeline that links research metadata keywords to Wikidata QIDs. These stable identifiers support semantically grounded cross-database search and provide a basis for future knowledge graph construction. CAREL processes heterogeneous keywords through a four-layer cascade built around a novel Cross-lingual Retrieval Consensus (CRC) signal, which turns the agreement among language-conditioned retrieval ranks into a measure of linking confidence without requiring annotated data. Routing through the layers follows the ambiguity of each keyword: rule-based layers resolve the clear cases, and keywords not resolved by the rule-based stages reach a locally deployed open-source large language model (LLM), which bounds inference cost. We evaluate the pipeline on two benchmarks constructed from our multilingual African studies research metadata, a domain characterised by culturally embedded concepts and cross-institutional vocabulary variation: subject headings anchored in the Library of Congress Subject Headings (LCSH) and researcher-supplied tags. We deploy locally hosted open-source LLMs to assess whether such LLMs can support the task without relying on commercial APIs. This matters for research data that should not be sent to external services, and for institutions that want to keep control over how their data is used. CAREL reaches 89.8% and 90.9% end-to-end accuracy on the LCSH benchmark with Gemma4-31B-it and Qwen3.5-27B, holds 88.8% and 89.5% on the tag benchmark, and stays above 86% on both with Gemma4-E4B-it, a model with 4.5B effective parameters that runs on a consumer GPU. It detects keywords with no Wikidata entity at an F1 of 88. A stratified evaluation of frequent headings shows similar accuracy across record-context quality tiers.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Keywords: Training-Free Entity Linking for Research Metadata via Cross-Lingual Retrieval Consensus

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) have substantially improved the capabilities of GUI agents, while memory augmentation has emerged as a promising approach for reusing knowledge from past interactions. However, existing memory augmented GUI agents typically adopt a fixed representation strategy, providing retrieved experience as a static modality. It remains unclear whether a single memory modality is consistently optimal, or how modality preference changes across interaction steps. In this work, we conduct a systematic study of memory modality in VLM based GUI agents. Across GUI benchmarks, we find that the preferred memory representation is strongly step dependent. Motivated by the finding, we introduce \textbf{SwitchMem}, a routing framework that dynamically selects between textual and visual memory representations at each step. Across three GUI benchmarks, SwitchMem outperforms memory augmented baselines that rely on static memory representations. Our findings validate our claim that memory modality is a step dependent decision rather than a fixed design choice. Code and project resources are available at https://txxnrd.github.io/switchmem
evidence_items.title: Learning How to Remember: Memory Modality Selection for GUI Agents

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have been widely adopted for document parsing and optical character recognition (OCR), as they can accurately extract page-level elements. However, downstream applications such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) also require coherent document-level structure. Although these models indicate heading levels using different numbers of preceding ``\#''symbols, page-by-page prediction often lacks document-level consistency. In practice, input-resolution and context-length constraints make it infeasible for a VLM to jointly process all page images in documents containing tens or hundreds of pages. To address this limitation, we propose a VLM-based framework that incrementally reconstructs heading hierarchies with a \emph{level-wise multimodal memory}. The memory retains a compact subset of all previously processed pages, selected by anchors. Our framework supports flexible anchor selection, and in this work we select the most recent node at each level, allowing the VLM to observe the visual, textual, and layout patterns of headings at every level. For comprehensive evaluation, we also introduce the Complex and Long Document Heading Hierarchy Reconstruction Benchmark (CLDoc-HHRBench), comprising 250 documents and 11,212 pages with expert-verified annotations. Experiments on CLDoc-HHRBench and three existing benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.
evidence_items.title: Heading Hierarchy Reconstruction for Complex and Long Documents with Level-Wise Multimodal Memory

evidence_items.summary: Research on gender-related online content is often operationalized through harm-centered tasks that collapse non-harmful gender-related and unrelated content, while existing datasets remain concentrated in high-resource languages and Global North settings. To bridge these gaps, we introduce GENDIS, a dataset of 9,600 multilingual, human-annotated YouTube comments from India, Kenya, and Nigeria (3,200 per country), annotated using a two-level framework that first identifies whether gender is referenced and then classifies gender-related content as negative, positive, or neutral. This separation provides a denominator for gender-related discourse independent of harm, enabling both prevalence estimation and characterization of its evaluative range. In the uniform random stratum, 23.8-35.0% of comments are gender-related, and among those with a resolved stance, 82% are neutral or positive. Across models, gender-reference detection is substantially easier than stance classification, especially for positive and neutral speech. Lightly supervised classifiers match frontier zero-shot large language models at substantially lower cost and outperform generic toxicity detection, while cross-country transfer remains limited. GENDIS provides a locally grounded resource for measuring when gender is invoked online and how that reference is framed.
evidence_items.title: GENDIS: Gender-Related Discourse and Stance in Multilingual YouTube Comments from India, Kenya, and Nigeria

evidence_items.summary: The rapid expansion of Industrial Internet of Things networks has increased the demand for intrusion detection systems that balance accuracy, efficiency, and cost. Most studies have focused on accuracy alone, ignoring practical deployment trade-offs. We propose a multi-dimensional evaluation framework that integrates Pareto Frontier Optimization, Attack Surface Coverage scoring, and Total Cost of Ownership modeling. We evaluate three Intrusion Detection System models on the Edge-IIoT 2022 dataset: Convolutional Neural Network-Gated Recurrent Unit-Long Short-Term Memory with Federated Learning, Decision Tree with Autoencoder, and Long Short-Term Memory-Convolutional Neural Network-Attention. Each model is assessed using normalized metrics combined via a weighted synthesis engine.The results show that the Decision Tree with Autoencoder achieved the highest composite score of 78.85%. LSTM-CNN-Attention delivered a maximum security coverage of 98.16%. Convolutional Neural Network-Gated Recurrent Unit Long Short-Term Memory achieved best accuracy with the lowest five-year cost of $1.385 million. The framework enables context-aware intrusion detection system selection for edge-based IIoT environments.
evidence_items.title: Multi-dimensional framework for context-aware IDS selection in edge-IIoT

evidence_items.summary: Global installed geothermal power capacity is approximately 18 GWe, and geothermal plants generally provide dispatchable electricity at high capacity factors. Expansion depends on reducing the capital costs and operational risks of reservoir management, plant control and equipment maintenance, and artificial intelligence has been applied to all three. Whether that work has produced evidence sufficient for deployment has not been assessed at the level of individual studies. This review reports a PRISMA-guided systematic evidence map. Searches of Scopus and Web of Science returned 8,113 records; 977 reports entered the full-text retrieval universe, 874 were assessed at full text, and 626 peer-reviewed journal articles published between 1987 and 2026 were included, resolving to 620 independent evidence units. Each included article has a full-text-grounded extraction record produced under a rule frozen before production use, with a page or section locator for every value reported quantitatively, and readiness was derived deterministically from the coded fields rather than assigned by a reader. Two thirds of the classifiable corpus is evaluated on simulation, synthetic or laboratory data, or on field data without a meaningful held-out design. Evaluation on data external to the development set is reported in 42 of the 614 articles for which the question could be determined, and three articles report a controlled pilot; none reports shadow operation or routine deployment. Maturity is stage-specific: surface conversion contributes 179 articles and four reach field evaluation, while exploration contributes 183 and more than half do. Transferability and operational integration do not advance together, so the review reports them on separate axes. The share of articles reaching field evaluation rose from 13 per cent in 2018 to 43 per cent in 2025 while externally validated work remained in single figures each year, indicating that access to field data is spreading faster than demonstrated transfer. Systematic evidence map of 626 peer-reviewed studies on AI in geothermal energy systems, coded from full text with locators. Evaluation on data external to the development set is reported in 42 of 614 determinable articles; three report a controlled pilot and none routine deployment. Readiness is derived from coded fields by a published rule, so every assignment is reproducible from the supplementary data. Transferability and operational integration do not advance together: the pilots and the external validations sit in different use cases. Field-data access is spreading while demonstrated transfer is not, rising from 13 per cent in 2018 to 43 per cent in 2025 with externally validated work flat.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence for geothermal energy systems: a systematic evidence map of validation, transferability and deployment readiness

evidence_items.summary: With recent developments in Artificial Intelligence (AI), the adoption of distributed learning paradigms such as Federated Learning (FL) has emerged. In simple terms, FL enables multiple entities to collaboratively train AI models without sharing local data. The FL paradigm is particularly valuable in privacy-sensitive settings, such as financial services, because it enables institutions to collaboratively improve fraud-detection models while keeping sensitive transaction data local. However, FL schemes are prone to security vulnerabilities, where malicious clients can poison local data or model updates and degrade the global model, and hence the performance of the resulting model might be affected. Therefore, in this work, we propose Enhanced Detective, a dual-stage robust aggregation strategy that combines Median Absolute Deviation (MAD), distance-based update filtering, and FedMedian aggregation. Experiments on an imbalanced credit card dataset evaluate targeted label-flipping and weight-scaling attacks over 50 communication rounds. With 40% malicious clients, Enhanced Detective achieves an AUPRC of 0.796 and a Recall of 0.847.
evidence_items.title: Enhanced Detective: A Dual-Stage Proactive Defense Against Internal Poisoning Attacks in Financial Fraud Detection Using Federated Learning

evidence_items.summary: Verifiable instruction-following benchmarks emphasize output-constraint satisfaction but can overlook whether responses meaningfully answer the underlying request, creating an evaluation blind spot. We show that frontier models can receive full credit for responses with little substantive answer content. Using the same verifier-based criterion as a training reward can induce reward hacking, as publicly released checkpoints exhibit higher constraint satisfaction but lower response quality after reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. To address this reward hacking, we introduce CALIF, a lightweight method that augments verifier rewards with a calibrated likelihood-based bonus to preserve response quality. CALIF evaluates response likelihood under the request alone using the existing frozen reference policy, requiring no additional judge or learned reward model. Across models ranging from 1.7B to 8B in reasoning and non-reasoning modes, CALIF improves constraint satisfaction on IFBench while maintaining response quality near or above pre-RL levels. It also outperforms corresponding base policies in 40 of 45 model-metric comparisons across three rubric-based instruction-following benchmarks, demonstrating gains beyond training verifiers.
evidence_items.title: Diagnosing and Correcting Reward Hacking in Verifiable Instruction Following

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Chronic non-communicable diseases are identified by the prolonged imbalance in the production of reactive oxygen species and antioxidant defense mechanism. Reactive species can directly attack DNA, and if there are no repairs of the lesions, these can lead to the identification of chromosomal damage, which is a well-established indicator of genomic stability and cancer risk. There is less data related to this relationship in the context of Iraq. The aim of the study was to examine the oxidative stress evaluation and chromosomal damage among patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), chronic kidney disease (CKD) and essential hypertension admitted at Al-Hussein Teaching Hospital from Al-Samawah city of Iraq. A case-control study was undertaken on 120 patients (40 T2DM, 40 non-dialysis CKD stages 3-4 and 40 essential hypertension patients), as well as on 40 control patients matched by age and sex. The study determined the level of serum malondialdehyde (MDA), total oxidant status (TOS), total antioxidant capacity (TAC), reduced glutathione (GSH), and activity of superoxide dismutase (SOD). The designed oxidative stress index (OSI) was also calculated. Chromosomal damage was evaluated among cultured peripheral blood lymphocytes using the metaphase chromosomal aberration (CA) technique and the cytokinesis-block micronucleus (CBMN) method. Findings: All patient groups showed higher amounts of MDA, TOS and OSI and lower amounts of TAC, GSH and SOD than controls (p < 0.001), most notably in CKD. The frequency of total CA (CKD 4.5 ± 1.4%, T2DM 3.6 ± 1.2%, hypertension 2.8 ± 1.0% vs 1.2 ± 0.6% in controls) and micronuclei (18.2, 14.9 and 12.1 vs 6.8 per 1000 binucleated cells respectively) was significantly increased (p < 0.001).
evidence_items.title: Relationship Between Oxidative Stress and Chromosomal Damage in Patients with Chronic Diseases

evidence_items.summary: Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming advertising by enabling marketers to create persuasive text, images, and other promotional content rapidly and at lower cost. At the same time, the ability of generative systems to produce highly realistic content creates concerns about deception, misinformation, transparency, and the credibility of consumer-facing information. The present study examines the consumer consequences of AI-generated false and misleading advertising, with particular emphasis on hallucinated product claims. The study focuses on whether AI-generated hallucinated product claims influence perceived deception, AI skepticism, and perceived information reliability, and whether these consumer responses subsequently shape purchase intention. Drawing on the stimulus-organism-response (S-O-R) framework, the study conceptualizes hallucinated product claims as the stimulus, the three consumer evaluations as the organism, and purchase intention as the response. A quantitative, cross-sectional, deductive research design was adopted. Data were collected from 320 business-school students and faculty members through a structured questionnaire using a five-point Likert scale, and the model was assessed using SmartPLS. The reported measurement results show Cronbach's alpha values above 0.70, composite reliability above the stated threshold, and average variance extracted above 0.50 for all constructs, indicating acceptable reliability and convergent validity. The reported discriminant-validity matrix also supports construct distinctiveness. The structural model reports a VIF range of 1.47-2.24 and an R² of 0.421 for purchase intention. Four of the six hypotheses are supported. AI-generated hallucinated product claims significantly increase perceived deception and significantly reduce perceived information reliability.
evidence_items.title: The Dark Side of Generative AI in Marketing: AI-Generated False and Misleading Advertising and Its Consumer Consequences

evidence_items.summary: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has increased the demand for reliable, efficient, and interpretable machine learning (ML) methods for complex prediction and decision-making tasks. However, conventional ML approaches often encounter challenges related to model optimization, generalization, computational efficiency, data imbalance, and limited interpretability. This study proposes an Advanced Machine Learning Framework for Algorithm Development, Optimization, and Explainable Intelligent Prediction that integrates data preprocessing, feature engineering, algorithm selection, Hyperparameter optimization, ensemble learning, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). Multiple ML algorithms, including Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, K-Nearest Neighbors, Gradient Boosting, and Extreme Gradient Boosting, are comparatively evaluated. Model performance is assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC), computational efficiency, and interpretability. Furthermore, SHAP and LIME techniques are incorporated to explain feature contributions and improve transparency in model predictions. The framework facilitates systematic comparison between conventional and optimized models while examining the trade-off between predictive performance, computational cost, and explainability. The proposed approach provides a generalizable pathway for developing robust and trustworthy intelligent prediction systems. Its applicability extends across healthcare, education, cyber security, finance, and other data-driven domains. The study contributes an integrated framework that combines algorithmic optimization with explainability to support accurate, transparent, efficient, and reliable ML-based decision-making systems.
evidence_items.title: An Advanced Machine Learning Framework for Algorithm Development, Optimization, and Explainable Intelligent Prediction

evidence_items.summary: The biogas production in anaerobic digesters occurs due to highly dynamic and nonlinear relationships between the properties of input substrate, environment parameters, and operational conditions of reactors. In this research, a multi-dimensional sequence-to-sequence LSTM model is proposed for predicting daily outputs of biogas by means of historical data recorded at operational level of anaerobic reactors presented in the attached database. The process of data preprocessing includes merging raw data records into daily timeseries, calculating the total feedstock as the sum of masses of all feedstock inputs, and representing five predictor variables such as ambient temperature, digester temperature, carbon-to-nitrogen ratio, total feedstock, and biogas production. After MinMax feature scaling, samples of a sequence-to-sequence learning are created with a 14-day look-back and 7-day prediction horizon to result in 5,459 timeseries of which 4,367 records are taken for training and 1,092 timeseries for evaluation. The sequence prediction network consists of an encoder LSTM with 128 units, RepeatVector component, and decoder LSTM with 64 units that use 0.2 dropout probability in recurrent layers. Training is conducted for up to 50 epochs, with the Adam optimizer, mean squared error as the loss function, mean absolute error metrics, and early stopping mechanism with patience equal to 10. The notebook reports a final visible training loss of 0.0129, validation loss of 0.0121, and validation mean absolute error of 0.0842 in normalized scale. On the test workflow, the mean absolute prediction error after inverse transformation is 18.31 m3, while an anomaly threshold of 48.34 m3 identifies 55 potential abnormal productio n days out of 1,092 evaluated days. Additionally, a SHAP-based interpretation stage is introduced to estimate the influence of features for the first forecasted day.
evidence_items.title: Biogas Yield Forecasting Using Sequence-to-Sequence LSTM With Error-Based Anomaly Detection and Post Hoc Usability

evidence_items.summary: This paper develops a mathematical framework for neonatal cardiorespiratory monitoring that moves beyond single-threshold alarms. Rather than asking whether one signal crosses a limit, it asks whether the monitored state can reach a clinically defined failure region within a stated time horizon. The author maps heart rate, respiration, and oxygen saturation into normalized transport coordinates that capture respiratory pauses, desaturation, bradycardia, recovery time, and overlapping events. The central quantity is an endpoint-specific thinness ratio: the predicted maximal approach toward failure, taken as an upper quantile over the horizon, divided by the current distance to failure. The paper proves several results. A ratio below one guarantees that the probability of entering the failure region within the horizon is at most a chosen small level, provided the quantile is valid. The mean-approach ratio also bounds that probability directly. By contrast, the earlier formulation based on expected endpoint displacement provides no such guarantee, because an infant can reach failure mid-horizon and recover by the end. In a Gaussian first-passage benchmark, the certificate is exact at a ratio of one and grows with the square root of the horizon for diffusive transport. Measurement error reduces the usable margin, giving signal quality a precise role, and the certificate transfers to the full physiological state only when failure is visible in the monitored coordinates. The author emphasizes that scale and pathway are independent: a warning described as a cardiorespiratory cascade requires both a large ratio and a connected temporal route from respiratory disturbance to the endpoint. The framework is explicitly a research instrument, not a clinical tool. It has not been validated in infants, applies only to its declared endpoint, horizon, coordinates, and model, and its central calibration claim can be tested directly on retrospective data.
evidence_items.title: Neonatal Thinness: An Endpoint-Specific Transport-to-Failure Ratio with a Probabilistic Non-Reachability Certificate for Cardiorespiratory Monitoring
