evidence_items.summary: Generated images often have coherent layouts and visual content, yet local errors in small text and complex characters still limit their readability and practical use. Scene-text refinement requires accuracy, preservation, and efficiency. Existing methods based on variational autoencoders (VAEs) can lose fine strokes during reconstruction, while full-image editing can shift background colors. In this work, we introduce PixText, a model that formulates local text refinement as grouped image generation in pixel space. Conditioned on the original image, PixText generates only the target regions, preserves unedited content, and uses MeanFlow for four-step generation. We further introduce Text Refinement Bench to evaluate text correction and image preservation in generated images. On this benchmark, PixText achieves 83.06% glyph pass and 94.66% exact target-character OCR accuracy, versus 36.77% and 52.31% for the strongest baseline. Its four-step MeanFlow variant retains an 81.84% pass rate with less than one GPU-second of amortized generation cost per image.
evidence_items.title: Efficient Scene-Text Refinement via Pixel-Space Grouped Image Generation

evidence_items.summary: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) are appealing for code generation because they can update many tokens in parallel, yet many are optimized for sequence synthesis rather than edit prediction. This setting is poorly matched to modern AI-assisted IDEs, where edit prediction must infer the next code change from recent edits, the current file, and cursor-local context. Such changes are usually sparse and preserve most source tokens, so regenerating a full code segment wastes computation. We propose Diff Diffusion, a diffusion-inspired LLM framework for code editing that predicts edit paths from an original snippet to its revised form. Diff Diffusion represents denoising as structured edit operations, and combines this formulation with multi-stage training and efficient parallel decoding. By focusing computation on changed regions, Diff Diffusion supports accurate low-latency edits and multi-position parallel modification. Across public edit-completion benchmarks, edit-prediction evaluations, and online validation, Diff Diffusion matches or leads autoregressive baselines while delivering 2.78 times faster inference on public edit-completion benchmarks and a 39.0% P50 model-latency reduction in production. This work provides a new modeling perspective for AI applications that require high accuracy and low latency.
evidence_items.title: Diff Diffusion: Predicting Edit Paths with Diffusion Models for Efficient Code Editing

evidence_items.summary: Benchmarks are essential for evaluating and improving large language models (LLMs). Yet many widely used benchmarks are redundant, making evaluation unnecessarily expensive. Benchmark compression lowers this cost by estimating full-benchmark scores and rankings from a partial evaluation. Research in this area has grown rapidly since 2024, but to our knowledge no survey has systematically organized its methods and findings. We review 119 papers to explain how methods choose what to evaluate, recover full-benchmark results, and verify their reliability. From this analysis, we develop a taxonomy covering compression within individual benchmarks, across benchmark suites, and during adaptive evaluation, together with work on redundancy and reliability. We compare their information needs, total costs, reliability checks, and limitations. Methods reduce evaluation costs by selecting representative subsets, using cheaper or reusable information, and testing adaptively, but risk poor coverage, inaccurate estimates, and sequential delays. The resulting taxonomy and practical guide help researchers choose, validate, and deploy methods for more efficient and reliable LLM evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Are We Testing Too Much? A Survey of Benchmark Compression for Efficient Evaluation of Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Constructing robust GUI agents relies on multimodal visual grounding: the ability to precisely map natural language intents to actionable on-screen components. Despite abundant desktop, web, and mobile benchmarks, high-fidelity resources tailored for diverse environments are surprisingly scarce. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Screen Referring Grounding Dataset (ScreenRef), a comprehensive GUI grounding dataset consisting of GUI screenshots paired with natural language referring expressions and box or point annotations. Spanning desktop, web, and mobile domains, ScreenRef comprises 586K screenshots and over 633K referring expression instances, covering tasks such as text recognition, visual matching, spatial understanding, and refusal scenarios. To boost the model's grounding performance, we propose the Distillation-to-Reinforcement Learning (D2RL) method to address the limited generalization of supervised fine-tuning and the sparse reward problem in reinforcement learning. Utilizing ScreenRef, we train Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct via sequential SFT and D2RL training, yielding GroundGUI-8B. GroundGUI-8B achieves 95.2% on ScreenSpot-V2, 63.9% on ScreenSpot-Pro, 65.4% on OSWorld-G, 86.8% on MMBench-GUI L2, and 38.3% on UI-Vision. Among 8B-scale models, it produces substantial gains over models trained on open-source datasets, with performance comparable or even superior to models trained on closed-source data. Code, models, and datasets are available at https://github.com/PrentisAI/GroundGUI.
evidence_items.title: GroundGUI: GUI Grounding by High-Quality Data and Distillation-to-Reinforcement Learning

evidence_items.summary: Few-step distillation reduces the sampling cost of diffusion and flow models, but existing approaches often require auxiliary score models or specialized architectures. We show that simple on-policy velocity regression already provides a strong foundation for 4-NFE generation. To represent teacher velocity variation within each coarse transition, we introduce Pivot, a training-only residual proxy that separates local corrections from the student's interval-mean prediction. We further repel the student from weaker teacher predictions, providing a lightweight mechanism for avoiding undesirable modes. The resulting framework, Simplified Matching Distillation (SMD), remains entirely regression-based, requires neither online score estimation nor adversarial training, and leaves the deployed generator unchanged. We evaluate SMD on image generation and editing, 3D generation, video synthesis, and joint audio--video generation, scaling to 33 billion parameters. At 4-NFE, SMD outperforms strong few-step baselines and surpasses multi-step teachers on several benchmarks. It also supports cross-model, multi-teacher, and causal-video distillation.
evidence_items.title: Simplifying and Improving On-Policy Distillation for Few-Step Diffusion

evidence_items.summary: System One models choose an agent's next action by scoring a supplied set of options in a single pass. This makes them fast and cheap, but when they choose wrongly there is nothing to inspect: did the model misread what the agent has seen, or read it correctly and still act wrongly? We answer behaviorally. On a frozen benchmark of agent decision states from simulated environments, customer-service policies, tool use, web navigation and coding, we pair every next-action question with factual probes about the same state, each answered independently. Across seventeen fast systems and a reasoning model, the answer is consistent: most wrong actions follow correct reading, and the more accurate a system, the more of its errors take this form. These errors are not noise; they gather on the same states across systems of every kind. Where the probed facts provably determine the action, models that read every fact still fail to combine them, and their own answers, composed by code, repair the failure. On real states, what is missing is often not a fact but the next sub-goal.
evidence_items.title: Reading Right, Acting Wrong: Diagnosing Decision Failures of System One Models in Agent Loops

evidence_items.summary: Controlling an acting LLM agent means deciding, at each step of a long-horizon task, whether to trust its next action, abstain, or hand off to a human. That decision needs a per-step confidence signal predicting whether the current rollout will eventually succeed. The agent's own self-reported verbalized confidence is the natural candidate, but existing reinforcement learning methods calibrate it against the correctness of a decision at the current step. We propose a method to calibrate it against the eventual outcome of a multi-step episode: under GRPO, the group of rollouts for a task supplies success labels, and a proper scoring rule scores each step's confidence against the realized outcome. In offline RL on recorded trajectories of a Qwen2.5-7B agent in ALFWorld, TextWorld, and WebShop environments, the AUROC of step confidence against episode outcome rises from near chance to 0.68-0.85, and the top-10% of steps the agent is most confident about succeed ~4.3x more often than average. In online RL on the live ALFWorld agent, four calibration rewards improve early-step AUROC, expected calibration error goes from 0.42 to below 0.12, and selective execution improves over both the untrained agent and a format-only RL control, without degrading task success. We also introduce an evaluation protocol that separates episode depth, task difficulty, and attempt-level foresight, which shows where the gain lies: the trained agent recognizes from its first step which tasks it will fail, while telling a succeeding attempt from a failing one at the same task is harder, with some early-window signal emerging on TextWorld.
evidence_items.title: Can an Agent Learn to Predict Its Own Failure? Outcome-Grounded Confidence Calibration in LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: A robot needs a world model that predicts how its actions will change the scene and a policy that chooses those actions. Models are usually built and evaluated for only one of these roles, and every robot records its actions in its own format. We ask whether one robot world model can serve both roles across different bodies, and what makes this work. We present GreenWAM, a world foundation model for robotics, together with the recipe that produces it: (1) a shared anatomical action space that describes 20 robot families, from bimanual arms to dexterous humanoids, in common joint coordinates; (2) joint training on these families in visual, action-conditioned and world-action modes; and (3) policies that split an action expert off the generator. As a world model, GreenWAM attains top-tier trajectory, depth and 3D accuracy on WorldArena 1.0, ahead of every world-action model and video generator in our comparison. As a policy, it scores among the top entries of the RoboTwin 2.0 leaderboard, reaches the highest zero-shot LIBERO-plus success among the compared methods and is competitive with dedicated vision-language-action and world-action policies on CALVIN and LIBERO. We further adapt GreenWAM to a real humanoid, where it succeeds more often than policies adapted from π_{0.5} and from Cosmos 3 Edge, and distill it into a single-step policy for real-time control. Controlled experiments yield three findings: robot specialization improves world prediction and control together; an action expert helps when split off at the start of adaptation; and keeping world-model modes during policy adaptation preserves robustness to scene changes.
evidence_items.title: GreenWAM: A World Foundation Model for Robotics

evidence_items.summary: Test-time scaling has enabled LLMs to solve increasingly complex reasoning, discovery, and optimization tasks. However, existing approaches often gather observations while seeking evidence for current hypotheses, then generate new hypotheses conditioned on those hypotheses and their associated evidence. This couples observation discovery to existing hypotheses, favoring local refinements over exploration of unknown hypotheses regions. Inspired by the hypothetico-deductive method (Hempel, 1945) and dual-space models of scientific discovery (Klahr & Dunbar, 1988), we introduce SHELDON, a scientific reasoning harness that separately represents and jointly explores hypothesis and observation spaces. By actively seeking new observations along with new hypotheses, SHELDON can discover observations that its current hypotheses do not explain. These unexplained observations expose gaps in its understanding, motivate new investigations, and guide the generation of hypotheses beyond refinements of existing ones. Across diagnosis, abstract reasoning, and optimization benchmarks, SHELDON outperforms evaluated baselines by up to 26.7 points. Additional analysis shows that SHELDON generates up to 4.5x more novel solutions.
evidence_items.title: SHELDON: Reasoning through Dual Search over Hypothesis and Observation Spaces

evidence_items.summary: Evaluating model uncertainty on real-world data is challenging because each instance provides only a single observed label, leaving true conditional class probabilities unknown. To address this, we introduce ProbabilityBench, a benchmark that provides exact, instance-level class probabilities across three simulated text-based domains: peer review, covert information transfer, and credit risk. By explicitly defining the full data-generating process for each environment, we analytically compute both exact class probabilities and Bayes error. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical guarantee that rendering these cases into natural-language memos strictly preserves their underlying generative probabilities. This exactness enables direct measurement of reported probability quality via KL divergence. Across 16 evaluated models, most models on the observed cost-quality Pareto frontiers are decision models, including Jev and Perplexity Decider. Finally, ProbabilityBench serves as a meta-evaluation framework, leveraging known ground-truth values to benchmark the accuracy of standard calibration metrics and Bayes-error estimators themselves.
evidence_items.title: ProbabilityBench: Model Evaluation and Calibration with Exact Ground-Truth Uncertainty

evidence_items.summary: Processing multilingual text requires both identifying a broad range of languages and distinguishing the language of each token in inputs containing multiple languages. We introduce MixLID, a token-level language identification model supporting 111 language-script combinations. MixLID follows a two-stage training process: it first learns to distinguish individual languages using the language labels of monolingual examples, then continues training on mixed-language data. The second stage uses concatenated examples from existing code-switching data alongside augmented examples created through word substitution based on correspondences between English source words and loanwords. For monolingual identification, MixLID outperforms all baselines in both accuracy and macro F1 on four benchmarks within the language coverage shared with each baseline. For mixed-language identification, it outperforms the baselines in identifying the language of individual tokens on every evaluated language pair. MixLID achieves high performance across a broad range of languages in both monolingual and mixed-language settings. The model is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/nlpai-lab/MixLID.
evidence_items.title: MixLID: Token-Level Language Identification in Mixed-Language Text

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models show strong potential for end-to-end autonomous driving by leveraging world knowledge and understanding to excel in long-tail scenarios. However, current VLAs have two limitations: 1) Degeneration into vision-action (VA) models. For low latency, regression/flow-based methods directly generate actions but underuse VLM understanding, causing unsafe, unexplainable actions. 2) Autoregressive high latency. Autoregressive methods sequentially generate chain-of-thought (CoT) and action tokens, fully leveraging VLM understanding, but high latency hinders deployment. To enable low-latency deployment while using CoT to assist action generation, we propose AUGUstus, an Autonomous-driving VLA model with Unified Generation and Understanding. We unify diffusion-based action generation and autoregressive CoT understanding in one model, where understanding only serves generation. Joint CoT supervision preserves VLM spatial understanding in shared representation for safer, more accurate trajectories. AUGUstus-mode orders action generation before CoT, so CoT supervises reliable actions during training while inference needs only action output, enabling low latency. AUGUstus-GRPO, a unified GRPO algorithm, jointly optimizes action and CoT, improving action performance. Experiments show AUGUstus achieves 94.6 PDMS on NAVSIMv1 and 90.7 EPDMS on NAVSIMv2, SOTA planning without scorer module. On nuScenes, it achieves average L2 error 0.27 m and average collision rate 0.05%, best among compared methods. To validate AUGUstus practicality, we train on in-house data with 512 NVIDIA H800 GPUs for ~2 days, evaluate on an internal 1,000 km dataset, and preliminarily deploy on a real vehicle, achieving 12 Hz operation. Project page: https://augustus-ad.github.io
evidence_items.title: AUGUstus: Autonomous Driving VLA Model with Unified Generation and Understanding

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly expected to orchestrate diverse tools over long-horizon tasks. Existing agents typically use Direct Tool Calling (DTC), where the model invokes tools sequentially, and tool responses accumulate in the model context, which can lead to context rot and orchestration breakdown. In contrast, Programmatic Tool Calling (PTC) invokes tools through executable code and stores intermediate results in runtime variables rather than appending them to the context. Prior work has explored PTC mainly as an inference-time optimization, but its benefits for agentic training remain unclear, and suitable verifiable training tasks are scarce. In this work, we introduce ProgAgent, a full PTC training stack, comprising a pipeline for synthesizing verifiable long-horizon tasks, a lightweight PTC runtime, and a two-stage training recipe. Using only 215 tasks instantiated at four environment scales, ProgAgent yields higher pass rates than the evaluated baselines of comparable size across four benchmarks. On LOCA-bench, ProgAgent-14B achieves a 30.7% pass rate at a 64k-token environment state, where these baselines score zero. Cross-harness experiments show that PTC-trained models outperform DTC-trained models under both evaluation interfaces, suggesting that the benefits of PTC training extend beyond the interface.
evidence_items.title: ProgAgent: Learning Tool Orchestration through Programmatic Training

evidence_items.summary: Asynchronous rollout improves the efficiency of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) by reducing under-utilization during long-tail generation. Sustained concurrency also concentrates context processing into fewer decode steps, increasing the KV workload per step. We characterize this KV concentration and find that KV cache quantization delivers substantially greater acceleration than weight-only and weight-activation quantization in our matched-workload comparisons. However, INT4 KV rollout can degrade learning even with token-level truncated importance sampling (TIS). We propose KV4-RL, which combines calibration-free INT4 KV quantization with selective INT8 protection of attention sinks and recent context. Protecting a bounded number of positions reduces sampler mismatch while retaining most of the speedup from INT4. Across 400 iterations of Qwen3-8B-Base GRPO training, KV4-RL achieves 1.80times cumulative rollout speedup and 1.27times cumulative full-iteration speedup over BF16 rollout, reaching 1.97times rollout speedup over the final 50 iterations. Under a common BF16 evaluator, its final six-benchmark mean accuracy is within 0.5 percentage points of BF16-rollout training for both Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base.
evidence_items.title: KV4-RL: Unlocking Faster Asynchronous Rollouts for RLVR with INT4 KV Cache Quantization

evidence_items.summary: Multi-robot systems (MRS) offer significant advantages over single-robot platforms by enabling information sharing and coordination for different tasks in complex environments. However, reliable cooperation critically depends on inferring trust over both information sources and their reported hypotheses, particularly under partial observability and potential adversarial interference. Existing approaches frequently depend on pre-established trust relationships or side-channel information, which may not be available or reliable in realistic MRS deployments. This work introduces NeST-Bayes, a neural-symbolic framework that jointly infers robot and hypothesis trust using only inter-robot observation consistency, without requiring preassigned robot trust, reputation information, or side-channel identity signals. NeST-Bayes infers instantaneous trust evidence scores for robots and object hypotheses by reasoning over ego-centric relational graphs constructed from cross-robot observation consistency. These evidence scores are accumulated over time through Bayesian updates of Beta-distributed trust beliefs to maintain temporally consistent trust estimates. Extensive evaluations show that NeST-Bayes achieves the highest mean object precision and robot recall across all benchmark settings, and the highest robot precision and object recall in most settings, compared to trust-based methods. Under aggressive optimized attacks, it achieves 98.8\% robot precision with 93.8\% recall and 98.3\% object precision with 95.4\% recall. In an occlusion-rich Webots warehouse, it maintains 92.5\% robot precision with 92.0\% recall and 97.3\% object precision with 85.0\% recall. These results demonstrate joint improvements in the reliability and coverage of retained information.
evidence_items.title: Who to Trust in Multi-Robot Systems: Joint Robot and Object Hypothesis Trust Inference via Neural-Symbolic Cross-Validation

evidence_items.summary: Contrastive learning has become the standard paradigm for multimodal representation learning, aligning semantically matched pairs while separating mismatched ones in a shared embedding space. Although various contrastive training strategies have been proposed across negative selection, batch construction, and gradient modulation, their actual effectiveness under controlled, reproducible conditions remains poorly understood. This motivates a fundamental question: Do sophisticated contrastive strategies consistently bring meaningful downstream gains in multimodal embedding learning? To address this, we systematically evaluate representative strategies under a unified benchmarking framework on MMEB. Surprisingly, direct evaluations reveal that most existing strategies offer marginal gains over a standard aligned baseline, with several even degrading overall performance. To uncover the underlying failure modes, we introduce an MLLM-as-a-Judge diagnostic framework that dissects top-1 retrieval behaviors into labeled positives, false negatives (unlabeled valid matches), and hard/easy negative errors. Our systematic analysis yields three key insights: (1) Gradient distortion: Upweighting gradients from high-similarity negatives consistently hurts downstream generalization; (2) Distribution illusion: Wider separation between positive and negative similarity distributions does not necessarily translate to better retrieval performance; and (3) Synergistic training: While false-negative mitigation or hard-batch construction yields limited gains in isolation, integrating hard-negative mining, false-negative mitigation, and hard-batch construction achieves optimal performance, delivering an average improvement of 6.0% on MMEB with Qwen2-VL-2B. Overall, our findings demystify popular contrastive strategies and provide actionable recipes for training universal multimodal embedding models.
evidence_items.title: What Really Works for Universal Multimodal Embeddings? A Controlled Study of Contrastive Training Strategies

evidence_items.summary: Coding agents increasingly interact with users by generating interactive software on the fly rather than replying in text, yet many bugs in such software reveal themselves only after multi-step interactions. Today, users must discover these bugs and wait for fixes, making the development loop slow and expensive. Existing benchmarks typically assume the bugs have already been identified, leaving agents' ability to find interaction-dependent failures largely unevaluated. We introduce SWEeper-Bench, 200 tasks built from real bug fixes in 200 widely used open-source web applications. Each task gives the agent only the codebase and an open-ended request such as "Find and fix issues in Focalboard's board sharing and membership." Because these bugs are hard to detect from code alone, agents must design interactive tests to uncover them. An agentic verifier then judges each repair by what a user would observe in the browser. The best of 15 frontier agents passes only 59.0% of tasks. Through stage-by-stage analysis of agent trajectories, we show that the biggest bottleneck is identifying the buggy behavior: agents often reach the relevant feature but never trigger the failure or fail to recognize it. SWEeper-Bench measures progress toward agents that close this loop themselves, delivering software that works without waiting for user feedback.
evidence_items.title: SWEeper-Bench: Can Agents Discover Bugs in Interactive Software?

evidence_items.summary: Improving embodied agents often focuses on optimizing the underlying model through training, while the surrounding agent harness that controls planning, context, and tool use is typically engineered. We ask whether this harness can instead improve itself directly from experience traces under sparse environmental feedback. We propose EMbodied Agent Harness Optimization (EMHO), a self-evolving framework that keeps the embodied model frozen and iteratively revises its harness by analyzing execution trajectories and prior harness history. EMHO optimizes beyond skills or recovery prompts, modifying how the agent monitors progress, uses vision tools, grounds observations, and responds to failures. To support multiple subtasks with a single harness, we introduce EMHO-Merge, which addresses trade-offs in jointly optimizing a single shared harness across subtasks by using episode-level gains and losses to guide evidence-supported refinement of when and how revised behaviors are applied. We evaluate EMHO on EmbodiedBench across navigation and manipulation tasks, and EMHO consistently improves task success for both Qwen 9B and 27B models. Qualitative analysis shows that EMHO goes beyond recovering from failures and unproductive actions to reshape how the embodied agent interprets and interacts with its environment.
evidence_items.title: EMHO: EMbodied Agent Harness Optimization via Experience Traces

evidence_items.summary: 2026 Frontier & Reasoning LLM Benchmarks: Elo, SWE-bench, MATH & Cost | artificial intelligence | nlp | deep learning
evidence_items.title: Top LLMs Frontier AI Benchmarks 2026

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in decision-support systems because of their ability to interpret complex queries, synthesize information, and generate contextually relevant responses. However, their use in reliability sensitive settings remains challenging because LLMs can produce incorrect or unsupported outputs while expressing a high degree of linguistic confidence. This paper presents a confidence aware explainable AI framework for improving the reliability of LLM-based decision support. The proposed approach combines model confidence, semantic consistency across multiple stochastic generations, and explanation support to construct a composite reliability score. A selective decision module then uses this score to determine whether a generated response should be accepted, flagged for review, or withheld through abstention. The framework is evaluated across factual, commonsense, and multi-step reasoning tasks using multiple open-weight LLMs. Performance is assessed in terms of answer accuracy, expected calibration error, failure-detection AUROC, selective accuracy, and response coverage. The evaluation investigates whether combining complementary reliability signals provides a more informative assessment of response correctness than self-reported confidence, model confidence, or semantic consistency alone. The proposed framework provides a practical reliability layer for LLM-based decision-support systems by jointly communicating confidence, explanation support, and an actionable response decision, thereby helping distinguish sufficiently reliable outputs from those requiring further verification or abstention.
evidence_items.title: Confidence-Aware Explainable AI for Reliable Large Language Model Decision Support

evidence_items.summary: Abstract A persistent gap separates academic research priorities from the operational challenges faced by manufacturing firms. Established identification methods, among them Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) workshops, Lean audits and consultant engagements, are episodic, bounded by participant expertise and organised along departmental lines, which makes cross-departmental issues hard to surface. Multi-agent systems built on large language models (LLMs) have meanwhile shown collaborative problem-solving ability in software engineering and, more recently, in shopfloor scheduling and supply chain coordination. This article is a Perspective. It develops a framework and a research agenda; implementation and empirical evaluation fall outside its scope and are set out as its first research priorities. Three contributions are offered. The first is a synthesis of literature from industrial problem identification, LLM-based autonomous agents and manufacturing AI, which positions the proposal against existing industrial LLM agent work. The second is a framework in which six domain-specialised agents (production, quality, maintenance, supply chain, safety, energy) would collaborate through a five-phase protocol: worker-driven discovery, cross-departmental analysis, candidate-relationship detection, consensus-based financial assessment and debate-driven prioritisation. The prioritisation procedure is fully specified, including the normalisation of financial estimates, a measure of estimate dispersion, the derivation of criteria weights, a non-compensatory gate for safety-critical items and a mandatory human verification step. The third is a worked calculation on a hypothetical steel manufacturing vignette, included so that the procedure can be reproduced and scrutinised rather than as evidence of effectiveness. A preliminary qualitative readiness assessment and a three-horizon agenda of fourteen research questions complete the paper.
evidence_items.title: Large language model multiagent systems for industrial problem discovery and prioritization

organizations: Department of Information and Computer Sciences, University of Hawai‘i at Mānoa, Honolulu, HI 96822, USA
College of Engineering, University of Hawai‘i at Mānoa, Honolulu, HI 96822, USA
evidence_items.summary: Electroencephalography analysis typically requires multistage processing pipelines for which configuration depends on recording characteristics and the intended analytical objective. Although automated pipelines improve reproducibility, they generally implement predefined processing sequences. We present an agentic framework in which a large language model (LLM) orchestrator synthesizes and executes task-specific EEG processing workflows by selecting, parameterizing, and ordering established signal processing components accessed through Model Context Protocol interfaces. Computational EEG processing and analysis operations are performed using established EEGLAB (version 2026.0.0) implementations running in MATLAB (R2026a) , while structured execution results and quality control information are returned to the orchestrator to support adaptation during execution. The framework is evaluated by examining tool-layer execution fidelity, independent pipeline synthesis, and the quality of the resulting EEG output relative to the established DISCOVER-EEG workflow. In an evaluation using eight resting state EEG recordings from four participants, mean epoch retention was 0.845 for the agent-generated pipeline and 0.843 for DISCOVER-EEG, while mean spectral entropy was 4.87 and 4.84 bits, respectively. Mean signal-to-noise ratio was 13.92 dB for the agent-generated pipeline and 11.14 dB for DISCOVER-EEG; however, this difference should be interpreted cautiously because the pipelines used different upper filter boundaries. A secondary analysis examined whether EEG processed using the generated pipeline retained features relevant to Alzheimer’s disease versus healthy control classification. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of coupling LLM-based orchestration with EEG processing software to generate executable task-specific workflows with structured execution records and provenance.
evidence_items.title: Agentic EEG Pipeline Synthesis Using Large Language Models and the Model Context Protocol

organizations: Department of Artificial Intelligence, Faculty of Information Technology and Artificial Intelligence, Abai Kazakh National Pedagogical University, 13 Dostyk Ave., Almaty 050010, Kazakhstan

Department of Informatics and Informatization of Education, Faculty of Information Technology and Artificial Intelligence, Abai Kazakh National Pedagogical University, 13 Dostyk Ave., Almaty 050010, Kazakhstan
evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in education, but evidence on their performance comes mainly from high-resource languages. We evaluated five commercial LLMs in Kazakh in a zero-shot setting: sentiment classification on 300 class-balanced KazSAnDRA reviews and question answering (QA) on the same 300 randomly sampled KazQAD questions with and without the gold supporting passage. Exact McNemar tests with Holm correction found no significant pairwise differences on sentiment classification, one with supporting context, and nine without context under the Containment criterion. For OpenAI and Anthropic, the higher-tier model had a larger advantage over its lower-tier counterpart when the supporting passage was removed (tier-by-regime interaction: OR = 1.92, 95% CI [1.52, 2.43]). Closed-book scores were affected by output format, inflectional morphology, and answer length. Human evaluation of 500 QA responses showed that string-based metrics substantially underestimated closed-book accuracy (0.55 by human judgement versus 0.26 by Containment). Under human judgement, the three higher-scoring models did not differ significantly from one another. Access to a relevant passage narrowed differences between models, although this oracle-context condition did not test a retrieval system. These findings support task-specific evaluation of Kazakh-language educational assistants and the use of answer-matching criteria checked against human judgement.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Kazakh-Language Educational Assistants: Sentiment Classification and Question Answering with and Without Context

organizations: University of Louisville School of Medicine, Louisville, KY
Norton Healthcare, Louisville Arm and Hand Institute, Louisville, KY
evidence_items.summary: Background: Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) is a common entrapment neuropathy, and as patients increasingly seek health information online, the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in providing accurate medical advice is gaining attention. This study evaluates the responses of two large language models (LLMs), ChatGPT and Google Gemini, regarding CTS management, comparing their outputs to established clinical practice guidelines in terms of accuracy, completeness, and readability. Methods: Seven questions related to CTS treatment were developed and posed to both ChatGPT and Google Gemini. The generated responses were assessed by eight fellowship-trained hand surgeons, who independently classified each answer as “appropriate,” “appropriate but incomplete,” or “inappropriate.” Readability was determined as grade level using a standardized online calculator that assessed multiple readability formulas. Results: Out of 112 total responses evaluated, 76 were deemed appropriate, with ChatGPT providing 46 appropriate responses compared with 30 from Gemini. Readability analysis indicated that ChatGPT’s responses averaged at a 12th-grade reading level, while Gemini’s averaged a 10th-grade level. Notably, 24 responses were graded as “appropriate but incomplete,” emphasizing the need for comprehensive information. Conclusion: This study demonstrates the potential of AI-driven platforms in enhancing patient education on CTS management. ChatGPT outperformed Gemini in accuracy, but both models showed limitations in completeness. The findings highlight the importance of ensuring that AI-generated health information is not only accurate but also accessible to patient populations. Future research should focus on improving the integration of AI with health care provider insights and quality resources to enhance patient outcomes and understanding.
evidence_items.title: Carpal tunnel syndrome: Do large language models utilize the clinical practice guidelines?

organizations: Instituto Politécnico Nacional, Mexico
evidence_items.summary: The objective of this chapter is to determine the implications of Artificial Intelligence in doctoral education to integrate it as a priority form of literacy at this educational level. In the case of doctoral education, the integration of AI is the main challenge because these future researchers will be the generators of scientific and technological knowledge who will face the challenges of an AI-influenced world. The chapter is structured in three parts. The first presents a theoretical framework focused on the characteristics of doctoral training in universities, mentioning its relevance and the different types of doctorates (research-oriented and professional). The second part discusses the concepts and dimensions of artificial intelligence literacy through an organized review of articles. The third part addresses doctoral training in the context of AI, specifically the proposed conceptual model based on student acceptance and evaluation, institutional policies, and hybrid writing-AI process.
evidence_items.title: Implications of Artificial Intelligence in Doctoral Education

evidence_items.summary: Introduction Construction delays remain a challenge in projects, often resulting in cost overruns, disputes, productivity losses, and schedule inefficiencies. Growing project complexity has increased the need for data-driven approaches to delay analysis and management. This study reviews the application of artificial intelligence in construction delay analysis and management by examining application areas, techniques, project contexts, implementation maturity, and research gaps. Methods A structured literature review was conducted using a PRISMA-guided search and screening process. Scopus and Web of Science were searched for studies published between 2021 and 2025. Following database filtering, title and abstract screening, and full-text eligibility assessment, 42 studies were retained for qualitative synthesis. Results The reviewed studies applied artificial intelligence to delay prediction, delay-cause identification, risk prioritisation, progress monitoring, schedule recovery, and optimisation using machine learning, deep learning, ensemble learning, and hybrid modelling approaches. Several studies reported predictive accuracy above 90%, particularly for artificial neural networks, ensemble techniques, and hybrid optimisation models. However, evidence remains constrained by limited datasets, project-specific applications, weak real-time data integration, and insufficient consideration of contractual and external factors. Discussion The reviewed studies indicate that Artificial Intelligence (AI) models have improved predictive capability in construction delay management. However, practical implementation remains limited by data availability, model interpretability, and weak integration with project decision-making processes. Conclusion Artificial intelligence can improve construction delay management through transparent and data-driven approaches.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Construction Delay Analysis and Management: A Review

organizations: Faculty of Education and Liberal Arts, Inti International University, 71800 Bandar Baru Nilai, Labu, Seremban, Negeri Sembilan, Malaysia
evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is often presented as a sequence of increasingly capable tools, yet educational outcomes do not rise automatically with model capability. This narrative review argues that the decisive variable is alignment: AI produces durable educational value when its affordances are aligned with pedagogy, assessment, educator agency, and institutional governance. The review traces the field from automation and learning analytics through adaptive support and generative co-production to an emerging model of responsible augmentation. Recent meta-analyses, controlled studies, systematic reviews, policy documents, and selected empirical studies were critically compared across three interdependent domains: resources and learning environments; teaching and learning; and management, assessment, and evaluation. The synthesis explains why apparently contradictory findings coexist. Structured, curriculum-aligned AI tutoring can improve immediate learning, whereas unconstrained answer generation can raise supported performance while weakening independent performance. Likewise, automated assessment can improve feedback speed but becomes educationally unsafe when opaque scores or unreliable detectors are treated as final decisions. Evidence concerning international and multilingual learners further shows that language, culture, affect, and data representation are not peripheral variables. The review proposes a responsible-augmentation framework in which alignment, agency, equity, and accountability operate across all three domains. It concludes with a research agenda prioritising longitudinal transfer, calibrated human–AI collaboration, subgroup validity, transparent governance, and institution-level implementation studies.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education From Automation to Responsible Augmentation

evidence_items.summary: Educators and researchers increasingly recognize the importance of Artificial Intelligence literacy. Despite the growing body of related literature, the challenges and enabling factors for its integration into preschool education remain insufficiently explored and theoretically documented. It is crucial to understand both the difficulties and the conditions that influence its promotion, as well as the perceptions formed in kindergartens, so that these can become subjects of further investigation and evaluation. The present study aims to capture teachers’ views on the importance of Artificial Intelligence literacy in preschool education, as well as to highlight the challenges and factors that influence its implementation. The data were collected from 97 educators through a structured digital questionnaire.
evidence_items.title: Kindergarten teachers’ perceptions of artificial intelligence in early childhood education.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Spaceflight instruments must undergo electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) testing under strict contamination-control requirements. In this context, local RF-transparent protective covers may be considered when the test facility cannot provide the required cleanliness conditions around the hardware. This work presents an application-oriented electromagnetic assessment of candidate RF-transparent protective covers for contamination-sensitive EMC testing. Several candidate materials are characterized using the open-ended coaxial probe (OECP) technique over the 2–20 GHz band to determine their effective dielectric properties and estimate their normal-incidence flat-wall transmission coefficients. Full-cover transfer-function (TF) measurements are then performed at INTA’s BIANCHA free-space anechoic facility over the 4.5–8 GHz band, using two receiving antennas with complementary radiation characteristics: a pyramidal horn and a top-hat bicone. Hemispherical covers fabricated with five candidate materials are first assessed, including repeatability and time-domain gating analyses. An alternative cubic cover is then evaluated to study the influence of cover geometry, angular incidence and edge/corner effects. An additional S 11 based mismatch assessment is also performed to distinguish antenna input-matching effects from broader system-level antenna–cover interactions. The results show that low-loss dielectric covers can introduce limited TF perturbations within the tested free-space configuration, while also demonstrating that cover geometry has a significant impact on the angular stability of the measured response. The conclusions are therefore restricted to the experimentally validated 4.5–8 GHz BIANCHA configuration.
evidence_items.title: Electromagnetic assessment of RF-transparent protective covers for contamination-sensitive EMC testing

organizations: Rivers State University, Port Harcourt, Rivers State, Nigeria
evidence_items.summary: This study assessed the physicochemical parameters and heavy metal (Pb, Cd, Cr, Ni, Cu, Zn) concentrations in surface water of Mgbuodahia River, Niger Delta, Nigeria, for six months (May– October 2025) across four stations (ST1–ST4). Physicochemical parameters were measured in situ, heavy metals were quantified by atomic absorption spectrophotometry, and data were evaluated using a General Linear Model ANOVA with Tukey’s pairwise comparison. Dissolved oxygen was low (0.62±0.12 mg/L) and biochemical oxygen demand elevated (8.41±4.20 mg/L), indicating organic pollution. Lead (0.33±0.10 mg/L) and cadmium (0.10±0.06 mg/L) exceeded WHO permissible limits (0.01 and 0.003 mg/L respectively) at every station and month. ANOVA showed significant monthly variation for pH, conductivity, temperature and most heavy metals, while chromium showed no significant station or month effect, suggesting a diffuse rather than point-source origin. Nickel showed a pronounced June peak roughly double every other month's mean, indicating an episodic input event. These concentrations are higher than values reported for several other Niger Delta water bodies, indicating that Mgbuodahia River is affected by lead and cadmium inputs. The study concludes that Mgbuodahia River is impacted by organic and heavy metal pollution and recommends continuous monitoring and regulation of discharge into the river.
evidence_items.title: Physicochemical Parameters and Heavy Metal Contamination of Surface Water of Mgbuodahia River, Niger Delta, Nigeria

evidence_items.summary: This study examined the relationships between Data Availability Statement (DAS) categories, citation counts, and the evolution of research data-sharing practices. We analysed 653,490 research articles published between 2010 and 2025 in the ten open-access journals with the most DAS-containing articles, using PubMed Central full-text records matched to Web of Science citation data. DASs were classified into seven categories with a validated large language model (LLM) framework, and associations with citations were evaluated by non-parametric tests and regressions controlling for journal and publication year. The associations varied across journals (DAS × journal interaction: joint Wald test F54 = 30.49, p < 0.001). After adjustment they were generally small: relative to articles reporting no data generated or not applicable (N), reuse of public third-party data (R) was the only category positive and significant in all four specifications; in-article or identifier-free availability (P) was also associated with slightly higher counts in most specifications; and full repository deposition (F) showed no clear advantage over N and lay slightly below author-request-only statements (A; − 0.029, 95% CI: − 0.036 to − 0.023). Longitudinally, rising DAS adoption was accompanied by a more heterogeneous pooled composition of sharing mechanisms rather than a single pathway towards open data, a shift driven largely by the staggered entry of journals. DAS categories thus provide a practical, scalable framework for characterising data-sharing practices, and journal context matters when interpreting them.
evidence_items.title: Research Data-Sharing Practices Through the Lens of Data Availability Statements

organizations: College of Artificial Intelligence, Henan Agricultural University, Zhengzhou 450002, China
Agricultural Information Institute, Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences, Beijing 100081, China
evidence_items.summary: Wheat pests and diseases threaten food security, but field management still lacks intelligent systems that can connect visual diagnosis with executable treatment recommendations. This study proposes WDPG, a knowledge-enhanced multi-agent framework that integrates a three-layer heterogeneous knowledge graph with a source-traceable prescription knowledge base, and combines DSPy-based diagnostic prompt optimization, DeepResearch-based evidence completion, and agentic prescription verification. The system takes wheat images or symptom descriptions as input and coordinates Diagnostic, Prescription, and Critic agents to generate structured prescriptions with traceable evidence, dosage, application method, and pre-harvest interval. On a 601-sample held-out test set, the integrated WDPG system achieved an end-to-end full-prescription accuracy of 0.9218 and demonstrated better overall performance than GPT-5.5 and GLM-4.6V for wheat pest and disease diagnosis and prescription generation. These results support the effectiveness of the integrated WDPG framework for structured and source-grounded wheat pest and disease diagnosis and prescription generation.
evidence_items.title: WDPG: An Integrated Agentic Framework for Wheat Pest and Disease Diagnosis and Prescription Generation

organizations: South China Normal University
Harbin Institute of Technology
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Age-related molecular heterogeneity in breast cancer complicates the prioritization of reproducible research candidates across heterogeneous molecular resources. We developed a bounded agentic in silico framework integrating curated ageing genes, The Cancer Genome Atlas Breast Invasive Carcinoma (TCGA-BRCA), the independent GSE42568 cohort, STRING protein-protein associations, and Gene Ontology and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes enrichment. Of 307 curated human ageing-related genes, 292 were expression-testable in 1,079 TCGA-BRCA primary tumors. Continuous-age screening identified 126 genes at a false discovery rate below 0.05, and 80 remained significant after adjustment for estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2, and pathological stage. Among 40 prespecified candidates tested in GSE42568, eight replicated directionally; IL7R, SQSTM1, EGR1, and IGF1 were both cross-cohort replicated and robust across estrogen-receptor strata. Stratified age-label permutation supported the overall discovery signal (empirical P = 0.001996). STRING hub rankings were stable across interaction-confidence thresholds (Spearman rho = 0.81–0.90), and 514 significant functional terms were reduced to 30 representative modules. A 760-scenario process-aware benchmark compared static, goal-planning, adaptive, and bounded controllers. The bounded controller achieved 1.000 for policy conformance, feasible-goal completion, action appropriateness, safety conformance, provenance conformance, and escalation conformance, with resource stewardship of 0.988. The framework provides a reproducible computational route for molecular candidate prioritization and hypothesis generation while explicitly excluding autonomous diagnosis, prognosis, treatment recommendation, and clinical biomarker declaration.
evidence_items.title: A Bounded Agentic In Silico Framework for Age-Aware Molecular Candidate Prioritization in Breast Cancer

organizations: University of Thessaly, Greece
evidence_items.summary: Utilising language models (LLMs) to prepare STEM activities can reduce lesson-planning time, but speed does not ensure quality. A standalone model may introduce factual errors or misconceptions, use language unsuitable for children's age, or suggest unsafe materials. This paper presents a theoretical and methodological framework that treats AI as an agentic system. Models with distinct roles cross-check one another and ground their work through RAG in an expert-reviewed, curated knowledge base. The knowledge base is locally owned and human-readable, with each note recording its source and review status. The system may use local models or privacy-protecting, low-cost services. It is paired with a TPACK-based professional development programme. Prompting matters, but teachers remain responsible for evaluating the evidence and deciding whether a draft suits their context. Four conditions are proposed: ordinary generation, RAG, matched self-review, and a reviewer-agent workflow. The framework has been partially implemented as an operational alpha but has not yet been formally evaluated.
evidence_items.title: Enhancing Teacher Professional Development for Preschool and Early STEM Education Through RAG and a Knowledge-Grounded Agentic System

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) routers reduce serving cost by choosing which model to call and how many output tokens to grant it for each query. Existing routers rank model-budget actions using a single quality metric. This does not work for mixed workloads. For ordinary queries, a good answer is correct and useful (utility); for security-sensitive queries, a good answer refuses harmful requests or resists malicious instructions (security). These two objectives prefer different models and budgets. We propose SCRouter, a router that learns when to prioritize security and how to allocate the token budget. For each model-budget pair, it estimates the probability that the response finishes within budget. It uses this probability to predict utility and security separately. A small probe determines how to weight these two predictions for each query. SCRouter then selects the model and budget by balancing the weighted utility and security against cost. We also build SCRouterBench, a benchmark of 38,869 utility and security queries spanning nine security dimensions, each answered under all 144 combinations of 12 models and 12 budgets, plus 2,753 out-of-domain queries. SCRouter improves the baselines by 13-29 points in-domain and 19-23 points out-of-domain.
evidence_items.title: Rethinking Quality in Large Language Model Routing: Security-Conditioned Model-and-Budget Selection

evidence_items.summary: Recently, Morris et al. introduced TinyLoRA, a strategy for LLM fine-tuning which introduces arbitrarily few parameters, and demonstrated accuracy improvements using less than $10$ parameters rather than the ${\gtrsim 10,000}$ typically demanded by LoRA-based methods. However, that study continued to use gradient-based local search methods of the kind deployed for training multi-billion parameter LLMs in the first place. This article is predicated on the observation that, in the low dimensional setting, global optimization methods become tractable, unlocking Large language Model Bayesian Optimization (LlMBO). LlMBO is sample-efficient, gradient-free, memory-light, parallelizes across devices without synchronization, and, unlike policy-gradient methods, can optimize greedy-decoding accuracy directly. We describe numerical experiments comparing LlMBO against GRPO on fine-tuning tasks for a variety of models on a math benchmark suite which show that LlMBO can be a suitable alternative in this regime, matching or exceeding GRPO's fine tuning gains, while using a fraction of the compute and memory.
evidence_items.title: How Low Can You Go: Fine-Tuning LLMs with Bayesian Optimization (LlMBO)

evidence_items.summary:
Cognitive bias in large language models (LLMs) undermines their reliability due to the practical limitations of existing mitigation methods. This study introduces a divergence-reflection-convergence (DRC) framework, which leverages a computationally efficient and inference-time strategy designed to identify and mitigate cognitive biases without costly retraining.
 
 
 
 This study proposes a novel three-stage DRC framework utilizing a competitive reasoning process where the model first generates divergent viewpoints, subsequently reflects on them to extract a decision rule, and finally converges on a robust output. Furthermore, we validate the DRC framework on five popular LLMs across four common dimensions of cognitive bias, quantifying performance with evaluation metrics including asymmetric kappa (AK) and total variation distance (TVD).
 
 
 
 The experimental results demonstrate that LLMs refined by the DRC framework provide more consistent and reliable outputs across all scenarios. Notably, this effect is more pronounced for mitigating internal biases than external biases, suggesting the DRC framework is highly effective at correcting LLMs' flawed internal heuristics. In terms of specific evaluation metrics, the DRC framework successfully transforms all negative or near-zero AK scores into positive values and markedly reduces TVD scores, both of which signify a substantial bias reduction.
 
 
 
 This study develops a DRC framework as a novel inference-time mitigation scheme for LLM bias that addresses the practical limitations of retraining-based approaches. Its competitive reasoning process offers a scalable solution for deploying responsible AI. Concurrently, we propose a more nuanced evaluation metric, the AK, tailored for quantifying LLM bias in subjective contexts.
evidence_items.title: Toward fairer large language models: a divergence-reflection-convergence framework for mitigating cognitive bias

evidence_items.summary: Aesthetic image cropping improves composition by balancing subjects, context, and image boundaries. Large vision-language models bring semantic knowledge to this task, but their scale limits lightweight photography assistance. We propose FrameLite, a compact cropping model built on Qwen3.5-0.8B. Our approach is motivated by the observation that a small model can generate better crops than its first answer suggests. We develop three-stage training to turn this potential into stronger direct predictions. Spatial and composition training establishes localization and framing preferences. Quality-Guided Online Supervision (QOS) then learns the highest-quality complete answers among the current policy's generated candidates. Greedy-Referenced Optimization (GRO) further refines the policy using positive and negative quality differences relative to its current greedy answer. Both online stages use annotation-derived feedback, while inference returns one coordinate answer without search or an external scorer. Experiments show that FrameLite outperforms the compared large-VLM croppers across public benchmarks with a substantially smaller backbone. Controlled studies confirm that selecting high-quality training answers improves the final model beyond online sampling alone. We will release our code and model weights at https://github.com/JianzeLi-114/FrameLite .
evidence_items.title: FrameLite: Decision-Oriented Aesthetic Cropping with a Compact Vision-Language Model

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for human mobility generation by modeling individual routines, activities, and mobility preferences. However, existing approaches remain largely resident-centric: generating realistic individual trajectories does not necessarily recover the encounters that emerge when multiple residents co-occur at the same place and time. To this end, we study encounter-aware human mobility generation, which jointly preserves individual mobility and population-level interaction structure. We propose EncounterMob, an encounter-driven LLM framework consisting of a coarse-to-fine Encounter Generator and an Iterative Coupling Framework. The Encounter Generator first captures city-level encounter rhythms and then instantiates participant-time-venue encounters, while the Iterative Coupling Framework coordinates these encounters with personal mobility behavior through successive refinement. We further introduce an encounter recovery protocol covering encounter marginal and joint distributions over residents, times, and venues. Experiments on the Japan and NYC datasets show that EncounterMob outperforms all external baselines on all seven encounter metrics and all six personal mobility metrics. Compared with ELLMob, it reduces the participant-time-venue joint error by 40.4%/41.7% and the mean personal mobility error by 58.8%/32.7% on Japan/NYC, respectively.
evidence_items.title: Encounter-Driven City-Scale Human Mobility Generation with Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary:
INTRODUCTION
Despite growing interest in large language models (LLMs) for endodontic diagnosis, prior studies have used simulated cases, examination formats, or small selected series. This multicenter retrospective study compared the diagnostic accuracy of ChatGPT-5.2 and Gemini 3.0 with that of calibrated endodontists across 645 teeth requiring initial root canal treatment.


METHODS
Cases were evaluated across four endpoints: pulpal diagnosis, periapical diagnosis, treatment planning, and case difficulty. Standardized clinical summaries and radiographs were submitted to endodontists and both LLMs using a fixed single-pass protocol. Exact-match accuracy, Cohen's κ, Gwet's AC1, macro-averaged F1 score, McNemar tests, and generalized estimating equations were used for statistical comparison.


RESULTS
Endpoint accuracies ranged from 74% to 88%. Macro F1 was highest for periapical diagnosis (ChatGPT-5.2, 0.724; Gemini 3.0, 0.719) and lowest for treatment planning (0.385; 0.550), where both models showed lower observed performance in minority categories, interpreted as suggestive given small subgroup sizes. Composite accuracy across the three clinical endpoints was 61.1% (95% CI, 57.4%-64.8%) and 59.4% (95% CI, 55.3%-63.3%), and four-endpoint accuracy was 47.3% (95% CI, 43.3%-51.2%) and 46.2% (95% CI, 42.3%-49.8%), indicating at least one clinically relevant error in about half of cases. Treatment planning was the only endpoint differing between models after Holm-Bonferroni correction, favoring Gemini 3.0 (OR, 1.457; adjusted p = .003).


CONCLUSIONS
Both models performed acceptably on individual endpoints and common presentations, but performance was endpoint-specific and substantially reduced on integrated assessment and low-prevalence categories. These findings support use of LLMs in endodontic diagnosis and treatment planning as adjunctive tools, but not without expert supervision.
evidence_items.title: Comparing Diagnostic Ability of Two Off-the-Shelf Large Language Models with That of Endodontists for Teeth Requiring Initial Root Canal Treatment: A Multicenter Retrospective Investigation.
Modality mismatch or clinical blind spot? Methodological considerations in benchmarking large language models against human raters of PET/CT radiation-safety videos.

evidence_items.summary: We trained Agaram 2.5B, a 2.5-billion-parameter Tamil-English language model, from scratch on about 50 billion tokens (58% Tamil, the rest English, math, code and parallel text) on one node of eight H100 GPUs in about six days, with a new tokenizer that, unlike our first model's, keeps line breaks. Supervised fine-tuning on 134,428 conversations, whose replies an open-weight teacher model wrote, and three short targeted rounds turned it into a chat model that answers in Tamil script, romanized Tamil (Tanglish) and English and can call tools: on 25 tool prompts whose schemas appear in training it picks the right tool 23 times and gives exactly the expected arguments 13 times. The released model translates better than Sarvam-1, a 2B Indic base model, in all six FLORES and IN22 directions (FLORES chrF 54.3 into Tamil and 55.2 into English, against 49.2 and 44.2), and nearly doubles its base model on native-Tamil IndicIFEval (19.3% from 10.0%). It is weak on knowledge: reading-comprehension and knowledge benchmarks sit near chance, and on 50 held-out everyday questions written by one native speaker, one LLM judge rated 46% of its replies usable (22-24 of 50 over three passes; 95% interval for 23 of 50, 33-60%), with nearly every failure a wrong fact. Our two further SFT experiments changed answer format but not the knowledge measures. We also describe our first model, Agaram 1.5B, whose failures shaped the choices here; how the judge's scores varied between passes on identical replies; and, item by item, what the targeted rounds trained against and where frontier-model text entered the data. The project ran on compute credits and our own funds, about USD 13,300 across both models; the weights are released (licence to be announced after legal review), with GGUF files for llama.cpp, at https://huggingface.co/murai-labs/agaram-2.5b-instruct; code at https://github.com/Murai-Labs/Agaram2.5b
evidence_items.title: Agaram 2.5B: The First Tamil-First Language Model Trained from Scratch with Tool Calling. A Playbook for Under-Represented Languages

evidence_items.summary: How should demonstration quality be used during vision-language-action (VLA) pretraining to improve performance after target-task fine-tuning? We compare weighting, filtering, and conditioning across reward definitions and label granularities using 5,000 naturally suboptimal human demonstrations and 24 target tasks. Within each VLA, we match demonstrations and training budgets. Additional comparisons examine pretraining data size and the roles of quality tags during fine-tuning and inference. Across three VLAs, we find that approach-aware episode conditioning improves mean success over plain behavioral cloning; conditioning and filtering favor episode and chunk labels, respectively, on average, with model-dependent reversals; and constant-tag fine-tuning improves mean success after conditioned pretraining with either tagged or untagged inference. We introduce AXIS-Bench to support these controlled comparisons. Built on crowdsourced simulation demonstrations, it provides recorded object and contact states for recomputing quality labels on shared trajectories. Replayable trajectories support workspace-aligned rendering and user-defined real-world target tasks. In our real-world experiment, simulation pretraining raises success from 9.6\% to 31.7\%. Project page: https://axis-bench.github.io/.
evidence_items.title: What Matters in Quality-Aware VLA Pretraining: A Benchmark and Empirical Study

evidence_items.summary: AI for Organizing Digital Collections is a half-day tutorial that introduces practical approaches for applying AI to organize textual, visual, and multimodal digital collections. The tutorial focuses on how Large Language Models (LLMs) can support classification, subject analysis, and vocabulary mapping, and how Vision-Language Models can support archival image description and visual subject term assignment. Through accessible explanations, demonstrations, and hands-on exercises, participants will learn how to train LLMs to support digital collection organizations, evaluate model outputs, and design AI-assisted workflows. The tutorial is intended for digital library researchers, metadata professionals, catalogers, LIS educators, students, and cultural heritage practitioners interested in using AI to improve collection organization and discoverability.
evidence_items.title: AI for Organizing Digital Collections: Practical Approaches with LLMs and Vision-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Scholarly metadata is an essential element in the scholarly ecosystem, empowering discovery, interoperability, and provenance and its efficacy relies on metadata quality and coverage. However, with the substantial increase in the number and diversity of research artifacts over time, it has become a cumbersome task to harvest metadata features for scholarly publications, datasets, source code, and machine learning models. These artifacts generate heterogeneous metadata features, which are distributed across various repositories. In addition, large language models (LLMs) and agents have emerged as powerful tools and are now being extensively adopted to facilitate a wide range of tasks across domains, ranging from information extraction to knowledge graphs. Nevertheless, numerous open questions persist regarding their adoption in diversified research disciplines, especially concerning their accuracy, robustness, biases, and societal impact when applied in the context of research metadata, scholarly information extraction, and open science. This workshop aims to cover these exciting aspects centered around metadata features from research artifacts, with a focus on large language models and knowledge graphs.
evidence_items.title: Smarter Extraction of Scholarly Metadata using Knowledge Graphs, Language Models, and Agents

evidence_items.summary: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive LLMs, yet remain susceptible to hallucination. Activation steering offers a promising mitigation approach by guiding parallel token predictions through internal representations. However, existing steering methods largely overlook two characteristics of dLLMs: dynamic denoising states and temporal hallucination risks, which challenge predefined steering vectors and uniform intervention strengths. We propose TRACESTEER, a trace-driven activation steering framework that uses preceding denoising predictions as feedback to jointly adapt steering direction and strength. Specifically, Denoising Feedback Steering (DF-Steering) constructs step-specific steering vectors from preceding predictions and current hidden states. Trajectory-Guided Steering Gate (TS-Gate) regulates their strength using prediction uncertainty and the denoising timestep. With the backbone frozen, factual supervision and magnitude regularization jointly guide the learning of adaptive steering interventions, promoting factual reliability and stability throughout denoising. Experiments on two dLLMs show improved factual reliability on TruthfulQA and generalization across five downstream benchmarks.
evidence_items.title: TRACESTEER: Trace Driven Activation Steering for Hallucination Mitigation in Diffusion Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Molecular fragments provide chemically meaningful units, but existing molecular languages rarely make their locations and connections explicit for editing. Here we introduce STAMP (Sequential Tree Attachment-based Motif-Preserving representation), a topology-aware molecular language that connects fragment-level representation learning with precise structural editing. STAMP separately encodes motif identity, attachment sites and tree topology, making fragments reusable across contexts and subtrees directly accessible. Learned representations capture motif similarity and recurring transformations, and lower activity-cliff prediction error on 23 of 30 targets versus a matched SMILES encoder. Compatible subtree operations support scaffold-preserving optimization, ranking first among six methods on 15 of 23 benchmark objectives. A deterministic compiler enables frozen language models to act on indexed fragments, improving molecular editing, optimization, transformation transfer and change identification by 9 to 56 percentage points over plain SMILES. Together, these results establish an executable molecular language in which learned chemical units remain directly operable during design.
evidence_items.title: STAMP as a topology-aware molecular language for fragment-level learning and editing

evidence_items.summary: BACKGROUND & AIMS: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is often diagnosed months to years after symptoms begin, and diagnostic delay is associated with complications. We tested whether longitudinal machine learning using electronic health record (EHR) data can identify incident IBD before diagnosis, and quantified lead time and deployment burden. METHODS: We studied adults with an IBD-compatible symptom, sign, or finding at UCSF (2012-2024). Incident cases were confirmed by structured filtering and validated large language model note review. We trained a state space model (Mamba) and comparators on pre-diagnostic EHR data, excluding diagnostic-workup features, and assessed discrimination at 6- and 12-month landmarks. We externally tested Mamba without recalibration at ZSFG, a safety-net hospital serving a demographically and socioeconomically distinct population, and simulated diagnosis-code-only deployment at UCSF. RESULTS: Six months after presentation, among patients still undiagnosed (67% of UCSF test cases), Mamba achieved an AUROC of 0.969 (95% CI, 0.928-0.999) at UCSF and 0.965 (0.952-0.976) at ZSFG. Median lead time was 20 months at UCSF and 15 months at ZSFG. Among future cases with an initially normal colonoscopy (N=32) or a histological finding of acute inflammation without chronicity (N=63), the model flagged 84% and 89% of these patients, respectively, before those procedures, indicating the potential for pre-diagnostic detection. Among 358,886 symptomatic patients not used for training (60 incident cases), the diagnosis-code-only model achieved an AUROC of 0.926; reviewing 20 alerts/month identified 34 cases (PPV, 1.09%; 64-fold above baseline). CONCLUSIONS: Longitudinal machine learning can identify increased IBD risk months to years before diagnosis and may define a population for prospective studies of early IBD biology. Prospective evaluation should determine whether earlier identification reduces diagnostic delay.
evidence_items.title: Prediction of incident inflammatory bowel disease from routine electronic health records: development and external validation of a longitudinal machine learning model

evidence_items.summary: Visual agents must turn video observations into timely decisions to track progress and choose what to do next. Building on the emerging System One paradigm, we introduce VideoJev, a family of models that cast video understanding and interaction as structured decision tasks. We adapt pretrained multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by replacing autoregressive answer decoding with a shared head that scores temporal intervals and textual options against video evidence. These scores yield event spans or answer choices, unifying temporal grounding and multiple-choice video question answering. This combines the semantic flexibility of MLLMs with efficient decisions that agents can use directly. As an interaction unfolds, new goals and intermediate results prompt further queries about the same visual history. VideoJev therefore reuses visual computation through Cached inference for queries as they arrive and Joint inference for multiple queries in a single forward pass. Across three temporal grounding benchmarks, VideoJev-4B and VideoJev-35B-A3B improve mean mIoU over their backbones by 6.7 and 10.8 points, respectively, with measured inference speedups of $2.8$-$3.1\times$. On four video QA benchmarks, both achieve performance comparable to their backbones in Thinking mode, with measured inference speedups exceeding $100\times$. These results offer a unified, reusable decision interface for composing structured visual judgments into complex, open-ended workflows.
evidence_items.title: VideoJev: System One Model for Video Understanding and Interaction

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) promise to automate one of higher education's most resource-intensive activities: assessing student writing. Existing evaluations are typically limited to a single model, a single prompt and a single institution. Using 761 undergraduate psychology assignments from three UK universities, we evaluated three frontier LLMs, individually and in ensemble, on accuracy, prompt sensitivity, error independence, generalisability and evidential basis. Agreement between human and machine marks varied widely, with no model or prompt optimal across institutions. All models compressed marks towards a common central tendency, overvaluing the weakest assignments and undervaluing the strongest. Because this error was shared, ensembling failed to remove it. Machine marks also rewarded linguistic features more strongly than human marks. Since human-machine agreement was a joint product of model, prompt and institution, we conclude that current LLMs lack evaluative capacity transferable across contexts, and that single-context validation overstates readiness for deployment.
evidence_items.title: Machine--human agreement in marking undergraduate assignments is specific to model, prompt and institution

evidence_items.summary: Understanding fluorescence microscopy images is fundamental to automating biological research. However, existing methods typically learn predefined concepts from closed-set data, limiting transfer across tasks and biological contexts. In this work, we introduce MicroCLIP, a vision-language model that learns generalizable cellular and subcellular representations from natural language supervision for open-set image classification and retrieval. To pretrain MicroCLIP, we construct MicroPool-2M, a dataset of approximately 2.5 million fluorescence microscopy image-text pairs spanning diverse cellular structures, cell lines, and imaging conditions. Aligning microscopy images with biological concepts in natural language is challenging because most images lack descriptive captions and biological knowledge annotations. We therefore progressively establish image-text associations at three levels to provide MicroCLIP with richer semantic supervision: (1) category-level alignment links images to standardized labels defined by subcellular structure-cell-line combinations; (2) knowledge-level alignment incorporates biological priors derived from these labels to capture relationships across species and cell types; and (3) detail-level alignment uses a multimodal large language model to recaption and verify image-text pairs at scale, emphasizing fine-grained visual characteristics. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MicroCLIP achieves leading performance in zero-shot classification and text-image retrieval on microscopy images. It retrieves images with specific cellular characteristics from thousands of candidates and generalizes to unseen biological concepts without additional supervision. These results highlight MicroCLIP's potential as a foundation model for fluorescence microscopy.
evidence_items.title: MicroCLIP: Connecting Text and Microscopy Images via Contrastive Language--Image Pretraining
