evidence_items.summary: AI systems now write long and difficult mathematical proofs, and checking their step-by-step validity is becoming a bottleneck. A learned verifier could check proofs cheaply, but training one requires a correctness label on every step, and such labels are hard to obtain for open-ended proofs. Existing methods take them from human annotators, which is costly, or derive them from final answers, which proofs do not have, and formalizing each proof in Lean requires expert effort. We introduce LeanPRM, a framework that uses the Lean proof assistant to create step-level labels for natural-language proofs. A model writes a natural-language proof together with a paired formal proof, without feedback from Lean. Lean then labels every step, and a second model discards failures caused only by the formal syntax, so that the negative labels mark errors in the mathematics. LeanPRM contains 10,634 proofs with 152K labeled steps and no human annotation. A Qwen3-4B verifier trained on LeanPRM raises exact step-label accuracy on a held-out set of 200 proofs (LeanPRM-Bench) from 48.2 to 74.7, as opposed to 60.3 when the same base model is trained on PRM800K. It also selects better proofs in best-of-N selection on IMO-level problems, and outperforms the PRM800K-trained verifier on three of four external verification benchmarks. Training on LeanPRM improves verifiers at every size from 0.6B to 8B parameters on LeanPRM-Bench, Hard2Verify and IMO-GradingBench. Given the labels need no human annotation, LeanPRM can grow with the supply of formal statements, offering a path to step-level feedback on AI-generated proofs that are hard for humans to check.
evidence_items.title: LeanPRM: Lean-Grounded Process Supervision for Natural Language Proof Verification

evidence_items.summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) have attracted wide attention for their fast, parallel decoding, but they are believed to be far less efficient to train than autoregressive language models (ARMs): a widely cited study reports that a DLM needs roughly 16x the training compute of an ARM to match its likelihood, a figure that has made pretraining DLMs from scratch look prohibitive at scale. We find that the methodology behind this figure has fallen out of step with current DLM practice: it scores the model with its evidence lower bound (ELBO) and trains a full-sequence, decoder-only model. We therefore revisit the scaling laws of DLMs, adopting the exact likelihood under the model's own decoding order, block diffusion training, an encoder-decoder architecture, and a sweep over the block sizes used in practice. Under this new protocol, we study across ten model variants, about 1,700 models in total, and find that pretraining DLMs is far cheaper than previously thought. Concretely, scoring with the exact likelihood reduces the compute multiple to 12.8x; block diffusion training and an encoder-decoder architecture further reduce it to 7.8x at block size 32, and smaller block sizes narrow it to 4.6x at block size 8 and 3.0x at block size 4. We complement these scaling analyses with an empirical rule for the optimal decoder depth of encoder-decoder block diffusion, a held-out compute budget beyond the fitting range at which the gap between variants persists, and downstream benchmark results where likelihood improvements carry over to accuracy. Overall, the 16x figure substantially overstates the pretraining cost gap between DLMs and ARMs, and pretraining DLMs from scratch is far more viable than previously assumed.
evidence_items.title: Revisiting the 16x Pretraining Compute Gap between Diffusion and Autoregressive Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Background: Vision-language models (VLMs) are being considered for estimating energy intake from meal photographs. Prompt descriptions such as a Japanese-dietitian persona shift the estimates, suggesting their use for calibration; what the estimates rest on was unknown. Objective: We examined whether prompt descriptions can serve as calibration, at which training stage responses to a nationality persona and to an amount instruction arise, and whether estimates follow the visible amount or one associated with the identified dish. Methods: Eleven commercial and 15 open-weight models were evaluated on NutriImage (887 Japanese single-dish photographs) and SNAPMe (1,134 US meal photographs) under eight prompt conditions (no description, five personas, and smaller- or larger-portion instructions). With one model, images were cropped or replaced by the dish name. Before- and after-meal photographs of 804 meals (ACETADA) were estimated. Pre-trained and post-trained weights of Gemma 3 and InternVL3.5 8B were compared by likelihood scoring. Prompts were compared with numerical calibration. Results: Where the dish was named as in the full image, a 25% crop changed neither the median absolute percentage error (MedAPE; 33.8% vs 34.4%) nor the persona shift (-20 vs -20 kcal); dish names alone gave similar accuracy (MedAPE 31.7%); nearly empty trays still received 39%-75% of the before-meal estimate, often described as already eaten. Between models, the persona shift was related to baseline bias (r = -0.77) and less to instruction following (r = -0.36); the instruction shift showed the reverse (r = -0.14 and -0.95). In Gemma 3, the Japan-US contrast was 2-4 times larger before post-training, and the instruction response 2-4 times larger after it (InternVL3.5 8B: 3 and 1.4 times). Across images, the Japan-US contrast was uniform on US meals and, for Japanese dishes in the commercial models, Gemma 3, and Qwen3-VL 32B, larger where overestimated. In these models, the persona lowered MedAPE for Japanese dishes as much as, or slightly more than, subtracting the mean bias, and no more than dividing by a ratio; on US meals it did not; in open-weight families that responded little, only numerical calibration lowered error. The smaller-portion instruction raised MedAPE in models with little bias (eg, 30.0% to 50.2%). Conclusions: In the model examined most closely, the estimates behaved as if anchored on an amount associated with the identified dish and only partly corrected by the visible amount. Prompt descriptions moved them by amounts depending on model and cuisine, not on the correction needed; a persona is therefore not proposed as a general means of calibration. In a facility, the findings suggest showing the identified dish for correction, calibrating by a ratio measured on reference meals with the deployed model, keeping amount statements out of the prompt, and not deriving intake from before-after-meal differences.
evidence_items.title: Effects of Dish Name, Visible Amount, Persona, and Explicit Instruction on Energy Estimates From Food Photographs by 26 Vision-Language Models: Comparative Evaluation Study

evidence_items.summary: Diffusion language models reconstruct masked tokens in parallel, offering an alternative to autoregressive generation. Yet their Transformer backbones typically carry visible evidence and evolving masked predictions through a single residual stream. We equip masked diffusion models with multiple residual streams that persist through depth and adaptive routing between them, then investigate how they support these complementary roles. On the pretraining task, two streams reduce reconstruction perplexity by 5.71% on validation data and 5.13% on average across external corpora compared with standard residual connections. We observe that, without predefined roles, visible and masked positions learn distinct routing patterns. Causal interventions show that this distinction organizes read and write routing, while token-specific write strength remains important within each role. Guided by these findings, a model trained with role-conditioned routing recovers half the validation gain from adding a second stream. State interventions explain the benefit of the additional stream: it preserves early token representations for later reuse while evidence accumulates at masked positions. This mechanism recurs at a larger model scale, showing how persistent streams support context preservation alongside prediction refinement.
evidence_items.title: Multi-Stream Residual Computation in Diffusion Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) enable flexible parallel generation by resolving tokens according to the model's evolving predictability rather than a fixed left-to-right order. This flexibility, however, introduces training choices absent from standard autoregressive teacher forcing: which reference tokens are visible when a target is supervised and how much generation space is allocated. Standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) typically makes these choices through random masking, independently of inference. Our analysis shows how this training-inference mismatch can misdirect supervision. Random masking can conceal prediction errors or penalize uncertainty that decoding would otherwise resolve, while the attention-visible input length can change which response formulations the model favors, even when the underlying solution is unchanged. Motivated by these findings, we propose Predictability-Aware Canvas Selection and Supervision (PACS), an SFT method. PACS uses the model's own predictability to select each example's attention-visible input length and supervises reference tokens immediately before their confidence-guided revelation. Across reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, PACS consistently achieves the highest mean accuracy among the compared SFT methods, with gains of up to 12.84 percentage points over vanilla SFT on individual benchmarks. Code will be released upon publication.
evidence_items.title: Match the Canvas, Not Just the Answer: Predictability-Aware SFT for Diffusion Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with metric and multi-view relationships that remain implicit in RGB observations. Geometry foundation models recover this structure from RGB, but existing methods either fuse the estimated features with visual tokens and learn to use them from question answering alone, or align VLM latents with geometry features. Capturing geometry, however, does not ensure its use: zeroing the aligned latents of a released feature-alignment model leaves its accuracy unchanged. We introduce GeoReader, a framework that learns geometric representations for the VLM that reads them. First, we train lightweight Geometric Readers to produce continuous input tokens, supervising them with geometry descriptions decoded by a frozen VLM, so that the Readers express geometry in a form the target model can already read. We then freeze the Readers to preserve this interface while fine-tuning the VLM on spatial QA, with geometry injection conditioned on the question. Geometry descriptions serve only as training targets: at inference, the VLM answers directly from the continuous geometric tokens without generating a geometry chain of thought. With geometry predicted from RGB images, our approach reaches 94.3 on MindCube-Tiny with Qwen3-VL-4B and, with a multi-source QA mixture, an average of 72.5 across six additional spatial benchmarks with Qwen3.5-9B. These results suggest that a useful geometric representation is one the receiving model can use, not merely one from which geometry can be reconstructed.
evidence_items.title: GeoReader: Learning Latent Geometry for Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Multi-agent deliberation can improve recognition by criticizing and revising candidate answers, but fixed controls cannot respond to changes in disagreement or reasoning quality. We present an adaptive multi-agent controller (ADMA) that learns continuous policies for proposal, challenge, arbitration, and coordination while keeping the task model frozen. Shared trace features describe quality, agreement, and progress, while role-specific features support decentralized control during inference. One controller trained on legal and financial reasoning is transferred without policy updates to four textual and multimodal benchmarks and two successive task-model versions. With Qwen3.5 held fixed, ADMA-Full improves accuracy by 6.2-14.2 percentage points over Direct and by 2.8-3.0 points over ADMA-Fixed. Paired bootstrap ranges for the Full-Fixed comparison are positive on three tasks. Outcome decompositions show that recoveries exceed introduced errors, while process assessment records fewer false-consensus events and more supported correct outcomes. Transfer to Qwen3.6 remains task dependent, which bounds the generality of the learned policy. Median token and latency ratios are 14.3-18.7 and 7.8-16.5 relative to Direct. These results show that adaptive deliberation can improve fixed-model recognition when its task-dependent gains justify the additional computation.
evidence_items.title: Learning Adaptive Deliberation Control for Reliable Recognition with Multi-Agent Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Gaussian wave packets provide an exact analytical foundation for modeling time-dependent quantum phenomena, effectively bridging the gap between classical trajectories and full quantum mechanics. We introduce GWPTools, a highly extensible Wolfram Language framework designed to compute exact time-dependent Gaussian wave packet dynamics using a unified symbolic-numeric architecture. Built upon a robust ``parameter bus''and polymorphic dispatch, the software serves as an interactive pedagogical tool for exploring quantum theory and an exact algebraic engine for rigorously benchmarking numerical grid-based and trajectory methodologies. Version 1.0.0 focuses on exact time evolution in driven one-dimensional quadratic potentials. Native extensions into quantum hydrodynamics and phase space representations enable exact energy decompositions, analytical Bohmian trajectories, and symbolic derivations of quasi-probability distributions and information metrics. We demonstrate the framework's modular scalability by prototyping interference in superpositions, open-system decoherence, and coupled two-dimensional oscillators. Ultimately, these capabilities establish a versatile foundation for maximizing the reach of exact analytical modeling toward increasingly complex driven quantum systems.
evidence_items.title: GWPTools: An extensible Wolfram Language framework for time-dependent Gaussian wave packet dynamics

evidence_items.summary: As generative language models become more capable and widely used, inference demand grows, making efficient serving increasingly important. Discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) offer a promising path to more efficient inference through parallel token generation. Prior dLLM decoding methods, however, focus on improving inference efficiency for individual sequences. We formulate fixed-budget dLLM batch decoding and introduce Batch-Paced, a training-free method that jointly optimizes the allocation of decoding compute across requests to improve overall batch quality. Across two dLLM backbones, five benchmarks and their representative mixtures, Batch-Paced improves batch performance under matched budgets; gains generally grow with batch size and largely persist across decoding configurations. Analysis of requests'decoding trajectories suggests that these gains arise largely by raising the committed-token confidence of lower-confidence requests. We further show that Batch-Paced's batch decode time remains competitive and that adding a decoding-depth allowance during Batch-Paced decoding can shorten it further at a modest performance cost.
evidence_items.title: Batch-Paced: Fixed-Budget Batch Decoding in Discrete Diffusion Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Long-lived technical organizations depend on senior subject matter experts whose knowledge is only partially preserved in reports, publications, and archival metadata. Digital libraries preserve those records, but they rarely provide centralized, expert-scoped, question-answering access to the knowledge of people who leave or change roles. We present an implemented knowledge-retention prototype, built on ALICE, an architecture for large language model (LLM)–knowledge-graph interaction and grounded evidence provenance, that creates virtual experts from digital-library records. Its core contribution is a data-organization layer for expert-scoped knowledge: author-scoped ingestion from the NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS), Docling-derived chunking, evidence-aligned triple extraction into per-expert Kuzu graphs, and a lifecycle model for creating, refreshing, and retiring expert knowledge bases; a trust-aware, persona-conditioned conversational interface is one application built on that layer. We also introduce Trust-Propagated Path Retrieval (TPPR), a graph retrieval mechanism that scores multi-hop evidence chains by the geometric mean of their edge certainty scores. On standard multihop question answering (QA) benchmarks, the ALICE retrieval architecture with GPT-4o achieves 56.5% exact match (EM) with TPPR on 2WikiMultihopQA and 32.5% EM with high-recall retrieval on MuSiQue. Oracle analysis indicates that MuSiQue is limited primarily by retrieval coverage, with a 37.5% retrieval failure rate versus 8.5% for 2WikiMultihopQA. The analysis snapshot includes two expert collections spanning 74 publications, 5,866 chunks, 25,534 entities, and 22,734 extracted relations. A formative masked pilot with 10 NASA domain experts suggests that virtual-expert responses are rated substantially more human-like than baseline LLM responses and can be identified above chance, while remaining too small for inferential claims.
evidence_items.title: From Digital Library Records to Trust-Grounded Virtual Experts for Knowledge Retention

evidence_items.summary: Pre-trained Large Language Model (LLMs) are effective on many tasks in zero-shot and few-shot settings. For machine translation of low-resource languages, the obvious options are few-shot prompting and fine-tuning on a small parallel set. We ask: what if moderate amounts of low-resource monolingual data are also available? We argue that, rather than continued pretraining, a more effective use of this data is the pre-LLM era technique of back-translation (BT). The current fine-tuned LLM translates monolingual sentences in each language, and the resulting pairs train it in the reverse direction. Updates on the parallel set are interleaved for stable learning. With 1K parallel pairs on Odia and Swahili, BT beats continued pretraining into the low-resource language by 7.7 to 16.4 XCOMET-XXL points in domain. With beam-decoded intermediate translations, it also beats a model with 10 time more parallel data. In-context examples retrieved from the parallel data further improve BT. We also analyze the source, quality and amount of monolingual text. Across five low-resource languages, with Hindi as a high-resource control, and two 3B backbones, BT improves translation into the low-resource language by 16 to 173% XCOMET-XXL over parallel-only fine-tuning. Blind human evaluation on Odia and Sanskrit agrees with the automatic metrics.
evidence_items.title: Back-Translation Still Matters: Leveraging Monolingual Data for Low-Resource Machine Translation with LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Multi-agent Large Language Model (LLM) systems typically commit to a deliberation protocol before inference. A fixed protocol cannot allocate computation differently to resolved and unresolved instances, and it may mistake repeated support for independent confirmation. We study this failure as semantic false consensus: a confident group answer supported by narrow, duplicated, or correlated rationales. We introduce ECMR, an evidence-aware controller over frozen role-conditioned LLMs. At each step, ECMR summarizes answer concentration, support diversity and independence, contradictions, role behavior, verification history, and remaining budget, then selects whether to propose, challenge, verify, arbitrate, diversify, correct a role, or stop. We formulate this decision as finite-horizon budgeted control and derive sufficient conditions under which state conditioning, risk-triggered verification, and role correction improve cost-adjusted utility. Across a declared held-out evaluation of 9,000 records from MedQA, CaseHOLD, and FinQA, ECMR-Full increases pooled accuracy from 62.1% to 84.9%, reduces false-consensus rate from 40.7% to 17.0%, and raises evidence-support rate from 58.0% to 88.7%. State shuffling loses 11.7 accuracy points with only 0.7 fewer rounds, while harder traces shift from early stopping toward arbitration. ECMR-Full uses the largest token budget, yielding the strongest absolute reliability rather than uniformly superior token efficiency.
evidence_items.title: ECMR: Evidence-Aware Deliberation Control for Multi-Agent LLM Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) serving systems use token-level continuous batching to improve resource utilization, but heterogeneous response lengths complicate request scheduling. Prediction-guided short-first scheduling reduces average latency but can severely delay long requests, while unrestricted aging may over-promote delayed long requests under congestion. We propose Quota-Based Aging (QBA), a lightweight policy that combines predicted short-first admission with quota-bounded, debt-enforced promotion of aged predicted-long requests. We also use a reduced M/G/n queueing surrogate, calibrated from simulator traces, to explain first-order mean-latency trends. QBA is evaluated using a serving-aware event-driven simulator that models decode-priority batching, chunked prefill, token-budget constraints, and KV-cache-safe admission. We compare QBA with FCFS, predicted short-first, and aggressive aging under asymmetric prediction errors on synthetic and production-derived workloads. The evaluation considers queueing delay, throughput, utilization, and class-conditional tail performance. Results show that QBA provides a controllable middle ground between aggressive short-first prioritization and unrestricted aging, substantially reducing long-request tail latency while retaining much of the mean-latency benefit of prediction-guided scheduling.
evidence_items.title: Quota-Based Aging for Prediction-Guided Scheduling in LLM Serving

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) are commonly organized around two coordination regimes. Centralized coordination provides explicit control but can create a bottleneck at a single coordination locus, whereas decentralized coordination offers local autonomy but must achieve effective collaboration through distributed decisions and experience. These trade-offs motivate a systematic study of the space between the two regimes. We introduce Degrees of Freedom (DoF), a continuous configuration framework that quantifies the size of the decision space delegated to downstream agents. DoF controls the granularity of delegated work and the target probability that each task unit is assigned to the branches. Its endpoints recover the two coordination regimes. Across multiple task domains, DoF reveals a hierarchy of organizational effects. Delegated granularity and within-regime routing produce structured but bounded profile reallocations, whereas task domain and retained experience are associated with stronger differences between the centralized- and decentralized-branch profiles. The resulting performance landscape is task-dependent: different domains favor different DoF configurations, while atomic-target conditions are more consistent across runs. In-domain retained experience brings the two branch profiles closer together. The same controlled sweep reveals a task-dependent coordination landscape: some domains exhibit higher-performing configurations, whereas others show flatter responses and no single configuration dominates across domains. In five of the six evaluated state, an intermediate DoF configuration achieves higher mean accuracy than both endpoints, demonstrating the value of exploring the coordination space between them. Together, these findings provide empirical guidance for studying and designing intermediate coordination regimes in LLM-based MAS.
evidence_items.title: Degrees of Freedom in Multi-Agent Coordination: Between Centralized and Decentralized Regimes

evidence_items.summary: Multi-objective molecular optimization is a critical process in drug discovery that aims to modify a given molecule to simultaneously improve multiple properties while maintaining a similar overall structure. This process often requires iterative modifications guided by computational or experimental feedback. Recent large language model (LLM)-based methods have begun to explore this iterative approach; however, these methods are not explicitly trained to leverage such feedback, while existing approaches primarily focus on single-turn molecular optimization. To address this gap, we introduce Multi-turn Feedback Guided (MFG) molecular optimization, a reinforcement learning framework that trains an LLM to progressively optimize molecules using feedback from previous turns. MFG introduces a feedback vector capturing both property improvements and source molecule similarity, alongside a feedback-aligned reward function that promotes progressive improvement across turns. We apply MFG over $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O}$, a state-of-the-art LLM model for multi-objective molecular optimization, evaluate $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O-MFG}$ on ten multi-objective molecular optimization tasks. The results demonstrate that $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O-MFG}$ achieves the highest average similarity-constrained success rate ($81.50%$), outperforming the base model $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O}$ ($70.81%$).
evidence_items.title: MFG: Multi-turn Feedback Guided Molecular Optimization

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Model (LLM) workflows increasingly decompose knowledge-intensive generation into planning, role assignment, subtask execution, and synthesis. Although this structure may support specialization, it also adds coordination and computational overhead. We present a preliminary task-level comparison of a Direct Generation Workflow and a Decomposed Generation Workflow under matched inputs and evaluation conditions. The study covers three grounded knowledge-generation tasks: public-event narrative synthesis, project-grounded research ideation, and scientific related-work generation. Across the evaluated configurations, decomposition produces the largest mean Task Quality Score (TQS) gain for research ideation (+0.053), a smaller gain for related-work generation (+0.025), and only a modest gain for public-event narrative synthesis (+0.013). These improvements require 95.1–126.2 seconds of additional runtime on average. The results provide preliminary evidence that the value of multi-agent decomposition is task-dependent.
evidence_items.title: The Decomposition Dilemma: When Do Multi-Agent LLM Workflows Help Grounded Knowledge Generation?

evidence_items.summary: The Key-Value (KV) cache constitutes a dominant source of memory consumption during large language model (LLM) inference, particularly in long-context and complex reasoning scenarios. Existing KV cache quantization methods have explored different compression granularities, including layer-wise precision adjustment and token-level information preservation. In practical deployment, however, the key challenge is not merely compression, but how to allocate limited quantization resources among heterogeneous precision preservation strategies under a fixed KV cache memory budget. We propose MultiAlloc, a profiling-guided precision allocation framework for KV cache quantization that adaptively distributes limited quantization resources between layer-wise precision enhancement and token-wise preservation. MultiAlloc employs lightweight offline profiling to characterize layer sensitivity and token importance, enabling adaptive precision allocation under a fixed memory constraint. Guided by the profiled memory--accuracy trade-off, it automatically derives an effective precision allocation strategy without online allocation search, and applies the resulting policy during inference. Extensive experiments on reasoning and long-context benchmarks demonstrate that MultiAlloc consistently improves over layer-wise, token-wise, and recent multi-granularity KV cache quantization methods under matched memory budgets across diverse models, including Mistral, Llama, DeepSeek-Qwen, and QwQ.
evidence_items.title: MultiAlloc: Budget-Aware Precision Allocation for KV Cache Quantization

evidence_items.summary: Practical remote sensing applications often require both understanding and generation capabilities for the same geographic scene. However, most existing methods address either understanding or generation in isolation, while existing unified remote sensing models'generative ability is limited to text-to-image. To bridge this gap, we propose Omni-RS, a unified framework supporting four remote sensing understanding tasks and five generation tasks. Specifically, we introduce the"Scene-Guided Two-Stage Training"strategy, which first adapts a multimodal large language model to remote sensing understanding and then uses its hidden states to guide a diffusion transformer for image generation. To enable joint learning across diverse generation tasks, we construct UniGen, a unified multi-task generation dataset, by organizing heterogeneous remote sensing data into a unified format. Furthermore, we introduce"Detailed Visual Conditioning", which uses visual conditions encoded by a VAE to guide the generation process, thereby supporting additional generation tasks that require reference images. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Omni-RS performs exceptionally well in understanding tasks and has achieved outstanding results in a variety of generative tasks.
evidence_items.title: Omni-RS: Unifying Multi-Task Understanding and Generation in Remote Sensing

evidence_items.summary: Many information needs are difficult to express as keyword queries, since users often lack the domain-specific terminology needed to retrieve relevant documents. We propose a Summaries-as-Queries (SaQ) framework that enables contextual document discovery by transforming a user-provided document into an effective retrieval representation. Rather than relying on a single summarization strategy, SaQ employs a hybrid summarization pipeline that first identifies salient concepts through extractive summarization and then guides abstractive summarization to generate concise, contextually faithful summaries. To improve retrieval coverage beyond a single summary query, the framework decomposes the generated summary into multiple topical subqueries using a large language model (LLM), allowing distinct semantic aspects of the source document to be searched independently. The resulting ranked lists are integrated through rank fusion to produce a unified set of relevant documents. By combining hybrid summarization, LLM-guided query decomposition, and rank fusion, SaQ bridges document understanding and information retrieval, providing an effective framework for contextual document discovery in digital libraries and large document collections. Experimental results on a large dataset demonstrate that SaQ consistently outperforms competitive retrieval baselines. These findings demonstrate that SaQ provides an effective new paradigm for contextual document discovery in digital libraries.
evidence_items.title: Contextual Document Discovery in Digital Libraries through Hybrid Summarization and LLM-Guided Query Decomposition

evidence_items.summary: Objectives: To assess the feasibility and early performance of an AI-assisted screening workflow that reviews inpatient discharge summaries to identify potential treatment injuries for clinician review and, where appropriate, Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC) treatment injury claim consideration in New Zealand. Design: Single-site, six-month pilot reported as a quality-improvement/service-evaluation activity. A large language model (LLM)-enabled system acted as an index screening test over discharge summaries to generate candidate treatment injury signals for structured clinician adjudication and escalation. Setting: A New Zealand district hospital (Wairarapa). Screening operated on routinely produced inpatient discharge summaries. Participants: All inpatient discharge summaries produced during the pilot period were screened (n = 2,642). The unit of analysis was one discharge summary per inpatient episode. Intervention: An LLM-based screening workflow that outputs structured candidate harm signals with supporting excerpts and a certainty label. Outputs were reviewed by clinicians using a structured adjudication template. Suitable cases could be escalated to senior clinicians and followed through the local ACC treatment injury process. Main outcome measures: Primary outcomes were yield, positive predictive value (PPV) of AI- flagged signals for clinician-adjudicated iatrogenic harm, and the rate of unsupported/hallucinated outputs. Secondary outcomes included overlap with incident reporting and administrative coding, downstream ACC claim outcomes, and clinician review workload. Results: Across 2,642 inpatient discharge summaries screened, the AI-assisted workflow generated 237 candidate signals (yield 9.0%; 95% CI 7.9% to 10.1%). Clinician adjudication classified 102 as confirmed iatrogenic harm, 43 as possible harm requiring additional context, 81 as no harm, and 11 as unsupported/hallucinated outputs. PPV for confirmed harm was 43.0% (95% CI 36.8% to 49.4%). PPV for confirmed-or-possible harm was 61.2% (95% CI 54.9% to 67.1%). Seven ACC treatment injury claims were lodged as a direct result of AI-assisted surfacing; three were accepted, two declined, and two were held/pending at analysis. Organisational ACC data identified 68 treatment injury claims lodged during the same period, of which 17 overlapped with AI-identified cases. Conclusions: AI-assisted screening of discharge summaries can feasibly increase detection of potential treatment injuries for structured clinician review and may support more systematic ACC consideration and safety learning. Safe scaling requires transparent reporting of model and prompt details, robust human adjudication and escalation pathways, and governance controls to mitigate false positives and unsupported outputs. A next-stage evaluation should estimate diagnostic accuracy against a chart-review reference standard and examine implementation outcomes including workload, acceptability, fidelity and sustainability.
evidence_items.title: AI-assisted identification of potential treatment injury from inpatient discharge summaries: an early-stage sociotechnical evaluation in a New Zealand district hospital

evidence_items.summary: Longer contexts allow large language models (LLMs) to condition their predictions on more information, but inference costs grow prohibitively with context length. An emerging alternative uses test-time updates to encode context as temporary changes to model weights. However, encoding this information into weights that already represent general knowledge obscures its role as context, so the LLM may fail to use it properly to condition subsequent inference. To restore this contextual role, we first associate each context with an identifier during encoding, thereby distinguishing the newly encoded information from pre-existing knowledge. Invoking the identifier at inference then enables the LLM to recite the encoded context. Nevertheless, successful recitation does not ensure that the LLM will use the recalled information as context. We therefore further introduce a prompting framework that explicitly guides the LLM to use this information as context. Across diverse controlled tasks and practical benchmarks, our method outperformed the baseline using only off-the-shelf LLMs, showing its advances in context encoding.
evidence_items.title: Encoding Context into LLM Weights: What Makes It Context?

evidence_items.summary: Scoring open-ended creativity is expensive. The gold standard for evaluating open-ended creativity responses, including divergent thinking tasks such as the Alternate Uses Task (AUT), is the Consensual Assessment Technique (CAT), where panels of human experts rate creative products. CAT is resource-intensive, limiting the extent to which institutions can measure creativity. Advances in large language models offer an alternative: a CAT-inspired persona panel using large language models (LLMs) as judges to score open-ended responses automatically. Our selected large language models, gpt-5.5, gpt-5-mini, and Claude Haiku 4.5, were assigned expert personas, and we aggregated each model's judgments and compared them against two controls: a self-consistency control using repeated judgments from a single generic judge, and a basic prompted baseline. On gpt-5-mini, the CAT-inspired persona panel improves over a single prompted judge ( r=0.48 to 0.55). It does not outperform the self-consistency control, suggesting that the benefit of the CAT-inspired persona panel is aggregation rather than persona diversity. Accuracy improves substantially with many-shot grounding: supplying many labeled in-context exemplars nearly closes the gap to Ocsai, the fine-tuned reference, while persona diversity adds nothing measurable. For digital libraries and learning repositories that collect open-ended submissions at scale, scalable scoring methods are especially consequential.
evidence_items.title: Can LLMs Simulate Expert Panels? Evaluating CAT-Inspired Persona Prompting for Automated Creativity Scoring

evidence_items.summary: Persistent textual memory lets language-model agents reuse lessons from past tasks to improve on future multi-step tasks without retraining. Systems such as ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet keep it as a playbook: lessons the agent writes after each task and reads in its prompt. A key challenge is to decide which lessons improve later tasks. Current systems leave the decision to the agent itself, which makes performance unstable: the same procedure can write a playbook that helps or one that falls up to 69.6 points below no playbook. These findings motivate valuing lessons by their measured effect on task success rather than by the agent's judgment. We propose Randomized Block Curation (RBC), which measures this effect with a randomized experiment on practice tasks. It groups related lessons into blocks large enough to move success measurably and, on each practice task, includes or leaves out every block at random. Random inclusion makes tasks with and without a block comparable, so the gap in their success estimates the block's effect. RBC keeps the blocks that help and, since the same procedure can write a helpful or a harmful playbook, grows several and serves whichever curated, whole or no playbook scores best on fresh practice episodes. Across two memory systems, three models and three benchmarks, RBC raises average success to 66.9, against 55.5 with the whole playbook, 54.1 with no playbook and 53.8 when the agent's own judgment picks the lessons to keep.
evidence_items.title: Reliable Memory from Unstable Growth: Curating Self-Written Agent Playbooks with Randomized Experiments

evidence_items.summary: With the growing volume of scientific literature, scholarly knowledge graphs are increasingly used to organize research findings, and large language models now build such graphs automatically. However, the facts extracted by these methods are often wrong. Since most facts cannot be compared against an external reference, users cannot tell which ones need rechecking. In this study we propose a way to flag such errors. We observed that a scholarly result graph contains several distinct classes of defect, and that detecting them calls for different kinds of evidence. A human audit shows that most audited disagreements are not extraction errors but correct values reported under a different experimental setting, which we separate from genuine source-extraction errors. We compare three signals, namely a value-blind extraction-reliability signal drawn from how a fact was extracted, graph-consistency checks over the reference structure, and a value-aware result-validity signal in which a model reads each stored value against its cited evidence. No single signal detects every kind of defect. Graph-consistency checks best separate disagreements with the reference. On a score-stratified human sample, the value-aware check best detects genuine extraction errors, raising their detection from an AUROC of 0.70 to 0.95; these are sample-conditional rankings, not graph-wide estimates. Each signal works best on a different target, while a combined score gives one triage ranking across both. We also tested whether flagged errors could be corrected automatically. This proved unsafe, since about 25 percent of the proposed corrections would overwrite a correct fact, so the tool prioritizes errors for human review rather than editing the graph. We release the error-scored graph, a benchmark with a 150-fact human-audited error breakdown, and the human validation set.
evidence_items.title: Triaging Defects in Scholarly Result Graphs with Extraction, Evidence, and Consistency Signals

evidence_items.summary: Running large language models (LLMs) on consumer hardware is bottlenecked by the key-value (KV) cache, which grows with every decoded token and quickly exhausts the memory and bandwidth of a single consumer GPU. We present SparPR (Sparse Partial Recomputation), a runtime KV-cache recovery mechanism that does not modify model weights and requires no offline training. SparPR couples three online decisions: Query-Aware key-block selection scores historical blocks against the current query; dynamic budget control estimates per-block copy and recompute costs to decide how many blocks to retain; and on-demand local recomputation with cost-aware fallback merges retained blocks into continuous spans and switches between sparse recomputation and full recovery according to a runtime cost comparison. Implemented on FlexGen/FlexLLMGen, SparPR is evaluated on a single consumer laptop (RTX 3070 Ti 8GB, Ryzen 9 6900HX, 16GB RAM). It cuts end-to-end latency by 31%, 52%, and 63% at 1k, 2k, and 4k prompt tokens respectively, with 1.4x-2.7x higher throughput, and completes an 8k-token workload in 44 minutes where the FlexGen baseline times out. Under a fixed cache budget, SparPR retains a Needle Accuracy that stays well above StreamingLLM and H2O at every keep ratio, and ablation studies confirm that the three mechanisms act jointly.
evidence_items.title: SparPR: Runtime KV-Cache Recovery for Resource-Constrained LLM Inference on Consumer Hardware

evidence_items.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) reduces hallucination in large language models by conditioning generation on retrieved evidence, but retrieved contexts are often compressed before inference to reduce cost and latency. Prior work evaluates compression primarily through answer accuracy, leaving open whether different compression strategies affect how faithfully model outputs are grounded in the provided evidence. We present a controlled study of hallucination behavior under context compression and introduce Attention-Based Semantic Preservation (ABSP), a lightweight query-agnostic method that retains tokens according to structural centrality in a proxy model’s self-attention patterns. Across 2,400 inference runs comparing no compression, random pruning, LLMLingua-2, and ABSP on TriviaQA and HotpotQA, structural compression consistently improves grounding faithfulness, measured by K-Precision. ABSP achieves the highest K-Precision among compressed methods at every compression ratio, outperforming LLMLingua-2 by + 0.111 on average and + 0.131 under aggressive compression, while matching its answer accuracy on single-hop retrieval. Cross-sample consistency is stable across methods, suggesting this hallucination signal is driven more by the generation model than by the compression strategy.
evidence_items.title: ABSP: Attention-Based Semantic Preservation for Faithful Context Compression

evidence_items.summary: Evaluating whether scholarly research contributes to a Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) requires an interpretive framework that combines the goal definition, its targets, contribution criteria, and the document itself. Instruction-tuned large language models can instantiate this framework in context, producing a consistent evaluative function that can be applied to every document in a collection. We present Goal-Conditioned Multi-Label Distillation (GCMLD), which distills this evaluative function into a compact multi-label model. A Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct teacher evaluates each document–SDG pair by constraining its generative output to two tokens ("0" and "1"), and the logit margin defines the teacher probability used to supervise the student. An 86-million-parameter DeBERTa-v3-base student learns to approximate the teacher’s evaluative function by predicting all seventeen SDG scores in a single model invocation. We test whether reducing the influence of intermediate teacher evaluations improves or impairs approximation by comparing plain binary cross-entropy with weighting, masking, and hard-label objectives. Masking small-margin evaluations reduced teacher fidelity with the teacher targets and temperature held fixed, and the reduction was largest for SDG–document pairs whose own margins are small. The loss of fidelity shows that intermediate teacher evaluations provide useful supervision for approximating the evaluative function. The student trained on publication abstracts continued to approximate the teacher on electronic thesis and dissertation (ETD) abstracts, with ETD-specific distillation producing modest additional gains. Replacing seventeen prompted teacher evaluations with one model invocation makes collection-scale evaluation practical. Aggregating document-level contribution probabilities by academic department demonstrates how the distilled model supports collection-scale analysis of institutional research.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Topic Matching: Goal-Conditioned Evaluation of Research Contributions in ETD Collections

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) execute billions of floating-point operations per output token across many hardware accelerators. At this scale, hardware-induced faults can bypass system-level detection mechanisms and cause Silent Data Corruption (SDC). Algorithm-Based Fault Tolerance (ABFT) is the state-of-the-art technique for protecting matrix multiplication from such faults, but it incurs non-negligible computational overhead and requires thresholds to distinguish hardware-induced errors from floating-point roundoff. In this paper, we revisit Cauchy--Schwarz Norm Bounds (CSNB) as a low-overhead alternative for detecting SDC during LLM inference. We compare CSNB against ABFT through controlled fault injection and evaluate the runtime overhead of both verification and threshold determination across multiple model sizes, batch sizes, and generation lengths. Our results show that, on average, CSNB retains 99% of the fault detection capability of ABFT for the evaluated dense linear layers while reducing verification overhead by 87% and threshold determination overhead by 67%. For Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) router gate computations, however, CSNB retains only 55% of the fault detection capability of ABFT. These findings suggest that CSNB is a promising low-overhead alternative for protecting dense linear layers in LLM inference, while checksum-based verification remains preferable for the evaluated MoE router gate.
evidence_items.title: Revisiting Cauchy-Schwarz Norm Bounds for SDC Detection in LLM Inference

evidence_items.summary: Large language models are increasingly used as judges to reduce reliance on costly human evaluation, yet their scores can systematically disagree with human judgments. We ask whether responses to an explicitly imposed evaluative bias can help correct a judge's implicit scoring biases. We introduce PRISM (Probe-based Residual Inference of Scoring Misalignment), which holds the evaluated content fixed and measures score changes when attributes are emphasized or de-emphasized. A local sensitivity model motivates representing these responses as a surrogate Jacobian. Ridge regression on human labels learns a correction to the baseline score. The resulting scoring protocol is rubric-free: it uses overall scores without requesting criterion-level ratings. In the main Jev and Sol comparisons on SummEval summarization and HANNA story evaluation, PRISM and its learned-baseline variant significantly improve agreement with human rankings over uncalibrated scores while remaining competitive with rubric-based methods. A controlled SummEval comparison yields similar agreement for rubric-derived quality probes and style probes, supporting calibration without reproducing rubric criteria. The learned coefficients reveal shared and opposing correction directions across judges.
evidence_items.title: PRISM: Calibrating Black-Box Judges with Counterfactual Probes

evidence_items.summary: Sycophancy in Large Language Models, the tendency to align responses with user preferences over ground truth, has largely been studied using questions without a clear ground truth and with a single, plainly stated user opinion. We present a systematic study of which framings of a user's claim trigger sycophancy in factual question answering, where every answer is objectively verifiable without extra context. Evaluating 14 models on 42K questions, we express correct and incorrect user opinions through various claim framings over 8 dimensions and 21 types, and measure a broad set of opinion-driven behaviors. We find that all models are susceptible to user opinions regardless of size. Models are most influenced by how confidently an opinion is stated, whom it is attributed to, and whether it is presented as shared between the user and the model. In contrast to prior work, framings based on the user's expertise, authority over the model, or social pressure matter little in our factual setting. Larger models resist incorrect opinions better but are no better at recovering from their own errors. Our results call for sycophancy evaluations that probe how an opinion is framed, not merely whether one is present, and that measure multiple behaviors beyond a single flip rate.
evidence_items.title: Claim Framing as a Driver of LLM Sycophancy

evidence_items.summary: Referees increasingly use large language models (LLMs), while finance and accounting journals disagree about whether to allow it. We ask which part of a referee's job the models can do. GPT-4o, whose training data end before the 2024 conference season, referees the papers presented at the 2024 AFA and NBER finance meetings, and we compare its verdicts with publication in the top-three finance journals over the next two years. Papers the model scores one standard deviation higher are 44\% more likely to be published, net of author reputation. The result is not driven by look-ahead bias, as the model does not recall the outcomes. The information comes from its judgements of correctness and exposition. Its judgements of originality and significance carry none, and a referee guide that stresses importance does not help. The split between correctness and contribution holds for accounting papers and for a newer model, GPT-5. LLMs can check whether research is right, but not whether it matters. The technical check can go to the model, while the judgement of contribution stays with people.
evidence_items.title: How Well Do LLMs Perform in Peer Review? Evidence from Finance and Accounting

evidence_items.summary: As digital libraries and information retrieval (IR) architectures increasingly integrate conversational artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLMs), understanding how pre-existing user cognitive frames shape interaction strategies becomes critical. Traditional user evaluations frequently overlook how novice users’ entrenched mental models formed through exposure to legacy search engines, bibliographic databases, and virtual assistants dictate their prompting behaviors. Utilizing a qualitative empirical study combining interaction logs, cognitive mapping sketches, and semi-structured post-session interviews (N = 7), we investigate how novice users interact with a GPT-4-powered conversational IR interface across diverse information-seeking tasks. We consolidate user conceptualizations into three primary mental model typologies: Database/Retrieval, Conversational/Synthesis, and Skeptical/Verification, mapping them to behavioral instructional hierarchies and prompt categorization frameworks. Findings reveal that extensive database experience predicts severe cognitive rigidity (functional fixedness), while age plays a secondary role. We conclude with implications for digital library architectures, advocating for transparent provenance, adaptive scaffolding, and XAI onboarding mechanisms.
evidence_items.title: Extending Search Habits: Unfolding Novice User Experience with Conversational AI through Information Retrieval Tasks

evidence_items.summary: Task planning for robots in off-site construction prefabrication is primarily manual, leading to planning inefficiencies and reluctance to adopt robotic solutions. Existing approaches provide limited support for scalable, modular automated task planning and localized runtime replanning. This paper proposes APTree, a model-driven framework that integrates automated task planning with modular task execution using behavior trees as the execution model. APTree repeatedly applies and coordinates heterogeneous symbolic planners to automatically generate and compose modular task plans at runtime. To support this approach, we develop a domain-specific language for the formal specification and validation of task plans, together with a compatible execution engine. We evaluate APTree on the real-world livMatS Biomimetic Shell pavilion, where it models the construction robotic fabrication domain, detects injected specification and planning errors at design time and runtime, and automatically generates large-scale task plans by coordinating three symbolic planners across numerous planning modules. A machine-checked formal analysis further shows that composed execution and local replanning are safe under explicitly stated assumptions, including planner soundness and non-interference of generated plans, providing practitioners with explicit conditions for dependable plan composition. APTree thus enables construction practitioners to leverage automated task planning without requiring detailed knowledge of symbolic planning techniques or APTree's internal implementation.
evidence_items.title: APTree: Extended Behavior Trees for Adaptive and Scalable Automated Robotic Task Planning in Construction

evidence_items.summary: Rare-disease knowledge presents a digital-library problem: clinically useful evidence is fragmented across case reports and clinical narratives, while conventional access remains largely document-centered. My prior work on primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) evaluated five open-source large language models (LLMs) on 58 real first-visit pediatric pulmonology notes. Models often identified patients who warranted further PCD evaluation, but clinician review showed that explanations and testing recommendations were frequently only partly sound. My doctoral research therefore asks how digital libraries can transform dispersed case-report collections into trustworthy, navigable representations of disease progression. I will curate PCD case reports, extract patient-level temporal trajectories with source origin, aggregate recurring and atypical patterns, and generate clinician-facing and patient-facing summaries from the same structured evidence. Evaluation will cover extraction accuracy, temporal reconstruction, factual support, omission, origin, audience appropriateness, and clinician usefulness, using automatic claim verification together with manual review. The intended contribution is not diagnostic automation, but an origin-preserving framework for organizing, synthesizing, and communicating sparse rare-disease evidence in digital libraries.
evidence_items.title: Building Evidence-Centered Digital Libraries for Rare Disease Trajectories

evidence_items.summary: Clinical communication is a fundamental skill that impacts patient satisfaction, treatment adherence, and clinical outcomes. Traditional training methods, such as standardized patients (SPs) or virtual standardized patients (VSPs), face barriers including high costs, logistical complexity, and lack of spontaneous interaction. This study addresses these challenges by developing a scalable alternative based on Large Language Models (LLMs) to train medical students in the anamnesis phase. We developed an interactive Conversational Virtual Patient (CVP) system, understood here as a text- and voice-based simulated patient without graphical embodiment. The conversational logic is orchestrated as an explicit state machine over the interview, implemented with LangGraph, a graph-based framework in which each node performs one processing stage and a shared state persists across turns. Clinical consistency across the interview is maintained by a semantic memory layer implemented with LangMem, a library that stores clinical facts as vector embeddings and retrieves them by similarity. Performance is measured by an automatic evaluation module assessing 24 communication criteria derived from validated instruments such as the Communication Assessment Tool (CAT) and the Communication Skills Scale (CSS). The platform was validated with 21 participants, comprising 9 eighth-semester medical students, 11 practising physicians, and 1 expert in healthcare technology. All sessions were conducted in Spanish. Considering the student cohort, which addresses the educational utility of the tool, the system obtained a Chatbot Usability Questionnaire (CUQ) score of 82.3/100 and an average acceptance of the automated feedback of 4.50/5. The physician and expert cohort, which provides expert clinical validation, obtained 96.5/100 and 4.21/5 respectively, yielding a pooled usability score of 90.4/100 and a pooled feedback acceptance of 4.33/5. In an exploratory comparison against eleven physician ratings of the same interviews, rank agreement was highest for “Interest” (\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\rho = 0.64$$\end{document}) and lowest for “Completeness” (\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\rho = 0.09$$\end{document}), and the automated scores fell below the physician scores in every dimension. No dimension attained significance after correction for six comparisons, and the confidence intervals were wide, so these coefficients describe the observed sample rather than the agreement attainable in general. The results support the feasibility of the system as a complement to traditional medical training, providing immediate and standardized feedback. Given the sample size and the single-institution design, these findings should be read as an initial validation of feasibility and acceptability rather than as evidence of pedagogical efficacy.
evidence_items.title: Towards clinical communication training with LLM-based conversational virtual patients and automatic evaluation systems

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as personal assistants; however, little is known about how they capture national-level preferences on a global scale. Given that"time"is a universal and representative concept, we examine LLMs'time preferences by varying only users'country and measuring the compensation LLMs deem appropriate for a 60-minute appointment delay. We then compare LLMs'responses with GDP per capita on Purchasing Power Parity (GDP_PPP), Mean Income, and a literature-based index (Patience Score). Our results across 193 countries and 5 LLMs demonstrate that people's time across the world is evaluated in noticeably different ways among LLMs, as well as varying levels of robustness under prompt variations. LLMs consistently recommend the highest compensation for Europe, but mostly the lowest for Africa. Based on GDP_PPP, LLMs underestimate the value of time for users living in Asia and South America. These findings indicate that geographical patterns are embedded in LLMs and may translate in different treatment in agentic settings.
evidence_items.title: A Global View of How LLMs Value Human Time

evidence_items.summary: Paper-to-patent citations connect scientific and technological documents, but their interpretability depends on how patents are used in the citing text. This study examines citation contexts and paper-level outcome associations in AI-related articles in PubMed Central (PMC). Screening 189,073 articles identified 746 with explicitly tagged patent references (0.395%), including 713 with 1,544 identifiable in-text patent-citation instances. Three large language models classified these instances by represented content, motivation, textual position, and evaluative stance. Regression models examined associations among these dimensions, and propensity-score-matched regressions compared patent-citing papers with XML-screened controls. Background-oriented citations were predominantly neutral and introductory, whereas adoption-oriented citations were more closely associated with methodological positions and supportive evaluations. These patterns suggest heuristic configurations of contextualization, operationalization, and problematization, although classification overlap and exclusion of rare categories limit their interpretation. In matched samples, the patent-citing indicator was associated with lower scholarly-citation measures and more citations received from patents. These associations are observational, not causal. Together, these findings show that paper-to-patent citations encode heterogeneous forms of engagement with patented technology and should be interpreted as selective bibliographic signals rather than direct indicators of technology-to-science knowledge transfer or research value.
evidence_items.title: Interpreting Paper-to-Patent Citations in AI-Related PMC Articles

evidence_items.summary: Named-entity recognition (NER) on historical and OCR-degraded text remains a difficult operating point for both supervised taggers and large language models (LLMs). Specialist encoders are fast and accurate in-domain but require task- and domain-specific training; frontier LLMs are strong general extractors, but their cost, deployment constraints, and run-to-run behaviour may be unsuitable for sovereign or high-throughput knowledge-graph construction pipelines. We ask whether structured orchestration can make an open-weight LLM operationally competitive for NER while preserving the cost, latency, stability, and sovereignty advantages that motivate open deployment. We study SOLE, a structured zero-shot architecture (specified extraction prompt, deterministic post-processing, entity-centric resolution) over an interchangeable substrate. Raw open-weight extraction collapses on historical OCR (0.216 partial-mention F1, zero predictions on 71.6% of documents); the same substrate under SOLE reaches about 0.78 entity-level F1. On HIPE-2020 French, SOLE on an open-weight substrate reaches per-mention parity with a frontier reference (0.818 vs 0.813, within run-to-run noise) at roughly 6.5 × lower cost and 3.3 × faster median latency, with several times tighter variance. The residual gap is confined to entity-level scoring; a substrate-swap decomposition shows it is corpus-dependent — roughly half substrate and half architecture on heavily degraded text, but essentially all architecture on cleaner text, where the frontier substrate adds no measurable quality. A stage-level pipeline autopsy localizes the architecture gap to never-emitted entities rather than resolver errors, and negative probes (intra-document rescan, prompt ensembling, higher reasoning effort) do not recover it. SOLE is not a frontier replacement; it is an operational point that makes open-weight NER cheap, stable, fast, and sovereign while making the remaining quality gap explicit and localized.
evidence_items.title: Toward Pareto-Efficient Sovereign NER with Open-Weight LLMs: Cost, Latency, Quality, and Stability Trade-offs in a Structured Zero-shot Extraction Pipeline on Clean and OCR-Degraded Text

evidence_items.summary: The stories told about artificial intelligence (AI) play a central role in shaping public understanding, policy debates, and expectations about technological change. News media are especially influential in this process. Using a cross-regional corpus of 12,924 English-language news articles about AI published since 2022, we examine how storytelling about AI varies across media systems in four regions: North America, China, India, and the Middle East. Leveraging large language models, we extract the implicit narrative lessons conveyed by each article---commonly known as story morals---capturing value-laden interpretations that extend beyond thematic content or sentiment. We find that North American AI coverage is uniquely characterized by narratives of caution, while under-emphasizing narratives of innovation and collaboration that are more prevalent elsewhere. However, this pattern is largely explained by a broader regional negativity bias in North American news sentiment, rather than by heightened concern about AI itself. Our findings bring into view the culturally conditioned nature of AI news narratives.
evidence_items.title: The Many Morals of AI: The cautionary bias of North American news narratives in global perspective

evidence_items.summary: Parallel generation is widely regarded as an inherent advantage of diffusion large language models. Yet our fixed-quota evaluation of four representative models reveals severe degradation across mathematics and code, with all scores below 15% at 16 tokens per step. Token-level probes identify local predictive potential near the observed prefix, especially in mathematical text. We propose RePara, which reinforces short consecutive token blocks through group-relative policy optimization and reduces rollout and log-probability recomputation costs. On LLaDA and SDAR, \ours improves GSM8K and MATH-500 accuracy over JustGRPO under reduced denoising budgets, with a 1.96x training-step speedup in our LLaDA/MATH setup.
evidence_items.title: A Few More Tokens Ahead: Reinforcing Parallelism in Diffusion LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Classical documents in digital libraries—such as Classical Chinese texts—are not only valuable cultural heritage but also core educational resources at the foundational education level. However, existing digital library systems predominantly focus on full-text retrieval and basic machine translation, making it difficult to support learners' deep cognitive construction. Meanwhile, the direct integration of large language models (LLMs) tends to trap learners in an answer-seeking mode, thereby diminishing the inquiry-based thinking essential to the humanities. This paper proposes and implements Classical-Tutor, an intelligent tutoring system for Classical Chinese digital resources. The system deeply integrates Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with a curriculum knowledge graph and introduces a graph-based dual-role dynamic scheduling engine (Dual-Role State Machine). Through a multi-trigger mechanism, the system adaptively switches between knowledge lecturing and heuristic guiding. In an LLM-simulated pilot evaluation the system sustains longer instructional interaction than a baseline RAG system, adapts retrieval granularity to learner profiles, and avoids the deadlocks of static Socratic prompting; the results characterize orchestration behavior rather than learning gains. The study offers an architectural reference for the intelligent utilization of humanities special collections in digital libraries.
evidence_items.title: Classical-Tutor: A Dual-Role RAG Architecture for Classical Document Resources in Digital Libraries

evidence_items.summary: Omnimodal large language models (OLLMs) are susceptible to cross-modal hallucinations under audio-visual interference. We find that, for a substantial fraction of incorrect joint predictions, the question-relevant unimodal branch can still recover the correct answer, suggesting that task-relevant evidence can remain recoverable from the relevant modality even when it is not reflected in the joint prediction. We refer to this recoverable failure pattern as \emph{modality misrouting}. We propose CaRe (Conflict-aware Residual Intervention), a training-free inference-time method for identifying and correcting modality misrouting. CaRe uses a text-only modality probe to identify a candidate modality-specific counterfactual branch, and flags potential misrouting when its prediction conflicts with the original joint prediction. For such cases, CaRe computes a residual direction from the discrepancy between the counterfactual and fused representations and uses it to steer the original multimodal state toward the relevant modality evidence, while retaining both modalities in the original audio-visual inference path. The intervention strength is adapted based on the confidence of the counterfactual branch. Experiments on CMM and AVHBench across two OLLMs show that CaRe consistently outperforms the evaluated inference-time hallucination-mitigation baselines.
evidence_items.title: Mitigating Cross-Modal Hallucinations by Correcting Modality Misrouting in Omnimodal LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have shown strong potential for remote sensing understanding, yet reliable reasoning remains challenging when tasks require fine-grained visual grounding and multi-step inference. Existing approaches typically rely on either costly pre-constructed reasoning trajectories or self-generated signals such as response consistency, which can reinforce shared errors and provide unreliable supervision. We introduce \textbf{Reasoning--Diagnosis Self-Evolution (ReDiS)}, a framework that separates reasoning exploration from candidate evaluation while allowing the two processes to evolve jointly. ReDiS instantiates two role-specific experts from a shared multimodal backbone: a \textbf{Reasoner} that explores diverse visual evidence--answer candidates and a \textbf{Diagnoser} that jointly evaluates the complete candidate set and provides credibility-aware feedback. As the Reasoner evolves, it exposes new candidate distributions and failure modes; the Diagnoser adapts to these changes and, in turn, reshapes the learning signal for subsequent exploration. To handle groups in which all sampled answers are incorrect and group-relative advantages vanish, we further introduce \textbf{Failure-Triggered Recovery (FTR)}, which provides minimal outcome-level correction without prescribing intermediate reasoning trajectories. Experiments on LHRS-Bench, MME-RS, and CHOICE show consistent improvements over Qwen3.5 backbones at 0.8B, 2B, and 4B scales. ReDiS improves category-averaged accuracy by 6.47 percentage points at 0.8B, while ReDiS-4B achieves the highest average performance among the compared remote sensing MLLMs.
evidence_items.title: ReDiS: Reasoning-Diagnosis Self-Evolution for Multimodal Reasoning in Remote Sensing

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal large language models have advanced rapidly, but most remain optimized for single-image inputs. Multi-image reasoning is costly because each image adds many visual tokens, increasing encoding and attention demands. Existing techniques that address the above issue, including visual token pruning, token merging, visual token compression, learned resampling, hierarchical compression, retrieval-augmented visual reasoning, and memory-based architectures, have largely been designed for single-image scenarios, where redundancy is primarily spatial and local. Multi-image reasoning introduces additional challenges: redundancy may occur across images, task-relevant evidence may be sparse or distributed, and aggressive per-image compression can remove details needed for comparison, counting, temporal reasoning, retrieval, or evidence grounding. Moreover, existing token-reduction methods are often either (i) training-free but inference-inefficient, typically relying on accessing attention matrices to get token-importance that may be impractical to access with memory-efficient attention implementations such as FlashAttention, or (ii) training-dependent, requiring the base MLLM to be retrained or adapted to a new compressed-token paradigm. In this work, we study scalable multi-image reasoning and understanding without retraining the base model and without accessing attention matrices at inference time. To this end, we propose mmVB, a lightweight plug-and-play module that assigns query-conditioned per-image token budgets via cross-image context, adding only 1.6M trainable parameters while reducing visual input tokens by 9x. This reduction yields 5x faster time-to-first-token and 7x fewer prefill FLOPs, while maintaining 94.4% of full-resolution accuracy across eight multi-image reasoning benchmarks.
evidence_items.title: Visual Tokens on Demand: Visual Budgeting for Scalable and Efficient Multi-Image Reasoning in Multimodal LLMs

evidence_items.summary: The LiteBIRD satellite mission aims to measure the tensor-to-scalar ratio $r$ with unprecedented sensitivity through observations of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) $B$-mode polarisation. Robust constraints on $r$ require accurate likelihood modelling across a wide range of angular scales. In this work, we validate harmonic-space likelihood methods against pixel-based benchmarks using 20\,000 end-to-end simulations that include CMB, instrumental noise, and Galactic foreground residuals processed through a realistic component-separation pipeline. We compare a debiased pixel-based likelihood, which serves as our benchmark on large scales ($\ell\leq32$), with an offset Hamimeche \&Lewis (oHL) likelihood applicable across the full multipole range. We systematically explore the space of analysis settings, identifying the number of simulations used for covariance estimation and the choice of beam window function as the most critical factors. Over the full multipole range considered ($\ell\leq128$), where the benchmark combines the pixel-based likelihood at $\ell\leq32$ with a harmonic one at smaller scales, the 68\% upper bound on $r$ from the oHL likelihood is $19$--$29\%$ larger than the benchmark one, depending on the beam window function. This demonstrates its viability as a computationally efficient baseline for LiteBIRD data analysis and cosmological inference from the polarisation $B$-mode field.
evidence_items.title: Validation of harmonic-space likelihood methods for LiteBIRD B-mode polarisation analysis

evidence_items.summary: Detectors of logical anomalies, such as missing, extra or wrongly combined parts, usually score a test image by its distance from normal (good) images. They achieve near-perfect image-level AUROC on standard industrial anomaly detection benchmarks such as MVTec LOCO, but their robustness to changes in capture conditions remains largely unexamined. Under a heterogeneous perturbation protocol in which each test image is randomly kept unaltered or subjected to a brightness reduction or a zoom-out transformation, the normal-reference methods we tested lose 9.7 to 34.1 AUROC points, and two of the strongest, CSAD and SALAD, fall from 97.7% and 96.4% to 68.1% and 62.3%. We propose a framework in which a classifier, trained on normal images and on synthetic anomalies, scores a test image without comparing it with normal data. From a short description of each product, a language model derives anomaly types and editing instructions, an image editor applies them to normal images, and the classifier learns to separate the edited images from automatically discovered normal sub-modes. With its full training recipe, the framework reaches 94.9% AUROC on clean images, 1.5 to 2.8 points below SALAD and CSAD, and 94.1% under the perturbation protocol. Trained without brightness or zoom-out augmentation, so that neither test perturbation occurs in training, it still reaches 92.5% (93.2% clean). These results suggest that clean benchmark scores can hide a strong sensitivity to capture conditions, and that learning the decision from both normal images and rule violations may reduce it.
evidence_items.title: Robust Logical Anomaly Detection under Capture Shifts via Synthetic Anomalies

evidence_items.summary: Bias scores in language-model evaluations often conflate what a model prefers with whether it answers at all. We identify this confound in \textsc{BBQ}, whose ambiguous score factorizes into answerability and signed preference. Across 11 categories, 28,}824 items, and five models, contrastive steering lowers the signed ambiguous score in 11/11 categories but lowers the signed disambiguated preference score in only 8/11. Across 99 configurations, the answerability channel exceeds half of the observed score change in 17\% and accounts for the entire change in 11%. In a six-category disambiguated evaluation, 20.8\% of 1,500 items flip to the unknown option, where abstention is incorrect; \textsc{StereoSet} shows no analogous answer-rate shift. The effect reflects selection and near-orthogonality between the contrastive and preference-gradient directions. We introduce Gradient-Constrained Direction Design (\textsc{GCD}), an option-gradient construction with a first-order unknown-logit constraint. Under a matched Qwen-7B protocol, GCD reduces answer-rate distortion 14-fold and yields a 4-fold larger preference change, while ablations show similar gains for alternative and unconstrained option-gradient directions; nulling the unknown gradient alone is not responsible for the gain. We recommend reporting answerability alongside published scores.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Bias Scores: Answerability Confounds in Activation Steering with Gradient-Constrained Direction Design (GCD)

evidence_items.summary: GUI grounding enables web agents to translate natural-language instructions into actionable interface locations. However, dense layouts and small, visually similar controls can lead models toward plausible but incorrect elements, while refinement around a single prediction may leave alternative targets unexplored. We propose the Multi-Hypothesis Verification Framework (MHVF) for training-free GUI grounding. It combines multi-hypothesis exploration with local visual verification using a single pretrained vision-language model. To explore alternative targets, MHVF constructs spatial hypotheses from multiple full-screen predictions and examines the corresponding regions through zoomed re-localization. To resolve ambiguity among the resulting candidates, it verifies their agreement with the instruction in marked local views.
